### Q027 Can AI meaningfully teach non-cognitive skills — empathy, collaboration, resilience, character? {#q027}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Can AI Meaningfully Teach Non-Cognitive Skills — Empathy, Collaboration, Resilience, Character?

The question turns on a distinction that the research community has not yet cleanly resolved: the difference between *practising* a non-cognitive skill and *developing* it. AI can plainly scaffold the first. Whether it can reliably produce the second remains genuinely open.

The most credible case for AI in this domain rests on simulation and scale. Building on work in game-based learning, more advanced AI systems can create dynamic, personalised social simulations — offering students diverse scenarios that adapt in real time to their interactions, enabling them to practise empathy and receive immediate feedback. The promise is especially tangible for populations with specific developmental needs: emotion-aware technologies implemented in serious games have shown value in assisting children with Autism Spectrum Disorder in developing social-emotional skills, and as AI grows more capable, such tools increasingly function as teaching instruments in their own right. For neurotypical learners, AI systems can facilitate better emotional regulation and increased focus by providing tailored learning experiences based on students' emotional and cognitive needs, and the evidence suggests that AI-enhanced social-emotional learning frameworks create a more emotionally supportive environment overall.

AI also offers something genuinely scarce in human pedagogy: tirelessness. An AI will not become impatient or burned out, and it can offer around-the-clock support with endless patience — valuable for students who need steady reassurance or a non-judgmental listener. Moreover, AI systems can track a student's emotional patterns over time, potentially flagging declines in engagement or signs of distress that a busy teacher might miss, enabling earlier interventions. A systematic review using virtual reality, chatbots, sentiment analysis, and wearable devices found that integrating AI technologies into social-emotional learning programs offers unique opportunities to personalise learning, provide real-time feedback, and support students' socio-emotional growth in a scalable manner.

Yet the honest assessment of the literature is that these are mostly proximal gains, not evidence of deep character formation. Research exploring AI as a moral mentor critiques its limitations: diminished human autonomy, insufficient mechanisms for deep moral revision, and the neglect of emotional and transformative experiences. Teaching, in this view, must model the intellectual and moral virtues that AI cannot supply. A particularly acute concern is what one research team calls "social deskilling": without intentional design promoting high-fidelity interaction modes such as live video or virtual-reality-based collaboration, students may experience the erosion of their capacity for empathy, negotiation, and non-verbal attunement.

There is also the question of authenticity. Doubts are being raised regarding the validity of empathic responses from machines and how they can influence students' emotional learning — and cross-cultural variations in emotional expression may further affect the suitability of emotional feedback provided by AI, necessitating culturally responsive design. Even among those sympathetic to AI-based social-emotional learning tools, a prevalent psychological concern remains: whether machine-empathy constitutes genuine emotional support.

The emerging consensus among character educators is that the co-curriculum — communities of practice, service, and shared responsibility — must be treated as a central site of formation, because it is in these human contexts that civic and moral virtues are actually exercised and strengthened. AI, on this view, is better understood as a rehearsal space than a formative one. It can help a student practise the moves of empathy or resilience, but character, in the classical sense, is forged through genuine stakes, genuine relationships, and the kind of friction that only other people provide. Empathy remains a fundamental skill whose most effective methods of cultivation are still an open question — and that uncertainty applies with compounded force to any system that cannot itself feel what it claims to teach.

### Q028 How do we assess learning authentically when AI can complete any traditional assessment? {#q028}

9 citations · 9 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Assessing Learning Authentically in the Age of AI

The question of how to assess learning when AI can complete virtually any traditional assignment is, at its core, a question about what assessment was always supposed to do. The proliferation of AI in education provides a valuable opportunity to reconsider why students are being assessed, what is being evaluated, and how evidence of learning is gathered. What the generative AI moment has exposed is not a new vulnerability but an old one: a great deal of conventional assessment was measuring compliance with a task format rather than the presence of genuine understanding.

The scale of the problem is not in dispute. The rapid adoption of generative AI among university students is reshaping traditional assessment methods, with 40% of surveyed UK students agreeing that AI-generated content could achieve a good grade in their subject. Traditional assessments such as essays and take-home assignments are increasingly susceptible to AI-assisted plagiarism, necessitating a re-evaluation of assessment strategies. The instinctive institutional response — detection tools, prohibition, a return to invigilated paper exams — is understandable but limited. Attempts to block remote access to technology can often easily be bypassed by students, and attempts to use other technology to detect such behaviour are unlikely to be effective or sustainable.

A more principled response begins with a distinction between what AI can produce and what it cannot perform. Authentic assessments differ from traditional tests by requiring students to apply their knowledge in practical, context-rich scenarios which reflect the complexities they will encounter in professional settings. No AI can attend a seminar and defend a position under cross-examination, conduct a supervised clinical consultation, or improvise in a live design critique. Oral examinations in higher education offer a comprehensive method of assessing student learning, and their advantage lies in their ability to evaluate a range of skills and competencies essential in today's rapidly evolving academic and professional landscapes — including depth of understanding and critical thinking in ways that written tests may not.

One of the more rigorous frameworks to emerge from this period is what has been called the "Two-Lane" model, developed at the University of Sydney and adopted by Australia's national quality agency. This validity-centred design recognises that different learning outcomes require different assessment approaches: foundational knowledge and skills that must be verified as genuinely human capability call for supervised environments such as proctored exams, oral presentations, or in-class demonstrations, while professional capabilities involving tool use call for assessments where AI engagement is transparent and the human contribution is measurable. The logic is honest: rather than pretending AI does not exist in professional life, the framework distinguishes between competencies that must be independently held and competencies that will, in practice, be AI-assisted.

A parallel movement emphasises process over product. Universities increasingly cite "authentic assessments (e.g., real-world tasks, projects), process-oriented assessments (e.g., portfolios), and assignments requiring higher-order thinking" as the most frequently mentioned approaches for adapting to the disruption caused by generative AI. There has been a broader shift in the literature toward greater emphasis on learning processes rather than solely on final products, with portfolios, staged drafting, in-class checkpoints, and reflective journals increasingly promoted as ways to protect validity and foster genuine assessment for learning.

Yet caution is warranted about treating any single format as a solution. Portfolio-based assessment, frequently suggested as a forward-looking option, faces the concern that generative AI could also produce outlines, drafts, or reflective commentaries, undermining intended authenticity. While some research appears to support the role of authentic assessment in reducing academic misconduct, the evidence is unclear, and the likely success of this approach will depend heavily on how it is done in its particular context and conditions. Even oral examinations present equity issues: handwritten and oral exams are known to significantly disadvantage students with physical or mental disabilities.

The most intellectually honest position is that there is no single AI-proof assessment format — only a more deliberately designed ecology of assessments that collectively make learning visible. Leading researchers argue that assessment quality, not cheating prevention, should drive AI-era reforms. Rather than investing in AI detection tools, institutions should invest in redesigning assessments to ensure validity. The disruption, in this reading, is not a crisis to be managed but a long-overdue invitation to ask what it actually means to know something — and to design the conditions under which that knowledge must be shown, not merely produced.

### Q030 How do we design AI systems that strengthen rather than substitute students' thinking (avoiding cognitive offloading)? {#q030}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Designing AI to Strengthen Rather Than Substitute Student Thinking

The central problem with AI in education is not that the technology is inherently hostile to learning — it is that the path of least resistance runs directly against the grain of how learning works. When a student asks a chatbot for an answer and receives one instantly, something cognitively significant is lost: the effortful struggle through which understanding is actually built. Learning happens only when the student does the effortful part, the wrestling that cognitive science calls productive struggle. Designing AI systems that protect rather than preempt that struggle is the defining pedagogical challenge of the moment.

The empirical evidence for concern is substantial and growing. A study by Gerlich (2025) surveying 666 participants across diverse age groups and educational backgrounds found a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool usage and critical thinking abilities, mediated by increased cognitive offloading. A laboratory experiment using neural imaging found that cognitive activity decreased when participants relied on external tools, and self-reported ownership of essays was lowest in the LLM group and highest in the Brain-only group. Perhaps most troubling for educators is the phenomenon researchers have termed "metacognitive laziness": when learners rely excessively on AI-generated outputs, they may not experience the necessary cognitive difficulty to trigger deeper metacognitive processes, reinforcing a state of metacognitive laziness — a phenomenon stemming from cognitive offloading, where reliance on external resources diminishes engagement in self-regulatory processes.

There is also a structural equity dimension often overlooked in these debates. The cognitive risks of AI — like metacognitive laziness and the illusion of competence — disproportionately affect novices and those with weaker self-regulation skills, thus potentially widening existing equity divides. The students who most need to build independent reasoning capacity are precisely those most vulnerable to having it quietly eroded.

What, then, does better design look like? The research converges on several principles, none of them simple to implement but all grounded in learning science rather than marketing convenience.

The tool must refuse to do the student's thinking. Key design principles include a hint-first tutoring stance, automated detection of assessment-relevant prompts, refusal of direct solutions during active assignments, and redirection toward conceptual explanation or strategy rehearsal. This is not merely a policy choice — it can be built into the architecture itself. Some systems are designed so that the system cannot give the answer because it is designed not to — a structural answer to the hallucination and cognitive outsourcing problem.

Scaffolding must be contingent and fading. The concept of contingent scaffolding, drawn from decades of educational psychology, holds that support must be responsive to the learner's current state, providing assistance only when needed and fading as competence develops. A well-designed AI system should not offer the same level of support at every moment; it should actively shrink its own footprint as a student's competence grows. Educational AI should support autonomy needs while actively fading its own scaffolding.

Friction can be a feature, not a bug. Research on so-called "desirable difficulties" demonstrates that learners often do not appreciate the beneficial effects of tasks that are experienced as effortful but have a positive effect on learning results and transfer of knowledge and skills — for example, retrieval practice is significantly more effective than simply re-reading material, though self-testing requires greater cognitive effort. Practically, this suggests that rate-limiting or introducing delays before providing help can preserve productive struggle: if students must wait before seeing a hint, or can only request help a certain number of times per session, they are more likely to attempt problems independently first.

AI can strengthen the teacher rather than replace them. One of the more promising design directions is using AI not to tutor students directly but to support the human tutors working with them. Stanford's Tutor CoPilot is an AI-powered system designed to provide live suggestions to human tutors on how to foster productive struggle, generating expert-like suggestions such as asking a guiding question or providing a hint. This approach keeps the cognitive labor where it belongs — with the student — while giving teachers real-time support for the moments when they would otherwise default to simply providing an answer.

The AI's role within the learning sequence matters enormously. Answer-giving where the student should struggle is what harms learning, while guarded design in the same place does not — and the upside is just as design-dependent. The practical question for institutions is therefore not whether to permit AI, but precisely where in the learning sequence the tool is placed and what cognitive job it is assigned to perform there.

The hardest design challenge is what researchers have named the autonomy–accessibility paradox: the design features that render AI support pedagogically effective — immediate availability, adaptive calibration, frictionless engagement — may simultaneously attenuate the productive struggle through which deeper understanding is formed. Making an AI that is genuinely useful without being cognitively substitutive requires deliberate constraint — building systems that are, in a meaningful sense, less convenient by design. That discipline of intentional restraint is the clearest line separating AI tools that build minds from those that quietly hollow them out.

### Q114 What happens to teacher expertise and professional identity when curriculum materials are machine-generated? {#q114}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

When curriculum materials are machine-generated, the most visible change is in the artifacts of teaching — lesson plans, worksheets, assessments. The deeper change is in the teacher: their expertise, their professional identity, and their place in the educational division of labor. The literature on this question is converging on a central tension: AI can make teachers more capable, or it can make them redundant in the tasks that defined their expertise — and which outcome occurs depends less on the technology than on how it is introduced and who controls it.

The first effect is a shift in the locus of expertise. Traditionally, a teacher's professional identity was built substantially on being the author of their curriculum: the person who decided what to teach, how to sequence it, and how to represent it to students. When materials are machine-generated, that authorship moves — at least in part — to the system and the vendor behind it. Teachers report experiencing this as a redefinition of their role from "gatekeeper of information" to "facilitator of AI-mediated learning." This is not inherently a loss: facilitation is a legitimate and demanding professional role. But the literature documents genuine uncertainty among teachers about what constitutes their unique expertise in an AI-saturated setting. If the machine can write the lesson, what is the teacher for? The answer that emerges is that the teacher's expertise shifts from production to judgment: evaluating the machine's output, adapting it to particular students, and deciding what is worth teaching. But this shift is only experienced as empowering if teachers actually exercise that judgment — which depends on whether the system and the institution leave room for it.

The second effect is the risk of deskilling. The concept of deskilling, drawn from labor process theory, describes what happens when the cognitive content of a job is automated and the worker is left with execution. When AI automates grading, assessment, content delivery, and lesson design — tasks that were central to the teacher's expertise — the teacher can be positioned as an operator of a system rather than a professional. The risk is most acute when implementation is top-down: when AI tools are imposed without meaningful teacher input, when vendors' discourse positions teachers as the bottleneck to be optimized, and when teachers are treated as "instrumental objects" of the technology rather than participants in its design. The literature links this to "AI education anxiety" — occupational stress rooted in concerns about professional irreplaceability and skill deficits — and to burnout and resistance.

The third effect is on professional identity and autonomy. Research on teacher professional identity in the AI era finds that identity is being reconstructed: teachers are moving from "digital immigrants" to "AI natives," from transmitters to designers and ethical guides. The reconstruction is not automatic; it requires institutional support. Studies find that professional wellbeing is positively correlated with instructional autonomy, teacher-student relationships, and a sense of professional competence — and negatively correlated with feeling marginalized by automated systems. The implication is that machine-generated curriculum materials do not, by themselves, destroy teacher expertise; they relocate it. But the relocation can go badly if teachers are not given the authority to review, refine, and reject AI-generated recommendations. The literature is explicit that teachers must retain the authority to reject the machine's output — and that this authority must be real, not nominal.

The fourth effect is on the quality of the materials themselves and the teacher's relationship to them. When a teacher writes a lesson, they know its assumptions, its gaps, and its intended audience; when a machine generates it, the teacher must reconstruct that knowledge through review. The evidence suggests that teachers who treat AI as a "creative thought partner" — generating drafts that the teacher then evaluates and adapts — report positive experiences, including for novice teachers developing their professional identity. The danger is the "set-it-and-forget-it" pattern: materials adopted without critical review, which erodes both quality and the teacher's sense of ownership. The literature recommends "curriculum-informed AI" — systems aligned with high-quality instructional materials and research-backed practices — precisely because the alternative is generic output that does not reflect the teacher's professional voice or the school's pedagogical goals.

The fifth effect is on the profession as a whole. If machine-generated materials become the norm, the apprenticeship structures of teaching change: novice teachers no longer learn their craft by writing lessons and having them critiqued; they learn by evaluating machine output. This can be an efficient induction — the literature finds that generative AI can support novice teachers' emerging identities by enabling successful implementation of innovative task designs — but it risks producing teachers who are skilled evaluators of AI output and less skilled authors of curriculum. The profession's collective expertise in curriculum design, which was built through generations of teachers authoring and sharing materials, may atrophy even as individual teachers become more efficient.

In sum, machine-generated curriculum materials do not automatically deskill teachers, but they do relocate expertise — from production to judgment — and the relocation is risky. The outcome depends on three conditions: teachers must retain real authority to review, adapt, and reject machine output; implementation must be collaborative rather than top-down; and professional development must build critical AI literacy — the capacity to evaluate algorithms, datasets, and the power structures embedded in AI platforms. Where these conditions hold, AI can make teachers more capable and their identity more secure; where they fail, teachers are positioned as operators of systems they do not control, and the profession's expertise is gradually transferred to the machine and its vendor. The question is not whether AI will change teacher expertise — it will — but who will hold the judgment that remains.

### Q116 What effect does AI support have on novice, substitute, and under-qualified teachers specifically? {#q116}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The effect of AI support on novice, substitute, and under-qualified teachers is distinct from its effect on experienced teachers, because these groups face a different problem: not how to save time on work they know how to do, but how to do work they do not yet know how to do. The evidence suggests that AI can be a powerful equalizer for these teachers — providing expert-level scaffolding on demand — but that the benefits are conditional on design, training, and the preservation of human mentorship.

For substitute teachers, the most immediate effect is on the emergency lesson. Substitute shortages have forced schools to rely on paraprofessionals, administrators, and under-qualified adults to supervise classrooms, often without prepared plans. AI tools can generate structured lesson plans, worksheets, and activities in seconds, tailored to grade level and subject — including lab experiments for science and discussion prompts for humanities. This converts a substitute from a supervisor into a teacher of record, at least for the lesson's duration. The evidence from practitioner accounts is that AI-generated plans help substitutes provide meaningful learning experiences even when they lack subject-matter expertise, and that AI can scaffold complex discussions and suggest classroom-management strategies. The effect is to reduce the instructional gap created by teacher absence — a gap that disproportionately harms students in under-resourced schools, where substitute shortages are most acute.

For novice teachers, the effect is on induction. Early-career teachers face a steep learning curve: planning, classroom management, differentiation, and the sheer volume of administrative work. The literature identifies AI as an "expert-level guide" that can shorten this curve by providing real-time feedback and pedagogical suggestions, and by automating the repetitive tasks — grading, tracking, parent communication — that consume novice time. Studies of generative AI in professional learning identify four affordance categories for teachers: functional (instructional design and content co-creation), cognitive (higher-order thinking and knowledge construction), social (human-AI partnership), and reflective (building self-efficacy through iterative feedback). For novices, the reflective affordance may be the most important: AI can synthesize data about their own practice and support self-directed professional development, which early-career teachers use with high levels of self-management and self-monitoring.

For under-qualified teachers — those teaching out of field, on emergency credentials, or in shortage areas such as mathematics and science — the effect is on competence. AI can provide the subject-matter scaffolding that these teachers lack: explanations, worked examples, and content knowledge on demand. The literature on the math teacher shortage, for example, describes AI as an evidence-based support that helps under-qualified teachers deliver instruction they could not otherwise deliver. The effect is to make the teacher's lack of formal preparation less damaging to students — a genuine equity benefit in systems that cannot staff every classroom with fully qualified teachers.

But the literature also identifies significant risks specific to these groups. The first is cognitive over-reliance. Novice and under-qualified teachers are the most likely to accept AI output without sufficient pedagogical judgment, precisely because they lack the expertise to evaluate it. The "descriptive-operational gap" in the literature — many studies describe what AI can do, few measure whether it develops professional competency — is a warning that AI support can produce dependence without development. A novice who learns to teach by accepting machine-generated plans may never develop the curriculum judgment that experienced teachers have. The second risk is the loss of the apprenticeship model. The literature on tacit knowledge warns of the "pipeline problem": when entry-level cognitive work is automated, the structures through which expertise is passed from generation to generation are disrupted. For teaching, this means that AI support for novices must not replace the human mentor. Studies find that teachers who work alongside experienced human mentors outperform those who rely solely on AI tools, because mentors provide context, emotional support, and pedagogical guidance that AI cannot replicate. The effective model is hybrid: AI provides the scaffolding, the mentor provides the formation.

The third risk is equity in reverse. AI support for substitutes and under-qualified teachers is most needed in under-resourced schools — but those are precisely the schools least likely to have the devices, connectivity, training, and support systems that make AI use effective. The literature on the AI divide warns that if AI support is available only where infrastructure and training exist, the technology will widen rather than narrow the gap between well-staffed and under-staffed schools. The effect of AI on novice, substitute, and under-qualified teachers is therefore not a single effect; it depends on the conditions under which these teachers work.

The fourth consideration is training. The evidence is consistent that AI tools are only as good as the training that surrounds them: without professional development, substitutes and novices either misuse the tools or underuse them. Schools that deploy AI for these groups without training are likely to see the tools fail — and to conclude, wrongly, that the technology does not work.

In sum, AI support has a distinctive and largely positive effect on novice, substitute, and under-qualified teachers: it provides expert-level scaffolding on demand, converts substitutes from supervisors into instructors, shortens the novice induction curve, and supplies subject-matter competence to under-qualified teachers. But the effect is conditional. It depends on training, on infrastructure, on the preservation of human mentorship, and on guarding against cognitive over-reliance. Used well, AI is a force multiplier for the teachers who need the most support; used carelessly, it can produce dependence without development and widen the very gaps it promises to close. The test is whether AI support builds these teachers' capacity or merely compensates for its absence.

### Q227 How is generative AI changing pedagogy, authorship, and assessment in creative arts education? {#q227}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

Generative AI in Creative Arts Education: Pedagogy, Authorship, and Assessment

Generative AI has arrived in creative arts education with particular force, because it directly engages with the core activities of arts disciplines — image creation, music composition, narrative writing, design, and performance — in ways that challenge fundamental assumptions about creativity, authorship, and the purpose of arts education. The evidence on AI in creative arts education is still nascent, concentrated in higher education, and methodologically limited, but it is sufficient to identify the key pedagogical opportunities, risks, and unresolved questions.

The Research Landscape

Systematic reviews published in 2024 and 2025 indicate a significant acceleration in empirical research on generative AI in arts education. Most studies are concentrated in higher education, with a notable prevalence of research from East Asia and the United States. Methodologically, research has shifted from theoretical discussions toward empirical, mixed-methods studies that evaluate the impact of generative AI on student learning outcomes, creative thinking, and engagement. The field remains in an early stage: most studies have small samples, short intervention durations, and lack control groups.

Generative AI as Creative Tool: Three Roles

Current literature categorises the role of generative AI in arts education into three primary functions. First, as a facilitator of human creativity: AI acts as an assistant to enhance ideation and problem-solving, used for brainstorming or initial concept generation. Second, as a collaborative partner: AI participates in the production process, allowing for rapid prototyping and style exploration. Third, as an autonomous generator: AI produces outputs with minimal human intervention, though this is less common in pedagogical settings where human agency remains a priority.

Research on AI as a creative tool finds that when integrated with intentional instructor design, it can significantly improve creative confidence (by lowering technical barriers, allowing students to focus on visual thinking and aesthetic judgment), personalised learning (providing real-time feedback and tailored support), and engagement (students report higher levels of interest and motivation when using AI to explore complex artistic concepts).

The Authorship Problem

The most contested issue in AI and creative arts education is authorship. When a student uses AI to generate an image, compose a melody, or draft a narrative, who is the author? The question is not merely philosophical — it has direct implications for assessment, intellectual property, and the educational purpose of arts disciplines.

The evidence suggests that the authorship question cannot be resolved by a simple rule. The degree of human creative contribution varies enormously across AI-assisted creative work: from minimal (accepting an AI-generated output with minor modifications) to substantial (using AI as a tool in a complex creative process that involves significant human judgment, selection, and refinement). Assessment frameworks that treat all AI-assisted work as equivalent — either all acceptable or all prohibited — fail to capture this variation.

Emerging assessment frameworks distinguish between process and product: they evaluate not just the final creative output but the creative process that produced it, including the student's ability to articulate their creative decisions, evaluate AI-generated options, and integrate AI assistance into a coherent creative vision. These process-sensitive frameworks are more demanding but also more pedagogically defensible.

The Aesthetic Homogenisation Risk

A significant concern in the literature is the risk of aesthetic homogenisation: if students across institutions and disciplines use the same AI tools with similar prompts, the diversity of creative output may decline. Research on AI-generated visual art finds that current models tend to produce outputs that reflect the aesthetic preferences embedded in their training data — predominantly Western, contemporary, and commercially oriented. Students who rely heavily on AI generation without critical engagement with these aesthetic defaults may produce work that is technically competent but aesthetically undifferentiated.

Arts educators have responded to this risk by emphasising critical AI literacy — the ability to recognise and interrogate the aesthetic assumptions embedded in AI tools — as a core competency for arts students. This includes understanding how training data shapes AI aesthetic preferences, how to use prompting strategies to push against default aesthetics, and how to evaluate AI-generated work critically rather than accepting it uncritically.

Copyright and Intellectual Property

The copyright status of AI-generated creative work remains legally unsettled in most jurisdictions. In the United States, the Copyright Office has ruled that purely AI-generated works are not eligible for copyright protection, but that works with sufficient human creative contribution may be protected. The threshold of human contribution required for copyright protection is not yet clearly defined. In the EU, the AI Act's transparency requirements for AI-generated content have implications for arts education, but the copyright framework for AI-assisted creative work is still developing.

Arts educators need to understand the copyright implications of AI use in student work, including the potential for AI-generated content to infringe on the copyright of works in the training data, and the implications for student intellectual property rights.

### Q230 How can educators design formative assessment with AI that strengthens feedback, self-regulation, and learning rather than task substitution? {#q230}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Designing Formative Assessment with AI: Feedback, Self-Regulation, and the Task Substitution Problem

Formative assessment — the ongoing process of gathering evidence about student learning and using it to adjust instruction — is one of the most powerful tools available to educators. The evidence that high-quality formative assessment improves learning outcomes is among the strongest in educational research. AI offers the potential to enhance formative assessment by providing more frequent, more personalised, and more timely feedback than human teachers can deliver at scale. However, it also introduces a significant risk: that AI-assisted formative assessment becomes task substitution — students improving a submitted product without acquiring the intended skill.

The Evidence Base for Formative Assessment

The foundational evidence for formative assessment comes from Black and Wiliam's landmark 1998 review, which found effect sizes of 0.4 to 0.7 for high-quality formative assessment — among the largest effects in educational research. Subsequent meta-analyses have confirmed these findings and identified the key mechanisms: effective formative assessment provides students with information about where they are relative to a learning goal, what they need to do to close the gap, and how to take the next step. It also develops students' capacity for self-assessment and self-regulation — the ability to monitor their own learning and adjust their strategies accordingly.

AI Feedback: Opportunities and Limitations

AI can provide formative feedback at a scale and frequency that human teachers cannot match. AI writing feedback tools can provide immediate, detailed feedback on grammar, style, structure, and argumentation. AI mathematics tutors can identify specific misconceptions and provide targeted explanations. AI coding assistants can detect errors and suggest corrections in real time. These capabilities address one of the most significant constraints on effective formative assessment: the time required for human teachers to provide detailed, personalised feedback to every student.

However, AI feedback has significant limitations. It tends to focus on surface features (grammar, syntax, code correctness) rather than deeper learning (conceptual understanding, argumentation quality, creative thinking). It can be generic rather than genuinely personalised. And it can enable students to improve a product without understanding why the improvement was made — the task substitution problem.

The Task Substitution Problem

The central risk of AI in formative assessment is task substitution: students use AI feedback to improve a submitted product without acquiring the intended skill. A student who uses AI to correct their grammar may produce a grammatically correct essay without developing their own grammatical competence. A student who uses AI to debug their code may produce working code without understanding the underlying programming concepts. This risk is not hypothetical: research on AI writing feedback finds that students who receive AI feedback without reflection or explanation show smaller gains in writing competence than those who engage actively with the feedback.

Design Principles for AI-Enhanced Formative Assessment

Based on the evidence, several design principles emerge for AI-enhanced formative assessment. First, connect feedback to learning goals: AI feedback should be explicitly linked to the learning objectives of the task, helping students understand not just what to change but why the change matters for their learning. Second, require explanation and reflection: students should be required to explain the changes they make in response to AI feedback, demonstrating that they understand the feedback rather than simply implementing it. Third, combine AI feedback with human, peer, and self-assessment: AI feedback is most effective when it is one component of a multi-source feedback system that includes teacher, peer, and self-assessment. Fourth, use process evidence rather than product evidence: assess the process of learning — including how students respond to feedback, how they revise their work, and how they explain their reasoning — rather than just the final product. Fifth, design for self-regulation: AI feedback should be designed to develop students' capacity for self-assessment and self-regulation, not to substitute for it.

### Q260 How do teachers maintain instructional authority, pedagogical presence, and classroom trust when AI systems are simultaneously delivering competing explanations to students? {#q260}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

For most of the history of schooling, the teacher was the primary source of explanations in the classroom, supplemented by textbooks that the teacher chose. Generative AI changes this arrangement. Students can now obtain instant, fluent explanations of almost any topic, sometimes different from the teacher's, sometimes wrong, and sometimes clearer. This raises a practical and professional question: how do teachers maintain instructional authority, pedagogical presence, and classroom trust when AI systems are delivering competing explanations at the same time?

The scale of student access makes the question pressing. The Pew Research Center's February 2026 report on how teens use and view AI found that 54 percent of U.S. teens had used AI chatbots for help with schoolwork, and about one in ten used them for all or most of their schoolwork. Many students therefore encounter AI explanations alongside, or in place of, their teachers' instruction.

One response would be for teachers to compete with AI on its own terms, as a source of answers. The evidence suggests this is neither feasible nor desirable. AI systems can produce explanations faster and on demand, and some carefully designed AI tutors have produced strong learning gains. Kestin and colleagues, in a 2025 randomised crossover study in Scientific Reports involving 194 Harvard physics students, found that students learned more from a structured AI tutor than from an in-class active learning session covering the same material. Importantly, the AI tutor in that study was designed by instructors, drew on solutions they supplied, and operated within their course structure. Its effectiveness derived partly from the teachers' pedagogical design.

This points to a different basis for authority: teachers as designers and orchestrators of learning rather than sole transmitters of information. The randomised trial by Bastani and colleagues in PNAS found that how AI was configured determined whether it helped or harmed learning: unrestricted access improved practice performance but was associated with worse unassisted exam performance, while a tutor that offered hints rather than answers largely avoided the harm. Teachers who decide when AI is used, for what tasks, and with what constraints exercise a form of authority that AI cannot replace, because it rests on knowledge of learning goals, students, and context.

A second basis for authority is critical evaluation. When students bring AI explanations that conflict with the teacher's, the conflict can become a teaching opportunity. Teachers can model how to check claims against sources, identify errors, and reason about why explanations differ. Demonstrating that AI can be wrong, and showing how to find out, reinforces the teacher's role as an expert guide in evaluating knowledge rather than a competitor in producing it. The U.S. Department of Education's 2023 report on AI and the future of teaching and learning emphasised keeping humans in the loop and positioning AI as a tool that supports rather than supplants teacher judgement.

A third basis is relational presence. Teaching involves knowing students, noticing confusion or disengagement, providing encouragement, and building a community in which students feel safe to make mistakes. These dimensions depend on human relationships and are central to what students value in good teachers. Teachers who invest in them maintain a presence that AI explanations do not displace.

Trust is the most fragile element. The Center for Democracy and Technology's 2024 report Up in the Air found that uncertainty about AI rules and reliance on unreliable detection tools contributed to distrust between students and teachers, with some students disciplined on the basis of flawed evidence. Classrooms where AI is treated primarily as a cheating threat may erode the trust on which authority depends. Transparent norms help: teachers who explain when AI use is encouraged, when it is limited, and why, and who apply rules fairly, appear better positioned to maintain trust than those who rely on surveillance.

Several practical strategies follow from this evidence. Teachers can discuss AI openly, including its strengths and failures, rather than ignoring it. They can design tasks that require students to work through reasoning in class, explain their thinking, or critique AI outputs. They can adopt or help configure AI tools aligned with their pedagogy, rather than leaving students to use unrestricted systems. They can invite students to bring AI explanations into discussion, treating discrepancies as material for inquiry.

Classroom authority has never rested on a single foundation, and the history of the concept helps clarify what generative AI does and does not threaten. Judith Pace and Annette Hemmings, in a 2007 review in the Review of Educational Research, traced how sociologists from Max Weber onwards distinguished authority grounded in tradition, in legal or institutional position, in charisma, and in professional expertise, and they argued that classroom authority is best understood as a social relationship that students and teachers negotiate rather than a possession the teacher simply holds. On this view, a teacher's authority depends on students granting legitimacy to the teacher's direction, and that legitimacy can come from many sources, including perceived fairness, care and moral purpose as well as knowledge. The review emphasised that authority built solely on institutional position tends to produce compliance without engagement, while authority grounded in shared educational purposes tends to be more durable. This framing implies that AI chiefly challenges one strand of authority, the teacher's status as the most accessible holder of information, while leaving the relational, moral and pedagogical strands largely intact. It also suggests that the challenge is not entirely new: printed textbooks, encyclopaedias, television and the open web each offered students explanations that did not originate with their teachers, and teachers adapted by shifting emphasis towards interpretation and guidance.

Research on how people respond to algorithmic advice helps explain why competing AI explanations can be unsettling in classrooms. Berkeley Dietvorst, Joseph Simmons and Cade Massey, in a 2015 set of experiments in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, found that participants who watched a forecasting algorithm make errors became less willing to rely on it than on a human forecaster, even when the algorithm was more accurate overall, a pattern they called algorithm aversion. Jennifer Logg, Julia Minson and Don Moore, in a 2019 series of experiments in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, found the opposite tendency in other conditions: lay participants often weighted advice more heavily when told it came from an algorithm than when told it came from a person, which they termed algorithm appreciation, although the effect weakened among participants with relevant expertise. Neither line of research studied school students, so their application to classrooms is an inference. Taken together, however, they suggest that students may oscillate between over-trusting fluent AI explanations and dismissing them entirely after noticing a mistake. A teacher who helps students calibrate their trust, neither deferring to the machine nor rejecting it reflexively, addresses a cognitive tendency that the AI system itself is poorly placed to correct.

The reliability of AI explanations matters directly for how teachers should respond when they conflict with instruction. Ziwei Ji and colleagues, in a 2023 survey in ACM Computing Surveys, reviewed the extensive research literature on hallucination, the tendency of language-generation systems to produce fluent text that is unsupported by or contradicts source information, and concluded that hallucination arises across tasks and model types and had not been eliminated by the mitigation methods then available. Enkelejda Kasneci and colleagues, in a 2023 position paper in Learning and Individual Differences written by a multidisciplinary group of education and computer science researchers, argued that large language models offer genuine opportunities for explanation and personalised support but that students and teachers need competencies to understand the models' limitations, recognise errors and bias, and avoid over-reliance. These analyses imply that competing explanations will sometimes reflect genuine alternative framings that enrich understanding, sometimes simplifications appropriate for a different level, and sometimes plain errors. Distinguishing among these cases requires subject knowledge and pedagogical judgement, which is precisely where the teacher's expertise remains distinctive. A conflict between a teacher's explanation and an AI's explanation is therefore not, in itself, evidence that either is wrong; it is an occasion for adjudication that the teacher is usually best equipped to lead.

Trust has been studied as a multidimensional construct in schools, which offers a more precise vocabulary for what teachers need to protect. Megan Tschannen-Moran and Wayne Hoy, in a 2000 multidisciplinary review in the Review of Educational Research, synthesised research from organisational studies, psychology and education and proposed that trust involves willingness to be vulnerable to another party based on confidence that the party is benevolent, reliable, competent, honest and open. Applied to AI-rich classrooms, this framework suggests that a teacher's trustworthiness does not depend on knowing every answer. Students may continue to trust a teacher who occasionally says "I need to check that" if the teacher is honest, consistent and visibly committed to their learning, and they may lose trust in a teacher who appears to hide uncertainty or to apply AI rules arbitrarily. Openness, in particular, maps onto practices such as explaining why an AI-generated explanation differs from the class textbook, admitting when the AI's version is clearer, and inviting students to scrutinise the teacher's own reasoning. The framework also clarifies why surveillance-centred approaches to AI may be self-defeating: treating students primarily as suspects signals a lack of benevolence and invites reciprocal distrust.

The relational dimension of teaching has a substantial evidence base that predates AI and helps explain why presence is hard to replace. Debora Roorda and colleagues, in a 2011 meta-analysis in the Review of Educational Research covering 99 studies from preschool to secondary school, found that positive affective relationships between teachers and students were associated with higher student engagement and achievement, and that negative relationships were associated with lower engagement and achievement, with associations generally larger for engagement than for achievement. Because the included studies were largely correlational, the meta-analysis cannot show that relationships cause better outcomes, and reverse influences, in which engaged students elicit warmer relationships, are plausible. The consistency of the associations across ages and settings nonetheless suggests that the relational work teachers do is closely bound up with how students engage with learning. AI systems can simulate encouragement in text, but they do not notice a student's absence, follow up on a difficult week at home, or carry accumulated knowledge of a class's history. These are among the sources of legitimacy that Pace and Hemmings identified, and they are not displaced by an alternative explanation of photosynthesis or quadratic equations.

Comparisons across subjects and age groups suggest that the challenge is uneven. In mathematics and the sciences, where explanations can often be checked against worked solutions or experiments, conflicting AI explanations lend themselves to structured comparison, and teachers can ask students to test which account predicts results correctly. In history, literature and civic education, where interpretation is contested, an AI system's confident synthesis may flatten legitimate disagreement or present one perspective as settled, and the teacher's role shifts towards showing how evidence and argument support different readings. Younger students may lack the background knowledge to notice discrepancies at all, which places more responsibility on teachers and on the configuration of the tools they use, while older students may use AI explanations to challenge the teacher openly. Each of these situations calls for a somewhat different response, and policies that treat AI explanations uniformly across subjects and ages may miss these distinctions.

Equity considerations shape who bears the costs of competing explanations. Students with access to well-informed adults at home can ask a parent or tutor to adjudicate when an AI explanation conflicts with the teacher's, while students without such support depend more heavily on their teachers to make sense of discrepancies. Teachers in under-resourced schools, who often manage larger classes with fewer planning hours, may have less time to examine the AI explanations students bring and to redesign tasks around them. Professional development, curriculum materials that anticipate common AI errors, and institutionally vetted tools configured to support rather than bypass instruction could reduce these disparities, but the evidence on which supports are most effective remains thin. Implementation therefore depends on school leaders treating the maintenance of teacher authority as a shared institutional responsibility rather than an individual skill each teacher must develop alone, with time, training and clear norms provided at the level of the school or system.

Evidence on these strategies is still developing, and few studies directly measure teacher authority or classroom trust in AI-rich settings. The available research nonetheless suggests that authority in the age of AI rests less on being the only source of explanations and more on the judgement, design, relationships, and critical modelling that only teachers provide.

## Chapter 4: The Learner's Experience {#chapter-04}

12 questions · 120 citations · 115 unique sources · 60 cross-references

### Q031 How does constant AI availability change motivation, curiosity, and the desire to learn? {#q031}

11 citations · 11 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Ambiguous Gift of the Always-Available Answer

Something unusual happens when a capable teacher is available at every moment, willing to answer any question without hesitation: the student may stop generating questions of their own. This tension — between the undeniable usefulness of constant AI access and the subtler costs it may impose on motivation, curiosity, and the desire to learn — is now the subject of serious empirical scrutiny, and the picture that emerges resists simple optimism or alarm.

The optimistic case rests on solid ground. Researchers argue that AI's ability to personalize content fosters intrinsic motivation, aligning with self-determination theory's emphasis on autonomy and competence. AI has been shown to improve students' self-efficacy through features such as providing adaptable learning environments and personalized learning experiences. Empirical data from 2024 reveals that 54% of students show increased engagement in their coursework when AI tools are incorporated into the learning experience. These effects are real. When a student who once stalled at a confusing concept can get an immediate, tailored explanation at midnight, the friction that previously killed curiosity before it could mature is removed. Access expands; engagement, in this mode, follows.

But the relationship between ease and learning is more complicated than simple access suggests. The risk of detrimental cognitive offloading is not theoretical. A growing body of empirical research provides clear evidence for a "performance paradox": AI can boost a student's performance on an immediate task while simultaneously diminishing the durable learning that is the goal. The most striking causal evidence comes from a large-scale randomized controlled trial: roughly 1,000 students were assigned unrestricted GPT-4 access during math practice or to a control group; AI-assisted performance improved by 48%, but unassisted exam performance fell by 17% relative to control — consistent with the cognitive-science prediction that active engagement with learning materials produces more durable learning than passive processing.

The damage to persistence may be even more immediate than that result suggests. Across a series of randomized controlled trials on 1,222 participants, researchers found causal evidence that although AI assistance improves performance in the short term, people perform significantly worse without AI and are more likely to give up — and these effects emerge after only brief interactions of around 10 minutes. The proposed mechanism is revealing: persistence is reduced because AI conditions people to expect immediate answers, thereby denying them the experience of working through challenges on their own. In other words, constant availability recalibrates the inner sense of what effort should feel like. Immediate, unfiltered AI answers rapidly adjust subjective expectations, making unaided effort aversive; metacognitive decay occurs as feedback from actual problem-solving is replaced by solution consumption.

This points to a deeper mechanism concerning curiosity itself. Curiosity, properly understood, is not merely the desire to receive information — it is a motivational state aroused by an uncertainty the mind wants to resolve through its own engagement. From the perspective of self-determination theory, intrinsic motivation depends on learners' autonomy and active engagement; delegating key metacognitive tasks such as planning, monitoring, and evaluating to generative AI might reduce learners' active participation and sense of control, thereby decreasing intrinsic motivation. When every uncertainty can be instantly dissolved by a competent external agent, the very experience that generates curiosity — sitting with not-knowing — is eliminated before it has a chance to deepen.

This is not, however, an argument for withholding AI from learners. Not all friction may be inherently beneficial, and not all ease may be harmful; in some cases, AI may reduce surface-level barriers such as organizing initial ideas or decoding, freeing up students to spend more time exploring and revising, and AI-facilitated ease may unlock curiosity, extend time-on-task, or enable students to reach cognitive depths they may not previously have accessed. The distinction is between AI that scaffolds thinking and AI that replaces it. AI-mediated outcomes depend on the balance between cognitive relief and motivational autonomy: when technology scaffolds reflection and supports agency, it strengthens resilience; when it substitutes intrinsic effort or distorts self-perception, it contributes to cognitive overload.

The central finding of the current research moment is therefore not that AI kills curiosity, but that the architecture of interaction matters enormously. AI systems are fundamentally short-term collaborators: extraordinarily helpful in the moment, but indifferent to what that help does to the person receiving it over time. Designing systems that preserve productive struggle — that guide rather than answer, that ask before they tell — is not a nostalgic preference; it is what the evidence increasingly demands. Whether that design discipline will prove commercially viable, given that users tend to reward instant gratification, is the question that remains genuinely open.

### Q032 What are the effects of AI companionship on students' social development and human relationships? {#q032}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI Companionship and the Social Lives of Students

The scale of the phenomenon demands attention before its consequences can be properly assessed. According to a recent U.S. survey of 13- to 17-year-olds, 72% of adolescents have used AI companions, and 52% qualified as regular users. A third of teenagers have chosen AI companions over humans for serious conversations, and a quarter have shared personal information with these platforms. What was once a niche technology has, in the span of a few years, become a routine feature of student life — and researchers are only beginning to understand what this means for the development of genuine human sociality.

The case for AI companionship rests on a real and well-documented problem. Individuals who experience elevated levels of loneliness may seek AI companions to fulfil unmet emotional needs; in such cases, AI companions may function as surrogate social partners, offering emotional connection and psychological support that help mitigate the adverse effects of loneliness. AI chatbots can facilitate companionship, mitigating loneliness and depression through socioemotional interactions. For students navigating the social pressures of adolescence, these tools can also serve a preparatory function: an AI companion can give teens space to talk without feeling afraid of social consequences. Scholars describe this as the "stimulation hypothesis" — the idea that AI companions can provide safe spaces for identity exploration and emotional expression, potentially building skills that transfer to human relationships.

Yet the evidence increasingly complicates this optimistic reading. The most methodologically rigorous study to date, conducted by researchers at Aalto University and presented at CHI 2026, examined nearly two thousand Replika users over a two-year period. While AI companions can provide meaningful short-term emotional support, long-term use is increasingly associated with rising signs of psychological distress and a gradual pullback from real-world relationships. A joint OpenAI–MIT Media Lab study reached a compatible conclusion: voice interactions with ChatGPT reduced loneliness and problematic dependence more effectively than text alone, but only with moderate use — heavy daily use correlated with increased loneliness, suggesting that excessive reliance displaces authentic human connection.

The mechanism behind this drift is becoming clearer. AI companions, being always available and frictionless, "quietly raise the perceived cost of human relationships, which are messy, unpredictable, and require effort." A self-reinforcing cycle may take hold: when AI becomes a primary source of emotional support, reduced human interaction weakens interpersonal skills, which makes human relationships feel more effortful and AI interaction more appealing. A study of over 1,100 AI companion users found that people with fewer human relationships were more likely to seek out chatbots, and that heavy emotional self-disclosure to AI was consistently associated with lower well-being.

For adolescents specifically, the developmental stakes are higher than for adults. AI companions create unprecedented opportunities for adolescents to form emotional bonds with nonhuman entities during a critical period for social development. The American Psychological Association notes that adolescents are less likely than adults to question a chatbot's accuracy or intent, and may mistake its simulated empathy for genuine human understanding — and warns that adolescent relationships with AI can displace healthy real-life friendships and family ties and foster unhealthy dependency. Mental health professionals are worried that AI companions may promote emotional dependence, interfere with therapeutic relationships, provide dangerous advice, and exacerbate existing mental health problems among adolescents. At the extreme end of the risk spectrum, these unique risks have already been linked to tragic cases, including the suicides of two adolescents after prolonged conversations with AI companions.

There is also the question of what students are learning from these interactions about the nature of relationships themselves. Studies suggest that such technologies may foster emotional dependence, distort users' perceptions of intimacy and, in some cases, contribute to negative psychological outcomes such as addiction, depression, and self-harm. Unlike traditional chatbots, AI companions are built on large language models, enabling them to memorize past information, hold in-depth and coherent conversations, emulate empathy, and provide personalized humanlike companionship with constant responsiveness in real time. The simulation is sophisticated enough that the boundaries between felt and fabricated intimacy become genuinely difficult to locate.

The honest summary is that the research is not yet settled. Short-term benefits for acutely lonely students appear real; long-term social costs — weakened interpersonal skills, inflated expectations of human partners, withdrawal from the effortful reciprocity that sustains actual friendship — appear equally real, and likely more consequential. Companion AI should be developed and deployed in ways that complement — not replace — genuine human connection, explicitly prioritize psychological safety over engagement maximization, and include safeguards against reinforcing isolation or vulnerability among already at-risk users. Whether the industry, which stands to profit handsomely from emotional dependency, will accept such constraints remains the central open question.

### Q033 How do we cultivate critical thinking in students who grow up trusting AI-generated answers? {#q033}

11 citations · 11 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Critical Thinking in the Age of the Oracular Machine

The urgency of the problem is no longer speculative. By December 2025, the share of middle and high school students using AI for homework had risen to 62 percent, and 67 percent of those students — up more than ten percentage points in under a year — agreed that the more students use AI for schoolwork, the more it will harm their critical thinking skills. Students, in other words, have already diagnosed their own condition. The question is what educators intend to do about it.

The core danger has a clinical name. Researchers term it "cognitive offloading" — a condition in which students who rely heavily on AI demonstrate substantial declines in analytical reasoning capabilities and decreased study motivation. This over-reliance occurs when students place undue trust in AI-generated content, often neglecting their analytical capabilities, which leads to superficial engagement with learning material. The machine does not merely answer questions; it gradually diminishes the felt need to ask them rigorously. The dominant paradigm of generative AI in education positions it as an omniscient oracle — a model that risks hindering genuine learning by fostering cognitive offloading.

What is particularly insidious is the texture of AI's errors. Many AI-generated responses appear confident and well-formatted, yet they may miss nuance, require detailed fact-checking, or reflect underlying biases from source materials. A student accustomed to receiving polished, authoritative-sounding prose has little obvious incentive to interrogate it. Confidence of presentation and accuracy of content are not the same thing, and learning to hold that distinction is precisely what AI makes harder.

The pedagogical response most supported by current research is not prohibition but deliberate reframing of the student's relationship to AI output. Treating AI outputs as starting points rather than definitive answers is the foundational shift. This can be structured concretely: students might analyze a ChatGPT-generated essay, identifying where it provides strong arguments and where it lacks depth or misinterprets the topic. AI reflects the biases in its training data, whether cultural, ideological, or systemic; teaching students to analyze these biases enables them to identify hidden assumptions and consider alternative perspectives.

Scaffolding and metacognition are, on current evidence, the most promising structural tools. Research suggests that scaffolding techniques — including prompt scaffolding, explicit reflection, and modelling — can help foster students' critical thinking skills in digital and AI-driven contexts. Critical thinking acts as a mediating factor, enabling students to assess AI suggestions more rigorously, adjust their trust levels, and ultimately engage more productively with AI. One emerging framework goes further, proposing a shift from "AI as Oracle" to a "Cognitive Mirror" paradigm — reconceptualizing AI as a teachable novice designed to reflect the quality of a learner's explanation, using AI's safety mechanisms as didactic tools to deliberately create a "pedagogically useful deficit." Whether such designs prove scalable remains to be seen.

At a higher conceptual level, scholars argue that the whole framework of AI literacy needs reconceiving. AI literacy must be reconceptualised as a metacognitive social practice that transcends individual competencies — one that encompasses a collective capacity for critical engagement with AI design, deployment, and governance, since the probabilistic nature and epistemic opacity of large language models render traditional rule-based digital literacy paradigms obsolete. Teaching students to use a search engine wisely was one kind of skill; teaching them to interrogate a system that synthesizes and confabulates with equal fluency is another order of problem entirely.

Researchers have called for decade-long studies tracking how sustained generative AI use reshapes foundational scholarly competencies — critical thinking, creativity, and epistemic humility — across disciplines. That such studies do not yet exist is itself telling. The generation now in school is the first to grow up with these tools as ambient infrastructure, and the pedagogy catching up to that fact is still, at best, provisional. What seems clear is that the habits of mind most worth cultivating — skepticism, source triangulation, tolerance for productive struggle — are precisely those that AI, used unreflectively, tends to erode. The institution that treats AI as a shortcut will produce graduates who cannot think without one.

### Q034 What new literacies (AI literacy, prompt literacy, epistemic hygiene) become as fundamental as reading and writing? {#q034}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The New Literacies: AI Fluency, Prompt Craft, and Epistemic Self-Defense

There is a recurring pattern in the history of communication technology: each transformative shift in how information is produced and distributed eventually forces a redefinition of what it means to be literate. The printing press made alphabetic reading non-negotiable; the internet elevated digital and media literacy from elective to essential. Generative AI represents a third such rupture, and the skills it demands are not supplementary refinements to existing education — they are foundational competencies in their own right.

**AI literacy** is the broadest of these emerging skills, and the one gaining the most institutional traction. The World Economic Forum's *Future of Jobs Report 2025* projects that nearly 40% of the skills required by the global workforce will change within five years. In response, preparing students for that future now means going beyond traditional curricula to include AI-specific capacities such as algorithmic thinking, prompt engineering, and understanding bias in data systems. Governments are beginning to formalize this. Article 4 of the EU AI Act mandates that those deploying AI systems must ensure users — including students and educators — have a sufficient level of AI literacy. The OECD and European Commission have jointly developed an AI Literacy Framework for primary and secondary education, and insights from more than 2,000 individuals helped shape its final version. In the United States, the Department of Education took actions prioritizing AI education in July 2025, releasing guidance on using AI to improve education outcomes. These are not isolated experiments — they signal an emerging consensus that AI literacy belongs alongside reading and arithmetic in the foundational curriculum.

**Prompt literacy** is a narrower but equally significant skill: the ability to communicate effectively with generative AI systems. Prompt literacy enables anyone to communicate with and direct generative AI systems without needing expertise in computer programming. Prompts are commands formulated in natural human language that unlock the capabilities of AI and guide its outputs — and with prompt literacy, people can successfully interact with generative AI to achieve defined objectives while exercising judgment and responsibility. This is not simply a technical trick. Prompt engineering can be viewed as a specialized form of computational communication — a literacy for strategically interacting with AI systems to achieve desired outcomes. Research confirms that the quality of a prompt shapes the quality of the answer: the quality of prompts directly impacts the relevance, accuracy, and creativity of AI-generated output. Crucially, prompt literacy goes beyond just providing initial input; it also involves evaluating the accuracy of results produced by generative AI and continually modifying the prompt until the desired information is obtained. In this sense, prompt literacy is inseparable from critical thinking — it is reasoning made operational.

**Epistemic hygiene** — the discipline of governing one's own belief-formation processes — may be the most urgent and least taught of the new literacies. AI systems impact not only beliefs, but belief revision itself — the reconfiguring of mechanisms by which people adopt, reject, or modify claims to knowledge. The danger is not only individual. As artificial intelligence rapidly evolves, the complexity of navigating an information landscape saturated with synthetic content, misinformation, and disinformation is amplified. Deepfakes, AI-generated texts, and algorithmically curated media increasingly challenge public trust and informed democratic participation. Research on student behavior reveals a troubling tendency: students increasingly see AI tools as trustworthy central sources of learning, a posture that skirts critical reflection on biases or model limits, producing automation bias in which AI results are trusted too much, even when errors are recognized — compromising basic epistemic practices such as evidence assessment, source triangulation, and epistemic modesty.

What unifies these three literacies is that none of them is purely technical, and none can be reduced to simple rule-following. Beyond technical know-how, learners will need the human skills that AI cannot replicate — empathy, judgment, ethical reasoning, and collaboration. Without this support, learners may uncritically accept AI-generated content, adopt habits that compromise academic integrity, or neglect skills like critical thinking and empathetic judgment. The analogy to reading and writing is therefore precise rather than rhetorical: just as a person who can decode letters but cannot evaluate an argument is not truly literate, a person who can use AI tools but cannot interrogate their outputs, probe their assumptions, or trace the origin of a claim is not equipped for the epistemic demands of the current moment. The new literacies are not additions to the curriculum — they are its necessary reformation.
