### Q035 What is the promise and the peril of AI-driven accessibility for learners with disabilities, neurodivergence, or language barriers, from the learner's own perspective? {#q035}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI-Driven Accessibility: Promise and Peril for Learners Who Have Been Left Behind

The most consequential thing AI may do in education is not raise average performance — it is lower the floor. For learners with disabilities, neurodivergent students, and those navigating instruction in a language not their own, the gap between what a system offers and what they can actually access has historically been vast. AI is beginning to close that gap in ways that matter, but it is simultaneously introducing new forms of exclusion that deserve equal scrutiny.

On the side of promise, the evidence is genuine. Generative AI tools can support academic writing, task planning, emotional regulation, and self-management by providing personalised, flexible, and multimodal support. For a student with dyslexia who has spent years watching peers draft fluent prose in the time it takes them to form a paragraph, or for an ADHD student whose executive function collapses under open-ended tasks, these are not marginal conveniences — they can be transformative. Positive outcomes documented in the research literature include improved writing fluency, time management, self-efficacy, and engagement. Meanwhile, AI-supported translation, summarisation, and speech-to-text features are transforming the accessibility of learning materials, particularly for multilingual and neurodiverse learners, enabling real-time adaptation of complex texts into multiple languages or simplified summaries. For a student who speaks Spanish at home and sits through science instruction in English, real-time comprehension support is not a shortcut — it is equity.

Participation in regular classes is now possible for disabled students with the use of AI-based assistive technologies, and such tools can also allow students with disabilities to pursue autonomous learning without depending on the availability of a human interpreter or aide. Extended Reality technologies can enable immersive, adaptable, and practice-oriented learning, while accessibility tools such as speech-to-text have become more accurate in recent years due to advances in AI and cloud computing. The cumulative effect is a set of accommodations that, for the first time, scale.

The peril, however, sits close to the promise. The first risk is bias in the underlying systems. Students with disabilities are particularly at risk of AI bias due to the lack of diverse user input in the training of most models — a notable example being the tendency of AI-generated captions to misinterpret dysarthric speech, creating accessibility barriers in online learning environments. An AI that cannot understand how a person with a motor speech disorder talks is not an accessibility tool; it is another wall. Most studies in the field lack neurodivergent user participation and fail to adequately address sensory and cognitive heterogeneity, accessibility barriers, and gender bias in their datasets — meaning that systems built without the input of those they claim to serve will reliably fail them in ways that remain invisible until deployment.

The second risk is more philosophical but no less real: the erosion of agency. AI can both foster and inadvertently constrain autonomy depending on system transparency and design; if recommendations are overly prescriptive or opaque, learners may follow AI-generated paths rather than initiate or evaluate their own choices, creating dependence rather than genuine self-direction. Experimental evidence reinforces this concern: the vulnerability of students' self-regulation and autonomy in AI-mediated learning is real, with exposure to AI interventions producing significant declines in autonomy in at least one subgroup across multiple experiments. For students who have already been defined by their deficits — who have spent years receiving accommodations framed as exceptions rather than rights — a system that further reduces their sense of authorship over their own learning does quiet, lasting damage.

The third risk is structural. If AI tools live up to their potential for neurodivergent learners, those learners may be more willing to accept privacy or security risks in exchange for the advantages — but if policymakers legislate on the basis of the risk-benefit ratio for the neurotypical population, they could prevent neurodivergent people from accessing tools that are genuinely helpful to them. Regulation calibrated to the majority will always be the wrong fit for those at the margins. Finally, AI technologies in education risk reproducing systemic inequalities by embedding ableist and normative assumptions into their design, marginalising non-normative ways of learning and knowing — precisely the ways of knowing that neurodivergent and differently-abled learners often exemplify.

The honest summary is this: AI-driven accessibility holds more concrete near-term promise for marginalised learners than for any other group, precisely because their baseline access is so constrained. But the same systems, if built without their participation and deployed without nuance, will encode new hierarchies in the language of inclusion. Neurodivergent people having a voice in these discussions is not a courtesy — it is the precondition for any of this working as intended.

### Q036 What does self-directed, lifelong learning look like when everyone has a personal AI mentor? {#q036}

9 citations · 9 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Perpetual Student: Self-Directed Learning in the Age of Personal AI Mentors

For most of human history, access to expert guidance was rationed by proximity, wealth, and institutional affiliation. A person curious about thermodynamics, contract law, or classical Arabic had to find a teacher, enroll in a program, or settle for books. The arrival of a capable AI that can serve as a persistent, personalized intellectual companion changes the structural logic of learning itself — and the change is not merely one of convenience.

The core shift is from scheduled instruction to continuous, demand-driven inquiry. Large language models can serve as interactive mentors that create a learning plan for the adult learner based on their needs and prior knowledge, and suggest sources and further steps toward desired learning goals. This maps surprisingly well onto older theories of adult education: this vision aligns with the andragogical model and principles of adult learning described by Malcolm Knowles, developed long before the rise of computers. What Knowles argued theoretically — that adults learn best when they direct their own inquiry, connect new material to lived experience, and see immediate relevance — an AI mentor can operationalize moment by moment.

The empirical results are beginning to catch up with the promise. The evidence base for AI tutoring shifted significantly in 2025, moving from promising pilots to peer-reviewed proof: a randomized controlled trial published in *Scientific Reports* by Harvard researchers found that students using a purpose-built AI tutor learned significantly more in less time compared to students in traditional in-class active learning, with effect sizes ranging between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. Crucially, for adult learners — who often return to education with diverse experiences and varying skill levels — this level of customization is particularly valuable, as AI systems can identify gaps in knowledge and propose targeted learning activities, supporting more efficient and meaningful learning pathways.

The mechanics work through something close to what developmental psychologists call the zone of proximal development. AI tutors are uniquely positioned to maintain learners in that productive sweet spot: they can instantly detect if a task is too easy or too hard and adjust difficulty in real time. Analytics dashboards that embed metacognitive nudges promote planning, progress monitoring, and effective time management, while large language model planners support goal setting and task strategy development.

Yet the picture is not uncomplicated. A crucial tension has emerged between assistance and autonomy. The mode of assistance delivery matters: user-initiated support tends to preserve autonomy and promote deeper engagement, whereas proactive, unsolicited prompts may introduce automation bias and reduce active reflection. In other words, a learner who is handed answers rather than guided toward them may be accumulating information while eroding the very metacognitive muscles that make lifelong learning durable. Research frequently evaluates AI applications based on immediate outcomes such as test scores or vocabulary retention, while overlooking learners' internal cognitive and affective processes — goal setting, motivation, and reflection — which are essential for long-term autonomy.

The evidence consistently points toward a hybrid model as the most effective arrangement. The human-AI hybrid model is becoming the dominant architecture: research shows that the best outcomes come not from fully autonomous AI tutoring, but from systems where AI handles adaptive instruction while human educators handle motivation, strategy, complex reasoning, and relationship building. Experimental schools have already restructured their days around this division of labor: AI tutors track each learner's mastery and identify gaps before presenting new concepts; by completing core academics in compressed morning sessions, students free up time for collaborative projects, while teachers transition into mentorship roles, leading work designed to develop communication, leadership, and problem-solving abilities.

There is also an equity problem that optimistic accounts tend to understate. The gap between students with access to cutting-edge AI tutors and those without could become a chasm. Research mapping AI's integration across the United States, China, and India has highlighted challenges related to data privacy and infrastructural inequality — meaning the democratizing potential of universal AI mentorship depends entirely on whether access is actually universal. The technology can, in principle, give every curious person the equivalent of a patient and knowledgeable tutor available at any hour. Whether it does so in practice is a question of political will and public investment, not of algorithmic capability.

What lifelong learning looks like in this world, at its best, is a learner who sets genuine goals, interrogates the AI's suggestions rather than merely consuming them, and uses the time saved on rote acquisition for the harder work of synthesis, creation, and judgment. The AI handles the scaffolding; the human provides the direction and the meaning.

### Q037 How do we protect and develop memory, attention, and deep reading in an AI-saturated environment? {#q037}

14 citations · 14 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Memory, Attention, and Deep Reading in an AI-Saturated Environment

The concern is not new in its structure — every powerful information technology, from the printing press to the search engine, has prompted anxiety about what the mind surrenders in exchange for what it gains. What distinguishes the present moment is the speed and intimacy of the trade. Generative AI does not merely retrieve information; it performs cognitive work — composing, reasoning, synthesizing — that was previously the exclusive province of the human mind. The question of what this does to memory, attention, and deep reading has moved from cultural commentary into empirical research, with findings that are sobering but not yet settled.

The Cognitive Offloading Problem

AI tools such as virtual assistants, search engines, and recommendation systems facilitate information retrieval, potentially altering how individuals store and recall knowledge. Sparrow, Liu, and Wegner introduced the concept of the "Google effect," suggesting that the availability of information at one's fingertips reduces the need for internal memory retention. Generative AI intensifies this tendency. AI tools like ChatGPT can create what researchers call "cognitive debt" — a hidden cost to mental abilities when machines are allowed to do the thinking. A 2025 MIT study found that when students used AI to help write essays, their brains were less active and their memory was weaker compared to students who wrote without AI assistance.

The mechanism here is well understood. When answers are instantly available, learners may overestimate their understanding, under-invest in monitoring and encoding, and drift toward transactive memory strategies — the result being short-term fluency but long-term fragility, especially when retrieval practice is bypassed. A separate neuroimaging study reinforces this point: measures of brain connectivity and executive control were worse in a scenario of AI-assisted essay writing than in a brain-only condition, indicating that the neural integration important for learning was diminished.

The relationship, however, is not simply linear. Evidence reveals a complex, non-linear relationship between AI use and cognition — moderate AI usage shows minimal cognitive impact, while excessive reliance correlates with decreased critical thinking abilities, reduced metacognitive accuracy, and lower retention. Notably, younger participants exhibit higher dependence on AI tools and lower critical thinking scores compared to older participants — a finding that carries significant implications for education.

The Deep Reading Crisis

The erosion of deep reading predates generative AI but is substantially worsened by it. Research by literacy neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf suggests that digital reading impairs the deep-reading circuit of the brain, weakening the ability to critically analyze, infer, and synthesize knowledge. Differences in processing depth have been observed between print and digital conditions, with evidence of shallower semantic integration during screen reading unless readers deploy compensatory strategies. When AI tools now offer instant summaries of long texts, the incentive to read at depth diminishes further. Digital platforms have ushered in what neuroscientists describe as "continuous partial attention" — a state of being perennially preoccupied and never fully attentive.

Deep reading activates areas of the brain associated with language, sensory processing, and emotional response; when we read deeply, we are more likely to understand complex concepts and perspectives different from our own. To lose this practice, then, is to lose something beyond literary enjoyment — it is to weaken the neural architecture that underlies empathy, sustained reasoning, and the tolerance for complexity.

What Can Be Done

The prescription that emerges from current research is neither blanket rejection of AI nor uncritical embrace, but deliberate architectural choices about when and how cognitive effort is preserved or surrendered. When AI surfaces definitions and local cues at the moment of need, it trims friction and limits split attention — provided that core generative moves remain with the learner. Benefits peak when help is short, local, and step-bound, then fades to promote independent problem-solving.

On the memory front, the most robust counter-strategy remains retrieval practice — the active recall of information rather than passive re-reading. Retrieval practice, or the active recall of information from memory, is a highly effective learning strategy that strengthens memory and comprehension, an effect robust and strongly backed by research in cognitive psychology. Spaced repetition and retrieval practice, empowered by AI, hold genuine promise for constructing personalized learning systems — here the technology serves consolidation rather than replacing it. When learners revisit content they have forgotten, the brain must work harder to retrieve the information, thereby reinforcing memory; over time, these retrieval events transform short-term memory into lasting understanding.

For deep reading, neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf's framework offers the clearest direction: digital reading may condition the brain to favor quick browsing over deep reading, which is why Wolf argues for the cultivation of "bi-literate brains" that can navigate both digital and print environments. This means intentionally reserving time for long-form print reading, treating it not as nostalgia but as cognitive training. As AI changes the way humans think across reflection, reasoning, and creative production, curriculum models are needed that not only build knowledge but encourage metacognition, problem-solving, and original creation.

The underlying principle threading all of this together is one of deliberate resistance to ease. The brain, like muscle, strengthens through effort and atrophies through disuse. An AI-saturated environment is, structurally, an environment that removes effort at every turn. Preserving memory, attention, and deep reading therefore requires treating friction — the discomfort of recalling, of sustaining focus, of following an argument to its end — not as a problem to be optimized away, but as the mechanism of growth itself.

### Q118 How does always-available tutoring change help-seeking behaviour and peer learning? {#q118}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Always-available AI tutoring changes help-seeking behaviour in two opposing directions at once: it lowers the social and logistical costs of asking for help, while simultaneously creating new forms of maladaptive help-seeking that decades of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) research have documented in detail. The net effect on peer learning is similarly double-edged — AI can free classroom time for collaboration and even orchestrate peer expertise exchange, but it can also displace the interpersonal friction through which collaborative skill is actually built.

Help-seeking before AI: the ITS evidence base. The most rigorous evidence on help-seeking in computer-based tutoring comes from the intelligent tutoring systems literature, which studied on-demand hints long before generative AI. Aleven and colleagues' foundational work on the Geometry Cognitive Tutor showed that students frequently engage in 'hint abuse' — clicking through hint levels in under a second to reach the bottom-out hint that gives the answer — or, conversely, in 'help avoidance', persisting in errors rather than requesting assistance. These patterns are not marginal: help-seeking behaviour accounted for as much variance in learning gains as students' raw error rates. The field's response was the 'Help Tutor', a metacognitive agent that gave real-time feedback on the quality of students' help-seeking itself. Classroom studies found that this feedback produced lasting improvements in help-seeking strategy — students became more deliberate hint users even after the agent was switched off — although it did not always translate into statistically significant domain-learning gains, a finding researchers attribute to the cognitive load of simultaneous metacognitive and domain feedback. The durable lesson is that the mere availability of help does not produce good help-seeking; the quality of the help-seeking behaviour must itself be scaffolded.

What always-available AI changes. Generative AI tutoring changes the economics of help-seeking in ways the ITS literature could not fully anticipate. First, it removes the social cost: students can ask 'stupid' questions of a non-judgemental system without fear of peer ridicule or teacher disappointment, which NORC's research on AI-enhanced high-dose tutoring identifies as a key mechanism for engaging students who would otherwise conceal confusion. Second, it removes the temporal cost: help is available at 2 a.m., during homework, and at the exact moment of need, which is precisely the design logic of the 'flipped' model in which AI handles routine practice outside class while teachers use class time for higher-value interaction. Third, it changes the perceived authority of the help source. A striking recent experiment found that simply warning students that a pedagogical agent might make mistakes significantly increased their rate of hint requests — students treated a fallible tutor as something to verify rather than absorb, engaging in more cautious, metacognitive interaction. This suggests that the perceived infallibility of AI tutors may suppress the very verification behaviour that good help-seeking requires.

The risk of over-reliance and help avoidance in reverse. The same affordances that lower help-seeking barriers create a mirror-image risk: help becomes so cheap that students skip the productive struggle that precedes a good help request. Research on generative AI in tutoring warns that systems which simply provide answers, without Socratic scaffolding or step-by-step guidance, encourage students to outsource problem-solving entirely. The Brookings synthesis of the tutoring evidence concludes that the pedagogical design of the AI — whether it prompts, questions, and withholds answers — matters more than the raw capability of the model. In effect, always-available tutoring can convert help-seeking from a strategic, effortful act into a reflexive one, and the ITS literature's finding that unregulated hint use undermines learning applies with even greater force to a tutor that can generate unlimited, bespoke answers.

Effects on peer learning. The evidence on peer learning is more encouraging but conditional. Multi-agent tutoring configurations — in which students interact with several AI agents playing different roles, or with AI mediating interaction between human classmates — have been shown to produce learning benefits that dyadic one-on-one tutoring does not. When multiple agents offer divergent perspectives or make different types of errors, students must reconcile conflicting information, which deepens critical thinking. In writing tasks, single-LLM assistance produces 'idea-level homogeneity' — students converge on similar content — whereas role-specialised multi-agent setups restore ideational diversity while maintaining quality. Some systems now support an 'expertise exchange' model in which the AI identifies students with complementary strengths and prompts them to teach one another, formalising peer tutoring at scale. These findings suggest AI is not inherently corrosive of peer learning; it depends on whether the system is designed to route students toward one another or to absorb interaction itself.

The displacement risk. The countervailing evidence is that AI can quietly erode the social core of student teamwork. When AI becomes the default intermediary in group work — summarising contributions, translating ideas into prose, smoothing over disagreements — the collaborative process becomes more efficient but less developmental. The interpersonal friction of negotiating meaning, managing disagreement, and justifying positions is precisely what builds collaborative skill, and it is bypassed when a machine mediates. The emerging design consensus is therefore that AI should handle the routine and the individual, while teachers deliberately protect and structure the collaborative and the interpersonal. The practical implication for schools is that always-available tutoring is best understood not as a replacement for the help-seeking and peer-learning ecosystem but as a new element within it — one that requires explicit pedagogical management of when students should ask the machine, when they should ask a peer, and when they should struggle alone.

### Q120 What does AI assistance do to students' self-assessment accuracy and metacognition? {#q120}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The evidence on AI assistance and metacognition points to a central paradox: AI can either sharpen or corrode students' self-assessment accuracy depending almost entirely on how the system is designed and how the student is positioned within it. The same technology that can scaffold calibrated self-judgement through structured reflection can also produce what researchers now call 'algorithmic self-deception' — inflated confidence born of agreeable, vague, or uniformly positive machine feedback.

The calibration problem and algorithmic self-deception. Self-assessment accuracy is conventionally measured as calibration: the gap between a student's perceived and actual performance. A growing body of research documents that generative AI feedback, left to its own devices, widens this gap. The mechanism is a combination of automation bias — the human tendency to uncritically trust machine outputs — and the stylistic properties of large language models, which tend toward agreeable, encouraging, and non-committal feedback. Studies of 'algorithmic self-deception' show students developing inflated perceptions of their competence when AI feedback is vague or uniformly positive, precisely because nothing in the interaction forces them to confront the difference between what they think they know and what they can actually produce. This is not a minor effect: calibration errors of this kind predict subsequent study choices, so students who are over-calibrated by AI feedback allocate their effort poorly and are less likely to seek the help they genuinely need.

When AI improves metacognition: the scaffolding evidence. The same literature shows that AI assistance can substantially improve metacognition when the system is designed to demand cognitive work from the student. In large-scale undergraduate settings, practice-exam systems that required students to provide confidence ratings and written explanations before receiving AI feedback transformed routine practice into a metacognitive exercise: students engaged more deeply with course material and transferred the self-assessment strategies to real examinations. Randomised evidence on self-regulated learning in generative AI environments found that students given an explicit metacognitive support framework — prompting goal-setting, monitoring, and evaluation — showed significant improvements in task strategy use and self-evaluation relative to controls, while students without such scaffolding experienced declines in self-regulation. The pattern across studies is consistent: metacognitive benefit is not a property of the AI but of the interaction design. AI that asks, prompts, and withholds produces better self-assessors; AI that answers, praises, and moves on produces worse ones.

The 'Cognitive Mirror' paradigm. A prominent design response to these findings is the proposal to reposition AI from an 'omniscient oracle' to a 'teachable novice'. In this paradigm, the AI is engineered to reflect the quality of the learner's explanation back at them — feigning confusion when an explanation is weak, asking clarifying questions, and modulating its responses according to a Teaching Quality Index derived from the learner's own output. The mechanism is the protégé effect: explaining a concept to a novice forces the explainer to structure their thought, expose misconceptions, and notice gaps in their own understanding. Because the AI's confusion is calibrated to the quality of the student's explanation, the system functions as an externalised mirror of the student's metacognitive state — making invisible misconceptions visible and repairable. Early evidence suggests this approach sustains engagement and improves conceptual understanding relative to answer-giving configurations, though the paradigm remains at the proof-of-concept stage rather than the scale-evidence stage.

AI versus human feedback: different regulatory pathways. Comparative studies of AI and human feedback complicate the simple story that human feedback is better. The emerging finding is that AI and human feedback support different regulatory processes rather than different levels of quality. AI feedback tends to be more actionable and more polite, and it correlates with content integration and quality judgement; human feedback is often more direct and more effective at driving students back to the source material. The implication is that the two feedback channels are complementary — AI for iterative refinement and immediate correction, humans for challenge, redirection, and the kind of directness that disrupts complacency. Notably, research on AI-mediated language learning found that the timing of AI feedback (immediate versus delayed) had little direct effect on the accuracy of metacognitive judgements, but that emotional valence and cognitive load were significant mediators — a reminder that the affective experience of receiving machine feedback shapes how students use it to judge themselves.

Practical implications for schools. Three conclusions follow for educators. First, self-assessment accuracy under AI is a design outcome, not a technology outcome: schools should prefer systems that require students to predict, explain, and reflect before receiving feedback, and should be suspicious of systems optimised purely for helpfulness. Second, metacognitive scaffolding should be embedded in AI use rather than bolted on — the evidence shows that unstructured AI interaction degrades self-regulation, while structured interaction improves it. Third, calibration should be measured, not assumed: schools adopting AI tools should track whether students' self-assessments become more or less accurate over time, since the most dangerous failure mode — confident ignorance — is invisible in aggregate grades. The weight of the evidence is that AI assistance is metacognitively neutral in itself; it amplifies whatever interaction structure surrounds it.

### Q121 How is AI reshaping collaboration, peer help, and cheating norms within student cultures? {#q121}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is reshaping student culture along two distinct axes: it is changing how students collaborate and help one another, and it is changing what students themselves regard as cheating. The two processes are connected, because both turn on a single question that student communities are actively renegotiating: where is the line between legitimate machine assistance and illegitimate delegation?

The perception–prevalence gap in cheating. Survey evidence reveals a striking disconnect between what educators and students believe about AI-driven cheating and what behavioural data show. A 2024 survey of more than 4,300 high school students found that overall self-reported cheating rates — around 72 per cent — were essentially unchanged from historical baselines established before ChatGPT. Analyses of multi-school data similarly found no significant spike in self-reported cheating following the arrival of generative AI. In higher education, however, perceptions are markedly more pessimistic: a 2024 Wiley survey of over 2,000 students and 850 instructors found that 68 per cent of faculty believed generative AI would negatively affect academic integrity over the following three years, and 53 per cent of students said more cheating was occurring than the year before, with 35 per cent naming ChatGPT as a contributing factor. The gap between perception and measured behaviour matters for policy: institutions that legislate against a cheating epidemic that the behavioural data do not show risk alienating students whose actual AI use is more modest and more defensible than faculty assume.

How students draw the line. Student norms around AI use are more differentiated than institutional policies often acknowledge. Across surveys, students consistently distinguish 'productive use' — brainstorming, generating ideas, explaining difficult concepts, checking understanding — from 'cheating', which they define as using AI to complete entire assignments or write full papers. There is broad consensus among students that whole-task delegation is unacceptable; the contested territory is everything in between. At the same time, a substantial minority of students (37 per cent in the Wiley survey) reported avoiding AI tools entirely because they feared instructors would interpret legitimate use as cheating — evidence that ambiguous norms impose a chilling effect on honest students. The definition of cheating is thus fluid and locally negotiated, and it varies by discipline, by assignment type, and by the perceived relevance of the task. Researchers describe this as a period of 'normative flux' in which student cultures are developing their own working distinctions faster than institutions are codifying theirs.

AI as a collaborator: the transformation of group work. Within student cultures, AI is increasingly treated not as a tool but as a teammate. In group work, students use AI to summarise peer contributions, clarify concepts, translate ideas into coherent prose, and mediate disagreements. This produces real efficiency gains and can improve inclusivity by giving less confident students a non-judgemental interlocutor. But it also risks bypassing the interpersonal friction — negotiating meaning, managing disagreement, justifying positions — through which collaborative skill is actually developed. When AI becomes the default intermediary, group work becomes more efficient and less developmental, and the traditional rationale for group assessment — that it proxies real-world collaborative competence — is quietly undermined. The design response emerging from the literature is to shift assessment from final outputs toward the visibility and quality of the collaborative process itself, making the interpersonal work legible to assessors.

From detection to integrity ecosystems. Institutional responses are themselves reshaping the norms they aim to govern. The early phase of AI policy — banning tools and deploying detection software — is giving way to what researchers call 'integrity ecosystems': systemic frameworks that treat academic integrity as an emergent property of governance, assessment design, institutional culture, and individual moral agency rather than as a property of individual student behaviour. This shift is driven partly by evidence that AI detection software is unreliable, produces false positives, and disproportionately flags non-native English speakers, and partly by a recognition that punitive, output-focused policies ignore the reality of technology-mediated knowledge production. The emerging toolkit includes assignment-specific 'AI use scales' that define acceptable levels of machine assistance, process-based assessment that requires students to document their work, and developmental integrity education that treats honesty as a learned value rather than a rule to be policed. The World Economic Forum's guidance on responsible AI in higher education similarly emphasises building skills, trust, and integrity through transparent policy and shared stewardship rather than surveillance.

Root causes and the direction of travel. Research on why students cheat suggests that dishonesty is often a coping mechanism for structural pressures — high-stakes testing, heavy workloads, and assignments perceived as irrelevant — and that AI has not changed these drivers. The most durable effect of AI on student culture may therefore be indirect: by forcing institutions to redesign assessment, AI is pushing schools toward tasks that are harder to automate, more process-visible, and more personally meaningful — precisely the conditions under which cheating loses its appeal. The emerging student norm, on the evidence, is not 'cheating is fine' but 'using AI is normal, and the line between assistance and delegation should be explicit and fair'. Schools that engage that norm openly — through transparent policy, honest dialogue, and assessment redesign — are likely to find that AI reshapes collaboration more than it inflates cheating.

### Q233 What are the specific opportunities and risks of AI-powered personalisation for gifted and high-ability learners? {#q233}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

AI-Powered Personalisation for Gifted and High-Ability Learners: Opportunities and Risks

Gifted and high-ability learners represent a population whose educational needs are frequently underserved by standard curricula and instructional approaches. AI-powered personalisation offers significant opportunities to address these needs — through acceleration, enrichment, and the provision of intellectually challenging content calibrated to individual ability levels — but also introduces distinctive risks related to identification bias, over-reliance on AI challenge, and the potential narrowing of gifted education to measurable cognitive performance.

Opportunities: Acceleration and Enrichment

AI adaptive learning systems can identify when a student has mastered content at a given level and automatically advance them to more challenging material, enabling a form of continuous acceleration that is difficult to achieve in traditional classroom settings. For gifted learners who are frequently bored or disengaged by grade-level content, this capability is potentially transformative. Research on AI-driven acceleration in mathematics and science demonstrates significant gains in both achievement and engagement for high-ability students, with some studies reporting that gifted students using AI adaptive systems progress through two to three years of curriculum content in a single academic year.

Beyond acceleration, AI systems can provide enrichment — exposure to content that extends beyond the standard curriculum in depth, breadth, or complexity — that is tailored to individual interests and learning styles. Large language models, in particular, can serve as intellectual sparring partners for gifted learners, engaging in Socratic dialogue, generating challenging problems, and providing expert-level explanations of complex topics. This capability is particularly valuable for gifted learners in under-resourced schools who lack access to specialist teachers or advanced coursework.

Opportunities: Identification and Early Intervention

AI systems can analyse patterns in student performance data to identify gifted learners who might otherwise be overlooked by traditional identification methods. Traditional gifted identification relies heavily on standardised tests and teacher nomination, both of which are subject to significant bias — particularly against students from low-income families, racial and ethnic minorities, and English language learners. AI-based identification systems that analyse a broader range of performance indicators — including response patterns, problem-solving strategies, and creative outputs — may be more equitable than traditional methods, though this remains an active area of research.

Risks: Identification Bias and Algorithmic Amplification

AI identification systems trained on historical data may amplify existing biases in gifted identification rather than correcting them. If the training data reflects historical patterns of under-identification of certain groups, the AI system will learn to replicate those patterns. Moreover, AI systems that define giftedness in terms of performance on measurable cognitive tasks may systematically overlook forms of giftedness — creative, social, emotional, leadership — that are less amenable to quantification.

Risks: Over-Reliance and Intellectual Dependency

There is a risk that gifted learners who rely heavily on AI for intellectual challenge may develop a form of intellectual dependency — becoming accustomed to AI-generated problems and explanations rather than developing the capacity for independent intellectual inquiry. This risk is particularly acute for gifted learners, whose defining characteristic is often their capacity for deep, self-directed intellectual engagement. If AI systems provide challenge in a way that is too structured or too responsive to student preferences, they may inadvertently undermine the development of intellectual resilience and tolerance for ambiguity.

Risks: Narrowing of Gifted Education

AI-powered personalisation tends to optimise for measurable outcomes — test scores, curriculum progression rates, problem-solving accuracy — which may narrow gifted education toward cognitive performance at the expense of social-emotional development, creative expression, and the cultivation of intellectual character. Gifted education research consistently emphasises the importance of addressing the social-emotional needs of gifted learners, including perfectionism, asynchronous development, and existential concerns, which are not well-served by AI adaptive systems focused on academic acceleration.

### Q261 What evidence, if any, links a student's AI usage patterns in early adolescence to their academic independence, metacognition, and critical thinking in later years? {#q261}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Early adolescence, roughly ages ten to fourteen, is a period of rapid development in executive function, self-regulation, and abstract reasoning. It is also the period when many students begin to use AI tools independently for schoolwork. A natural concern is that patterns of AI use established during these years might shape students' later academic independence, metacognitive skills, and capacity for critical thinking. The honest answer to what evidence links the two is that direct longitudinal evidence does not yet exist. Generative AI has been widely available only since late 2022, so no cohort has yet been followed from early adolescence into later schooling. What exists instead is a set of cross-sectional, experimental, and theoretical findings that suggest plausible pathways.

Usage data establish the relevance of the question. The Pew Research Center's February 2026 report on teens found that 54 percent of U.S. teens aged 13 to 17 had used AI chatbots for schoolwork and that about one in ten used them for all or most of their schoolwork. Use among younger adolescents is less well measured, but many encounter AI through school platforms, search engines, and messaging apps.

The most frequently cited correlational evidence comes from Gerlich's 2025 study in the journal Societies, which surveyed and interviewed 666 participants across age groups. It found a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool use and critical-thinking scores, mediated by cognitive offloading, the practice of delegating mental tasks to external tools. Younger participants, aged 17 to 25, showed higher dependence on AI and lower critical-thinking scores than older participants. Because the design was cross-sectional, it cannot determine whether AI use reduces critical thinking, whether people with weaker critical-thinking skills rely more on AI, or whether other factors explain both. The sample also did not include early adolescents.

Lee and colleagues at Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University, in a survey of 319 knowledge workers presented at CHI 2025 and covering 936 examples of AI use, found that higher confidence in AI was associated with less reported critical thinking, while higher self-confidence was associated with more. Although conducted with adults, the finding suggests that the disposition with which users approach AI matters, a disposition that may be shaped early.

Experimental studies provide stronger causal evidence about short-term effects. Fan and colleagues, in a 2024 study in the British Journal of Educational Technology with 117 university students, found that ChatGPT support improved essay scores but not knowledge gain or transfer, and that students engaged less in metacognitive activities such as monitoring and evaluating their work, which the authors called metacognitive laziness. The randomised trial by Bastani and colleagues in PNAS, involving high-school students in Turkey, found that unrestricted GPT-4 access improved practice performance but was associated with lower performance on subsequent unassisted exams, while a guardrailed tutor largely mitigated this harm. These findings suggest that the way AI is used, rather than use as such, influences whether students develop independent capabilities.

Developmental considerations suggest that early adolescents may be particularly sensitive to these effects. Executive functions and metacognitive skills are still maturing, and habits formed during this period may persist. The American Psychological Association's 2025 health advisory on AI and adolescent well-being noted that adolescents' developing brains may make them more susceptible to the influence of AI systems, and urged designs and practices that protect healthy development. If young adolescents routinely offload planning, monitoring, and evaluation to AI, they may have fewer opportunities to practise these skills during a formative period.

Plausible pathways also run in positive directions. AI tools designed to prompt reflection, ask questions, and provide hints rather than answers could support metacognitive development by modelling self-questioning. Students taught to evaluate AI outputs critically may strengthen rather than weaken their critical thinking. Whether early AI use helps or harms long-term independence may depend on the guidance and structure surrounding it.

The concepts at stake in this question have a long research history that predates AI and that shapes how any future evidence should be interpreted. John Flavell, in a 1979 article in American Psychologist, introduced metacognition as a field of developmental inquiry, describing it as knowledge about one's own cognition together with the monitoring and regulation of cognitive activity, and he argued that children's metacognitive abilities develop gradually and remain limited well into the school years. Subsequent research on self-regulated learning extended this idea, framing academic independence as a recurring cycle of planning, monitoring and reflection that students acquire through practice, feedback and gradually withdrawn support from teachers. In this tradition, independence is not a fixed trait but a set of learned habits, and the conditions under which students practise those habits matter for whether they become durable. Correlational studies in this tradition have generally linked stronger self-regulation to higher achievement, although they leave open how much of the relationship reflects other influences such as prior knowledge, motivation and family support. Any account of how AI might affect later independence therefore has to explain how it alters the opportunities students have to plan, monitor and evaluate their own work during the years when those capacities are consolidating.

The broader literature on cognitive offloading provides a framework that is more general than AI and offers some reassurance as well as caution. Evan Risko and Sam Gilbert, in a 2016 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, defined cognitive offloading as the use of physical action or external tools to reduce the cognitive demands of a task, and noted that offloading is pervasive, from writing shopping lists to using calculators, and is often adaptive because it frees limited internal resources for other purposes. They also noted that offloading can reduce memory for offloaded information and that people's decisions about when to offload are influenced by metacognitive beliefs about their own abilities, which can be inaccurate. This framing suggests that the relevant question is not whether adolescents offload thinking to AI, since all learners offload to some degree, but which processes are offloaded, whether the offloading is chosen deliberately, and whether students retain the capacity to perform the task without assistance when needed. Offloading arithmetic to a calculator after fluency has been established differs from offloading the planning and evaluation of an argument before those skills have developed.

Earlier research on digital technology illustrates how easily headline findings in this area can outrun the evidence. During the 2010s, public debate about smartphones and social media often asserted large harms to adolescents on the basis of modest correlations. Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski, in a 2019 analysis in Nature Human Behaviour using specification curve analysis on three large datasets covering more than 350,000 adolescents, found that the association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being was negative but very small, accounting for at most 0.4 percent of the variation in well-being, comparable to the associations of everyday activities such as eating potatoes. This episode suggests caution towards early claims about AI and cognition, whether alarming or reassuring, and they highlight the value of preregistration, replication and transparent analytic choices in the research that is now beginning.

Newer neuroscientific work on AI-assisted writing has attracted attention but remains preliminary. Nataliya Kosmyna and colleagues at the MIT Media Lab, in a 2025 preprint posted to arXiv, used electroencephalography to compare 54 adult participants writing essays with a large language model, with a search engine, or without tools, and reported that the group using the language model showed weaker measures of neural connectivity and lower ability to quote from their own essays. The study had not been peer reviewed at the time of posting, involved a small sample of university-affiliated adults, measured effects over a few sessions, and its neural measures do not map straightforwardly onto educational outcomes. It is therefore best treated as a hypothesis-generating signal rather than evidence about how adolescents' long-term metacognition develops. Its value for the present question lies mainly in illustrating measures that future longitudinal studies with younger participants might incorporate, alongside behavioural assessments of independent performance.

Developmental science explains why the early adolescent years may be a period of particular sensitivity, although it does not establish that AI effects will be lasting. Laurence Steinberg, in a 2005 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, described adolescence as a period in which basic reasoning abilities approach adult levels by mid-adolescence while executive functions such as planning, response inhibition and the coordination of thought and emotion continue to mature, with brain regions supporting these functions developing over a longer timeframe. This uneven development suggests that adolescents may be capable of using sophisticated tools before they have fully developed the self-regulatory capacities that would help them decide when not to use them. It also suggests a window in which instruction that explicitly teaches planning, monitoring and evaluation could be especially valuable. Whether patterns of tool use established at twelve persist to sixteen, however, is an empirical question, and research on other habits indicates that adolescent behaviour is often malleable as contexts, peers and expectations change.

Existing longitudinal infrastructure suggests how the evidence gap might be closed. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, whose design Nora Volkow and colleagues described in 2018 in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience, enrolled roughly 11,800 children aged nine and ten across 21 U.S. sites with the aim of following them for about a decade with repeated neuroimaging, cognitive testing and measures of screen media use. Because the cohort was entering early adolescence as generative AI became widely available, studies of this kind could in principle add measures of AI use and relate them to later cognitive and academic outcomes while controlling for earlier measurements of the same capacities. Such designs would still be observational and could not establish causation on their own, but repeated measures allow researchers to examine whether changes in AI use precede changes in metacognition or follow them, which cross-sectional surveys cannot. Complementary randomised trials, in which schools are assigned different configurations of AI support over a full school year or longer, would provide stronger causal evidence about medium-term effects.

Equity and implementation considerations bear on how a precautionary approach should be applied in the meantime. Adolescents whose families and schools can provide structured guidance, such as teachers who design tasks requiring independent drafts before AI assistance or parents who discuss how tools are used, may develop more deliberate habits than those who encounter AI mainly through unsupervised consumer apps. If unstructured use is concentrated among students with fewer supports, any adverse associations could compound existing gaps in achievement. At the same time, restrictive policies that deny some students access while peers elsewhere learn to use AI skilfully could create a different disadvantage. A balanced implementation would introduce AI in early adolescence alongside explicit instruction in metacognitive strategies, preserve regular opportunities for unassisted work, configure school tools to prompt reflection rather than supply finished answers, and collect data on how students use these tools so that schools can contribute to the evidence the field currently lacks.

Measurement is a further obstacle that any future study will have to address. Self-reported AI use is vulnerable to recall error and social desirability, particularly among adolescents who know that some uses are prohibited at school, and simple frequency measures do not distinguish between asking a chatbot to explain a concept, to check a finished draft, or to write an assignment outright. Metacognition is similarly difficult to measure, since questionnaires capture what students believe about their own thinking, while think-aloud protocols and log data capture what they actually do but are costly to collect at scale. Studies that combine logged interaction data from school-provided tools with performance on unassisted tasks would offer more informative evidence than surveys alone, provided that data collection respects students' privacy and is governed by clear consent arrangements involving families.

The research gap is clear. Answering the question would require longitudinal studies that measure AI usage patterns in early adolescence with objective data, track metacognition and critical thinking with validated instruments over several years, and account for confounding factors such as prior achievement, socio-economic status, and school context. Until such studies are available, claims that early AI use causes later deficits or benefits should be treated as hypotheses. The existing evidence nonetheless supports a precautionary approach: structuring young adolescents' AI use to preserve opportunities for independent effort and to teach critical evaluation from the start.

## Chapter 5: Institutions and Systems {#chapter-05}

11 questions · 106 citations · 101 unique sources · 55 cross-references

### Q038 Is the industrial-era school model (grades, classrooms, standardized curricula) still viable, and what replaces it? {#q038}

11 citations · 11 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Industrial School Model and Its Discontents

The architecture of modern schooling — fixed grade levels sorted by age, forty-five-minute periods punctuated by bells, a uniform curriculum delivered to everyone simultaneously — was not designed with learning as its primary goal. For decades, the structure of high school education has remained largely unchanged, rooted in a model that mirrors the industrial factory system, with its 45-minute class periods, ringing bells, and standardized curricula tracing back to an era when schools were designed to prepare students for factory work. The critical question of the present moment is whether that architecture has simply aged, or whether it has become actively counterproductive.

Before accepting the critique wholesale, one important caveat deserves attention. The terms "factory model school" and "industrial era school" are, according to educational historians, ahistorical phrases that emerged in the mid-to-late twentieth century and function largely as rhetorical devices by those advocating change — descriptions that historians characterize as misleading and inaccurate representations of how American public education actually developed. The critique, in other words, contains a mythological element: the industrial school was never quite as mechanically uniform as its detractors imply, and invoking the factory metaphor can obscure more than it reveals.

That said, the structural tensions are real. Nearly all major reform efforts of the past several decades left the basic tenets of the industrial-paradigm classroom intact — an approach where groups of same-aged students all learn the same thing at the same time, advanced more than a century ago as a means to rank and sort students into different life pathways. The system's central flaw is its indifference to where any individual student actually stands. It is unforgiving to those who fall behind: what is taught is based on age, not on what a student knows, so that stumbling for any reason — a pandemic, a family crisis — can make it genuinely difficult to catch back up, especially in cumulative subjects like mathematics.

Employers increasingly report that graduates lack critical thinking, problem-solving, and digital literacy skills, and that the industrial-age model's focus on standardized testing and memorization leaves students ill-equipped for innovation. Meanwhile, critics of standardized curricula highlight an overemphasis on assessment leading to narrowed instruction, insufficient flexibility for diverse learners, and rising achievement gaps.

The most serious contender to replace the age-grade-curriculum triad is competency-based education (CBE), which reorients schooling around demonstrated mastery rather than time served. CBE focuses on skill mastery rather than seat time or letter grades, allowing students to progress at their own pace and demonstrate real understanding. The logic is intuitive: traditional education has students spend a set amount of time on a subject, take an exam, and move on whether or not they have truly mastered the material, while competency-based learning flips this by asking whether a student can actually demonstrate mastery of specific skills and knowledge. The growth in adoption is measurable: as of 2025, over 1,500 institutions in the United States have adopted approximately 2,400 undergraduate and 750 graduate competency-based education programs.

Alongside CBE, personalized learning — powered increasingly by artificial intelligence — is moving from experimental to mainstream. Personalized learning is shifting from theory to standard practice, with schools moving toward teaching methods that focus on each student's pace, interests, and goals, using digital tools to track progress and make rapid adjustments — an approach that, when it works well, helps close learning gaps and keeps students more engaged. Adaptive learning systems can adjust content delivery in real time based on learner performance, while AI-based systems help educators identify gaps and align content with existing standards.

Yet a note of realism is warranted. The only change processes ever used in public education to significantly alter practice reflect industrial-age thinking and methodologies — and there is a deep irony in trying to end the era of factory-model schools by using factory-model strategies for change. Many educators also report limited training in how to manage personalized instruction at scale — a bottleneck that no technology resolves on its own. What is emerging, then, is less a clean replacement than a prolonged and contested transition: the shell of the old model persists in most public institutions while its logic is eroded, incrementally and unevenly, by competency frameworks, adaptive tools, and a growing recognition that sorting children by birth year was always a convenience, not a pedagogy.

### Q039 How should curricula be redesigned when factual content is instantly accessible and rapidly obsolete? {#q039}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Curriculum in the Age of Instant Knowledge

The central paradox confronting educators today is one of abundance: the very tool that renders a fact instantly retrievable also makes the memorization of that fact seem pedagogically pointless. Students can now access instant factual answers through AI platforms, making traditional rote-recall exams increasingly ineffective and outdated. Yet the conclusion that content no longer matters would be as mistaken as the assumption that it matters in exactly the way it once did. The real challenge is finer-grained: to distinguish which kinds of knowledge are genuinely outsourceable to machines, and which must remain deeply internalized by human minds.

One useful map for this distinction comes from cognitive science. Declarative knowledge — the memorization of facts and data — is considered the simplest level, while procedural knowledge involves the automated understanding of *how* to use problem-solving strategies, and conditional knowledge, the highest level, requires understanding *how*, *when*, and *why* to use each strategy. AI systems, as currently constituted, are remarkably good at the first level and serviceable at the second. The third — knowing when a tool or argument is appropriate to a given situation — remains stubbornly human. Curriculum redesign, on this view, should shift weight steadily upward through these levels, treating the declarative layer not as the destination but as the scaffolding through which deeper understanding is constructed.

This does not mean abandoning content altogether. The question "if AI knows everything, why learn anything?" is a dead-wrong framing — AI neither "knows" everything nor is capable of acting on its own. A student who has never grappled with the internal logic of evolutionary biology, the structure of a legal argument, or the arithmetic of compound interest cannot meaningfully direct, evaluate, or contest an AI-generated answer on those subjects. Conceptual and epistemic knowledge — understanding *why* a field is structured as it is, and how its claims are validated — may actually become *more* valuable as AI handles more of the retrieval work. Knowledge should be assessed for relevance, developing the right mix between declarative, procedural, conceptual, and epistemic layers, and modernizing traditional disciplines accordingly.

The institutional implications of this shift are substantial. Assessment is the most immediate battleground. With 40% of surveyed UK students agreeing that AI-generated content could achieve a good grade in their subject, faculty are increasingly concerned about academic rigor — and rather than engaging in a reactive "AI-detection arms race," educators are advised to proactively redesign assessment strategies. At the national policy level, governments are beginning to act: the UK's 2025 curriculum reforms include making media literacy and financial literacy compulsory in primary school, and replacing the narrowly focused computer science GCSE with a broader, future-facing computing qualification, alongside exploring a new credential in data science and AI for sixteen-to-eighteen-year-olds.

A related and underappreciated danger is what researchers call automation bias. Students increasingly treat AI outputs as the central, trustworthy source of learning, skipping critical reflection on the model's limits — a tendency that compromises ground-level epistemic practices such as evidence assessment, source triangulation, and epistemic modesty. A curriculum redesigned for this environment must therefore treat epistemics — knowing *how* one knows, and how to evaluate competing claims — as a core subject rather than an implicit byproduct of other learning.

Perhaps the deepest reorientation concerns the temporal dimension of knowledge itself. The first quarter of the twenty-first century has been defined by shocks and long-run transformations that have reshaped economic and social systems, with changes rapid enough to leave individuals, firms, and governments less time to adapt. As skill demands evolve faster than policy cycles, investing in lifelong learning and using timely labour-market intelligence are crucial to help people adapt. This implies that curricula should be designed less around a fixed canon of content and more around the meta-cognitive capacity to keep learning — what the Center for Curriculum Redesign calls adaptability, arguing that adaptability is more essential than ever given AI, and that schools must actively teach it.

The risk in all of this, however, is a false binary that discards disciplinary knowledge in favor of vague "twenty-first-century skills." Reform efforts have largely failed because they focus on fixing past problems with uniform solutions; applying new technologies within outdated paradigms is equally ineffective. What is needed is neither the old cathedral of facts nor a content-free skills gymnasium, but a redesigned architecture in which durable conceptual knowledge, practiced judgment, epistemic self-awareness, and genuine adaptability are woven together — with the specific factual content serving as the material through which those capacities are built, not the end in itself.

### Q040 What is the future of universities, credentials, and degrees when skills can be learned and demonstrated outside institutions? {#q040}

13 citations · 13 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Credential in Question

The institution of the university degree is not collapsing, but it is no longer uncontested. For most of the twentieth century, a bachelor's degree served as a reliable proxy for capability, discipline, and general readiness for professional life. That arrangement is under genuine pressure — not because universities have grown less rigorous, but because the labour market is changing faster than four-year curricula can follow. The labour market now changes faster than curricula. A degree takes four to five years to complete, but technology and required skills change every six to twelve months. The result is a structural mismatch that no amount of curriculum review can fully close.

The Rise of the Alternative

Into this gap has rushed a proliferating array of shorter-form credentials. Out of the 1.8 million credentials now offered across the United States, digital badges and certificates dominate — with digital badges alone numbering over one million, according to a recent report from Credential Engine. Degrees, by comparison, made up a smaller fraction of the credentials tallied: 264,099 programmes. The microcredential market itself is not trivial in economic terms; the global microcredential market is projected to exceed USD 3.5 billion in 2025, with an annual growth rate above 17 percent through 2030, with strong presence in technology, healthcare, education, and sustainability sectors.

The appeal is straightforward. Microcredentials have advantages over standard degrees in cost, duration, and structure: they are shorter in duration, more focused in terms of skills and subject matter, and more adaptable in curriculum and delivery than a conventional degree programme. There is "growing appetite, more demand from learners for more efficient and direct routes to employment opportunities," as one analyst at Jobs for the Future has put it. In the most recent enrollment data, students pursuing short-term credentials increased 6.6 percent in a single year, outpacing growth in associate and bachelor's degree programmes.

The Gap Between Policy and Practice

Yet the most revealing data concerns not the supply of alternatives, but what employers actually do when confronted with them. Here the evidence is striking and sobering. While 85 percent of companies claim to use skills-based hiring, only 0.14 percent of hires are actually impacted by degree requirement removal. At least 26 states and major private companies including IBM and Accenture have stripped degree requirements from job listings, with seven states showing double-digit percentage increases in postings without degree requirements between 2019 and 2024. But less evidence has emerged of employers actually hiring non-degreed job seekers in substantial numbers: Burning Glass and Harvard Business School found that fewer than 1 in 700 hires in 2023 benefited from the shift to skills-based hiring.

The explanation is cultural as much as structural. The people in charge of hiring are typically senior managers accustomed to college-related data — school attended, courses taken, grades earned, degree attained — and without those reference points, they need an entirely new template for assessing candidates. Cultural biases will not simply evaporate because a CEO issues a press release. There is also a regulatory obstacle: many of the same states that have eliminated degree requirements still regulate non-degree training providers as if they were traditional college institutions, forcing them through a labyrinth of licensing rules and reporting mandates never designed for their models.

Unbundling, Not Replacement

The most durable forecast from those studying the field is not disruption but transformation through what might be called unbundling. The future of higher education will likely not be about replacing degrees, but unbundling them into independent modules. Universities are not sitting still: Arizona State University has developed "stackable" microcredentials that can accumulate toward a master's degree, while European universities are integrating microcredentials into the Bologna Process to allow cross-border recognition. At the same time, the gap between skills-based hiring intent and actual practice exists partly because the infrastructure for verifying skills did not exist until recently; the emerging standard is Open Badges 3.0, built on the W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model.

What appears to be emerging, then, is a layered system: rather than degrees being replaced, a hybrid system is developing — perhaps something like a "skills passport" or "lifelong learning credential" that records all learning, from a first degree to the microcredentials accumulated throughout a working life. Traditional degrees remain essential for leadership roles, advanced research, and professions that require intensive accreditation, while shorter credentials gain ground in technical fields where demonstrable, current competence matters more than breadth. The World Economic Forum estimates that over one billion workers will need to reskill by 2030, and LinkedIn Learning reports that the technical skill half-life, from a marketability standpoint, is approximately two years — a pace at which no four-year degree, however well designed, can keep up on its own. The university will survive, but likely as one node in a much larger, more fluid learning infrastructure rather than as the sole gateway to professional life.

### Q041 How can public education systems keep pace with private AI development without surrendering governance to tech companies? {#q041}

9 citations · 9 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The tension between public education and private AI development is not a future problem — it is an acute, present one, and the recent record makes clear that governments at every level are scrambling to catch up rather than lead.

The Scale of the Asymmetry

The speed differential between private AI development and public institutional response is almost comically lopsided. The 2025 State EdTech Trends Report, released by SETDA in collaboration with Whiteboard Advisors, captures a pivotal moment: for the first time, artificial intelligence has overtaken cybersecurity as the top state education technology priority. Yet this priority status arrived largely in reaction to commercial products already saturating classrooms. According to CoSN's May 2025 State of EdTech District Leadership report, 43 percent of districts lack formal policies or guidance for AI use — even as 80 percent of districts have generative AI initiatives underway. The tools arrived before the governance did.

The Legislative Response: Active but Fragmented

Legislatures are not standing still. During the 2025 legislative session, 53 bills were proposed on the use of AI in education across 21 states, including 51 that apply specifically to K-12 schools; four states — Illinois, Louisiana, Nevada, and New Mexico — enacted legislation. Across these bills, five themes emerge: advancing AI literacy for students and professional development for teachers; requiring guidance on responsible use including privacy and transparency; creating studies or task forces; prohibiting specific AI uses such as those related to student mental health support or replacing teachers; and addressing AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery. The breadth is encouraging; the fragmentation is not. A patchwork of state-level rules — some permissive, some restrictive — creates an uneven landscape that sophisticated vendors can navigate at will, adapting their terms of service to whichever jurisdiction offers the least friction.

At the federal level, the posture has been more promotional than regulatory. The White House launched a "Pledge to America's Youth: Investing in AI Education" that now includes commitments from over 200 tech companies and organizations including Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Salesforce. America's AI Action Plan highlights the current administration's aversion toward regulation by providing that states should not have access to federal funding on AI-related matters should they implement "burdensome AI regulations." This creates a structural incentive for states to compete on permissiveness rather than protection.

The Data Governance Crisis

The governance vacuum is not theoretical. In December 2024, PowerSchool — a leading provider of cloud-based software managing student grades, attendance, and records for approximately 16,000 schools — detected unauthorized access; by January 2025, the scope was clear: more than 62 million student records and nearly 10 million teacher records had been exfiltrated, representing the largest breach of children's data in US history. The breach exposed an industry governance model that has normalized the centralization of children's data at unprecedented scale without commensurate security architecture, regulatory oversight, or enforceable data minimization requirements — and one year later, that model remains largely intact.

More insidious than spectacular breaches is the routine opacity of how student data flows. More than half of education technology companies did not fully disclose how learner data was being collected and shared, creating ethical and reputational risks for universities and schools. This lack of visibility has led to the rise of what experts call "shadow AI" — unapproved apps and browser extensions that process student inputs, store them indefinitely, or reuse them to train commercial models, often free, widely adopted, and nearly invisible to IT teams.

What Public Governance Can Actually Do

Three strategies carry genuine promise. The first is the creation of public AI infrastructure as a counterweight to proprietary systems. Digital Promise has launched a K-12 AI Infrastructure Program, a \$26 million, multi-year effort to create openly shared and freely available models, datasets, and benchmarks designed for education. The logic here is important: if public institutions depend entirely on proprietary models, they can only govern those models from the outside. Owning or co-developing public-interest AI infrastructure is a different kind of leverage.

The second is what some governments are calling regulatory sandboxes — formally supervised frameworks where governments can engage innovators to test tools that challenge existing legal frameworks, in order to understand risks and safeguards and help shape regulation. This allows regulators to develop genuine technical knowledge before committing to rules, rather than legislating from ignorance.

The third is institutional self-defense through procurement power. Some higher education institutions are addressing data risk by maintaining local control of AI infrastructure — for example, the University of Montana worked with Amazon Web Services and Microsoft to create a university-owned data center that runs enterprise-grade models directly from these companies, ensuring all data is hosted in the university system and is not used to train any models. Public institutions collectively represent enormous purchasing leverage; exercising that leverage through coordinated procurement standards could reshape vendor incentives across the entire sector.

The Deeper Question

Realizing the benefits of AI in education while managing its risks calls for collaboration across public, private, and civic actors, supported by strong public oversight and safeguards; as Big Tech companies expand their presence in education ecosystems, it is critical for governments to strengthen their capacity to engage with private sector partnerships on their own terms. The phrase "on their own terms" carries real weight. The risk is not merely that public systems will fall behind technically — it is that, in the scramble to catch up, they will accept the terms set by the companies whose products they adopt, effectively outsourcing not just the tools but the values embedded in them. Keeping pace, in this context, means something more demanding than speed: it means building the institutional knowledge, legal architecture, and public infrastructure to remain the authoritative party in every negotiation.
