### Q047 How do we manage the transition for current workers whose skills are being obsoleted faster than retraining systems can respond? {#q047}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Retraining Gap: When Skills Obsolescence Outpaces the Systems Built to Address It

The arithmetic of the current moment is genuinely alarming. The World Economic Forum's 2025 Future of Jobs report estimates that workers can expect two-fifths of their existing skill sets to be transformed or become outdated over the 2025–2030 period. Meanwhile, SHRM's 2025 research estimates that 19.2 million U.S. jobs face a high or very high risk of automation displacement across clerical, logistics, and finance sectors. The retraining systems expected to absorb this disruption were not built for its scale or velocity, and the evidence accumulated over decades suggests they are not becoming adequate fast enough to matter.

The public architecture of worker support reveals a structural underfunding that predates the current crisis. Federal workforce development spending has fallen from 0.35 percent of GDP in the 1980s to under 0.1 percent today. In absolute terms, the United States spends roughly five billion dollars per year on public workforce programs. The historical track record of dedicated programs such as Trade Adjustment Assistance is damning across administrations and decades: past efforts to respond to economic displacement have not lived up to the hopes of those who devised them, reflecting failures of both design and implementation, with major consequences for workers and the broader political landscape.

The private sector offers some countervailing examples, but they remain exceptional rather than systemic. AT&T committed one billion dollars to a multiyear program called Future Ready to retrain about 100,000 employees for new tech roles, partnering with online education providers and universities to create tailored courses; by 2020, tens of thousands of workers had completed training in software development, data science, and cybersecurity. Such cases demonstrate that large-scale internal retraining is technically possible — but a 2025 Brookings survey of HR leaders at companies that had deployed AI tools found that only 7 percent were working on reskilling strategies for AI-impacted roles, while 62 percent were focused on piloting AI in HR management itself. The private sector is, in other words, more likely to automate its human resources department than to retrain the workers that automation displaces.

Three structural failures recur through the research with uncomfortable consistency. The standard retraining theory assumes that for every automated job that disappears, a new skilled job emerges somewhere else — but evidence suggests technological change can reduce the number of available middle-wage positions faster than workers can retrain into them. You cannot retrain your way into a job that does not exist. Second, the people who need retraining most are often the least able to access it: retraining takes weeks or months of classes, often without income, and workers living paycheck to paycheck cannot afford to stop earning. Third, even when workers do retrain, the destination may be insecure: Harvard Kennedy School–affiliated research found that retraining raises earnings on average but produces smaller gains when workers move into occupations with high AI exposure, concluding that retraining works best when it targets roles with long-term stability rather than those vulnerable to additional automation. This is a moving target that existing programs have no mechanism to track in real time.

A further problem concerns what gets taught. The skills that AI is perceived to be most useful in helping to teach — procedural, closed skills — appear to be the same ones most susceptible to workplace automation, creating a potential "training for obsolescence" trap where educational systems inadvertently prepare workers for roles that will not exist by the time they complete their programs.

Current reform proposals cluster around three approaches, none yet proven at scale. The first is structural overhaul of public programs: workforce programs are currently evaluated on how participants are doing a year after completing their training, which creates an incentive to nudge workers into the first available job rather than what may be a better long-term alternative — a preferable approach would align program incentives with securing long-term, meaningful employment. The second concerns income continuity: a 2024 study found that wage insurance increased rates of employment and long-run earnings by cushioning wage losses and encouraging displaced workers to accept new jobs, suggesting that bridging income rather than mandating rapid retraining may paradoxically produce better outcomes. The third is distributional: some economists suggest mechanisms to share productivity gains more broadly, including profit-sharing plans that extend to all employees, or new forms of taxation where companies that benefit enormously from AI contribute to retraining funds or basic income for displaced workers.

What the evidence converges on is a need for a system that enables exposed and displaced workers to prepare for and transition to future occupations mid-career rather than only early-career — an infrastructure that does not yet exist in any country at meaningful scale. The retraining gap is not primarily a pedagogical problem. It is a political economy problem: the costs of displacement fall on individuals and communities, while the gains from automation accrue to firms and shareholders, and no durable mechanism yet redistributes between the two with sufficient speed or adequacy.

### Q048 How does AI in education affect democracy — the formation of citizens capable of judgment, deliberation, and resistance to manipulation? {#q048}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI in Education and the Democratic Citizen

Democracy does not merely require voters; it requires people capable of forming independent judgments, tolerating disagreement, deliberating with those who hold different views, and resisting the sophisticated manipulation that modern information environments make ever easier. Whether AI in education strengthens or erodes these capacities is one of the most consequential questions of the present moment — and the honest answer is that the evidence points in genuinely opposing directions simultaneously.

Begin with the cognitive dimension. Research examining AI's broader impact on human thought identifies a "cognitive offloading effect," in which the externalization of mental functions to AI can reduce intellectual engagement and weaken critical thinking. This is not a fringe concern. A 2025 study presented at the ACM CHI conference, surveying 319 knowledge workers, found that while GenAI tools often prompt a kind of quality-checking vigilance, a key irony of automation is that by mechanizing routine tasks and leaving exception-handling to the human, it deprives the user of routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive capacities, leaving them atrophied and unprepared when harder cases arise. The classroom is not exempt from this logic. Research using Bloom's taxonomy suggests that AI assistance may be more effective for knowledge-based recall tasks than for the higher-order thinking skills that require analysis, synthesis, and evaluation — precisely the skills democratic deliberation demands.

The personalization problem compounds this. Critics of high-level AI personalization argue that over-tailored content may inadvertently create "filter bubbles" or "knowledge silos," where students are shielded from the productive struggle necessary for deep conceptual change. Just as social media algorithms can narrow our worldview by feeding us only opinions we already agree with, hyper-optimized AI tutors might be stunting intellectual resilience by removing the vital struggle from the learning process. The connection to democratic life is direct: on the social level, algorithmic personalization creates filter bubbles that limit the diversity of opinions and can lead to the homogenization of thought and polarization. A student raised inside a perfectly tailored learning environment may develop competence within a narrow range while losing the habit — and appetite — for encountering genuinely alien ideas.

Today's learners are digital citizens first, encountering AI in their social media feeds, search engines, and recommendation systems; democratic competence must therefore include a critical understanding of AI itself. Learners need to recognize how AI shapes their exposure to information, how biases can be embedded in systems, and how automated tools can empower or constrain civic engagement. This is a relatively new but serious demand: the citizen must now be able to read not just texts but the architectures that select those texts.

Yet the picture is not only one of erosion. Civic educators have argued that AI could move students beyond merely learning a set of facts into an "opportunity to practice the skills of negotiation, the skills of engagement, the skills of give-and-take" essential to democratic life. AI-powered platforms can simulate scenarios involving misinformation, enabling learners to distinguish between credible and misleading content — a skill whose civic importance is self-evident. And research on teaching AI literacy directly to adolescents shows real promise: because adolescents' nascent digital footprints make them particularly susceptible to misrepresentation by AI systems, educational modules on algorithmic bias and filter bubbles have produced substantial learning gains in early trials.

The condition on which the optimistic case depends is, however, demanding. The goal of genuine civic co-intelligence in education is achieved when teachers and students co-create a culture of inquiry, skepticism, and ethical responsibility around AI use — ensuring that AI is a catalyst for deeper thinking and democratic citizenship, not a substitute for creativity, empathy, or human judgment. There is evidence that teacher care and relational engagement are fundamental to student character development and well-being, raising real questions about whether AI-mediated education can replicate the affective and relational dimensions essential for authentic moral growth.

The deepest worry, then, is not that AI will teach students wrong answers. It is that AI — if deployed without pedagogical intention — will teach students to outsource the hardest parts of thinking: sitting with uncertainty, weighing competing claims, arguing a position across genuine disagreement. Those are not skills that any algorithm can practice on a student's behalf. They require friction, and friction is precisely what the most commercially successful AI tools are designed to remove.

### Q049 What shared human culture and values should education transmit when AI fragments information into personalized realities? {#q049}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The Epistemic Commons: What Education Must Preserve When AI Splinters Reality

The deepest threat posed by AI-driven personalization is not misinformation in the conventional sense — it is the dissolution of a shared world. At a societal level, if everyone interacts with differently personalized systems calibrated to their particular preferences and beliefs, shared reality and common knowledge may erode. This is the civilizational wager now sitting, largely unexamined, at the heart of educational policy. The question is not only what children should learn, but what they must learn *in common* — and why that commonality itself is a moral and political good.

The problem is more layered than early warnings about filter bubbles suggested. In increasingly personalized media environments, individuals encounter information that aligns with their existing beliefs, raising concerns about polarization, intergroup hostility, and the erosion of shared political reality — and filter bubbles emerge not from algorithms alone, but through the recursive interaction of motivated cognitive processing, identity-based social networks, and algorithmic amplification. AI does not simply distort the information landscape from the outside; it reshapes the internal habits by which people seek, weigh, and revise knowledge. AI systems impact not only beliefs, but belief revision itself — and in the classroom, this implies students will update their knowledge in response to algorithmic authority, without recourse to further justification or reflection.

This is where the educational stakes become philosophical rather than merely technical. The values underpinning current forms of educational AI — individualism, mastery-based learning, automation of teaching — work directly against many of the core elements of how democratic education has been understood by educationalists such as John Dewey over the past century. Personalized learning optimizes the individual learner's trajectory through content; democratic education, by contrast, has always been partly about the friction of encountering minds unlike one's own, negotiating disagreement, and building the civic capacity to inhabit a world held in common. The current push for educational AI is resulting in technologies that diminish students' opportunities for communication and collaboration with others.

What, then, should education transmit? Three clusters of value emerge from current scholarship as non-negotiable, regardless of what AI systems can deliver efficiently.

The first is *epistemic agency* — the cultivated capacity to interrogate sources, tolerate uncertainty, and resist the seduction of algorithmic fluency. AI tools that prioritize speed and convenience risk amplifying automation bias, reducing cognitive struggle, and weakening critical thinking; to counteract this, AI must preserve cognitive friction — prompting retrieval, offering delayed feedback, framing uncertainty as opportunity — so that it fosters intellectual resilience and the critical thinking skills vital for democratic society. The transmission of this value requires teachers who model doubt, not just delivery.

The second is *shared factual ground* — a curriculum that insists certain things are true, contested, or false independent of any individual's preference profile. Through algorithmic filtering and personalized content, individuals are nudged toward specific viewpoints without awareness, limiting exposure to diverse information and weakening their capacity for independent thought — and the resulting manipulation diminishes individuals' ability to make informed choices, undermining democratic participation. Education's answer must be a commitment to evidence, method, and the disciplines that have developed collectively-validated ways of knowing: scientific reasoning, historical analysis, literary interpretation, mathematical proof.

The third is *solidarity through encounter* — the experience of being educated alongside people whose lives, backgrounds, and conclusions differ from one's own. Education for democracy is a holistic and participatory approach that fosters the knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes needed for active and responsible citizenship, going beyond textbooks by emphasising experiential and inclusive learning that strengthens democratic competencies such as critical thinking, dialogue, agency, and meaningful participation. No AI tutor, however sophisticated, replicates the moral education that occurs when a classroom must reach understanding across genuine disagreement.

Ultimately, an ethical use of AI in education is about preserving education as a space for autonomy, critical inquiry, and democratic formation — because if AI systems undermine these values, they risk weakening not just learning outcomes, but the social institutions that depend on educated, reflective, and empowered citizens. The curriculum of the future will need to be deliberately, even stubbornly, common: not because uniformity is a virtue, but because a democracy requires citizens who can, at minimum, argue about the same world.

### Q050 Which current decisions about AI in education do researchers and policymakers identify as most consequential, and on what grounds? {#q050}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Looking Back from 2050: The Decisions That Shaped a Generation

History rarely announces the moments that will matter most. The decisions now being made about artificial intelligence and education — rushed, improvised, and only partially understood — are almost certainly among them. From the vantage point of 2050, this decade will likely look like an inflection point comparable to the introduction of mass printing or compulsory schooling: a period when the architecture of human learning was renegotiated under enormous pressure, with consequences that outlasted everyone who made the choices.

The first decisions likely to be judged harshly concern the heedless substitution of AI for cognitive effort. The share of students in middle school grades and up who reported using AI for help with their homework rose from 48 percent in May 2025 to 62 percent in December of the same year. That trajectory, if it continues unchecked, points toward a generation that has never had to sustain the productive discomfort of not knowing. The research already accumulating is sobering: overreliance on AI tools can lead to a decline in critical and analytical thinking skills, especially when students become overly dependent on AI-generated content, with over-reliance linked to diminished creativity and increased dependency. More specifically, the most significant improvements from AI assistance appear at lower levels of cognitive taxonomy, suggesting that AI may be more effective for knowledge-based recall tasks than for higher-order thinking skills that require analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. The 2026 International AI Safety Report identified the deeper stakes plainly: children's early interactions with AI systems may influence how their key skills and habits develop over time, and it can be difficult to assess whether observed changes in behavior represent short-term adjustments or more persistent shifts that could affect autonomy.

What makes this particularly consequential is that students themselves already sense the danger. As of December 2025, 67 percent of students endorsed the view that the more students use AI for schoolwork, the more it will harm their critical thinking skills — up more than 10 percentage points from ten months earlier. A society whose children recognize a trap they feel unable to avoid is one that has failed at the level of institutional design, not individual virtue.

The second class of decisions likely to haunt the future involves equity. Unequal access to AI is widening the educational gap between those who are privileged and those who are underprivileged. The emerging geography of this divide is already being mapped. In tech-rich cities, students use AI to think critically and solve problems with expert guidance ensuring they learn, not just use; while elsewhere, with good connectivity but little oversight, students offload work to AI, gaining convenience but missing real learning. Meanwhile, fragmented adoption driven by decentralized decision-making is leading to inequities, with some districts leveraging AI effectively and others struggling to integrate it. The cruel irony is that the same technology capable of acting as a private tutor for every child — a democratizing force of enormous potential — is reproducing and amplifying the very hierarchies it might have dissolved. Without adequate safeguards, the same systems that promise to close learning gaps may reinforce them.

The third set of decisions involves governance, and here the picture is more ambiguous. By April 2025, at least 28 states had published guidance on AI in K-12 settings — an encouraging sign of institutional attention, though guidance documents are not the same as thoughtful policy. Organisational and governmental incentives to deploy AI systems quickly can limit opportunities to evaluate their effects carefully and to implement appropriate safeguards. The pressure to adopt — from vendors, from parents worried their children will fall behind, from administrators seduced by efficiency — is structurally different from the pressure to reflect.

What, then, does choosing wisely look like? The answer is not a moratorium on AI in education, which would be neither desirable nor achievable. It looks, rather, like distinguishing between AI as a tool for amplifying what teachers do and AI as a replacement for the cognitive struggle that is the mechanism of learning itself. Assignments built on assumptions of no AI use are increasingly disconnected from how students actually work — but that does not mean the answer is to simply surrender the design of learning to the convenience of the tool. When students externalize cognitive tasks to AI systems, it reduces internal cognitive demands but may compromise deeper cognitive processes such as inference, synthesis, and evaluation; over time, habitual offloading may foster cognitive laziness and impede the development of higher-order thinking skills.

The decisions that 2050 will celebrate are likely to be those made now with deliberate restraint: institutions that asked not "what can AI do in our classrooms?" but "what must humans still do for themselves, and why?" The regrets will belong to those who moved fast and assumed that what was efficient was therefore good.

### Q127 Which educational credentials are losing labour-market signalling value because of AI, and which are gaining it? {#q127}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is revaluing educational credentials along two distinct axes: it is eroding the signalling value of credentials that certify routine, automatable skills — most notably the general four-year degree as a blanket signal of white-collar readiness — while simultaneously inflating the value of credentials that certify applied, verifiable, and AI-adjacent competence. The result is a labour market in which the traditional hierarchy of credentials is flattening at the bottom and fragmenting at the top.

What is losing value: the general degree as a blanket signal. The most consequential change is the erosion of the 'college premium' as a default signal of employability. The mechanism is twofold. First, AI has automated precisely the entry-level white-collar tasks — document drafting, basic coding, standardised data analysis, clerical work — that the degree historically certified readiness for. Census Bureau working-paper data show employment among 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations declining significantly since the widespread adoption of large language models in 2022, with the steepest declines concentrated among graduates of mid-tier institutions rather than elite ones. Second, the signalling value of the degree itself has been degraded by grade inflation and declining foundational skills: analysis of university grading patterns shows the share of 'A' grades in writing and coding courses rising sharply since the launch of ChatGPT, which employers increasingly read as evidence that AI is completing assignments rather than that students are learning. When a credential no longer certifies the skills it nominally certifies, its market value falls regardless of its institutional prestige. The Gallup polling of students reflects the resulting uncertainty: students are actively reweighting majors and career plans in response to perceived AI exposure.

The shift to skills-based hiring. The erosion of degree signalling is being accelerated by a structural shift in employer behaviour. Surveys now report that roughly 70 per cent of employers say they prioritise skills over traditional degrees, and hiring managers increasingly weight demonstrated project portfolios at least as heavily as formal credentials — with a substantial share saying a strong portfolio can entirely compensate for a lack of credentials. This is not a rejection of higher education but a reweighting of its signal: the degree is becoming a necessary-but-insufficient condition, and the marginal credential that moves a candidate is increasingly a demonstrable skill rather than an additional certificate. The credential that is losing value is therefore not the degree per se but the degree as a complete signal — the assumption that holding one certifies readiness for a broad class of work.

What is gaining value: applied and verified AI credentials. At the same time, a new credential market has emerged around AI itself, and its internal hierarchy is steep. The market is saturated — more than 400 AI credentials now exist, most with employer recognition below 20 per cent — but a short list of credentials with genuine signalling power has consolidated: Google's Professional Machine Learning Engineer (61 per cent employer recognition), AWS Certified Machine Learning – Specialty (58 per cent), Microsoft Azure AI Engineer Associate (54 per cent), DeepLearning.AI specialisations (47 per cent), and IBM's AI Engineering certificate (31 per cent). The pattern beneath these numbers is that value accrues to credentials that are proctored, third-party-validated, and occupationally relevant. Brookings' research on the credential boom finds that wage premiums are driven almost entirely by job relevance: a job-relevant credential commands a premium more than double that of a non-relevant one. 'Literacy-level' badges and generic AI certificates, by contrast, carry little weight unless paired with tangible work output.

What is gaining value: skilled trades and vocational credentials. The other major gainer is the credential system that AI cannot easily devalue: skilled trades and vocational certification. Severe labour shortages in electrical, plumbing, welding, and related trades have driven up wages and job security in sectors that are largely shielded from AI-driven automation and that certify through apprenticeships and licences rather than degrees. The signalling logic is different: these credentials certify hands-on, inspected, and often legally required competence, and their value is rising precisely because the supply of certified workers is falling. The broader lesson is that credentials gain value when they certify something scarce, verifiable, and non-automatable — and lose it when they certify something abundant, unverifiable, or automatable.

The emerging hierarchy. The evidence points to a re-sorting rather than a collapse of the credential market. At the top, elite-institution degrees and advanced applied credentials retain and even gain value, because they signal access to networks, selection effects, and hard-to-fake competence. In the middle, the general degree is losing its automatic premium and is being supplemented — or in some cases replaced — by portfolios, skills transcripts, and occupationally relevant certifications. At the bottom, generic and literacy-level credentials are being commoditised to near-zero signalling value. For education systems, the implication is that the credential's value is no longer a property of the institution that issues it but of the verifiability and scarcity of the competence it certifies — a shift that rewards precisely the kind of assessment reform that AI itself is forcing on schools.

### Q128 How is AI changing entry-level work, and what does that mean for the school-to-work transition? {#q128}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is changing entry-level work by automating the very tasks that used to define it. The routine, foundational work of junior employees — data cleaning, meeting summarisation, basic research, document drafting, standardised coding — is precisely the work that large language models now perform, and the consequences are visible in the labour market: declining entry-level postings, rising underemployment among young graduates, and a structural 'experience gap' in which the bottom rungs of the career ladder are being removed before new workers have climbed them.

The hollowing out of the entry level. The evidence of contraction is now substantial. Research on job postings shows declines of roughly a third in entry-level roles in recent periods, and Census Bureau working-paper data document falling employment among 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations — software development, clerical work, editing — since the widespread adoption of large language models in 2022, even as employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations has continued to grow. Harvard Business School's Joseph Fuller describes the dynamic as a 'talent shift' in which AI is hollowing out the bottom of the career ladder: companies automate the tasks that junior staff used to do, reduce entry-level hiring, and then discover that they have depleted the pipeline of talent needed for future mid-level and senior roles. The paradox is that the efficiency gain is real and the long-term cost is structural.

The experience gap. The most consequential effect for the school-to-work transition is the erosion of the training function that entry-level work used to perform. Traditionally, the first years of employment were where graduates built professional judgement, communication skills, and workplace confidence through supervised practice on routine tasks. When AI performs those tasks, junior workers are increasingly expected to operate at a higher level immediately — supervising AI outputs, handling complex judgement-based responsibilities — without the gradual learning curve that built the tacit knowledge to do so. The concern, articulated across the literature, is that workers who skip the 'task rungs' of routine work may never develop the foundational understanding needed to oversee AI agents, spot hallucinations, or exercise the judgement that the new division of labour demands of them. The experience gap is thus not simply a hiring problem; it is a capability-formation problem that compounds over a career.

What employers now want. The skill requirements of entry-level hiring are shifting in response. Employers increasingly prioritise AI fluency — the ability to define problems, orchestrate models, and use tools ethically and effectively — alongside the human capabilities that remain scarce: critical thinking, collaboration, empathy, and communication. The emerging formulation is a shift from 'pedigree' to 'proof': candidates are evaluated on demonstrable ability to use AI tools, verify outputs, and solve problems, rather than on the institution that issued their degree. Deloitte's analysis of AI in the workplace frames the new entry-level profile as someone who can work alongside AI as a 'digital teammate' — accelerating their own output while retaining ownership of the final result and the judgement behind it. The skills that are losing value are the rules-based, procedural skills that AI can now perform; the skills gaining value are verification, interpretation, stakeholder management, and the ethical application of machine outputs.

Implications for the school-to-work transition. The implications for education systems are profound and are already reshaping institutional strategy. First, the transition can no longer be assumed to happen after graduation: the 'experience gap' means that work-based learning — internships, apprenticeships, project-based learning — is moving from optional enrichment to core curriculum, with institutions partnering with employers to embed real work into the academic programme. Second, the portfolio is becoming the credential: students are being encouraged to build performance-based projects, skills transcripts, and documented evidence of capability, because employers increasingly weight demonstrated work over degrees. Third, the transition itself is becoming a two-way street: as entry-level work disappears, the school-to-work bridge must be built earlier, with schools taking on more of the responsibility for the applied, judgement-based learning that the first job used to provide. The Stanford Social Innovation Review's analysis of AI and entry-level jobs concludes that organisations must redesign their training models — creating new infrastructures of work-based learning and performance-based hiring — to replace the training ground that routine work used to be. For students, the practical guidance from career research is consistent: maintain ownership of outcomes rather than offloading judgement to AI, build relationships and mentorship that machines cannot provide, and treat AI as an accelerator of higher-value work rather than a substitute for the human capabilities that entry-level roles increasingly demand.

What this means for schools. For schools, the transition has two direct consequences. The first is curricular: if the first job no longer provides the training ground it once did, then the applied, judgement-based learning that used to happen in the workplace must move into the school — through project-based assessment, work placements, and explicit instruction in verifying and supervising machine outputs. The second is informational: students need accurate, current guidance about which pathways lead to work, and the traditional advice to 'get a degree and the rest follows' is no longer reliable. Career education must now teach students to read the labour market itself — to understand which of their prospective tasks are automatable, and to build portfolios of demonstrated work rather than relying on credentials alone. The school-to-work transition is thus becoming less a handover and more a shared responsibility, with schools retaining students longer in the formation of applied competence and employers redesigning entry-level roles to preserve the training function that automation has eroded.

### Q129 What is happening to the economics of private tutoring, test preparation, and supplementary education? {#q129}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The economics of private tutoring, test preparation, and supplementary education are being transformed by AI in a pattern that is simultaneously expansionary and disruptive: the market is growing rapidly, AI is both a driver of that growth and a force reshaping its cost structure, and the competitive dynamics between human tutors, AI tutors, and free tools are redrawing the industry's boundaries. The result is a sector in which the overall pie is getting larger while the position of every incumbent player is being renegotiated.

A growing market with a changing cost structure. The private tutoring market is large and expanding. Global estimates value it at roughly \$133.8 billion in 2025, with projections of \$248.4 billion by 2034 and a compound annual growth rate around 7 per cent; the US market alone is forecast to grow by about \$28.85 billion between 2025 and 2029, at an accelerated rate of roughly 11 per cent. The AI tutoring and personalised-learning segment is growing far faster, with valuations projected to rise from about \$6.8 billion in 2025 to \$37.4 billion by 2034 — a compound annual growth rate near 20 per cent. The demand drivers are structural and largely pre-AI: high-stakes examination systems, intensifying academic competition, and the expansion of STEM-focused supplementary education. What AI changes is the cost structure. Traditional tutoring is labour-intensive and therefore expensive and hard to scale; AI tutoring has near-zero marginal cost per additional student, which is why the market forecasts treat AI as the industry's principal growth vector. The economics of the sector are thus bifurcating between a premium human-tutoring segment and a commodity AI segment, with hybrid models in between.

The Khanmigo experience: the economics of student-facing AI. The most instructive case study in the new economics is Khan Academy's Khanmigo, the highest-profile student-facing AI tutor. Its trajectory reveals the sector's central economic problem: inference costs. Early AI tutors found that the cost of running large language models for individual users threatened profit margins, and the economics only work when usage is structured, batched, or subsidised. Khanmigo's experience also exposed the engagement problem that shapes the market's structure: research found that while nearly all students tried the tool, median usage was low — students engaged on only a fraction of their practice days, and a Stanford study documented a 60 per cent drop in engagement after three weeks of unfacilitated use. The 'Socratic paradox' — Khanmigo's design avoids giving direct answers, which is pedagogically sound but friction-generating for students seeking immediate help — meant that engagement, not capability, became the binding constraint on the business model. The market's response has been a bifurcation: teacher-facing productivity tools (lesson planning, rubric generation, grading support) have seen strong adoption and viable procurement economics, while general-purpose student-facing chatbots have struggled with churn and are being redesigned around gamified interfaces, multi-agent orchestration, and stricter compliance.

Competitive dynamics: human tutors, AI tutors, and free tools. The competitive landscape is being redrawn along three fronts. First, free and near-free AI tools are compressing the bottom of the market: the availability of high-quality free assistance from general-purpose chatbots and platforms like Khanmigo (at low subscription prices) undercuts the low-end paid tutoring segment, particularly for routine homework help and basic test preparation. Second, the premium segment is consolidating upward: the market is seeing 'premiumisation', in which high-income households pay more for human tutors with verified credentials, guaranteed outcomes, and personalised service — the qualities AI cannot yet replicate. Third, the middle is being squeezed and hybridised: traditional tutoring companies are integrating AI into their offerings, using AI for diagnostics, practice generation, and between-session support while retaining human tutors for the core instructional relationship. The Asia-Pacific region, which accounts for roughly 35 per cent of global tutoring revenue and has the deepest 'shadow education' culture, is the leading laboratory for these dynamics, and China's 2021 'double reduction' policy demonstrates the sector's exposure to sudden regulatory shocks that can force rapid restructuring.

Equity and the new economics. The economic transformation carries a clear equity dimension. The cost structure of AI tutoring makes high-quality supplementary education cheaper than ever at the margin, which in principle narrows the gap between households that can afford tutoring and those that cannot. But the premiumisation of human tutoring and the quality gap between free and paid AI tiers cut the other way, and the market forecasts themselves note that affordability barriers for lower-income households are contributing to a widening attainment gap. The emerging economics of the sector can be summarised as follows: AI is expanding the market, compressing its low end, inflating its high end, and forcing every provider — human or machine — to compete on the specific value they add that the other cannot. For schools and families, the practical implication is that the economics of supplementary education are now more favourable than at any point in history for basic assistance, and more stratified than ever for the premium services that confer positional advantage.

### Q130 How is AI affecting adult retraining and mid-career education systems? {#q130}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is affecting adult retraining and mid-career education in two connected ways: it is massively increasing the demand for retraining, and it is simultaneously transforming the systems that deliver it. The demand side is driven by the scale of AI's disruption of existing jobs — with roughly 40 per cent of core worker skills expected to be disrupted by 2027, and nearly half of US workers reporting monthly AI use by 2025 — while the supply side is being reshaped by AI-powered learning platforms, new credential structures, and a reorientation of community colleges and corporate training toward applied AI competence. The evidence on whether these systems can meet the demand is sobering: the infrastructure is underfunded, the outcomes are hard to measure, and the risk of reskilling workers into equally automatable roles is real.

The demand: upskilling versus reskilling. The workforce-development literature now distinguishes two strategies. Upskilling augments an employee's existing skill set to improve performance or advance within a current career path; reskilling trains workers for entirely new competencies, typically because their current role is being altered or automated. The distinction matters for system design, because the two strategies have different economics and different success criteria. Upskilling is cheaper, faster, and easier to justify to employers; reskilling is expensive, slow, and carries the risk that the new occupation will itself be disrupted. Brookings' analysis of AI labour displacement and the limits of worker retraining is the most sceptical major treatment: it argues that public retraining programmes face a fundamental economic mismatch — workers may be reskilled into occupations that are also susceptible to automation, or into a surplus of 'skilled' workers relative to the number of high-quality jobs available — and that the methodological difficulty of separating training effects from the self-selection of motivated participants makes the evidence base weaker than the policy enthusiasm suggests.

The infrastructure problem. The National Academies' assessment of retraining for the age of AI documents a structural funding problem: US workforce development spends only about 0.1 per cent of GDP on active labour-market policies, which is chronically insufficient to scale successful training models to the population that needs them. Individual barriers compound the system-level ones: the opportunity cost of lost wages during training, lower take-up among older workers, and competing social and health concerns all suppress participation. The result is that the systems most in demand are the least funded, and the gap between the scale of AI-driven displacement and the scale of the retraining response is one of the defining features of the current transition.

What works: the corporate evidence. Against this backdrop, research on large corporate reskilling initiatives — including billion-dollar programmes at Amazon, JPMorgan, and AT&T — has identified the design features that distinguish effective from ineffective training. Successful programmes begin with broad AI literacy for all staff, explaining the capabilities and limitations of AI before any specialised technical training. They use blended learning models: combining self-paced online coursework with live cohort sessions and real-world project applications produces completion rates up to 65 per cent, versus roughly 8 per cent for pure self-paced models. They tie training to concrete career pathways — specific role transitions, salary increases, or title changes — rather than vague mandates to 'learn AI'. And they integrate 'learning in the flow of work', embedding bite-sized micro-learning into daily tasks so that new skills are applied immediately. The pattern is consistent with the wider learning-science evidence: adult retraining works when it is contextual, social, and career-anchored, and fails when it is abstract, solitary, and credential-agnostic.

The community college reorientation. The institutional response in the United States has centred on community colleges, which are widely described as uniquely positioned to serve as the primary engine of AI reskilling. Their advantages are structural: deep integration with local labour markets, agility in adapting curricula to regional economic needs, and accessibility for mid-career and non-traditional students. The emerging model, exemplified by the National Applied AI Consortium, combines stackable credentials (certificates that ladder into associate and bachelor's degrees, allowing workers to enter and exit the workforce at multiple competency stages), competency-based education (mastery of specific skills rather than seat-time, with credit for prior learning), and industry alignment through Business and Industry Leadership Teams that keep curricula tied to employer needs. The goal is to train the 'missing middle' of the AI workforce — practitioners who apply AI in healthcare, logistics, manufacturing, and public services rather than the researchers who build it. Georgetown's CSET analysis of AI and workforce training frames this as the central challenge: the applied, operational layer of AI competence is where the labour-market demand is, and it is the layer the traditional system is least equipped to supply.

AI as the delivery mechanism. Finally, AI is transforming the delivery of retraining itself. AI-powered platforms now personalise learning paths by identifying skill gaps through resume analysis and skills taxonomies, and adaptive systems adjust content to individual pace and prior knowledge. The World Economic Forum's guidance on navigating the new tech landscape emphasises that every career now involves continuous learning, and that AI tools are both the subject and the medium of that learning. The overall picture is of a system under double pressure: the demand for retraining is expanding faster than the infrastructure can scale, the evidence on what works is clearer for corporate programmes than for public ones, and the technology driving the disruption is also the technology being deployed to respond to it — with the risk, identified across the literature, that the response is too slow, too small, and too often aimed at the wrong target.

### Q131 Who profits from AI in education, and what business models are emerging around students? {#q131}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The profits from AI in education are flowing to a narrower set of actors than the market's headline growth figures suggest, and the business models emerging around students are consolidating around a few durable patterns: institutional software with high switching costs, habitual consumer subscriptions, teacher-facing productivity tools that convert individual adoption into district contracts, and trusted assessment and credentialing. The market itself is large and growing — estimates of the AI-in-education market range from roughly \$2.2 billion in 2024 to over \$5.8 billion by 2030, with longer-horizon projections reaching \$92 billion by 2033 — but the distribution of that value is highly uneven, and the sector's history already contains a clear lesson about which models profit and which are disrupted.

The institutional layer: where the durable profits are. The most defensible business models in AI education are the ones that own institutional infrastructure. Companies providing core systems — student records, enrolment workflows, learning management systems — are highly valued because they create high switching costs: once a district or university runs its operations through a platform, the cost of leaving is prohibitive, and the vendor captures predictable, long-term revenue. This is the 'sticky SaaS' model, and it is where the most reliable profits in the sector sit. The same logic applies to assessment and credentialing: while AI can generate content for free, it cannot replicate a credential that employers or regulators trust, which makes certification one of the most defensible segments in the market. The strategic implication is that value accrues to whoever controls the system of record or the system of trust, not to whoever generates the content that flows through them.

The consumer layer: habitual use versus answer-selling. The consumer-facing segment has produced the sector's most dramatic profit-and-loss lesson. Companies that built their business on selling access to academic answers — most prominently Chegg — have seen significant revenue declines as general-purpose AI made answer-selling nearly free. The models that profit instead are those that monetise habitual behaviour: Duolingo is the canonical case, succeeding by monetising a repeated learning routine rather than a one-time answer. The distinction is fundamental to the emerging economics: AI commoditises content, so consumer education businesses must sell engagement, habit, and outcomes rather than information. Subscription models built on daily use, streaks, and progress loops are the consumer pattern that survives; pay-per-answer and content-access models are the pattern being destroyed.

The teacher-facing layer: bottom-up adoption as a sales strategy. The most successful recent business-model innovation is the teacher-facing productivity tool with a 'bottom-up' go-to-market strategy. Companies like MagicSchool AI and Brisk Teaching built products that save teachers time — lesson planning, rubric generation, grading support, with teachers using AI at least weekly reporting average savings of around 5–6 hours per week — and grew through individual teacher adoption before converting that grassroots usage into district-level contracts for privacy, governance, and administration. This model solves the sector's classic sales problem: institutional procurement is slow and complex, but a product that teachers themselves demand creates pull that administrators cannot ignore. The economics are attractive because the value proposition is immediate and measurable (time saved), and the expansion path is natural (from individual licences to district-wide agreements).

Investment patterns and the AI-native advantage. The investment data show where the market believes the profits will be. Overall edtech venture funding has declined from pandemic-era peaks — dropping roughly 26 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the prior year — but capital is concentrating in AI-native platforms with proven unit economics, and in fewer, larger growth-stage rounds. Investors are prioritising companies that own specific workflows — curriculum platforms, adaptive practice tools, institutional infrastructure — over generic AI tutoring interfaces, and they favour models with clear cost savings for institutions or measurable improvements in student outcomes. The 'AI-native versus AI-augmented' distinction is also shaping the market: startups built on AI from day one dominate early-stage funding, while established platforms adding AI layers capture larger growth-stage checks on the strength of their existing user bases. The competitive threat to both comes from the largest technology companies, which are increasingly bundling education-specific AI features into products already used by schools at little or no additional cost — a dynamic that compresses the market for specialised tools.

Who profits, and who does not. The emerging answer to 'who profits' is therefore specific. The actors capturing durable value are: the large platform and infrastructure providers (through switching costs and scale); teacher-facing productivity tools that convert adoption into contracts; habitual-use consumer apps; and trusted assessment and credentialing bodies. The actors being squeezed are: answer-selling content providers (disrupted by free general-purpose AI), generic chatbot interfaces without workflow integration, and startups that 'build for students but sell to administrators' without understanding institutional procurement. The actors whose position is most contested are the students themselves, whose data, attention, and learning outcomes are the raw material of these models — and whose interests are protected only to the extent that privacy regulation, procurement scrutiny, and evidence requirements constrain the market. The business models emerging around students are thus a mirror of the wider AI economy: value concentrates in infrastructure, distribution, and trust, while the content layer is commoditised toward zero.

### Q262 What micro-credentials, digital badges, and AI-verified competency records are emerging as alternatives or supplements to traditional degrees, and what is their current labour-market traction? {#q262}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The traditional degree has long served as the dominant signal of competence in labour markets, but its cost, duration, and coarse granularity have prompted interest in alternatives. Micro-credentials, digital badges, and machine-verifiable competency records promise to recognise specific skills, accommodate lifelong learning, and allow employers to verify claims instantly. AI is accelerating this interest in two ways: by changing which skills employers value and by enabling new forms of assessment and verification. Yet enthusiasm about these credentials has run ahead of evidence about their labour-market value.

The landscape of credentials has expanded dramatically. Credential Engine, a U.S. non-profit that maintains a registry of credentials, has documented in its Counting U.S. Postsecondary and Secondary Credentials reports that more than one million unique credentials are offered in the United States, including degrees, certificates, licences, apprenticeships, industry certifications, and a rapidly growing number of non-degree credentials such as course certificates and digital badges. This proliferation makes it difficult for employers and learners to judge quality, a problem that registries and common descriptors aim to address.

Technical infrastructure for verifiable credentials has matured. The 1EdTech Consortium's Open Badges 3.0 specification aligns digital badges with the World Wide Web Consortium's Verifiable Credentials data model, enabling cryptographically signed records that can be checked without contacting the issuer. In Europe, the European Digital Credentials for Learning infrastructure, part of Europass, allows institutions to issue tamper-evident digital credentials that learners can store and share across borders. The Council of the European Union's 2022 Recommendation on a European approach to micro-credentials established common elements for describing micro-credentials, including learning outcomes, workload, assessment, and quality assurance, and encouraged member states to integrate them into qualification frameworks.

AI-verified competency records represent a newer and less established development. Some platforms use AI to assess performance on simulations, coding tasks, or portfolios and issue credentials based on these assessments, while others use AI to map learners' experiences to skills taxonomies. The reliability and fairness of such AI-based assessments are not yet well documented, and they raise the same concerns about bias, transparency, and validity that apply to AI in grading and hiring.

Labour-market traction is the crucial question, and here evidence suggests caution. The Burning Glass Institute and the Harvard Business School Project on Managing the Future of Work, in their 2024 report Skills-Based Hiring: The Long Road from Pronouncements to Practice, analysed job postings and hiring data for large U.S. employers that had announced removal of degree requirements. They found that while many firms removed degree requirements from postings, actual hiring of workers without degrees into those roles increased by only about 3.5 percentage points on average, and that the change affected fewer than one in 700 hires overall. They classified 37 percent of firms as genuine leaders in skills-based hiring, 45 percent as skills-based in name only, and 18 percent as backsliders. These findings suggest that formal openness to alternative credentials has not yet translated into widespread change in who is hired.

Employer survey evidence is more positive but comes largely from interested parties. Coursera's 2025 Micro-Credentials Impact Report reported that 90 percent of employers surveyed would be willing to offer a higher starting salary to candidates holding professional certificates. Because Coursera sells such certificates, these findings should be treated as indicative of employer attitudes rather than as independent evidence of labour-market returns, and stated willingness may not match actual hiring and pay decisions.

Several factors appear to shape whether alternative credentials gain traction. Credentials linked to recognised employers, industry bodies, or licensing requirements tend to carry more weight than generic badges. Stackability, the ability to combine micro-credentials into larger qualifications, may increase value by connecting them to established pathways. Quality assurance and transparency about what a credential certifies help employers interpret it. Verification infrastructure reduces fraud, which may become more important as AI makes it easier to fabricate documents.

Equity implications cut both ways. Alternative credentials could open opportunities for workers without degrees, but if employers continue to favour degree holders, learners may invest time and money in credentials with limited payoff. Workers who already hold degrees may also accumulate micro-credentials more readily, potentially widening rather than narrowing gaps.

Economic theory offers a useful lens for understanding why degrees have proved so durable and why alternatives struggle to displace them. Michael Spence, in his 1973 article Job Market Signaling in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, modelled education as a costly signal: if acquiring a credential is less costly for more productive workers, employers can use the credential to infer productivity even when the education itself adds little to skills. Signalling theory does not imply that degrees teach nothing, and later empirical research has found evidence for both skill-building and signalling functions, but it explains why the value of a credential depends on what employers believe it reveals rather than solely on what it certifies. A four-year degree signals persistence, conformity to institutional expectations and the ability to complete a long programme, qualities that a short course certificate cannot easily convey, however precisely it documents a specific skill. This perspective suggests that micro-credentials may gain most traction where they certify skills that are directly observable and job-relevant, and where degrees have been used as a crude proxy for such skills, rather than where employers value the broader attributes that long programmes are thought to signal.

Experimental evidence on how employers respond to unfamiliar credentials supports caution. David Deming, Noam Yuchtman, Amira Abulafi, Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz, in a 2016 study in the American Economic Review, sent fictitious résumés to real job vacancies, varying the type of institution that had awarded applicants' credentials. They found that business bachelor's degrees from large online for-profit institutions received substantially fewer callbacks than similar degrees from nonselective public institutions, and that in health occupations, certificates from for-profit institutions generated no more callbacks than résumés with no postsecondary credential at all, except where the occupation required a licence. Because the design randomly assigned credentials to otherwise similar résumés, it provides causal evidence about employer screening responses, although it measures callbacks rather than eventual hiring or pay. The findings suggest that employers discount credentials from providers they do not know or trust, which is directly relevant to new micro-credentials and digital badges from issuers without established reputations.

Evidence on sub-degree certificates, the closest established analogue to micro-credentials, points to modest and uneven returns. Christopher Jepsen, Kenneth Troske and Paul Coomes, in a 2014 study in the Journal of Labor Economics using administrative data from Kentucky's community colleges, compared earnings before and after enrolment and found that associate degrees and diplomas were associated with substantial earnings gains, while shorter certificates were associated with smaller gains, with returns varying considerably by field of study and by gender. Studies of this kind rely on individual fixed-effects methods rather than randomisation, so they cannot fully rule out the possibility that students who complete credentials differ in unobserved ways from those who do not. They nonetheless suggest that credential length and field matter, and that short credentials in fields with clear occupational demand, such as health and skilled trades, tend to show stronger associations with earnings than short credentials in general fields. Whether online micro-credentials behave similarly to community college certificates remains largely untested, since most lack comparable administrative data on completers' earnings.

The case for alternatives partly rests on evidence that degree requirements have been applied more widely than jobs require. Joseph Fuller and Manjari Raman of Harvard Business School, in their 2017 report Dismissed by Degrees, analysed job postings and found that employers frequently requested bachelor's degrees for middle-skill roles in which most current incumbents did not hold degrees, a phenomenon they called degree inflation. They argued that this practice raised hiring costs, lengthened vacancies and excluded capable workers without degrees, disproportionately affecting lower-income workers and some racial and ethnic groups. The report relied on posting data and employer surveys rather than causal analysis, and its estimates of affected jobs depend on assumptions about which requirements are unnecessary. It nonetheless helped motivate the skills-based hiring movement whose implementation the later Burning Glass Institute analysis found to be limited, a sequence that illustrates the gap between recognising a problem in credentialing and changing hiring behaviour.

AI-based assessment of competencies raises questions that research on algorithmic hiring has begun to document. Manish Raghavan, Solon Barocas, Jon Kleinberg and Karen Levy, in a 2020 paper presented at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, reviewed the publicly available claims and practices of 18 vendors of algorithmic pre-employment assessments. They found that vendors disclosed limited information about how their assessments were validated, what outcomes they predicted, and how bias was measured and mitigated, and that many relied on a legal threshold for adverse impact that does not capture all forms of unfairness. AI-verified competency records share many features with these assessment tools, since both infer skills from performance data using models whose validity may be difficult for employers or learners to evaluate. If AI-issued credentials lack transparent validation, employers may discount them, and learners may be unable to contest inaccurate assessments that follow them across job applications.

Regulation of automated employment tools is beginning to address some of these concerns, with implications for AI-verified credentials used in hiring. New York City's Local Law 144, enforced by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection from July 2023, requires employers and employment agencies that use automated employment decision tools to substantially assist hiring or promotion decisions to obtain an independent bias audit, publish a summary of the results, and notify candidates that such tools are being used. The law applies to tools used in employment decisions rather than to credential issuers directly, but an employer that relied on an AI system to screen candidates based on machine-assessed competencies could fall within its scope. In Europe, the AI Act's classification of AI used in recruitment and in evaluating learning outcomes as high-risk, discussed in other answers in this collection, creates parallel obligations. These developments suggest that AI-verified credentials will increasingly need documented validation and bias testing if they are to be used in consequential decisions.

International comparisons show that the institutional setting strongly shapes how alternative credentials are received. In countries with strong vocational education systems and established qualification frameworks, such as Germany and Switzerland, new credentials tend to gain recognition when they are linked to existing occupational standards negotiated among employers, unions and the state. The European Union's 2022 Recommendation on micro-credentials reflects this approach by encouraging integration into national qualification frameworks rather than leaving recognition entirely to the market. In the United States, where credentialing is more decentralised and market-driven, alternatives have proliferated more rapidly but with less consistent quality assurance, which helps explain the mismatch between supply growth and employer uptake. Comparative research on labour-market returns to micro-credentials across these different systems remains scarce, but the contrast suggests that technical standards alone are unlikely to produce traction without institutional arrangements that give employers reasons to trust what a credential certifies.

Quality assurance remains the unresolved link between the technical infrastructure described earlier and employer trust. Open Badges 3.0 and European Digital Credentials make it possible to verify that a credential was genuinely issued and has not been altered, but cryptographic verification says nothing about whether the underlying assessment was rigorous or whether the skills it certifies are relevant to a job. Degrees are backed, however imperfectly, by accreditation systems, while many micro-credentials are issued by providers subject to no external review. The European Union's 2022 Recommendation addresses this by asking that micro-credentials be subject to internal and external quality assurance, and registries such as Credential Engine's aim to make descriptive information comparable. Until such mechanisms are widespread and employers understand them, the evidence reviewed here suggests that a verified badge from an unfamiliar issuer may carry little more weight than an unverified one.

The overall picture is one of rapid growth in supply, maturing technical standards, and supportive policy, alongside limited evidence of substantial labour-market returns. Independent longitudinal research tracking earnings and employment outcomes for holders of specific credentials, compared with similar workers without them, would be needed to establish whether these credentials function as genuine alternatives or remain supplements to traditional degrees.

## Chapter 7: The Evidence Base — What Research Actually Shows {#chapter-07}

12 questions · 119 citations · 112 unique sources · 60 cross-references

### Q051 What does current peer-reviewed evidence show about the effects of AI tutoring systems on learning outcomes, and how strong is that evidence? {#q051}

9 citations · 9 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI Tutoring Systems and Learning Outcomes: What the Evidence Shows

The question of whether AI tutoring systems genuinely improve learning is one of the most consequential in contemporary education research — and the honest answer, as of mid-2026, is that the evidence is promising but still maturing, with its quality varying considerably depending on the generation of technology being evaluated.

The older, pre-generative-AI strand of evidence is comparatively well-established. A meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations of intelligent tutoring systems found a median effect size of 0.66 standard deviations over conventional instruction — equivalent to moving a student from the 50th to the 75th percentile. Positive effect sizes were found at all levels of education and in nearly all subject domains evaluated, and the pattern held even after accounting for potential publication bias. These are meaningful numbers by educational research standards, where effect sizes above 0.4 are generally considered substantive. However, the magnitude of improvement depended heavily on whether outcomes were measured using locally developed or standardized tests, suggesting that alignment between test content and instructional objectives is a critical determinant of results.

The more recent wave of research concerns generative AI — systems built on large language models rather than rule-based logic — and here the evidence base is thinner but expanding rapidly. Many claims about the educational benefits of generative AI have outpaced high-quality evidence, but a number of recent rigorous studies suggest that tutoring systems integrating generative AI can deliver learning gains and offer a path to individualized education at scale. A 2025 randomized controlled trial published in *Scientific Reports* by researchers at Harvard is among the most cited: the study measured college students' learning when content was delivered through an AI-powered tutor compared with an active-learning class, finding that students learned significantly more in less time with the AI tutor, and also reported feeling more engaged and motivated. A separate exploratory RCT in UK secondary school classrooms found that an AI tutor integrated into a mathematics platform and supervised by human tutors produced a 5.5 percentage-point increase in students' likelihood of correctly answering novel questions.

Yet the picture is not uniformly positive, and a crucial caveat emerges from a large-scale field experiment published in *PNAS*. That study examined GPT-4's impact on student learning in mathematics and found that although AI-based tutoring improved performance during practice sessions, students who relied on the technology tended to underperform when AI access was subsequently removed — indicating reduced independent skill acquisition. The remedy, the researchers found, was deliberate design: carefully designed safeguards, especially asking the AI tutor to provide teacher-designed hints rather than giving away answers, can mitigate these negative effects. This finding is echoed in the broader literature: there are studies indicating that over-reliance on AI hints can worsen outcomes, and a systematic review by Zhai et al. (2024) associated regular use of AI dialogue and tutoring systems with a decline in students' cognitive abilities and an increased tendency for cognitive offloading.

The K-12 systematic review published in *npj Science of Learning* in 2025 provides a useful summary of where the evidence currently stands for younger learners: the effects of intelligent tutoring systems on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive but are mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems, and additional research with longer interventions and more diverse samples is warranted. The methodological problems are not trivial: empirical evidence remains scarce, and most published evaluations rely on user satisfaction metrics or short-duration laboratory tasks rather than rigorous field experimentation with validated learning outcome measures.

Two conclusions emerge from the current body of work. First, well-designed AI tutoring systems — particularly those that adapt to the learner, provide formative feedback, and resist simply handing over answers — can produce real academic gains, especially in structured domains like mathematics and science. Second, design choices matter enormously: safeguards that constrain how the AI assists are not merely a safety feature but a pedagogical necessity, required to ensure that human learning is actually preserved. The gap between a well-designed AI tutor and an unconstrained language model is not cosmetic — it may determine whether the technology helps students learn or merely helps them complete tasks.

### Q052 What does research reveal about how students actually use generative AI when unsupervised — as distinct from how they report using it? {#q052}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The gap between what students say they do with generative AI and what they actually do — when unobserved and unsurveyed — has become one of the more revealing and methodologically vexed problems in contemporary education research. The evidence accumulated by 2025 and 2026 cuts in several directions at once, but certain patterns are now firm enough to hold.

The headline numbers on self-reported usage are staggering on their own terms. Based on a survey of over one thousand UK undergraduates, the Higher Education Policy Institute found that the proportion of students using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for assessments jumped from 53 percent in 2024 to 88 percent in 2025. By 2026, AI use had become nearly universal, with 95 percent of students reporting using it in at least one way and 94 percent saying they use it to help with assessed work. The Copyleaks 2025 report broadly corroborates this trajectory: nearly 90 percent of students have used AI for academic purposes, with almost a third doing so daily and another 24 percent doing so several times per week.

These are self-reported figures, however, and the distance between what students declare and what they do in practice is precisely where the more interesting research lies. The most direct evidence of systematic underreporting comes from studies using list experiments — an anonymization technique that allows respondents to admit socially stigmatized behaviors without direct attribution. A study based on interviews and list experiments with 305 Indonesian undergraduates found that students were often reluctant to admit dishonest behavior when asked directly, but the anonymous list experiment method produced substantially higher admissions of AI-assisted cheating. A comparable quantitative study of 1,386 Vietnamese undergraduates using list experiments found a similar pattern: students tended to conceal AI-assisted cheating when asked directly. The mechanism, across both contexts, appears to be shame and social pressure rather than simple ignorance of the rules.

A further dimension of the gap concerns not misconduct per se, but covert use more broadly. Qualitative research from 2026, drawing on interviews with college students, found that there is a growing misalignment between students' AI adoption and existing institutional practices — around assessment, policy, and limited AI resources — and that this misalignment has led to covert AI usage, increased student anxiety, and an intention-behavior gap where students feel pressured into disregulated AI engagement. The title of that study captures the phenomenology with precision: "Everyone's using it, but no one is allowed to talk about it." Its results show that traditional assessment structures — characterized by tight deadlines, exam stacking, and graded homework — incentivize students to use AI for task completion rather than deep engagement. In other words, institutional design is actively producing the covert behavior it nominally prohibits.

What students actually use AI *for*, when conditions allow honesty, also diverges from the catastrophizing narratives common in faculty discourse. The most common reported uses are for AI to explain concepts, summarize articles, and suggest research ideas — functions closer to an advanced reference tool than a ghost-writing service. The proportion of students directly including AI-generated text in assessed work, while rising, stands at 12 percent as of 2026, up from 8 percent in 2025 and 3 percent in 2024. This matters: even as near-universal engagement is reported, wholesale text submission remains a minority behavior. The more common, less dramatic reality is iterative assistance at earlier stages of work.

What distorts disclosure, research suggests, is not chiefly moral recklessness but institutional ambiguity. Roughly one third of respondents in one study admitted some AI use, yet disclosure was rare — and this silence appeared to reflect not dishonesty but rational caution in the face of ambiguous policies and perceived academic risk. Contrary to what institutional leaders might assume, mere awareness of a university's AI policy does little to sway student views on whether using AI is ethical; formal guidance often trails behind the informal norms students create for themselves.

The picture that emerges is thus more complicated than either the "students are cheating en masse" or "students are using AI responsibly" framings allow. Students are using generative AI far more extensively than they disclose, particularly in high-stakes assessment contexts. That concealment is shaped less by calculated dishonesty than by a policy environment that criminalizes a technology students experience as ordinary, and by assessment structures that reward speed over depth. The behavior gap, in this sense, is partly an institutional creation.
