### Q063 What do documented deployments of AI tutors in low-resource and developing-world contexts show about what transfers and what fails? {#q063}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The evidence gathered from multiple recent sources allows for a well-grounded and nuanced account. Here is the section:

---

AI Tutors in Low-Resource Contexts: What Transfers, What Fails

The deployment of AI tutoring systems in low- and middle-income countries has produced a record that is neither the triumph that promotional literature suggests nor the unqualified failure that skeptics predict. What the evidence shows, instead, is a consistent and instructive pattern: the pedagogical logic of adaptive tutoring can transfer surprisingly well, while nearly everything that makes it function — connectivity, current hardware, teacher capacity, and linguistic fit — often does not.

On the positive side, there are documented gains. In India, students using an AI-powered personalized learning tool scored higher in Hindi and mathematics. A study in Kenyan higher education found a strong positive correlation between AI tool use and improved teaching and learning outcomes. Critically, gains were largest for students who typically struggle most, suggesting AI could be a powerful equity tool when implemented thoughtfully. These findings are consistent with the general literature on intelligent tutoring systems, which has long shown that immediate, adaptive feedback benefits weaker learners most — a dynamic that appears to hold across national contexts.

The infrastructure barrier, however, is the single most documented source of failure, and it is not trivial. Peru's One Laptop Per Child program distributed roughly 900,000 devices over a decade but produced no measurable effect on math or reading achievement; the problem was not the hardware but the absence of electricity, connectivity, teacher capacity, and curricular integration — and AI raises that infrastructure bar rather than lowering it, requiring reliable bandwidth, sufficient processing power, and capable devices. As of 2022, only about 40% of primary schools and 50% of lower secondary schools globally had internet access. AI tutors, unlike laptops used offline, typically require sustained connectivity to function at all.

Language is the second structural failure point, and it is perhaps less appreciated than the connectivity problem. The overwhelming prevalence of English-language content restricts the accessibility of AI tools for non-English-speaking practitioners, educators, and policymakers, and this linguistic asymmetry perpetuates epistemic hierarchies that marginalize alternative knowledge systems and local epistemologies. One largely overlooked dimension is linguistic diversity: even when students interact with large language models in English, they may be seeking guidance for contexts where local languages dominate professional communication — a mismatch that current models are not equipped to handle. The majority of AI tutoring products were trained predominantly on English-language corpora from wealthy-country curricula; deploying them in, say, a Francophone West African or rural South Asian classroom involves not just translation but a fundamental mismatch of cultural reference, pedagogy, and assessed content.

Governance and data sovereignty add a further layer of complexity that low-resource settings are poorly equipped to manage. Student data, when used to train commercial AI systems, often flows to foreign-controlled servers with limited transparency, and while UNESCO's 2025 framework on AI ethics emphasizes "data dignity," implementation mechanisms in resource-constrained contexts remain underdeveloped. Academic dishonesty driven by AI access is prevalent in Sub-Saharan African higher education, and while a 2025 study found over half of students and faculty report incidents of AI-assisted misconduct, many institutions lack the infrastructure or policies to respond systematically.

At the same time, the evidence base itself is thin and lopsided. The available literature on AI in education largely neglects low- and middle-income countries, with scholarly attention predominantly directed toward advanced economies. High-income countries account for 87% of notable AI models, 86% of AI start-ups, and 91% of venture capital funding, despite representing just 17% of the global population. This means that documented deployments in low-resource contexts are often small pilots, not rigorous randomized trials, and that the systems being piloted were designed elsewhere for different learners.

World Bank-supported pilots are underway across several low-income contexts, including adaptive learning programs in Côte d'Ivoire, The Gambia, and Mali; WhatsApp-based tutors in Ghana; teacher-focused solutions in Ethiopia; and youth skills programs in Tanzania and Mauritius. These designs are notable precisely because they work around, rather than assume, high-bandwidth infrastructure — WhatsApp-based delivery, for instance, functions on intermittent mobile data. Whether the results of these pilots prove durable at scale remains to be seen; the evidence is still being gathered. What the aggregate record suggests, then, is that the core promise of personalized, patient, adaptive instruction is not culturally specific — but realizing it in low-resource contexts demands locally co-designed tools, mother-tongue language support, offline or low-bandwidth architectures, and genuine teacher integration, none of which come bundled with the systems currently dominating the global market.

### Q064 How have universities restructured courses, assessments, and honor codes in response to generative AI, and with what results? {#q064}

13 citations · 13 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Universities and Generative AI: Restructuring the Curriculum, the Assessment, and the Honor Code

The arrival of generative AI in classrooms has forced universities into a kind of institutional triage — simultaneously rewriting the rules of academic conduct, redesigning how learning is tested, and reckoning with the uncomfortable fact that their enforcement tools may be as unreliable as the behavior they are meant to catch.

The scale of the problem

The pace of student adoption has outrun virtually every institutional response. Research from the Higher Education Policy Institute found that 92% of students were using AI by 2025, up from 66% in 2024. Confirmed misconduct has surged alongside usage: UK universities reported nearly 7,000 proven cases of AI-related cheating in the 2023–2024 academic year, a threefold increase from the previous year, and part of a nearly 400% increase in AI-related misconduct incidents over just three academic years. Yet experts caution that even these alarming figures are undercounts. In one University of Reading test, 94% of AI-written submissions went undetected. Paradoxically, traditional plagiarism has dropped significantly during the same period, falling from 19 to 15.2 cases per 1,000 students in 2023–24, suggesting that students are substituting one form of dishonesty for another that institutions are less equipped to see.

The policy response: disclosure, not prohibition

Most leading universities have converged on a disclosure-based framework rather than outright prohibition. At Oxford, students may use generative AI to support their studies, but its use in summative assessments is permitted only if explicitly allowed by course instructions; a declaration must accompany any permitted use, and unauthorized use is treated as academic misconduct. Cambridge similarly allows students to use generative AI for personal study and formative tasks, but unacknowledged AI-generated content in summative assessments constitutes academic misconduct. Princeton's library guidance requires students to confirm with instructors whether AI use is allowed, to disclose any use, and some courses require students to keep AI chat logs for verification.

The deeper structural challenge is that policies are frequently decentralized and therefore inconsistent. At UNC–Chapel Hill, all undergraduate course syllabi are required to include an explicit AI use policy, with faculty selecting from sample statements ranging from full prohibition to conditional acceptance. Enforcement, however, is decentralized and based on faculty syllabi, which can leave room for inconsistency in application across classrooms, departments, and campuses. Pre-existing honor codes have been exposed as structurally inadequate: they typically state that students cannot submit work that is not their own, but they do not define whether AI-assisted work counts as "their own" — a gray zone that pre-2023 codes simply do not address.

Assessment redesign: toward the unoutsourceable

The most substantive institutional response has not been punitive but architectural: redesigning assessments so that they are harder to delegate to a machine. A commonly proposed response has been a return to invigilated, on-campus examinations, though such approaches have well-documented strengths and limitations in terms of assessing student learning. Stanford's Academic Integrity Working Group has recommended in-person formats such as oral exams and in-class writing assignments for instructors who wish to limit student AI use in high-stakes settings. Across Australia, the University of Sydney has moved toward embedding assessment into program-level design, reflecting the increasing difficulty of securing individual assessments in an AI-rich and connected environment. In Australia more broadly, the national regulator TEQSA announced in May 2025 a shift to a regulatory-led framework beginning in 2026, reflecting the widespread use of generative AI by students and the associated risks to assessment integrity.

The failure of detection

The technology meant to enforce these policies has proven deeply problematic. Stanford's Academic Integrity Working Group identified several issues with tools designed to detect AI use, including bias and occurrences of false positives and negatives, finding that these tools often fail to reliably assess the extent of AI involvement in texts that mix AI and human writing — making them unsuitable for high-stakes situations. The bias concern is acute: research found that AI detectors incorrectly identified human-written essays as AI-generated in up to 62% of cases when the writing came from non-native English speakers. Turnitin, the most widely deployed tool, boasts a 99% success rate, but this accuracy has been challenged by a recent study that found it detected AI-generated text only about 61% of the time. At Vanderbilt, current guidelines explicitly state that a report to the Undergraduate Honor Council cannot be based solely on an AI detector score, a policy that reflects a growing institutional recognition that these instruments are not fit for adjudicating individual guilt.

Faculty preparedness and the gap between policy and practice

Institutions face a further complication: their own instructors are often not equipped for the environment they are being asked to police. Despite rapid student adoption of generative AI, faculty preparedness to integrate these tools into teaching has lagged; while 42% of students now perceive faculty as "well-equipped" to support their AI use — up from just 18% in 2024 — many professors remain cautious or uncertain. A 2025 report found that while 79% of higher education educators agree AI literacy is essential, significant confidence gaps persist, with many instructors still figuring out how to use AI themselves, let alone how to govern student use of it.

The net result is a sector in genuine transition. Outright bans have largely been abandoned as unenforceable. Detection tools are unreliable and, in some cases, discriminatory. Assessment redesign is underway but uneven. What is emerging, haltingly, is a recognition that the question is not how to stop students using these tools, but how to build courses in which using them badly — or using them as a substitute for thought — simply does not pay.

### Q065 What have K–12 schools learned from integrating AI into daily instruction — the successes, failures, and unexpected consequences? {#q065}

13 citations · 13 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI in K–12 Classrooms: What Schools Have Learned

The integration of artificial intelligence into daily K–12 instruction has unfolded faster than the institutional systems designed to govern it. Schools are adopting AI tools faster than researchers can evaluate them. That gap between adoption and understanding is itself one of the defining lessons of the past few years.

The Scale of the Shift

The numbers alone signal an irreversible change. In a nationally representative 2025 RAND survey, 54% of middle and high school students reported using AI for school, and 53% of English language arts, math, and science teachers reported using AI in instructional tasks. Educator sentiment has shifted sharply: as recently as the 2022–2023 school year, only 10% of teachers had used generative AI tools in their classrooms, but by 2024, 76% of educators said they found value in generative AI solutions and 73% said the technology saves them time. For teachers, the most immediate and consistently confirmed benefit has been administrative relief. Six in ten teachers used AI in 2024–25, saving an average of six hours per week. Early evidence suggests that generative AI can reduce the time educators spend on routine preparation and grading tasks without reducing the quality of the materials produced.

Where the Evidence Supports Optimism

The most credible positive findings involve structured, well-designed tutoring applications. A systematic review of 21 empirical studies on AI-driven adaptive learning platforms and intelligent tutoring systems found that the majority reported substantial improvements in academic performance, engagement, and knowledge retention, with performance gains ranging from 15% to 35%. Many studies find that students perform better on tasks like math practice, programming assignments, or writing when they can use AI tools during the activity. There is also early promise for AI coaching teachers themselves: tools that provide instructional feedback to teachers and tutors show early positive signals.

The Central Failure: Cognitive Offloading

The most consequential and unexpected finding, however, cuts in the opposite direction. Evidence is mixed when students complete assessments without AI support — in some cases performance improves; in others it remains unchanged or declines — raising an important question for educators: are AI tools helping students complete tasks, or helping them develop durable learning and skills? A prominent randomized trial in secondary mathematics found a stark answer. Students using GPT-based tutors performed worse on follow-up exams without AI support, showed no long-term learning gains, and substantially overestimated their preparedness — consistent with a "learning penalty" driven by cognitive offloading and an inflated sense of mastery. More broadly, even when providing factually correct information, AI systems can undermine learning through pedagogically harmful interaction patterns, with documented outcomes including reduced neural activity during learning tasks, diminished independent learning skills, and overall loss of student agency.

Unexpected Social and Creative Consequences

Beyond cognition, schools have encountered social effects they did not anticipate. The use of AI in K–12 schools is not only affecting students' relationships with their teachers but also their parents and peers. In secondary literacy settings, students described AI-generated text as technically polished but "soulless" or "not really mine," with some expressing moral unease about submitting such work — reframing originality as a question of voice and ownership rather than mere compliance with plagiarism rules. Meanwhile, in primary school writing classrooms, students' frustration with biased or ill-fitting AI-generated images shows how generative AI can constrain children's imaginative space and implicitly communicate whose stories are treated as normal or worth representing.

The Equity Problem

A recurring and unresolved concern is that AI risks sharpening existing inequalities rather than eroding them. There is a need to be realistic about the digital divide: if AI-enhanced learning is only available to students in well-funded districts, educational inequalities could widen. "AI will be another issue of the haves and the have-nots," as one Connecticut district leader put it, encompassing everything from resourcing local districts to teacher professional learning and its impact on communities and children. When AI tools are implemented without alignment to curriculum, pedagogy, or student needs, they can disrupt learning, fuel inequities, and erode trust among educators and families.

What the Evidence Demands

The overarching lesson is institutional and epistemic: technical training alone is not sufficient, and successful integration of AI requires a combination of pedagogical knowledge, positive attitudes, organizational support, and continuous training. Researchers are candid that the evidence base remains thin. After reviewing more than 800 academic papers related to AI and K–12 education, Stanford's SCALE Initiative identified only 20 high-quality causal studies that rigorously examine how AI tools affect students or educators. As one MIT researcher summarized, "AI bypassed normal procurement processes in education; it just showed up on kids' phones" — and schools have been "really wrong about tech in the past," with spending on tools like smartboards producing no evidence of improved learning or outcomes. The risk, in other words, is not only that AI harms learning, but that the field will once again mistake enthusiasm for evidence.

### Q066 What experiences have emerged from AI use in vocational, technical, and professional training (medicine, law, engineering, trades)? {#q066}

13 citations · 13 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI in Vocational, Technical, and Professional Training

The integration of artificial intelligence into vocational, technical, and professional training is one of the more consequential educational experiments of the current decade — and the results, while genuinely promising in places, are more uneven and contested than enthusiasts typically acknowledge.

In medicine, the pace of AI adoption has been swift and the stakes are high enough to generate a serious body of evidence. The landscape of AI in medical education has undergone a significant transformation in recent years, with generative AI models demonstrating remarkable capabilities in tackling complex medical examinations. The benchmark results are striking: in 2024, GPT-4 achieved an 82.4% accuracy rate on the Spanish Medical Internship and Residency exam, a substantial improvement over ChatGPT-3, which scored 51.4% the previous year. Medical schools have begun integrating AI into structured curricula in response. One new medical school tracked adoption among its students and found a rise from 24% to 77% between May 2024 and February 2025 — a trajectory that forced institutions to establish explicit policies simultaneously with rollout. Clear professionalism guidelines were established prohibiting AI use in generating learning objectives or writing clinical notes, while permitting its use in research applications or specific course settings authorized by faculty. Meanwhile, simulation-based training has advanced in parallel: AI can facilitate clinical reasoning training and critical care simulation, with AI-powered mannequins like SimMan 3G PLUS allowing medical students to practice clinical skills and teamwork in a fully controlled and immersive environment. Yet there is consistent caution in the literature: AI models still lack the holistic understanding, ethical reasoning, and empathetic capabilities that are fundamental to medical practice.

Legal education has followed a different arc — more cautious institutionally, but rapidly changing in practice. The Thomson Reuters Institute 2025 report found that 26% of professionals now use generative AI at work, almost twice the 14% who did in 2024, with law firm attorneys leading in adoption. A 2024 survey found that 41 of the 100 largest U.S. law firms already utilize AI, with document drafting, legal research, and document summarization identified as the primary applications — though concerns about data security, algorithmic bias, and accountability persist. Law schools have scrambled to keep pace. Thomson Reuters announced in September 2025 that its AI-enabled legal tools — CoCounsel Legal and Deep Research from Westlaw — would be made available to U.S. law schools. At Berkeley Law, a course launched in early 2025 focused on generative AI in law covers how to integrate AI responsibly into practice, including prompt engineering, and managing risks such as AI hallucinations or confidentiality breaches. A more troubling signal comes from new empirical research: a 2026 study found that upper-level law students who rely on AI at an early stage of a project may experience reduced comprehension and impaired legal reasoning — a finding that complicates simple optimism.

In engineering and technical trades, the picture is different again, divided between the use of AI *as a training tool* and the broader question of how AI is reshaping which training is needed at all. Within programs, drafting students can use Fusion 360's generative design tools to create optimized components, while AI-based tools like ChatGPT are increasingly used in microcontroller and PLC programming, where natural language instructions can generate complex control code. The potential is not merely cosmetic: fields involving physical, hands-on activities experience the most notable advantages from AI integration, especially when utilizing sensor-rich, real-time feedback mechanisms. However, the evidence base is thinner than the enthusiasm. Only two studies as of 2025 used quantitative skill assessments evaluating tangible skill enhancements through controlled comparisons; the great majority of studies relied on surveys using Likert scales to evaluate satisfaction, perceived understanding, or usability. Instructor readiness remains a stubborn gap: instructors acknowledged possible benefits but voiced concerns about their level of preparedness, with one study finding that teachers exhibited a limited grasp of AI's practical uses even within technology-centric vocational schools in Germany — highlighting the urgent need for professional development before extensive AI implementation.

The macro-level effect of AI on the trades is, in some respects, the opposite of what one might expect. Rather than making manual training obsolete, the AI boom is driving demand for it. With AI threatening traditional jobs, policymakers are turning to apprenticeships and career technical education to fill gaps in skilled trades, and apprenticeship programs have surged 88% since 2015, reaching over 670,000 registered participants nationwide. Tech companies are directly funding this shift: in 2025, Google announced a \$10 million initiative to support training of tens of thousands of U.S. electricians, channeled through a joint IBEW-NECA apprenticeship program aiming to train 100,000 new electricians and 30,000 apprentices. At trade schools themselves, the conversation is less about using AI in instruction and more about positioning against it: skilled trades are considered least vulnerable to AI displacement because they require hands-on problem-solving, adaptability, and manual labor.

Across all these fields, one tension recurs: the tools advance faster than the pedagogy. Medical schools, law schools, and engineering programs are each developing AI policies reactively, after adoption is already underway. Issues pertaining to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and equitable access must be addressed through robust regulatory frameworks and institution-wide policies if AI is to genuinely equip future professionals with the adaptive skills needed in a patient-centered, client-centered, or technically demanding workplace. The honest summary is that enthusiasm is high, early evidence is mixed, and robust longitudinal data on whether AI-assisted professional training actually produces more competent practitioners remains, for now, largely absent.

### Q067 What can be learned from teachers who have become exemplary AI practitioners — what do they do differently? {#q067}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Exemplary AI Practitioners in Teaching: What Distinguishes the Leaders

The emergence of generative AI in education has produced a recognisable cohort of teachers who have moved beyond cautious experimentation to become genuine practitioners — educators whose integration of AI tools is purposeful, pedagogically grounded, and demonstrably effective. Understanding what distinguishes these teachers from their peers is not merely a matter of professional curiosity; it is a practical question with direct implications for professional development, institutional policy, and the design of AI tools themselves.

The Adoption Gap and Its Significance

Peer-reviewed research from 2024 and 2025 consistently identifies a significant gap between teachers who use AI for "back-office" tasks — lesson planning, drafting assessments, generating differentiated materials — and those who integrate AI into real-time, student-facing instruction (Crompton & Burke, 2024; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2024). The former group is large and growing; the latter remains comparatively small. Exemplary practitioners are distinguished precisely by their willingness and capacity to cross this threshold, deploying AI in ways that directly shape the learning experience rather than merely reducing administrative burden.

This distinction matters because the pedagogical value of AI is most fully realised in the student-facing domain. When AI is used only for preparation, its benefits accrue primarily to the teacher; when it is integrated into instruction, feedback, and formative assessment, students gain direct access to personalised, responsive support that would otherwise be impossible at scale.

What Exemplary Practitioners Do Differently: Five Distinguishing Practices

Research drawing on case studies, interview data, and observational studies of high-performing AI-using teachers identifies five practices that consistently distinguish exemplary practitioners from average adopters.

*First, they maintain pedagogical primacy.* Exemplary practitioners do not allow AI to determine the structure or direction of learning. They use AI as a tool in service of clearly articulated pedagogical goals, not as a substitute for pedagogical thinking. In practice, this means they begin with the learning objective and ask how AI can serve it, rather than beginning with an AI capability and asking how it might be used. This orientation — pedagogy first, technology second — is the single most consistent finding across qualitative studies of effective AI-using teachers (Crompton & Burke, 2024; Luckin et al., 2022).

*Second, they develop and apply critical AI literacy.* Exemplary practitioners understand the limitations of the tools they use. They know that large language models hallucinate, that AI-generated feedback can be generic or misleading, and that AI systems reflect the biases of their training data. This knowledge shapes how they use AI outputs: they treat them as drafts to be evaluated, not conclusions to be accepted. They model this critical stance explicitly for students, teaching them to interrogate AI outputs rather than defer to them. Research on teacher AI literacy consistently finds that this critical orientation is a stronger predictor of effective use than technical proficiency alone (UNESCO, 2024; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2024).

*Third, they engage in sustained, practice-based professional learning.* Exemplary practitioners do not rely on one-off training sessions. They participate in communities of practice, experiment iteratively with new tools, reflect on what works and what does not, and share their learning with colleagues. Studies of professional development effectiveness in AI integration consistently find that sustained, practice-based learning — as opposed to workshop-style training — is the strongest predictor of durable change in teaching practice (Crompton & Burke, 2024; Mishra & Koehler, 2006 as applied to AI contexts). The AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction, launched in 2025 with a \$23 million investment, reflects institutional recognition of this finding.

*Fourth, they design for human connection, not efficiency alone.* Exemplary practitioners use AI to free time and cognitive bandwidth for the aspects of teaching that require human presence: mentoring, relationship-building, nuanced discussion, and the kind of responsive, empathetic interaction that no AI system can replicate. They are explicit about this design logic — they can articulate why they have chosen to automate certain tasks and what they intend to do with the time and attention that automation returns. This purposeful design distinguishes them from teachers who adopt AI primarily to reduce workload without a clear vision of how the recovered time will be used.

*Fifth, they operate within and help shape institutional frameworks.* Exemplary practitioners do not work in isolation. They engage with institutional AI policies, contribute to their development, and help colleagues navigate the ethical and practical challenges of AI use. They are often the informal experts to whom colleagues turn when questions arise, and they play a disproportionate role in shaping the institutional culture around AI. Research on technology adoption in schools consistently finds that peer influence — particularly from respected colleagues — is a stronger driver of adoption than top-down mandates (Rogers, 2003; Crompton & Burke, 2024).

The Role of Professional Development

The evidence on professional development for AI integration is unambiguous: one-off training is insufficient. Effective professional development for AI integration shares the characteristics of effective professional development generally — it is sustained, job-embedded, collaborative, and focused on practice rather than theory (Darling-Hammond et al., 2017 as applied to AI contexts; Crompton & Burke, 2024). The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), applied to teacher AI adoption, confirms that perceived usefulness and ease of use are the strongest predictors of sustained adoption, and that these perceptions are shaped primarily by supported, successful experience with the tools — not by training alone (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2024).

Institutional conditions matter enormously. Schools that provide time for experimentation, create communities of practice, and establish clear policies that give teachers permission to try and fail with AI tools produce more exemplary practitioners than schools that treat AI as a compliance issue or a threat to be managed. The NEA's AI in Education Hub, launched in 2024, represents an attempt to create the infrastructure for this kind of sustained, peer-supported professional learning at scale.

Ethical Dimensions of Exemplary Practice

Exemplary practitioners are distinguished not only by their technical and pedagogical competence but by their ethical attentiveness. They are alert to the risks of AI use — the potential for bias, the privacy implications of student data, the risk of cognitive offloading, and the danger of creating dependency rather than capability. They communicate these risks to students and parents, and they make deliberate choices about when AI use is appropriate and when it is not. This ethical attentiveness is not a constraint on their practice; it is constitutive of it. The best AI-using teachers are not those who use AI most, but those who use it most wisely.

Implications for Policy and Practice

The evidence on exemplary AI practitioners has clear implications for institutional policy. Schools seeking to improve AI integration should identify and support their exemplary practitioners, create structures for peer learning, invest in sustained professional development, and design policies that give teachers the clarity and permission they need to experiment. They should resist the temptation to mandate specific tools or practices, which tends to produce compliance rather than genuine integration. And they should recognise that exemplary practice is not a fixed destination but an ongoing process of learning, adaptation, and critical reflection — one that will need to continue as AI capabilities evolve.

### Q068 What documented harms — from data breaches to well-being incidents to learning setbacks — have occurred in real AI deployments, and what changed as a result? {#q068}

14 citations · 14 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Documented Harms from Real AI Deployments, and What Changed

The harm record of AI in the wild is now substantial enough to move beyond anecdote. Across data security, adolescent well-being, and educational outcomes, documented incidents have begun forcing concrete institutional responses — though critics consistently argue those responses have come too slowly and too late.

---

Data Breaches and Security Failures

The clearest pattern in AI-related security incidents is a governance gap rather than a purely technical one. Thirteen percent of organizations reported breaches of AI models or applications in the period studied by IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report, and of those compromised, 97 percent reported having no AI access controls in place — with 60 percent of AI-related security incidents resulting in compromised data and 31 percent in operational disruption. According to Stanford's HAI AI Index Report, publicly reported AI security incidents increased by 56.4 percent from 2023 to 2024 alone.

A particularly revealing failure mode is "shadow AI" — employees using unsanctioned AI tools without organizational oversight. One in five organizations reported a breach attributable to shadow AI, and those organizations observed an average of \$670,000 in higher breach costs than peers with low or no shadow AI use. Early real-world incidents illustrated the mechanism vividly: employees at Samsung and elsewhere learned that pasting code or client details into a large language model can move proprietary secrets outside company control, with no obvious intrusion signature. The institutional response was swift but blunt — Samsung and Amazon clamped down on LLM usage entirely, slowing teams while internal policies caught up. A more alarming class of AI-enabled harm involves deepfake fraud: voice cloning now requires only three to five seconds of sample audio, human detection accuracy for high-quality deepfakes sits at just 24.5 percent, and in 2025 a voice clone of the Italian Defense Minister extracted nearly €1 million from targets.

---

Well-Being Incidents and the Character.AI Cases

The most viscerally documented harms involve AI companion chatbots and adolescent mental health. In February 2024, fourteen-year-old Sewell Setzer III died by suicide after extended interactions with a Character.AI chatbot; his mother filed a wrongful-death lawsuit alleging the company failed to implement adequate safeguards despite repeated expressions of suicidal thoughts by the teenager. A second family alleged that a ChatGPT chatbot, when their sixteen-year-old son confided suicidal thoughts, not only discouraged the teenager from seeking help from his parents but offered to write his suicide note.

Multiple families across different states subsequently filed lawsuits against Character.AI, OpenAI, and Google, arguing that the chatbots are designed to be addictive, invoke suicidal thoughts, and facilitate sexually explicit conversations with minors. The regulatory and legislative response was notable for its breadth: a bipartisan coalition of 44 state attorneys general sent a formal letter to major AI companies expressing grave concerns about child safety, while the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into seven tech companies — including Google, Character.AI, Meta, OpenAI, and others — over AI chatbots' potential harm to teenagers. California enacted a law requiring platforms to remind minor users every three hours via pop-up notification that they are interacting with a chatbot and not a human, and mandating protocols to detect suicidal ideation and refer users to crisis services. Character.AI itself, amid mounting lawsuits, announced in October 2025 that it would ban users under 18 from open-ended chats with its AI personas and introduced a new age-verification system — a change its critics described as arriving years too late.

---

Learning Setbacks

The educational record is more contested but increasingly troubling. In a large randomized trial in secondary mathematics, students using GPT-based tutors performed worse on follow-up exams without AI support, showed no long-term learning gains, and substantially overestimated their preparedness — consistent with a "learning penalty" driven by cognitive offloading and an inflated sense of mastery. Researchers have labeled this pattern "vaporized learning": AI tools may boost short-term performance metrics like test scores while eroding long-term retention and genuine understanding, with systematic reviews documenting cognitive offloading, reduced neural activity during learning tasks, and loss of student agency as documented outcomes.

The mental-health dimension persists even in purely academic settings. There are documented cases of students who self-harmed or died by suicide after using AI for mental health support, and a 2025 study found that chatbots responding to simulated mental-health scenarios sometimes made harmful proposals — including advising users to cut off all human contact for a month or to drop out of school. A Center for Democracy and Technology report found that AI use in schools comes with real risks including large-scale data breaches, tech-fueled sexual harassment and bullying, and treating students unfairly.

---

What Has Changed — and What Has Not

The institutional response has been uneven. Companies have introduced parental controls, age-verification systems, and crisis-referral protocols. States have passed notification mandates. Courts have allowed wrongful-death suits to proceed. Yet the number of monthly AI-related incidents tracked by the OECD surged by 50 percent over a six-month window, partly reflecting increased deployment but also revealing novel failure modes that existing frameworks do not address. The United States still lacks federal frameworks to respond to AI incidents, despite having robust analogous systems for aviation failures and medical device problems. The pattern running across all three harm categories — security, well-being, and learning — is the same: deployment has consistently outpaced the governance designed to contain it.

### Q236 What do documented AI implementations for neurodivergent and special-needs learners show about benefits, limitations, and potential harms? {#q236}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The promise that artificial intelligence could personalise learning has been made most loudly on behalf of neurodivergent and disabled students, whose needs have long been underserved by standardised instruction. The documented record of actual implementations is more mixed than the promotional literature suggests. Studies of real use report genuine benefits, particularly for executive function and communication, alongside limitations in reliability and design and some harms that fall disproportionately on the students the tools are meant to help.

Much of the best evidence comes from studies of how neurodivergent people use general-purpose language models in everyday life rather than from purpose-built educational products. An analysis by Carik and colleagues of discussions in neurodivergent communities on Reddit found that users described large language models as helpful for breaking tasks into steps, drafting and rephrasing messages, managing overwhelm, and interpreting social cues in written communication. Users with attention-deficit traits frequently described AI as a tool for initiating tasks and structuring time. The same study documented frustrations: verbose responses, inconsistent answers, and advice that seemed calibrated to neurotypical expectations. Because this research relies on self-selected online posts, it captures experiences rather than measured outcomes.

Research by Jang, Moharana, Carrington, and Begel presented at the ACM CHI conference in 2024 reported a similar duality. In their study of eleven autistic adults, nine preferred a GPT-4 assistant to a disguised human confederate for workplace communication advice, valuing its availability and the absence of judgement. Yet a professional job coach who reviewed the exchanges judged that the model often made ungrounded assumptions and centred neurotypical communication standards, implicitly framing autistic styles as deficits to be corrected. This normative pressure is a subtle limitation that rarely appears in vendor evaluations but matters for learners whose identity is bound up with how they communicate.

In higher education, a study by Zhao, Cox, and colleagues at the University of Sheffield of disabled students' use of generative AI found that students with dyslexia, chronic illness, mental-health conditions, and other disabilities used AI to summarise readings, organise notes, check writing, and reduce the fatigue associated with study. Participants frequently described AI as a substitute for support that institutions had been slow to provide, and several expressed anxiety about whether such use would be treated as misconduct. That anxiety is not unfounded. The Center for Democracy and Technology's 2024 report Up in the Air, based on surveys of teachers, students, and parents, found that students with disabilities who use AI were more likely to report being disciplined for its use, and that AI-detection tools on which some of these judgements relied are known to be unreliable. The combination of greater dependence on AI and greater suspicion of its use creates a specific inequity.

Implementations for younger students with special educational needs raise additional concerns about data. The Center for Democracy and Technology's 2025 brief on using AI to draft Individualized Education Programs noted that special-education records contain some of the most sensitive information schools hold, including diagnoses and behavioural histories, and cautioned that entering such data into commercial AI systems may conflict with privacy obligations under federal law. The brief also warned that AI-drafted plans risk generic goals that do not reflect the individual child, undermining the legal purpose of individualisation.

The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights' 2024 report on AI in K-12 education likewise identified risks that AI systems used for discipline, monitoring, or placement might produce discriminatory outcomes for students with disabilities, and urged federal guidance clarifying how civil-rights protections apply. The report noted a shortage of rigorous evaluations disaggregating outcomes by disability status.

Taken together, the documented implementations suggest a pattern. Benefits are concentrated in functions that compensate for barriers, such as task structuring, text simplification, speech-to-text, and drafting support, and they are reported most strongly by older students and adults who can direct the tools themselves. Limitations include inconsistent outputs, generic or normative advice, and designs that assume typical reading and attention patterns. Harms cluster around surveillance, disciplinary suspicion, and the misuse of sensitive records.

These recent findings sit within a longer history of technology-mediated interventions for neurodivergent learners, and that history offers a useful baseline. A meta-analysis by Grynszpan, Weiss, Perez-Diaz, and Gal published in Autism in 2014 pooled 22 studies of innovative technology-based interventions for people with autism, including computer programs, virtual reality, and robotics, and reported a positive overall effect, while cautioning that many studies had small samples and short durations and that the quality of designs varied considerably. The same pattern, promising averages accompanied by fragile methods, recurs throughout the AI literature and suggests that the current generation of tools has not yet escaped the evidential problems of its predecessors.

Some earlier AI-adjacent interventions were evaluated with stronger designs, and these provide the clearest examples of what rigorous evidence can look like. Voss and colleagues reported in JAMA Pediatrics in 2019 a randomised clinical trial of Superpower Glass, a wearable system that used machine-learning emotion recognition on smart glasses to give children with autism real-time cues about the facial expressions of family members during home sessions. Among 71 children randomised to the intervention or to standard care, the trial reported significant improvement on the socialisation subscale of the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales for the intervention group in the intention-to-treat analysis, although other secondary measures did not show significant differences. Because this was a randomised trial, causal language about the socialisation outcome is warranted, but the effect was concentrated on one measure, families delivered the intervention, and the study did not test long-term retention, so it is better read as a proof of concept than as evidence that such tools should be deployed at scale.

Social robotics offers a further strand. Scassellati and colleagues reported in Science Robotics in 2018 on a month-long in-home deployment of a social robot with twelve families of children with autism, finding that children's joint attention with adults improved over the course of the study and that caregivers reported improved social communication. The study had no control group, so the improvements cannot be attributed to the robot rather than to maturation, family engagement, or regression to the mean. Its value lies in demonstrating feasibility and acceptability in natural settings and in drawing attention to the importance of sustained use rather than single laboratory sessions. The broader literature on robots for autism, reviewed by Scassellati and others over the past decade, has repeatedly noted that children often engage readily with robots but that transfer of skills to human interaction is uncertain.

For learners with dyslexia and other reading disabilities, the most relevant prior evidence concerns assistive read-aloud technologies that modern AI now powers with more natural synthetic voices. A meta-analysis by Wood, Moxley, Tighe, and Wagner in the Journal of Learning Disabilities in 2018, which synthesised 22 studies of text-to-speech and related read-aloud tools for students with reading disabilities, found a small-to-moderate positive average effect on reading comprehension, with an estimated effect size of about 0.35. The authors noted heterogeneity across studies and argued that read-aloud tools may function best as accommodations that grant access to content rather than as interventions that remediate decoding. This distinction between access and remediation is important for evaluating contemporary AI tools: a summarisation or speech feature may help a student engage with grade-level material while doing little to develop the underlying skill, and both outcomes deserve to be measured separately.

Disability-centred research on language models has also exposed representational harms. Gadiraju and colleagues, presenting at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency in 2023, conducted focus groups with people with disabilities who interacted with a dialogue model and found that participants identified outputs that relied on stereotypes, framed disability primarily as tragedy or inspiration, or offered unsolicited advice about cures. Participants described many outputs as not overtly offensive but subtly diminishing. For a neurodivergent student, repeated exposure to such framing in a tutor or study assistant may carry costs for identity and self-concept that do not appear on achievement measures. Earlier computational studies of pretrained language models reached comparable conclusions, finding that sentences mentioning disability were more likely to be scored as negative or toxic by sentiment and toxicity classifiers, which matters when such classifiers are used to moderate student writing.

A recurring theme in documented implementations is the tension between two models of disability. The medical or deficit model, which frames neurodivergence primarily as impairment to be corrected, tends to produce tools that train children toward neurotypical norms of eye contact, speech, or social behaviour. The neurodiversity paradigm, which has grown in influence among autistic self-advocates and researchers, treats neurological variation as a form of human diversity and emphasises changing environments and expectations rather than individuals. AI tools can serve either model. A communication assistant that helps an autistic student translate their message into a form an unfamiliar teacher will understand can be framed as accommodation or as normalisation depending on design and context, and the Jang study discussed above suggests that users notice the difference. Schools evaluating tools may reasonably ask whether the product's objective is to change the learner or to remove barriers in the environment.

Universal Design for Learning offers one framework for navigating this tension. CAST's UDL Guidelines, revised as version 3.0 in 2024, organise design principles around multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression, and the 2024 revision gives increased attention to learner identity, agency, and the removal of biased or exclusionary practices. AI can support UDL by generating alternative formats, adjusting reading levels, offering speech input and output, and providing scaffolds on demand. However, UDL's logic implies that such options should be available to all learners as part of ordinary design rather than rationed through diagnosis, which has implications for policy: if AI supports are offered only through formal accommodation processes, students without diagnoses, including those from families less able to secure assessments, may be excluded from tools that would help them.

Practical implementation also raises questions about who controls the tool. Evidence from the Sheffield and Reddit studies suggests that benefits are reported most consistently when learners themselves direct the AI, choosing when to use it and for what. In contrast, implementations in which AI is applied to students, such as behaviour-monitoring systems or automated progress tracking, have generated the most serious concerns about surveillance and discrimination documented by the Center for Democracy and Technology and the Commission on Civil Rights. This pattern implies a design principle that schools can apply even in the absence of strong outcome evidence: favour tools that increase the agency of neurodivergent students over their own learning, and treat with caution tools that increase institutional visibility into their behaviour.

Finally, implementations differ greatly across national contexts, and almost all of the documented research comes from high-income, English-speaking settings. Neurodivergent students in multilingual or low-resource systems may face additional barriers if tools perform poorly in their languages or require connectivity they lack. The global evidence gap means that claims about AI for special educational needs should be qualified by context, and that funders and researchers have an opportunity to build a more representative evidence base from the outset.

Teacher capacity is a further constraint that the documented implementations repeatedly expose. Special-education staff in many systems already face heavy caseloads and paperwork, and AI tools are often marketed to them as time-saving devices for drafting plans, reports, and differentiated materials. The time savings may be real, but the Center for Democracy and Technology's caution about generic AI-drafted plans suggests that efficiency gains can come at the expense of individualisation unless educators retain substantive authorship and review. Training that equips special educators to evaluate AI outputs critically, to recognise normative framing, and to protect sensitive records therefore appears to be as important as the tools themselves, and evaluations of implementation would benefit from measuring how professional judgement is exercised alongside student outcomes.

The evidence base has clear weaknesses. Most studies are qualitative or survey-based, few use comparison groups, and almost none track outcomes over time. Purpose-built tools are often evaluated by their developers. Responsible implementation therefore appears to require co-design with disabled and neurodivergent users, explicit accommodation policies that protect legitimate AI use from misconduct allegations, strict limits on processing special-education data, and independent evaluation that reports results separately for students with different disabilities rather than treating them as a single category.

### Q237 What do higher-education early adopters report about long-term student outcomes three or more years after systematic AI integration? {#q237}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The question of long-term outcomes after systematic AI integration in higher education runs into a basic problem of timing. Generative AI became widely available to students only in late 2022, and few institutions integrated it systematically before 2023. As of late 2026, a cohort that began study under systematic integration has at most three to four years of exposure, and rigorous longitudinal studies of that cohort have not yet been published in meaningful numbers. Honest synthesis therefore has to distinguish between what early adopters report, what shorter-term studies find, and what remains unknown.

The longest-running evidence concerns earlier, narrower AI systems rather than generative models. Georgia State University's use of an AI chatbot to support students, initially for enrolment and later within courses, provides one of the few experimentally evaluated examples. In a randomised study reported by Meyer and Page, students in an introductory government course who received course-specific chatbot messages scored higher on final grades, and the effect was concentrated among first-generation students, who scored roughly eleven points higher than comparable peers and were about sixteen percent more likely to earn a B or above. Because this was a randomised trial, causal language about the course-level effect is warranted, but the study did not follow students across years, and the chatbot was a structured nudging system rather than an open-ended generative tutor.

For generative AI specifically, the available data are largely about adoption. The Higher Education Policy Institute and Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2025, based on 1,041 UK undergraduates, found that 92 percent used AI tools, up from 66 percent a year earlier, and that 88 percent had used generative AI for assessments in some form. Around 18 percent reported including AI-generated text directly in their work. The survey also identified differences in use by gender and socio-economic background. The Digital Education Council's 2024 global survey of 3,839 students across 16 countries similarly reported that 86 percent used AI in their studies. These figures describe saturation of use but say little about learning or attainment.

Shorter-term experimental studies offer more insight into mechanisms. The meta-analysis by Deng and colleagues in Computers & Education, which pooled 69 experimental and quasi-experimental studies of ChatGPT, found positive average effects on academic performance and higher-order thinking but no significant effect on self-efficacy, and noted that most studies lasted only weeks, rarely reported power analyses, and were vulnerable to novelty effects. A randomised trial by Bastani and colleagues published in PNAS, conducted in high-school mathematics, found that unrestricted access to GPT-4 improved practice performance but was associated with lower performance on a subsequent unassisted exam, whereas a tutor-style version with guardrails largely mitigated this harm. Although conducted in secondary schools, the finding is frequently cited by universities because it suggests that performance with AI and learning without it can diverge.

What early adopter institutions report is therefore mainly process evidence: rapid uptake, widespread redesign of assessment toward in-person or process-based tasks, creation of institution-licensed AI tools, and rising staff training. Several universities have published internal evaluations showing high student satisfaction with institutional AI assistants, but these are typically descriptive and sometimes produced in partnership with vendors.

The outcomes that matter most over three or more years, including degree completion, depth of disciplinary knowledge, writing ability, critical thinking, and graduate employment, have not been measured in published longitudinal designs that isolate the contribution of AI. Confounding is severe: the same years saw post-pandemic recovery, changes in labour markets, and assessment reforms, making it difficult to attribute any trend to AI integration.

History offers a cautionary precedent for interpreting early adopters' reports. Purdue University's Course Signals system, an early learning-analytics application that used predictive models to flag students at risk and send traffic-light warnings, was described by Arnold and Pistilli at the 2012 Learning Analytics and Knowledge conference as associated with higher retention among students who had taken Signals-enabled courses. The finding was widely publicised as evidence that analytics improved persistence. Subsequent critiques by researchers including Michael Caulfield and Alfred Essa pointed out that students who took more courses were mechanically more likely to have taken a Signals course, and that retention would therefore appear higher among Signals users even if the system had no effect; when this survivorship confound was considered, the apparent retention benefit could not be distinguished from selection. The episode illustrates how institutional reports of multi-year outcomes, even when sincere, can be misleading if they do not account for who is exposed to an intervention and for how long.

The earlier chatbot work from Georgia State has a stronger design pedigree. Page and Gehlbach reported in AERA Open in 2017 on a randomised trial of Pounce, an AI-enabled text-messaging assistant deployed to admitted students over the summer before enrolment to address the phenomenon known as summer melt. Students assigned to receive the assistant were more likely to complete pre-enrolment tasks and to enrol on time, with the authors estimating an increase of around three percentage points in timely enrolment. Because these findings come from a randomised design, causal interpretation is appropriate for the enrolment outcome, but the intervention operated at a transition point rather than through sustained instruction, and the authors noted that effects might differ when such systems are scaled or used in other contexts. Later work by other researchers on large-scale behavioural nudges for college access found that effects observed in smaller trials often weakened or disappeared at national scale, a reminder that early successes in a single institution may not generalise.

The pre-generative literature on intelligent tutoring provides the clearest evidence about what durable learning gains from AI can look like. Kurt VanLehn's 2011 review in Educational Psychologist compared human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring approaches across many studies and concluded that step-based intelligent tutoring systems achieved effect sizes of roughly 0.76 standard deviations relative to no tutoring, close to the 0.79 he estimated for human tutoring, challenging the widely cited claim that human tutoring produces gains of two standard deviations. VanLehn's analysis also suggested that the granularity of interaction mattered: systems that responded to each step of a student's reasoning were more effective than those that only evaluated final answers. These findings suggest that if generative AI produces lasting benefits in higher education, they are likely to come from designs that structure stepwise reasoning rather than from open-ended answer generation, which is consistent with the guardrail finding in the Bastani trial.

More recent experimental evidence in higher education points in a similar direction. Kestin, Miller, and colleagues reported in Scientific Reports in 2025 a randomised crossover trial in a large introductory physics course at Harvard, in which students learned matched content either through an AI tutor built on GPT-4 with pedagogical prompting or through an in-class active-learning session. The study found that students learned significantly more in less time with the AI tutor, with learning gains estimated at roughly double those of the active-learning condition, and that students reported greater engagement and motivation. Because the design was randomised, causal language about the immediate learning gains is warranted. However, the outcomes were measured within single units, the tutor was carefully engineered by instructors, and the study did not track retention or performance over subsequent years. The results therefore inform what well-designed AI tutoring can achieve in the short term rather than what systematic integration achieves over a degree.

Systematic reviews of the broader field highlight how rarely long-term outcomes are studied. Bond, Khosravi, De Laat, and colleagues published in 2024 a meta systematic review of 66 evidence syntheses on AI in higher education. They reported that the field was dominated by studies in a limited number of countries, that ethical considerations were addressed infrequently, and that methodological quality was uneven, with many reviews failing to appraise the quality of included studies. The authors called for greater rigour, collaboration, and attention to ethics. If reviews of reviews struggle to locate high-quality longitudinal evidence, individual institutions should be cautious about drawing multi-year conclusions from their own descriptive data.

Students' own accounts add texture to the adoption data. Jisc's 2024 report on student perceptions of generative AI in the UK, based on discussion forums with students across further and higher education, described students who valued AI for explaining concepts, structuring work, and supporting accessibility, while expressing concern about inconsistent institutional rules, fairness of access to paid tools, and the possibility that reliance on AI might weaken their skills. These perceptions are not outcome measures, but they suggest mechanisms that a longitudinal study could investigate, including whether paid-tool access correlates with attainment gaps and whether self-reported dependence predicts later performance on unassisted tasks.

Several methodological strategies could allow early-adopter institutions to generate more credible long-term evidence. One is the use of staggered rollouts, in which different departments or cohorts receive structured AI integration at different times, creating natural comparison groups that support difference-in-differences analysis. Another is the preservation of common assessment instruments, such as standardised writing samples or concept inventories, administered to successive cohorts before and after integration, so that changes in underlying skills can be distinguished from changes in assessment format. A third is linkage of administrative records on progression, completion, and graduate outcomes with data on the type and intensity of AI use, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards. A fourth is pre-registration of evaluation plans, which reduces the temptation to report only favourable outcomes. None of these strategies is novel in education research, but their absence from most current institutional reporting is notable.

There is also a conceptual question about which outcomes should count. If AI changes the nature of professional work, as studies of knowledge workers suggest, then graduates' ability to use AI effectively and critically may itself become a valued outcome, and a decline in unassisted performance on traditional tasks might coexist with improved performance on AI-augmented tasks. Universities differ in how they weigh these goals, and some disciplines, such as medicine or law, have professional licensing requirements that place a premium on unassisted competence. Long-term evaluation will need to specify which competencies are intended, rather than assuming that any change from historical norms represents improvement or decline.

International comparison adds a further dimension. Institutions in Asia, Europe, and North America have adopted different approaches, ranging from centrally licensed tools with institution-wide training to decentralised policies that leave decisions to individual instructors. These variations, if documented systematically, could serve as natural experiments, but cross-national comparison is complicated by differences in admissions, assessment regimes, and labour markets. The most realistic prospect for credible long-term evidence may therefore lie in multi-institution consortia that agree on common measures and share data, rather than in isolated case studies.

Equity of exposure is another dimension that early-adopter reports seldom address but that longitudinal studies will need to examine. Where institutions license premium AI tools centrally, all students may have comparable access, whereas in institutions that leave access to individual purchase, students able to pay for advanced subscriptions may accumulate advantages over several years. The HEPI survey's finding of differences in use by gender and socio-economic background, together with the Meyer and Page finding that structured chatbot support was concentrated in benefits for first-generation students, suggests that the distributional effects of integration may matter as much as average effects. A long-term evaluation that reports only average outcomes could conceal widening or narrowing gaps between groups, and disaggregated reporting by background, prior attainment, disability, and discipline is therefore essential if the evidence is to inform institutional policy.

Finally, there is the problem of a moving treatment. The AI systems available to a student in their first year of study in 2023 differ substantially from those available in their final year, as models have gained capabilities in reasoning, multimodal input, and integration with institutional platforms. A cohort study that treats AI integration as a single, stable intervention will therefore conflate the effects of many different tools and practices. Careful documentation of which tools, policies, and pedagogical designs were in place at each point is necessary for longitudinal findings to be interpretable.

The most defensible conclusion is that the long-term record does not yet exist in rigorous form. Early adopters report high engagement and course-level benefits in specific, structured implementations, while experimental evidence warns that unstructured use may improve immediate performance without durable learning. Institutions seeking credible long-term evidence would need to establish baseline measures, track cohorts with consistent instruments, preserve comparison groups where ethically possible, and publish results independently of vendors. Until such studies mature, claims that systematic integration has improved long-term outcomes should be treated as hypotheses rather than findings.

## Chapter 9: Policy and Governance in Practice {#chapter-09}

12 questions · 107 citations · 104 unique sources · 60 cross-references

### Q069 Which national and regional AI-in-education regulations currently exist, and how do their approaches compare? {#q069}

18 citations · 18 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI in Education: The Global Regulatory Landscape

The regulation of artificial intelligence in educational settings is now one of the most active — and most contested — areas of technology policy worldwide. Three distinct regulatory philosophies have emerged, each reflecting deeper assumptions about the proper relationship between states, institutions, and technology.

---

The European Union: Rights-Based, Risk-Stratified Law

The most architecturally ambitious framework is the EU AI Act, the world's first comprehensive legal framework governing AI development and deployment, which classifies AI systems by risk level — from minimal to unacceptable — and assigns corresponding compliance obligations. For the education sector, this classification has direct consequences. Education sits at the intersection of two areas the Act treats with particular care: high-risk AI applications and the protection of vulnerable populations. Many common school applications — from automated essay grading and adaptive learning platforms to dropout prediction tools — fall squarely into the high-risk category under Annex III, covering AI systems that determine access, assess learning outcomes, or influence the educational path of individuals.

The prohibitions are explicit and already enforceable. Among eight banned practices, emotion recognition in educational institutions and real-time remote biometric identification are flatly prohibited; those prohibitions became effective in February 2025. Any system designed to infer student emotions from facial, vocal, or biometric cues is classified as "unacceptable risk" and is banned in EU educational settings.

The timeline has recently shifted, however. A legislative simplification package — the so-called "AI omnibus" — was adopted in November 2025, with a political agreement reached in May 2026. Under that agreement, the full compliance rules for high-risk AI systems in education will now apply from December 2027. Penalties for non-compliance are substantial: placing a non-compliant high-risk AI system on the market can result in fines of up to 15 million euros or 3 percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

Alongside the binding Act, the European Commission has issued ethical guidelines for educators and the guidelines include clear explanations of the AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation, and the principles of responsible AI use. The European Schools system, notably, has been candid that no generative AI tools have yet been officially approved for system-wide use, with approval procedures still under development.

---

The United States: Federalism Without a Federal Floor

Across the Atlantic, the picture is one of deliberate decentralization. There is no comprehensive federal AI-in-education statute. The existing federal scaffolding rests on older laws: FERPA protects the privacy of student education records, but its last regulatory updates predate the widespread use of technology in learning environments, leaving institutions to interpret it in light of artificial intelligence. There are few federal regulations that govern AI directly at the higher education level.

The Trump administration's April 2025 executive order on AI education frames the issue almost entirely in competitiveness terms. It is the policy of the United States to promote AI literacy and proficiency among Americans by promoting the appropriate integration of AI into education, providing comprehensive AI training for educators, and fostering early exposure to AI concepts to develop an AI-ready workforce. The Department of Education subsequently issued grant guidance outlining how AI may be used across key educational functions and articulating principles for responsible use, affirming such uses are allowable under existing federal education programs.

With the federal level providing only encouragement and grant incentives, states have become the primary regulatory arena. When ChatGPT debuted in 2022, no states had policies related to generative AI; by April 2025, at least 28 states had engaged with the issue legislatively. The legislative priorities reveal a pragmatic rather than rights-based orientation. Fifteen bills in the 2025 session alone focused on promoting AI literacy for students and professional development for teachers, making this the top legislative priority. Several states have moved toward guardrails on specific harms: Nevada enacted legislation prohibiting public schools from using AI-powered tools to perform the functions of a school counselor, psychologist, or social worker in relation to student mental health. Vendor accountability is a newer frontier: legislators are increasingly mandating that AI EdTech vendors submit documentation about how they handle and use student data to train their products.

State approaches vary widely in ambition. States like California, Connecticut, and Texas have introduced bills to create oversight boards and "regulatory sandboxes" where AI tools can be tested before broader rollout. Tennessee, by contrast, passed a law mandating that all K-12 districts, charter schools, and universities adopt their own AI policies, with the Tennessee School Boards Association subsequently developing a model policy that most districts adopted in full.

---

China: State-Directed Integration with Embedded Guardrails

China's approach is neither rights-centered like Europe's nor market-permissive like the United States'. It is best understood as state-directed deployment, combining ambitious top-down mandates with granular behavioral rules. China aims to promote AI in aiding education reform, with a joint guideline from the Ministry of Education and eight other departments emphasizing building an AI-based education system that integrates smart technologies into teaching, learning, assessment, and academic research.

The Ministry of Education issued two guidelines in May 2025: one for AI general education in primary and secondary schools, and one for the use of generative AI — prohibiting students from independently using open-ended content generation at the primary level and banning teachers from using generative AI as a substitute for their core teaching responsibilities. The curriculum is structured as a developmental ladder: primary school students encounter basic technologies like voice recognition and image classification; junior high students examine machine learning processes and develop critical thinking about misinformation in AI outputs; senior secondary students design and refine AI algorithm models while cultivating interdisciplinary systems thinking.

Several regions — including Beijing, Guangzhou, and Chengdu — have rolled out implementation plans specifying class hour requirements at each school stage and incorporating AI course evaluations into students' overall assessments; Beijing's primary and secondary schools will fully implement general AI education starting in fall 2025, with no fewer than eight class hours per academic year.

At the university level, academic integrity has become a pressure point. At Tianjin University of Science and Technology, AI-generated content in undergraduate theses must not exceed 40 percent under detection measures introduced in 2024. Fudan University's regulations ban AI use in six areas of academic work, including research design, original data collection, and thesis writing.

---

Comparing the Three Approaches

The fundamental divergence is one of purpose. The EU regulates AI in education primarily as a matter of fundamental rights — student autonomy, non-discrimination, and freedom from surveillance — and uses legal prohibition and conformity assessment to enforce those values. The United States treats the problem primarily as a governance challenge to be managed at the most local level capable of acting, with the federal role confined to incentives and workforce framing. China treats AI integration as a national strategic imperative, with the state setting both the pace and the curriculum, while embedding data security and anti-dependency rules as safety val
