## Chapter 13: Knowledge Integrity and the Information Environment {#chapter-13}

10 questions · 81 citations · 71 unique sources · 50 cross-references

### Q162 How can schools establish the provenance of the teaching materials they use, now that AI-generated content is indistinguishable in form from authored content? {#q162}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

Establishing Provenance of Teaching Materials in the Age of AI-Generated Content

The question of how schools can establish the provenance of the teaching materials they use has become urgent as AI-generated content has become indistinguishable in form from human-authored content. A worksheet, lesson plan, or assessment that appears professionally produced may have been authored by a subject-matter expert, generated by a large language model, or produced through some combination of human and AI effort. The implications for educational quality, accuracy, and accountability are significant.

The Provenance Problem

Provenance — the documented history of an object's origin and ownership — has always mattered in education. Schools have traditionally relied on publisher reputation, author credentials, and institutional endorsement as proxies for content quality. These proxies are increasingly unreliable in an environment where AI can generate plausible-looking educational content at scale, where the distinction between "authored" and "generated" is blurring, and where the traditional publishing infrastructure is being disrupted by direct-to-teacher content distribution.

The provenance problem has two dimensions. The first is accuracy: AI-generated content can contain factual errors, outdated information, or subtle misconceptions that are difficult to detect without subject-matter expertise. The second is accountability: when AI-generated content causes harm — by teaching incorrect information, embedding bias, or violating copyright — it is often unclear who is responsible.

Technical Provenance Standards: C2PA and Content Credentials

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed an open technical standard — Content Credentials — that provides cryptographically signed metadata documenting the origin and editing history of digital content. The C2PA 2.4 specification (2026) includes a dedicated AI disclosure assertion that can document whether AI was used in content creation, the model type, and the level of human oversight. This standard is supported by major technology companies including Adobe, Microsoft, and Google, and is beginning to be adopted by content creation tools.

However, C2PA has significant limitations for educational use. It is a voluntary, opt-in system: content creators must choose to attach Content Credentials, and the absence of credentials does not prove that AI was not used. The system verifies provenance metadata but not the accuracy of the content itself. Security research has identified vulnerabilities in the C2PA specification, including the ability to replace timestamps and modify metadata without detection. And the system requires compatible tools throughout the content creation and distribution chain — a requirement that is far from universally met.

Practical Approaches for Schools

In the absence of reliable technical provenance standards, schools must rely on a combination of institutional processes and professional judgment. Practical approaches include: establishing clear procurement policies that require vendors and content providers to disclose AI use in materials; developing internal review processes that evaluate content accuracy and appropriateness before use; building teacher capacity to critically evaluate AI-generated content, including the ability to identify common AI error patterns; and creating feedback mechanisms that allow teachers to flag inaccurate or inappropriate content.

Schools should also develop clear policies on teacher-generated AI content: when teachers use AI to generate materials, what disclosure is required, what review process applies, and who is responsible for accuracy. These policies should be consistent with the institution's broader AI governance framework and should be communicated clearly to students and parents.

The Curriculum Integrity Dimension

Beyond individual materials, schools face a curriculum integrity challenge: ensuring that the overall curriculum — the sequence of learning experiences, the progression of concepts, the balance of perspectives — reflects deliberate educational design rather than the accumulated output of AI generation. AI-generated materials, even when individually accurate, may not cohere into a curriculum that achieves the intended educational goals. Schools need processes for evaluating curriculum coherence and alignment, not just individual material quality.

### Q163 To what extent are textbooks, worksheets, and reference works used in schools now AI-generated, and is this disclosed? {#q163}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

The honest answer to the first part of this question is that nobody knows with precision, because the systematic measurement of AI content in educational materials has not been conducted at scale, and what data exists is largely anecdotal or derived from small studies. What can be said with confidence is that the conditions for widespread AI-generated content in educational materials exist and that disclosure practices are inconsistent.

Evidence on AI use in lesson planning and worksheet creation. Survey data reported in the research indicates that approximately 80% of K-12 teachers indicated that disclosing AI use in lesson planning is unnecessary. This suggests not that teachers are not using AI for lesson preparation — usage is widespread — but that many do not consider such use to require disclosure. The boundary between AI-assisted editing and AI-generated content creation is blurring in practice, even as publishers and institutions attempt to define it. Academic studies of AI-generated lesson plans have found consistent quality limitations: a study of 310 civics lesson plans generated by AI found that approximately 90% promoted only basic cognitive levels (memorising, reciting, summarising) rather than higher-order skills. These materials were also found to be largely monocultural, with only around 6% incorporating diverse or inclusive perspectives. If such materials are entering classrooms without disclosure or human curation, they represent a quiet pedagogical problem — not because they were AI-generated but because they were undisclosed and unreviewed.

Publisher disclosure policies. Major academic publishers — Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, SAGE, and IEEE — have now established disclosure requirements for AI use in authored works. These policies require that any use of generative AI in drafting or creating content be declared, typically in an acknowledgments statement or dedicated declaration section. AI tools cannot be listed as authors under any major publisher's current policy. The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) has added "undisclosed involvement of artificial intelligence" as grounds for potential retraction. However, these requirements primarily apply to formal academic publications. The market for K-12 worksheets, reference works, and supplementary materials is less well-governed. Online platforms distributing teacher-created resources — a significant and growing source of classroom materials in many systems — have variable and often absent disclosure requirements.

The specific problem of fabricated references. One documented quality failure directly relevant to reference works is the AI tendency to fabricate citations. Librarians have reported a pattern of students presenting requests to locate books and journal articles that simply do not exist, having been invented by AI in response to research queries. A federal government report — the "Make America Healthy Again Commission" report — was found to contain citations for non-existent journal articles, suggesting AI involvement in its production. In 2025, newspapers including the Chicago Sun-Times and Philadelphia Inquirer published summer reading lists containing non-existent books, drafted by a third-party AI content provider. These cases are not hypothetical — they are documented instances of AI-generated content containing fabricated references entering distribution channels without adequate human review. If analogous materials were distributed as classroom reference works, students would be directing research effort toward sources that do not exist.

Compliance rates for disclosure. The evidence on disclosure compliance is discouraging. A study at King's Business School during the 2023–2024 academic year found that 74% of students failed to declare AI usage despite it being a mandatory requirement on coursework coversheets. The factors identified — fear of penalties, ambiguous policies, peer normalisation, and uncertainty about what counts as "AI use" — apply to teacher and publisher disclosure as well as student disclosure.

Implications. The evidence supports the conclusion that AI-generated content is entering school materials through multiple channels — teacher-created resources, commercially distributed worksheets, online platforms — at a rate that is currently unmeasured and largely undisclosed. The risk is not that AI was involved in creating materials but that undisclosed, unreviewed AI content may carry inaccuracies, pedagogical limitations, and fabricated references that no human expert has caught. Disclosure requirements, human curation mandates, and provenance tracking are all necessary responses.

Platform governance and school responses. The online platforms through which teachers share and purchase resources are a particular governance gap. Marketplaces for teacher-created materials have grown rapidly and now function as de facto curriculum suppliers in many systems, yet their disclosure requirements for AI-generated content are variable and often absent. A worksheet downloaded from such a platform may carry no indication of whether it was written by a teacher, adapted with AI assistance, or generated wholesale by a model. Schools can respond at the point of use: requiring that any externally sourced material be accompanied by a named author or an explicit AI disclosure, maintaining internal review processes for high-stakes materials, and favouring platforms and publishers that have adopted transparent policies. Teacher education and professional development should also address the disclosure question directly, since the survey evidence suggests that many teachers do not regard AI use in lesson preparation as requiring disclosure at all — a norm that will need to change if provenance is to become meaningful.

### Q164 What documented cases exist of AI-generated misinformation entering curricula or classroom materials? {#q164}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI-generated misinformation in educational contexts takes several forms: fabricated citations and non-existent sources; factually incorrect explanations that appear authoritative; culturally biased or stereotyping content; and simplified or misleading accounts of complex phenomena. The documented cases span professional and educational contexts, and while it is not yet possible to state how frequently such misinformation enters formal curricula undetected, specific instances across multiple domains have been recorded.

Fabricated academic citations. The most thoroughly documented pattern involves AI systems fabricating academic sources that do not exist. Librarians have reported a measurable increase in student requests to locate books and articles that turn out to be entirely fictional — invented by AI-powered research assistants and presented to students as real citations. These fabricated citations are qualitatively different from simple errors: they typically appear in correct bibliographic format, with plausible journal names, author names, and publication years, making them difficult to identify without actually attempting to locate them. A specific case from the federal government illustrates the broader reach of this problem: the "Make America Healthy Again Commission" report was found to contain citations for non-existent journal articles, consistent with AI-generated content in a government publication that reached public distribution. In 2025, the Chicago Sun-Times and Philadelphia Inquirer published summer reading lists containing non-existent books — materials that had been drafted by a third-party AI content provider engaged by the news organisations. While these are not directly classroom curricula, they illustrate how AI-generated content with fabricated references can pass through institutional distribution channels without adequate review.

Legal and professional misinformation with educational relevance. In late 2024, a Stanford University professor apologised for including AI-generated, non-existent citations in a court filing regarding political deepfakes. The significance for education is dual: it demonstrates that the hallucination problem affects expert users in professional contexts, not only novice student users, and it shows that AI misinformation can enter high-stakes, formally reviewed documents. If experts are vulnerable, students and teachers working under less rigorous review conditions face at least equivalent risk.

Scientific misinformation. In 2022 and 2023, instances were documented where ChatGPT cited non-existent studies from reputable journals, including the Journal of the American Medical Association, to support false claims about COVID-19 vaccine efficacy. If a teacher or student used such AI-generated summaries as a basis for classroom instruction, the result would be the teaching of fabricated scientific evidence as fact. AI's tendency to oversimplify complex scientific feedback loops, miss critical variables, or — in safety-critical contexts — provide dangerous instructions for laboratory demonstrations has also been flagged by science educators. The National Science Teaching Association's guidance specifically addresses the risk of AI-generated science content that omits critical safety considerations or presents oversimplified causal relationships as established fact.

Pedagogical limitations as curriculum risk. A study of AI-generated civics lesson plans found not only that the materials were cognitively shallow — promoting memorisation and recall over analysis — but that they were also culturally homogeneous, with only approximately 6% incorporating diverse perspectives. When educators use such materials without critical review, the effect is that students receive instruction shaped by the AI's training data biases rather than deliberate curriculum design. This is misinformation in a structural sense: it misrepresents the diversity of civic life and the complexity of civic reasoning.

Automation bias as an amplifying factor. Research indicates that students tend to exhibit "automation bias" — trusting AI outputs more readily than they trust equivalent human-written content. This makes AI-generated misinformation particularly dangerous in educational settings: it is simultaneously more likely to be trusted and more difficult for students to detect than human-produced errors. The combination of AI's confident presentational style with students' tendency toward automation bias creates conditions in which misinformation can be accepted and internalised rapidly.

Educator responses. Educational institutions are responding through AI literacy initiatives — teaching students to identify inaccuracies, fabricated references, and logical fallacies in AI outputs. Oregon State University has established an AI literacy and ethics centre specifically focused on evaluating AI inputs, processes, and outputs. The consensus among educational experts is that AI should be treated as a starting point for inquiry that requires verification, not as an endpoint.

The scale of the problem and measurement challenges. Quantifying how often AI-generated misinformation enters curricula is difficult, because the phenomenon is only visible when someone attempts to verify a specific claim or source. Surveys of student AI use suggest the scale of exposure is substantial: the 2025 HEPI-Kortext survey of UK higher education students found widespread use of generative AI for coursework, with a significant minority reporting that they had submitted AI-generated text without disclosure. If similar patterns hold in secondary education, the volume of AI-influenced work flowing through classrooms is large, and the proportion that contains undetected inaccuracies is unknown but non-trivial. Systematic monitoring would require schools to sample and audit materials and student work for fabricated sources and factual errors — a practice that is rare. The absence of measurement should not be read as the absence of a problem; it reflects the fact that the verification infrastructure has not yet caught up with the scale of AI-generated content.

### Q165 How are school librarians and media specialists adapting their role to synthetic information environments? {#q165}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

School librarians and media specialists occupy a structurally important position in the response to AI-generated content: they are the professional figures within schools most explicitly trained in information evaluation, source verification, and the epistemological principles that distinguish credible knowledge from plausible-sounding fabrication. Their role is not being displaced by AI; it is being fundamentally reoriented — from helping students find information to helping students evaluate information whose origin, accuracy, and integrity can no longer be assumed.

From information literacy to AI literacy. The academic library profession's primary professional bodies — the American Library Association (ALA) and the Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) — have framed AI literacy as a direct evolution of information literacy rather than a separate discipline. This framing is important because it situates librarians as the natural institutional home for AI literacy instruction rather than positioning it as solely a technology department or computer science function. The ACRL has drafted "AI Competencies for Academic Library Workers," organising skills into four categories: Knowledge and Understanding; Analysis and Evaluation; Use and Application; and Ethical Considerations. These competencies are explicitly designed to be product-agnostic — focused on foundational principles rather than specific platforms — which is appropriate given the rapid pace of tool change. The Public Library Association's Guide for Library Staff specifies the practical skills required, including prompt engineering, identifying AI-generated content, and understanding training data limitations. These are not trivial additions to existing librarian skill sets; they require professional development investment and ongoing learning.

Addressing AI-specific misinformation challenges. A primary concern in the library literature is that AI-generated misinformation is qualitatively different from earlier forms of misinformation that librarians were trained to address. Unlike traditional fake news or intentionally misleading sources, AI-generated misinformation is often highly plausible in form, correctly formatted in bibliographic style, and presented with confident authority — making it difficult for even subject experts to detect without independent verification. Librarians are therefore developing new instructional approaches: teaching students that AI hallucinations — fabricated citations, invented statistics, non-existent historical events — are not unusual edge cases but a structural feature of how language models work. The instruction shifts from "evaluate this source" to "verify whether this source exists" as a preliminary step before any deeper quality evaluation.

New instructional roles and frameworks. The ALA has published formal "Guidance on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Libraries," asserting that AI should complement — not replace — human judgment and accountability. This guidance directly addresses intellectual freedom: libraries must ensure that information ranking or recommendation by AI is transparent, and users must have opportunities to opt out of AI-automated systems. Librarians are creating AI toolkits, LibGuides, and syllabus statements to assist students and faculty in navigating AI responsibly. The EDUCAUSE ALTL framework has been adopted by library professionals as a structure for professional development, focusing on technical understanding, evaluative skills, practical application, and ethical considerations. EBSCO and ACRL are providing short courses specifically designed for library workers building AI literacy competencies.

Scholarly integrity and citation practices. Librarians are raising specific concerns about how AI undermines traditional scholarly communication and citation practices. When students use AI-generated references without verification, they submit citations to non-existent sources — a problem that only becomes visible when the librarian or instructor attempts to locate the source. The library profession is developing instructional responses: teaching students that verification is not optional for AI-generated citations and that the ability to locate the source through an independent database search is a minimum requirement before any AI-generated citation is used.

Roles in collection development and institutional policy. The ALA guidance extends to collection development: libraries are advised to establish policies regarding the acquisition of AI-assisted materials, prioritising quality and transparency over automated defaults. In technical services such as cataloguing and metadata enrichment, the human-in-the-loop principle applies: AI-generated suggestions require human review before they become institutional records. Librarians are also increasingly involved in institutional AI governance — sitting on AI task forces and policy committees — given their professional expertise in information evaluation and their institutional neutrality relative to vendor relationships. This governance role is expanding as the profession recognises that the synthetic information environment requires institutional, not merely individual, responses.

Challenges and open questions. The reorientation of the librarian's role is not without friction. The pace of tool change makes it difficult for professional development to keep up, and many school libraries are under-resourced relative to the scale of the new responsibilities. There is also an unresolved question about how AI literacy instruction should be distributed: if it is treated as primarily a library function, it may reach students only in scheduled library sessions rather than being embedded across the curriculum; if it is distributed across subjects, the librarian's distinctive expertise in verification may be diluted. The professional bodies have responded by building competency frameworks and training infrastructure, but implementation depends on institutional commitment — staffing, time, and budget. The direction of travel is clear: the librarian is becoming the school's designated expert on the integrity of the information environment, a role that is likely to grow in importance as synthetic content becomes more prevalent.

### Q166 What verification and source-evaluation skills should now be taught explicitly, and at what ages? {#q166}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Previous approaches to information literacy often embedded source evaluation as a sub-skill within existing subject teaching — research projects, essay writing, media studies. The synthetic information environment created by generative AI has made this implicit approach insufficient. AI can produce content that passes all the traditional surface-level quality checks: correct grammar, appropriate register, plausible citations, credible-seeming authority. The skills required to evaluate AI-generated content go beyond traditional source evaluation and must now be taught explicitly, sequentially, and across subjects rather than treated as a library add-on.

A developmental progression. The scholarly literature supports an age-banded framework for AI literacy instruction that maps onto cognitive development. For ages 8–12 (primary school), the cognitive goal is "conceptual hygiene" — establishing that AI is a pattern-matching system rather than a truth-finding authority. The practical routine recommended in the literature is "Stop–Ask–Check": before acting on any AI output, stop to consider whether the claim matters; ask whether it has been verified; check against a trusted source such as a teacher, book, or verified database. UNESCO's guidance on media and information literacy for this age group similarly emphasises building the basic ability to distinguish between information, opinion, belief, and narrative. A key concept to introduce at this stage — in age-appropriate terms — is that AI "finds patterns" rather than "knowing things," and that confident presentation does not equal accuracy. Children who internalise this concept are less vulnerable to the automation bias that makes AI misinformation effective. For ages 12–14 (middle school), the focus shifts to structured risk classification and verification protocols. Students at this stage can engage with the "Claim–Source–Match–Decision" model: identify the specific claim, locate an independent source that addresses it, compare the claim with the source's actual content, and decide whether the claim is supported. This is the stage at which students learn to interrogate fabricated citations specifically — to distinguish between a citation that appears in correct format and a citation that can actually be located through a library database. The American Psychological Association's guidance for this age group emphasises the risks of overtrust and anthropomorphism — the tendency to treat AI responses as having the status of expert advice — and recommends explicit instruction on the difference between simulated confidence and warranted authority. For ages 14–18 (secondary school), the focus expands to governance and delegation: when should I use AI as a tool, and when would doing so undermine my own skill development? Students at this stage can engage with the concept of "generation lines" — explicitly distinguishing between their own thinking and AI-assisted output — and with the institutional standards for AI disclosure that they will encounter in higher education and professional life. UNESCO's Media and Information Literacy framework for secondary students includes algorithmic literacy — understanding how AI systems collect data, prioritise content, and create "filter bubbles" — as a core component. Students should also understand that bias in AI output is not random but reflects patterns in training data; this is a concept that connects AI literacy to broader critical thinking about who produces knowledge and whose perspectives are represented.

Subject-integrated approaches. Multiple sources advise against creating separate "AI time" for verification instruction; instead, AI-checking routines should be embedded in existing subjects. History classes can use AI-generated accounts of historical events as objects of critical analysis. Science classes can use AI explanations of natural phenomena as starting points for identifying oversimplifications or missing variables. English classes can examine AI-generated text for the stylistic patterns and limitations that distinguish it from human writing.

The librarian's role. School librarians are positioned as the primary institutional resource for explicit verification instruction. The ALA's AI competency frameworks for library workers include prompt engineering skills — translating traditional database search skills into effective AI querying — alongside critical evaluation of AI outputs. Libraries are developing instructional programmes that teach the specific steps required to verify AI-generated citations: database searching, author identification, publisher verification, and date checking.

Implications. The skills that now require explicit, age-appropriate teaching are: recognising that AI outputs are probabilistic rather than factual; applying the Stop–Ask–Check routine (younger students) and Claim–Source–Match–Decision model (older students); verifying citations independently before using them; identifying when AI output reflects training data bias; understanding disclosure obligations; and evaluating when AI assistance is appropriate versus when it undermines skill development. These skills should be treated as core components of information literacy curricula at all levels, not as optional enrichment.

Assessing whether the skills have been acquired. If verification skills are to be taught explicitly, they must also be assessed explicitly. Performance-based assessment is the most direct method: students can be given an AI-generated passage containing a fabricated citation or a plausible-sounding but false claim, and asked to verify it against library databases and independent sources. Such tasks test the actual skill rather than knowledge about the skill, and they can be calibrated to the age bands described above — simpler verification tasks in primary school, multi-source triangulation and bias analysis in secondary school. Schools should also consider whether their existing information literacy assessments capture the new competencies, and should treat the ability to verify an AI-generated citation as a threshold skill for research-based assignments. The goal is not to make verification burdensome but to make it habitual, so that checking a claim against an independent source becomes as automatic as checking spelling.

### Q167 What happens to citation practice in schools when the cited source may itself be machine-written? {#q167}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Citation practice in schools has traditionally served two epistemological functions: accountability (enabling readers to verify claims by tracing them to sources) and authority (signalling that a claim is grounded in expert or credible knowledge). When a cited source may itself have been machine-generated — whether a ChatGPT response, an AI-assisted article, or a text produced by a model trained on synthetic data — both functions are degraded. The source cannot be independently verified in the traditional sense (the same AI prompt produces different outputs on different occasions), and its authority depends on a chain of epistemic trust that the AI system cannot itself establish.

How style guides are responding. The major academic style guides have developed AI citation frameworks, but these frameworks reveal as many problems as they solve. APA Style now provides specific guidance: AI company name and date in the reference, tool name and description in brackets, and a URL if the specific chat is retrievable. If the chat is not retrievable via a stable link — which is frequently the case — a general reference to the tool is used. APA explicitly requires that the use of AI be disclosed in the paper's methodology or author note, not merely cited. MLA treats AI-generated content as a source without a human author. Citations include the prompt used, the name of the AI tool, the version/model, the company, the date, and a stable URL if available. In-text citations typically use a shortened version of the prompt. Chicago recommends acknowledging AI use via footnotes, endnotes, or parenthetical citations rather than formal bibliography entries, including the prompt if not described in the main text. IEEE requires disclosure in the acknowledgments section rather than a formal citation, identifying which sections of the paper used AI assistance.

The fundamental epistemological problem. These formatting solutions address the transparency requirement but do not resolve the deeper epistemological problem: an AI citation cannot be verified in the way that a peer-reviewed source can be verified. The reader cannot examine the same AI output the student examined, because AI systems produce variable outputs. The cited "source" is not a stable, fixed text that an independent reader can retrieve and evaluate. This means that AI citations function as disclosure statements — indicating that AI was used and what it was asked — rather than as traditional source citations that enable independent verification. This is a meaningful distinction that needs to be taught explicitly to students. An AI citation tells readers about the student's research process; it does not provide an independently verifiable foundation for factual claims in the way that a primary source or peer-reviewed article does.

The hallucination problem in citations. AI systems themselves generate citations that do not exist. This creates a compounding problem: a student uses AI to research a topic, the AI provides a plausible-seeming list of sources, the student cites those sources, and the teacher or librarian attempts to verify them — only to find that several or all do not exist. This phenomenon has become common enough that librarians treat it as a standard verification task: before any AI-generated citation is used, check that the source actually exists through an independent database. The practical implication for citation instruction is that students must be taught a two-stage verification process: first, confirm that any AI-generated citation refers to an actually existing source; second, if the source exists, read it and confirm that it actually supports the claim for which it is being cited.

Institutional and publisher standards. Major publishers generally prohibit AI from being listed as an author and require explicit declarations of AI use in the writing process. Universities including Princeton have integrated these requirements into academic regulations. These institutional standards are beginning to trickle into secondary education through university preparation curricula, but their uptake at the K-12 level is inconsistent.

Implications for teaching citation. Schools need to update citation instruction to address these new realities. Students should be taught that: AI outputs are process disclosures, not independent sources; all AI-generated citations must be independently verified before use; the citation of AI should describe the prompt and the tool, not merely the output; and AI cannot itself be an author or authority, only a tool whose use is disclosed. These are not minor additions to existing citation instruction — they require reconceptualising what citation is for and what it can accomplish.

Broader implications for research education. The changes to citation practice ripple outward into how schools teach research itself. If citation is reconceived as disclosure rather than verification, students need to understand both functions and when each applies: a peer-reviewed article is cited to enable verification; an AI interaction is disclosed to document process. This distinction is teachable, but it requires schools to update research-methods instruction, library lessons, and assessment rubrics together. There is also a question of proportionality: schools should avoid either banning AI citation outright (which drives use underground and prevents the disclosure habit from forming) or treating AI citations as equivalent to traditional ones (which teaches students a false equivalence). The middle path — explicit disclosure, mandatory verification of any AI-supplied source, and clear consequences for fabricated citations — is the position toward which institutional guidance is converging.

### Q168 What technical provenance standards — watermarking, content credentials, signed provenance — exist, and do they work in educational settings? {#q168}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

Technical Provenance Standards for AI-Generated Content: Capabilities and Limitations in Educational Settings

The rapid proliferation of AI-generated content has created urgent demand for technical standards that can establish the provenance of digital content — documenting whether it was created by a human, generated by an AI, or produced through some combination of human and AI effort. Several technical approaches have been developed, each with distinct capabilities and limitations. Understanding these approaches — and their applicability to educational settings — is essential for schools seeking to govern AI-generated content effectively.

The C2PA Standard and Content Credentials

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed the most widely adopted technical standard for content provenance. C2PA Content Credentials are cryptographically signed metadata manifests that document the origin and editing history of digital content. The C2PA 2.4 specification (2026) includes a dedicated AI disclosure assertion that can document whether AI was used in content creation, the model type, the scientific domain, and the level of human oversight. The standard supports both "hard bindings" (cryptographic hashes that link the manifest to the content's binary data) and "soft bindings" (invisible watermarks that allow manifest recovery even if metadata is stripped).

C2PA is supported by major technology companies including Adobe, Microsoft, Google, and Sony, and is beginning to be integrated into content creation tools including Adobe Photoshop, Microsoft Designer, and several AI image generation platforms. The standard has a conformance programme that provides third-party testing and validation.

However, C2PA has significant limitations. It is a voluntary, opt-in system: content creators must choose to attach Content Credentials, and the absence of credentials does not prove that AI was not used. The system verifies provenance metadata but not the accuracy or quality of the content itself. Security research (Golaszewski et al., 2026) has identified vulnerabilities including the ability to replace timestamps, bypass revoked certificate checks, and modify metadata in "exclusion ranges" without detection. Different validation tools may yield contradictory results for the same file. And the system requires compatible tools throughout the content creation and distribution chain — a requirement that is far from universally met in educational settings.

AI Watermarking

AI watermarking involves embedding unique, algorithmic signatures during the model training or content generation phase. These markers serve two purposes: documenting the origin of content (provenance) and providing a mechanism for detecting AI-generated content (authentication). Watermarking techniques vary by modality — text, image, audio, and video — and generally fall into spatial-domain (direct modification of content features) and frequency-domain (modification of transformed coefficients) approaches.

For text, probabilistic token-level watermarking biases token selection during generation to embed detectable patterns. For images, deep learning-based watermarking encodes signatures into latent representations. These approaches can be robust to common transformations (compression, cropping, paraphrasing) but are susceptible to adversarial attacks designed to remove or forge watermarks.

A critical limitation of AI watermarking for educational use is the accuracy problem: detection tools can yield false positives — incorrectly identifying human-authored work as AI-generated — which limits their reliability in high-stakes academic settings. The EU AI Act's November 2026 transparency obligations require that AI-generated content be clearly watermarked or labelled, but the technical standards for compliance are still being developed.

Signed Provenance and Blockchain

Blockchain-based provenance systems use distributed ledger technology to create tamper-evident records of content origin and ownership. These systems can provide strong provenance guarantees for content that is registered at creation, but they face the same fundamental limitation as C2PA: they can only document what is voluntarily disclosed, and they cannot detect AI use in content that was not registered.

Applicability to Educational Settings

The honest assessment of current technical provenance standards for educational use is that they are promising but immature. C2PA provides a useful framework for content that is created using compatible tools and that is voluntarily registered, but it cannot provide reliable provenance guarantees for the vast majority of educational content currently in circulation. AI watermarking is developing rapidly but is not yet reliable enough for high-stakes academic integrity applications. Blockchain provenance is technically sound but requires infrastructure and adoption that educational institutions do not currently have.

In the near term, schools must rely on a combination of technical tools (where available), institutional processes (procurement policies, content review), and professional judgment (teacher capacity to evaluate content quality and accuracy). Technical provenance standards are likely to become more reliable and more widely adopted over the next five years, but they are not yet a substitute for human judgment in educational content governance.

### Q169 How should a school decide whether a claim delivered by an AI system is reliable enough to teach? {#q169}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

This question sits at the intersection of epistemology, pedagogy, and institutional risk management. When an AI system delivers a claim to a teacher — through a tutoring platform, a content generation tool, or a general-purpose chatbot — the school's responsibility is to determine whether that claim is accurate and reliable enough to be taught to students as true. This is not a peripheral concern: it is a foundational requirement for maintaining the integrity of education as a knowledge-transmitting institution. The fundamental difficulty is that AI systems, including the most capable current LLMs, generate outputs through probabilistic pattern matching rather than factual verification. They produce confident-sounding text in domains where they may have little or no reliable training data. They fabricate citations. They oversimplify complex phenomena. They reflect the biases — cultural, temporal, and methodological — of their training corpora.

A risk-stratified evaluation framework. Not all AI-delivered claims carry the same risk if taught incorrectly. A risk-stratified framework for evaluating AI claims should distinguish between: high-stakes factual claims — specific scientific data, historical facts, statistical figures, legal or medical information, information about living or recently deceased people — which require independent verification through primary or peer-reviewed sources before teaching, regardless of how confident the AI's presentation appears; structural or conceptual explanations — how a biological system works, the logic of a mathematical proof, the causes of a historical event — which require expert review by a subject-matter specialist, since the AI's explanation may be a useful starting point but may also oversimplify, omit critical nuances, or reflect outdated understanding; and low-stakes or illustrative content — worked examples with easily verifiable answers, explanations of well-established, uncontested facts, creative or hypothetical scenarios clearly labelled as such — which carry lower risk if the teacher or an expert can quickly verify correctness.

Institutional frameworks for claim evaluation. EDUCAUSE's institutional AI governance framework, drawing on the Belmont Report's ethical principles, includes "Assessment of Risks and Benefits" as a core requirement: institutions must conduct ongoing evaluations of AI tools' actual outputs against the risks of error. The ALTL framework's evaluative dimension — "critically assessing AI applications, outputs, and potential biases" — is directly applicable to teacher claim evaluation. For educational institutions, this means building into any AI tool deployment process: regular human subject-matter expert review of AI-generated content in use; mechanisms for teachers to flag AI outputs that appear incorrect or misleading; and feedback channels that allow errors to be reported to vendors with documented expectations for correction. UNESCO recommends that governments require AI tools to undergo institutional validation analogous to the standards applied to textbooks, which include checks for age-appropriateness, content accuracy, and cultural suitability. Schools that cannot rely on national governments having conducted this validation should develop their own validation processes, or adopt the process standards their national curriculum authority or professional body recommends.

The role of teacher subject expertise. A finding from the university context is instructive: researchers studying LLMs in academic settings have identified a "minimal threshold of experience" required to use these tools effectively. Professors report that LLMs provide a useful starting point but require significant human subject knowledge to verify facts and logic. Teachers without strong subject knowledge are therefore more vulnerable to accepting AI-generated errors — which suggests that AI deployment in schools should be accompanied by professional development that deepens, not substitutes for, teacher content knowledge. The New Zealand Ministry of Education's guidance makes this point in practical terms: teachers are advised that the most effective detection of inauthenticity in student work comes from knowing their students and their work — not from detection software. The same principle applies to AI claims: the most reliable check is a teacher who knows the subject well enough to recognise when an AI claim is wrong.

A practical decision protocol. Drawing the evidence together, a practical decision protocol for schools evaluating AI claims involves: (1) domain identification — is this claim in a domain where the AI has documented reliability limitations (medical, legal, statistical, recently contested, culturally specific)? (2) independent verification — can the specific claim be confirmed through a primary or peer-reviewed source that exists and is accessible? (3) expert review — has a human subject-matter specialist reviewed the claim in context? (4) pedagogical risk assessment — what is the consequence if the claim is wrong? (A factually incorrect claim in a science lesson about safety procedures carries higher risk than a minor historical inaccuracy in a low-stakes discussion activity.) (5) disclosure to students — even for verified AI-delivered content, teaching students that the claim was AI-generated and has been independently verified models the verification practice the students themselves should develop. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides the broader institutional risk vocabulary within which this individual claim evaluation sits: distinguishing high-risk AI applications (those with significant consequences if incorrect) from lower-risk applications, and proportioning oversight accordingly.

### Q240 How do AI systems trained predominantly on older data handle rapidly evolving topics, and how should educators communicate this temporal limitation to students? {#q240}

11 citations · 11 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Large language models learn from a snapshot of text collected up to a particular date, after which their internal knowledge stops growing. For stable subjects such as the rules of arithmetic or the plot of a classic novel, this matters little. For rapidly evolving topics, including current affairs, scientific fields with fast-moving literatures, technology, law, public health guidance, and the state of AI itself, the temporal limitation can produce answers that are outdated, incomplete, or confidently wrong, and students often have no way to tell.

The problem is more complicated than a single cutoff date. Research by Cheng and colleagues, titled Dated Data, examined whether models' effective knowledge matched the cutoffs reported by their developers. They found that effective cutoffs frequently differed from reported ones, and that different subjects within the same model could have different effective dates, partly because recent material is underrepresented in training corpora and because deduplication and the persistence of older versions of web pages skew the data toward earlier information. In practical terms, a model may technically include data from a given month while still reflecting the state of knowledge from considerably earlier on many topics. Recent events are often thinly represented, so the model's account of them can be sparse and distorted.

Models also tend not to signal uncertainty about time. When asked about a recent development, a model without retrieval may describe the situation as it stood in its training data without noting that circumstances could have changed, or it may infer plausible but invented details. The tendency to generate fluent text where knowledge is thin is related to the broader phenomenon of fabrication documented by Walters and Wilder in Scientific Reports in 2023, who found that a majority of citations produced by GPT-3.5 in their sample were fabricated and that a smaller but substantial share produced by GPT-4 were as well. Outdated content and invented content can appear identical to a student.

Many contemporary systems now incorporate web search or retrieval, which partially addresses the problem by grounding responses in current documents. Retrieval introduces its own issues, however, including dependence on the quality of retrieved sources, possible misreading of those sources, and inconsistent behaviour about when search is triggered. Students may not know whether a particular answer drew on live sources or on stale training data, and interfaces do not always make this clear.

Communicating these limitations to students appears most effective when it is concrete and practised rather than delivered as a generic warning. UNESCO's 2023 Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research emphasises developing users' understanding of how generative systems are built, including their dependence on training data, and the U.S. Department of Education's 2023 report argued that AI literacy should help students and teachers understand the limitations and failure modes of these systems. Several practical strategies follow from that guidance.

One strategy is to teach the concept of a training cutoff explicitly, with demonstrations. Teachers can ask a model about an event the class knows occurred recently and examine whether it acknowledges the event, describes it accurately, or fills gaps with speculation. Seeing the limitation firsthand tends to be more memorable than being told about it. Another strategy is to establish a habit of date-checking: for any claim about something that could change, students should ask when the information was true and confirm it against a dated, authoritative source. A third strategy is to categorise topics by volatility, distinguishing stable knowledge from fast-moving domains, so that students learn when AI output can be treated as a reasonable starting point and when it must be verified. A fourth is to require that AI-assisted work on current topics cite primary, dated sources rather than the AI itself.

Educators can also model appropriate language. Describing AI outputs as reflecting the information the system was trained on, rather than as statements of current fact, helps students internalise a more accurate mental model. School guidance documents, such as the TeachAI toolkit, encourage teaching students to evaluate AI outputs critically and to understand that systems can be outdated or wrong.

The technical literature has documented temporal degradation for several years. Lazaridou and colleagues at DeepMind, in a paper presented at NeurIPS in 2021 titled Mind the Gap, trained language models on data up to a particular point and evaluated them on text from subsequent periods. They found that model performance deteriorated progressively as the gap between training and test periods grew, with the decline especially pronounced for text involving named entities and topics that emerged or changed after the training period, and that simply increasing model size did not solve the problem. Their analysis suggested that temporal generalisation is a structural challenge for any system that learns from a fixed corpus, rather than a quirk of particular models.

Related work has explored how models represent time explicitly. Dhingra and colleagues, in a 2022 article in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, showed that standard language models trained on text from many years tend to conflate facts that were true at different times, for example the holder of a political office, and proposed time-aware training in which text is tagged with its date. Their experiments found that such conditioning improved the model's ability to answer questions about facts as they stood at particular times and to update more efficiently with new data. The broader implication for educators is that a model's answer about who holds a position or what a policy says may blend information from multiple periods, producing an answer that was never simultaneously true.

Evaluations of how models handle questions with changing answers confirm the classroom relevance of these findings. Vu and colleagues introduced FreshQA in 2023, a benchmark of questions spanning those whose answers never change, those that change slowly, those that change quickly, and those based on false premises. They reported that models without search augmentation performed poorly on fast-changing questions and on questions with false premises, often answering confidently rather than flagging outdated knowledge or challenging the premise. They also found that augmenting models with search results, particularly when the prompt presented evidence in date order, substantially improved accuracy. The false-premise finding deserves emphasis for educators: when a student's question embeds a mistaken assumption, perhaps about an event that did not happen as described, a model may elaborate on the assumption rather than correct it.

Retrieval-augmented generation, introduced in an influential 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues, combines a language model with a mechanism that retrieves relevant documents and conditions generation on them. The approach underpins many contemporary search-enabled assistants and institutional chatbots that draw on curated document collections. It offers a principled way to keep answers current, because the document store can be updated without retraining the model, and it can make sources visible to users. For schools, retrieval systems built on curated, dated materials, such as a district's current policies or a vetted set of science resources, may be more trustworthy for evolving topics than general-purpose models, provided that the curated sources are themselves maintained.

Yet the reliability of retrieval-based systems in practice remains uneven. The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia University reported in March 2025 on tests in which eight AI search tools were given excerpts from news articles and asked to identify the original article, publisher, date, and link. The researchers found that the tools collectively provided incorrect answers to more than 60 percent of queries, often with confident language and without acknowledging uncertainty, and that premium versions were in some respects more confidently wrong than free ones. Some tools fabricated links or cited syndicated copies rather than original sources. These findings suggest that the presence of citations in an AI answer is not in itself evidence of accuracy or currency, and that students need to check that cited sources exist, say what is claimed, and are dated appropriately.

The research on how skilled readers evaluate online information offers a complementary pedagogical foundation. Wineburg and McGrew, in a 2019 article in Teachers College Record, compared how professional fact-checkers, historians, and university students evaluated unfamiliar websites. They found that fact-checkers reached more accurate judgements more quickly by reading laterally, leaving the site to see what other sources said about it, rather than reading vertically within the site and relying on its appearance. Subsequent classroom studies by the Stanford History Education Group and others reported that brief instruction in lateral reading was associated with improved student performance on online evaluation tasks. Lateral reading transfers naturally to AI outputs: rather than judging an answer by its fluency, students can check key claims against independent, dated sources.

Information literacy frameworks provide a vocabulary for embedding these practices. The Association of College and Research Libraries' Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, adopted in 2016, includes frames such as authority is constructed and contextual and information creation as a process, which emphasise that the credibility of information depends on its origin, purpose, and timing. Teaching about AI temporal limitations can be integrated into such frames: an AI output is a product of a particular creation process, trained on materials from particular periods, and its authority on a given topic depends on whether that process could plausibly have captured current knowledge.

Subject-specific considerations also matter. In science education, students can be shown that fields such as genomics, climate science, or materials research publish findings continuously and that consensus statements are periodically revised, so that an AI answer may reflect an earlier consensus. In civics and social studies, election results, legislation, and court decisions change rapidly and carry high stakes for accuracy. In health education, outdated guidance on topics such as vaccination schedules or nutrition could cause harm. In computing, AI's descriptions of its own capabilities and of other AI systems are especially likely to be outdated, which creates an instructive paradox that teachers can use to illustrate the problem.

Educators themselves face the same limitation when using AI to prepare materials. A teacher who uses an AI system to draft a lesson on a recent scientific development or a current policy debate risks embedding outdated information in instruction. Professional guidance for teachers can therefore encourage date-checking of AI-generated lesson content, particularly for topics flagged as volatile, and can recommend that schools maintain curated, regularly updated resources for such topics.

Finally, there are questions of equity. Students with access to premium, search-enabled tools may receive more current answers than those using free versions without retrieval, while students in under-resourced languages may encounter even greater temporal gaps, since recent content in those languages is sparse in training data. Communicating temporal limitations therefore involves not only teaching a general concept but also helping students understand how the particular tools available to them behave.

Assessment design can reinforce these habits. Tasks that require students to establish the current state of a fast-moving question, to document the dates of their sources, and to note where AI outputs diverged from current evidence reward exactly the verification practices that temporal limitations demand. Such tasks also make AI use visible and discussable rather than covert. Teachers have reported that asking students to annotate AI outputs with corrections and dates is a manageable way to integrate the tools while preserving the intellectual work of inquiry, although evidence on the effectiveness of such approaches remains largely descriptive and would benefit from systematic evaluation.

The communication of temporal limits also has an affective dimension. Students who discover that a trusted tool has misled them may swing from overconfidence to blanket distrust, neither of which supports good judgement. Framing temporal limitations as a predictable property of how these systems are built, rather than as a scandal, appears more likely to foster calibrated trust.

The temporal limitation is not a temporary defect likely to disappear entirely, because any model trained on past data faces some lag, and retrieval only partially compensates. Treating AI responses on evolving topics as provisional, and building verification into ordinary classroom practice, appears to offer the most durable protection. It also teaches a broader lesson about knowledge itself: that what is known changes over time and that responsible inquiry requires attention to when, as well as what, a source claims.

### Q241 What is the epistemic status of AI-generated summaries and syntheses — when, if ever, can they serve as academically citable sources? {#q241}

11 citations · 11 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Academic citation serves several purposes at once. It gives credit to those whose work is used, it allows readers to locate and verify the evidence on which claims rest, and it situates an argument within a community of accountable authors. Asking whether an AI-generated summary or synthesis can be cited is therefore asking whether such outputs can perform these functions. The emerging consensus across publishers, research funders, and style authorities suggests that they generally cannot serve as evidentiary sources, although their use can and should be documented.

The first difficulty is accountability. The Committee on Publication Ethics stated in 2023 that AI tools cannot meet the requirements for authorship because they cannot take responsibility for submitted work, assert the presence or absence of conflicts of interest, or manage copyright and licence agreements. The European Commission's Living Guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research, updated in a third edition in May 2026, similarly maintain that AI systems cannot be authors and that researchers remain fully responsible for scientific output. If a source has no accountable author, it cannot fulfil the social function of citation, which is to attach claims to agents who can be questioned and corrected.

The second difficulty is verifiability and reproducibility. A journal article or book has a fixed, retrievable text. An AI-generated summary is produced on demand, may differ each time the same prompt is entered, and may be impossible for a reader to reproduce, particularly once model versions are retired. Even where a conversation link is preserved, the reader cannot inspect how the model arrived at its synthesis. A citation that cannot be checked weakens rather than strengthens an argument.

The third difficulty is accuracy. Walters and Wilder, in a 2023 study in Scientific Reports, examined 636 bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT for short literature reviews. They found that 55 percent of the citations produced by GPT-3.5 and 18 percent of those produced by GPT-4 were fabricated, and that among the real citations, substantive errors appeared in 43 percent and 24 percent respectively. Although newer systems with retrieval have reduced some of these problems, a synthesis may still misrepresent, overgeneralise, or omit the findings it summarises, and errors are hard to detect without consulting the originals. Citing the summary rather than the originals would propagate any such errors with an appearance of authority.

The fourth difficulty concerns the integrity of the literature itself. Kobak and colleagues, writing in Science Advances in 2025, used excess vocabulary analysis to estimate that at least 13.5 percent of biomedical abstracts published in 2024 were processed with large language models, with much higher rates in some subcorpora. As AI-assisted text becomes widespread, the risk grows that unverified syntheses enter the record and are later cited as if they were independent findings, creating circular chains of reference.

These considerations do not mean that AI summaries are useless or that their use should be hidden. Style authorities have provided ways to document use. The APA Style guidance on citing ChatGPT recommends describing how the tool was used and, where the output is quoted or paraphrased, crediting the developer and model version, while encouraging authors to include prompts and responses in an appendix. This form of citation functions as methodological disclosure rather than as an appeal to authority: it tells readers how a text was produced, not that the AI is a reliable source of the claims.

A defensible position for students and researchers therefore distinguishes three cases. When an AI tool is used to locate, organise, or draft, its use should be disclosed according to institutional and publisher policy, and claims should be traced back to and cited from the primary sources. When AI output is itself the object of study, as in research on model behaviour, it can and should be cited and archived as data. When a writer is tempted to cite an AI summary as evidence for a substantive claim, the appropriate response is to read and cite the underlying work instead.

The publishing establishment moved quickly to articulate these principles once generative systems became widely available. In January 2023, H. Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the Science family of journals, published an editorial titled ChatGPT is fun, but not an author, announcing that text generated by AI tools could not be used in Science papers without explicit permission and that such tools could not be listed as authors, and characterising violation as scientific misconduct comparable to altered images or plagiarism. Science later relaxed the prohibition on AI-generated text to permit disclosed use, but maintained the authorship bar. In the same month, Nature published an editorial setting out two ground rules: that no large language model would be accepted as a credited author on a research paper, because attribution of authorship carries accountability, and that researchers using such tools should document their use in the methods or acknowledgements. These editorials framed the issue not as a matter of style but as one of responsibility and transparency, which are the same functions that citation is meant to serve.

Philosophical analysis has sharpened the question of what kind of epistemic object an AI output is. Hicks, Humphries, and Slater argued in Ethics and Information Technology in 2024 that the outputs of large language models are best described, in the technical sense introduced by the philosopher Harry Frankfurt, as bullshit: speech produced without concern for truth. Their argument was not that outputs are usually false, but that the systems are designed to produce plausible text rather than to track truth, so that when they are accurate it is not because they aim at accuracy. Whether or not one accepts the label, the argument identifies a significant difference between AI outputs and ordinary testimony. In epistemology, the reliability of testimony is commonly grounded in the speaker's competence and sincerity, and in social mechanisms that hold speakers to account. An AI system has neither sincerity in the ordinary sense nor accountability, which helps explain why its outputs fit poorly into practices of citation designed for accountable testimony.

A counterargument holds that reliability, not sincerity, is what matters for knowledge, and that many trusted instruments, such as calculators or encyclopedias, are cited or relied upon without any notion of sincerity. Proponents of this view suggest that if an AI system could be shown to be reliable for a particular class of questions, its outputs might warrant belief in the way that the readings of a well-calibrated instrument do. The difficulty is that current generative systems are not reliable in a stable, domain-specific way that users can easily assess; their reliability varies by topic, phrasing, model version, and retrieval context, and error rates are often unknown for any given query. Instruments earn trust through calibration against known standards, a process that has not been completed for open-ended synthesis.

Empirical studies of AI systems that present citations reinforce the concern. Liu, Zhang, and Liang, in a study published in the Findings of the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in 2023, audited four popular generative search engines across a diverse set of queries. They found that on average only about half of generated sentences were fully supported by the citations provided, and that about three quarters of citations fully supported the sentences to which they were attached. They also observed an inverse relationship between how fluent and useful responses appeared and how well they were supported by citations. These findings suggest that even systems explicitly designed to ground their answers in sources produce syntheses that cannot be trusted without checking, and that apparent quality may be a poor guide to verifiability.

Information scientists have also raised concerns about how AI synthesis reshapes the process of inquiry itself. Shah and Bender argued in a 2022 paper at the ACM Conference on Human Information Interaction and Retrieval, Situating Search, that presenting users with a single synthesised answer rather than a set of sources removes opportunities for users to evaluate provenance, encounter diverse perspectives, and develop their own understanding of a topic. They suggested that search systems should support information seeking as a process rather than collapsing it into answer delivery. From this perspective, citing an AI summary is problematic not only because the summary may be wrong but also because it short-circuits the scholarly practice of engaging with the range of available evidence. A student who cites a synthesis has not encountered the disagreements, qualifications, and methods that the underlying sources contain.

Style guides other than APA have taken similar positions while differing in detail. The Modern Language Association's guidance, published in 2023, recommends citing generative AI whenever its output is paraphrased, quoted, or incorporated, using a template that describes the prompt, names the tool and version, credits the developer, and gives the date of generation. The MLA also advises writers to acknowledge functional uses, such as editing or translating, in a note or the text, and cautions that writers should vet secondary sources the tool cites. The Chicago Manual of Style has suggested that AI-generated text be acknowledged in the text or a note rather than in a bibliography, partly because the output cannot be retrieved by readers. These differences in format reflect a shared underlying view: documentation of AI use is about transparency of process, not about elevating the output to the status of a source.

Legal practice has supplied vivid illustrations of the risks of treating AI output as authoritative. In the 2023 case Mata v. Avianca in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, lawyers submitted a brief citing judicial opinions that had been generated by ChatGPT and did not exist, and the court imposed sanctions. Similar incidents have since been reported in courts in several countries. Although these are professional rather than academic contexts, they demonstrate the consequences of citing AI-generated syntheses without checking the underlying sources, and they offer teachers memorable examples for discussion.

For educators, these considerations translate into pedagogical opportunities rather than merely prohibitions. Assignments can ask students to use an AI system to produce a synthesis on a topic and then to verify each claim against primary sources, documenting which claims were supported, distorted, or unsupported. Such exercises build the habits of source-tracing that scholarship requires and make the epistemic limits of AI concrete. Instructors can also ask students to compare an AI synthesis with a published systematic review, examining differences in scope, method, and transparency, which illuminates why the latter is citable and the former is not.

Institutional policies vary in how they treat AI disclosure, and students may face inconsistent expectations across courses. Clear guidance that distinguishes between disclosure of AI use, citation of AI as an object of study, and citation of evidence would reduce confusion. Libraries and writing centres are well placed to provide such guidance, drawing on the publisher and style-guide positions described above.

Research integrity offices face a related set of questions about AI-generated literature reviews submitted in theses and grant applications. Where a review section has been substantially drafted by AI, examiners may not be able to tell whether the candidate has read the sources cited, and the fabrication rates documented by Walters and Wilder suggest that unchecked AI reviews can contain references that do not exist. Some universities have responded by requiring candidates to declare AI use and to be prepared to discuss any cited source in an oral examination, which restores a form of accountability by tying citations back to a person who can answer for them. This approach is consistent with the broader principle that what makes a citation meaningful is not the origin of the text but the willingness and ability of an identifiable person to stand behind the claims it supports.

There may be narrow future cases in which curated, versioned, and human-verified AI syntheses, published with accountable editors and stable identifiers, acquire a status closer to that of a reference work. In such cases, however, it would be the human editorial accountability and the fixed record that make the source citable, not the AI generation. For now, the epistemic status of AI summaries is that of a useful but fallible instrument whose use is recorded, not a source that warrants belief.
