## Chapter 14: Language, Culture, and Global Asymmetry {#chapter-14}

9 questions · 86 citations · 81 unique sources · 45 cross-references

### Q170 Which languages do current AI systems serve well in educational use, and which do they serve poorly? {#q170}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Current AI systems serve a small set of high-resource languages — above all English — very well in educational use, and serve the vast majority of the world's languages poorly or not at all. The divide is not incidental but structural: it follows directly from the composition of the web-scale corpora on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, and it has concrete, measurable consequences for learners, teachers, and education systems.

The resource hierarchy. The single most important determinant of how well an AI system serves a language is the volume of digitized text available for it in pre-training data. Analyses of Common Crawl, the dominant source of LLM training data, consistently find that English accounts for roughly 40–44% of crawled web content, followed at a distance by German (\~5.7%), Japanese (\~5.1%), French (\~4.6%), Spanish (\~4.6%), and Chinese (\~4.2%). A small tier of additional languages — Portuguese, Russian, Italian, Dutch, Korean, Arabic, and a few others — commands enough data to support reasonably fluent model behaviour. Beyond this tier of perhaps twenty languages, representation collapses: more than forty languages are estimated to constitute less than 0.01% of Common Crawl, and languages such as Hausa and Amharic fall below 0.004%. Because model quality tracks data volume closely, performance gaps between high- and low-resource languages on reasoning and comprehension tasks have been measured at up to 24 percentage points.

What 'served well' means in practice. In educational use, a language is well served when an AI tutor, writing assistant, or translation tool produces fluent, accurate, culturally appropriate output; when speech-to-text and text-to-speech work; and when the vendor has quality-tested the experience. By this standard, the set of well-served languages is very small. Khan Academy's Khanmigo, one of the most widely deployed AI tutoring systems, lists English, Spanish, Hindi, and Portuguese as its only fully quality-tested languages, with text-to-speech available exclusively in those four; more than thirty further languages are offered only in an 'experimental' capacity, with users warned to expect translation and formatting errors, and speech-to-text works only in English. This pattern — a handful of fully supported languages plus a long tail of experimental ones — is typical of the educational AI market. Even among high-resource languages, performance is not uniform: models trained and benchmarked primarily on English exhibit degraded reasoning when operating in other languages, in part because they internally translate prompts to English, reason in English, and translate the result back, a process that is both costlier and more error-prone.

Why low-resource languages are served poorly. Three mechanisms compound the data-scarcity problem. First, tokenizers are optimized for English, so non-English text is fragmented into more tokens, raising cost and degrading the model's ability to maintain context. Second, benchmarks and evaluation tasks are frequently translated from English, importing English-specific constraints (for example, word-count limits calibrated to English morphology) that are ill-defined or impossible in other languages, and importing US-centric cultural assumptions that produce factual errors elsewhere. Third, less-resourced languages occupy isolated, shallow regions of the model's latent space rather than a shared conceptual space, so reasoning skills transfer poorly to them. The result is a vicious cycle: models perform badly in a language, so the tools are not used by its speakers, so little new digital content is generated in that language, so the language remains under-represented in the next round of training data.

Consequences for education. The educational consequences are concrete and inequitable. Roughly 40% of the global population lacks access to education in a language they speak and understand fluently, a figure that reaches 90% in some low- and middle-income countries; AI tools that function only in English or a few major languages add a new layer of exclusion on top of this existing deficit. UNESCO has identified language as a compounding factor in the digital divide, alongside gender, disability, and age, and warns that when AI becomes the backbone of educational delivery, linguistic exclusion becomes more severe. There is also evidence of direct harm: AI writing detectors have been shown to flag the prose of non-native English speakers as AI-generated at far higher rates than native speakers' writing, penalizing precisely the students who are already disadvantaged. And because models are trained on predominantly North American content, their output in any language tends to reflect US-centric cultural norms, which can distort curricula and erode local linguistic and cultural knowledge when adopted uncritically.

Which languages are served poorly, concretely. The poorly served set includes most of the world's languages: the majority of African languages (Amharic, Hausa, Swahili, Yoruba, and hundreds more), many South Asian languages (Kannada, Telugu, Punjabi, and others), indigenous languages of the Americas (Cherokee, Quechua, Aymara, and others), and numerous smaller European and Asian languages. For these, current systems produce higher rates of hallucination, lower fluency, difficulty with idiomatic expression, and unreliable translation. Even widely spoken languages with large speaker populations but thin digital footprints — such as Bengali in some assessments, or many languages of the Horn of Africa — fall into this category. The practical educational consequence is that a student whose home language is not in the high-resource tier cannot rely on AI tutoring, feedback, or translation with the same confidence as an English-speaking student, and teachers working in these languages receive materially worse AI support.

Responses and the direction of travel. The problem is well recognized, and responses are emerging at several levels. UNESCO launched a Global Roadmap on Multilingualism in the Digital Era, built on the commitment to 'leave no language behind', and has issued policy guidance urging ministries of education to collect sociolinguistic data, develop learning materials in local languages, and recruit teachers fluent in both mother tongue and official language of instruction. Community-centred research collectives such as AI4Bharat and the Masakhane Collective model an alternative to 'parachute' data extraction, prioritizing data sovereignty and community control over language resources. Technically, targeted post-training on high-quality language-specific datasets, synthetic data augmentation, and cross-lingual transfer are improving performance in some low-resource languages, though these efforts remain small relative to the scale of the gap. The realistic near-term picture for education is therefore one of persistent asymmetry: the quality gap between the languages AI serves well and those it serves poorly is narrowing only slowly, and for the majority of the world's learners, the language of the AI system remains a significant, and largely unexamined, determinant of the quality of their education.

### Q171 How is AI being used in multilingual and newcomer classrooms, and with what measured results? {#q171}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is being used in multilingual and newcomer classrooms in three broad ways — real-time translation and interpretation, automated translation of instructional and family-facing materials, and AI-mediated language practice and feedback — and the measured results are mixed: clear benefits for access, inclusion, and teacher workload, alongside documented risks of overdependence, reduced productive language output, and algorithmic bias against non-native writers.

The scale of the need. In the United States alone, more than 5.3 million students are classified as English language learners, and the literacy gap is stark: roughly 71% of English learners do not reach reading proficiency by fourth grade, compared with 31% of their non-ELL peers. Multilingual classrooms in many OECD countries face similar pressures, with newcomer students expected to access grade-level content while still acquiring the language of instruction. This is the context in which schools have turned to AI tools, often with limited evidence and under pressure to respond quickly.

How the tools are used. The most visible use is real-time translation. Schools are deploying handheld AI interpretation devices (for example, Pocketalk and Timekettle devices), browser extensions, and platform-integrated translation so that newcomer students can follow lessons, participate in group work, and communicate with teachers and peers in real time. A second use is the automated conversion of lesson plans, worksheets, assessments, and family communications into multiple languages, which teachers report as a major time saving: materials that previously required hours of manual translation or external services can now be produced in minutes. A third use is AI-mediated language practice — conversational AI that gives students low-pressure speaking and writing practice with immediate feedback, often aligned to proficiency frameworks such as the Global Scale of English. Some districts also use AI to generate translated versions of high-stakes documents such as Individualized Education Program (IEP) notes and discipline reports, though guidance bodies consistently warn that these require human review.

What the measured results show. The evidence base is thinner than the adoption rate, but several findings recur. First, students generally report positive attitudes toward machine translation, viewing it as a vocabulary aid and a way to express complex ideas they could not yet formulate independently; studies find it can help students produce more cohesive and complex texts. Second, outcomes depend heavily on pedagogical integration: students who receive explicit training in how to use machine translation — including post-editing and evaluating multiple translation options — outperform untrained peers on spelling, grammar, and content accuracy, and engage more critically with the tool. Untrained use, by contrast, is associated with 'telltale signs' of over-reliance, such as vocabulary and clause structures beyond the student's demonstrated proficiency. Third, AI-mediated feedback has been linked in empirical studies to improved self-reflection and reduced performance anxiety, as students can practise and self-correct without the embarrassment of errors in front of peers. Fourth, teacher perceptions lag behind student perceptions: many language instructors remain skeptical, viewing translation tools as disruptive or as a form of academic dishonesty, and some respond by designing 'Google-irrelevant' assignments, which researchers note can inadvertently reduce opportunities for digital literacy development.

Documented risks and failures. The risks are as well evidenced as the benefits. Over-reliance on translation reduces opportunities for productive language output — speaking and writing — which is precisely the practice that drives acquisition of grammar and vocabulary; experts therefore describe translation tools as a scaffold to be withdrawn, not a permanent accommodation. There is also a documented equity failure in AI-based assessment: automated writing scoring and AI-detection systems trained predominantly on native-speaker data have been shown to misidentify the writing of English learners as AI-generated or to score it unfairly, with bias most pronounced when training datasets are small. This means the same AI systems that are supposed to support multilingual learners can, in assessment contexts, penalize them. Data privacy is a further concern: schools must ensure that tools processing student speech and writing comply with FERPA and GDPR, and that children's voices — which are under-represented in training data — are not captured into vendor systems without consent.

Guidance and the direction of practice. Professional bodies have begun to codify practice. The National Education Association's guidance for AI and multilingual learners recommends a human-in-the-loop approach: AI-generated translations of high-stakes documents must be reviewed by qualified staff; tools should be piloted in defined contexts before wider rollout; and schools should develop usage timelines so that newcomers transition toward independent English proficiency rather than permanent reliance. The emerging consensus across the literature is that AI translation functions best as a bridge — providing immediate access to grade-level content and reducing isolation — while the core work of language acquisition, including peer interaction and productive output, remains a human and pedagogical task. The measured results to date support this framing: AI demonstrably improves access and reduces teacher workload, but no study shows it replacing structured language instruction, and several show that unguided use can slow acquisition. For schools, the practical implication is that the value of AI in multilingual classrooms is determined less by the capability of the tools than by the quality of the pedagogical framework around them.

### Q174 How is AI being applied in indigenous and minority-language education, and who controls those projects? {#q174}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is being applied to indigenous and minority-language education primarily through automatic speech recognition, transcription of oral archives, conversational practice tools, pronunciation coaching, and translation assistance — and the defining feature of the field is the question of control. The most prominent projects are explicitly community-led, built on data-sovereignty frameworks designed to prevent the extraction of indigenous linguistic data by technology corporations, while a parallel set of risks — data colonialism, cultural misrepresentation, and environmental cost — shapes how these projects are governed.

How AI is being applied. The dominant application is automatic speech recognition (ASR). Because many indigenous languages are primarily oral, with limited written corpora, the ability to transcribe recorded speech is the foundational capability on which other tools depend. The First Languages AI Reality (FLAIR) program, based at Mila in Quebec and led by indigenous technologists, develops ASR and voice-based educational tools for First Nations languages, including portable 'language in a box' hardware that works offline for communities without reliable broadband. Te Hiku Media in Aotearoa New Zealand built ASR models for te reo Māori that transcribe the language with 92% accuracy and bilingual Māori–English speech with 82% accuracy — results that outperformed offerings from major technology companies at the time. Beyond transcription, projects include bilingual conversational chatbots for low-pressure practice, such as Masheli, a Choctaw–English chatbot, and Skobot, a wearable robot that converses in Anishinaabemowin; pronunciation-coaching applications such as Rongo, which helps learners recover native pronunciation and regional dialects; and generative-AI translation and tutoring tools, including the Te Rau o te Huia project, which uses a virtual elder persona to connect younger generations with traditional knowledge. In education, these tools are used to transcribe and make accessible vast archives of oral histories, to provide scalable practice opportunities that supplement — but are explicitly designed not to replace — in-person teaching by elders and fluent speakers, and to preserve regional dialect variation by training models on iwi- or community-specific data.

Who controls the projects. Control is the central axis of this field, and the leading projects are structured to keep it in community hands. Te Hiku Media pioneered the Kaitiakitanga licence, a community-governed framework that permits the use of Māori language data only for the benefit of Māori people, and built its own infrastructure, including the Whare Kōrero content platform, rather than surrendering data to global platforms. The Cherokee Nation established an AI, Data Sovereignty, and Cybersecurity Task Force and requires prospective technology partners to answer an AI questionnaire ensuring tools serve the collective good and uphold Cherokee values. In Canada, First Nations projects operate under the OCAP principles (Ownership, Control, Access, Possession), and internationally the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) and Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) are increasingly treated as preconditions for any AI work involving indigenous data. UNESCO has issued guidelines on indigenous data sovereignty in AI development, and the UN has framed the issue in terms of the right of indigenous peoples to govern data about themselves. The Maasai Language AI Project in Kenya exemplifies the community-led model: elders guide every stage of development to ensure cultural accuracy. The contrast with the mainstream AI industry is stark: most large language models are trained on web-scale data scraped without consent, and indigenous linguistic content — where it exists online — has been absorbed into commercial models without community authorization, a pattern researchers describe as data colonialism.

Measured outcomes and unresolved problems. The evidence that these tools work is strongest for transcription and speech recognition, where accuracy figures are published and independently meaningful, and for learner engagement, where conversational tools demonstrably increase practice time, particularly for younger learners who may be reluctant to practise with elders. What is less established is the long-term effect on language vitality: no study yet shows that AI tools alone reverse language shift, and practitioners consistently frame AI as a supplement to intergenerational transmission rather than a substitute for it. The risks are well documented. Generative models trained on limited data can produce stereotyped or inaccurate cultural content, including misattributed imagery and flattened dialect variation. The energy and water costs of data centres fall disproportionately on indigenous territories, creating a tension between language revitalization and environmental stewardship. And there is a persistent governance gap: for every community-led project, there are commercial products that use indigenous languages without consent, licensing, or benefit-sharing, which is why data sovereignty has become the organizing principle of the field.

The educational bottom line. For schools, the practical implications are threefold. First, AI can genuinely expand access to indigenous and minority-language learning — providing pronunciation models, transcription of elders' recordings, and low-pressure practice environments that are otherwise unavailable in most classrooms. Second, the quality and legitimacy of these tools depend on who controls them: tools built with community data governance are more accurate, more culturally faithful, and more durable than tools built by extraction. Third, schools adopting such tools should ask the same questions the communities ask — who owns the data, who can withdraw it, who benefits — and should prefer projects governed by the community whose language is being taught. The field's trajectory is toward community-controlled 'small data' models rather than reliance on general-purpose commercial systems, and that trajectory is itself an educational outcome: indigenous students are not only learning their languages with AI, but learning that their languages' digital futures are theirs to govern.

### Q175 Is there evidence that AI use accelerates linguistic homogenisation in student writing and speech? {#q175}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Yes — a growing body of empirical research shows that AI use measurably accelerates linguistic homogenisation in student writing, and the effect operates at two distinct levels: the individual text and the collective corpus. The evidence is strongest for written output, where studies document convergence in structure, style, and cultural reference, and it is driven by mechanisms — training-data bias, alignment procedures, and recursive feedback loops — that are intrinsic to how current systems are built.

The quality–homogenisation tradeoff. The most consistent finding in the literature is that AI assistance improves surface quality while reducing diversity. Studies of AI-augmented writing report higher scores on grammar, coherence, lexical richness, and argumentative structure, but simultaneously find reduced structural and creative variety. Researchers have formalized this as a 'quality–homogenisation tradeoff': as the volume of AI-assisted content grows, the collective contribution of novel ideas declines relative to human-only writing. The effect is dimension-specific rather than monolithic. Structural features such as cohesion architecture and structural originality are highly susceptible, with studies reporting losses of variance of up to 70–78% when AI is used; other dimensions, such as perspective plurality, may actually show increased diversity, because AI can help writers explore viewpoints they would not have generated themselves. The net effect, however, is convergence: individual essays become more polished while the ecosystem of student writing becomes more alike.

Cultural homogenisation. A second line of evidence shows that homogenisation is not merely stylistic but cultural. Because most large language models are developed by Western companies and trained on predominantly Western, English-language data, their suggestions systematically privilege Western values, artefacts, and linguistic norms. A widely reported study from Cornell found that AI writing suggestions made text 'more generic and Western': when writers from India used AI assistance, their writing shifted toward Western norms, with AI suggestions omitting or replacing local cultural details — proposing 'pizza' or 'Christmas' where the writer had described local food or festivals — and prompting users to describe their own cultural artefacts through a 'Western gaze'. The same study found that non-Western users experienced smaller productivity gains, because they had to invest additional effort correcting suggestions that did not fit their cultural context, a pattern researchers describe as a form of 'AI colonialism'. For students, this means that AI use does not merely standardize prose; it can actively erode culturally specific expression in writing.

Mechanisms of convergence. Three mechanisms explain why homogenisation is systematic rather than accidental. First, training data: models are trained to predict the statistically most likely next token, which privileges frequent, dominant linguistic patterns and suppresses rare or culturally distinct expression. Second, alignment: reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) rewards outputs that match rater consensus, which collapses output variance toward 'safe', canonical registers. Third, recursive feedback loops: as AI-generated text is re-ingested into the training data of future models, the system becomes self-reinforcing — a process researchers call 'modelized' text or linguistic monoculture. Quantitative studies document a stepwise drop in stylistic variance following the widespread adoption of LLMs, with newer models exhibiting lower variance in language and style than human writers on classical metrics such as type–token ratio and entropy. In multi-agent simulations, models even collapse distinct personas into a single 'helpful assistant' archetype, and they portray socially subordinate groups as more semantically homogeneous than dominant groups.

Evidence specific to student writing. Studies of student populations confirm that these effects reach the classroom. Research on high-stakes college admissions essays found that generative AI use is associated with measurable changes in writing style, and that lower-socioeconomic-status applicants adopted AI at disproportionately higher rates — using it as a substitute for the professional essay coaching that wealthier peers can afford — while simultaneously facing greater evaluative penalties, as admissions readers interpreted AI-assisted writing differently depending on the applicant's background. In multilingual higher education, students increasingly use AI to mediate between their full linguistic repertoires, and educators report concerns that improper use diminishes metacognitive engagement and authorial voice. There is also evidence that AI-based writing assessment compounds the problem: automated scoring systems assign lower scores to writing on culturally proximal topics than on Western-familiar ones, a bias not mirrored by context-familiar human raters, meaning the same systems that homogenize writing can also penalize the diversity that remains.

Is homogenisation inevitable? The evidence suggests it is not a fixed property of AI but a function of interaction design and pedagogy. Research shows that sophisticated prompt design can reverse homogenisation on specific metrics such as argument depth, turning convergence into diversification. Pedagogical models that involve students in prompt formulation, comparison of multiple AI-generated alternatives, critical revision, and justification of final linguistic choices have been shown to preserve — and in some studies enhance — linguistic creativity and authorial agency, provided the student remains the final author. Diversity-aware training objectives, pluralistic alignment, and data curation that prioritizes under-represented corpora are proposed technical remedies, though none is yet standard practice. The practical implication for schools is that unguided AI use in writing instruction is likely to accelerate homogenisation — in structure, style, and cultural content — while structured, critical use can mitigate it. The question for educators is therefore not whether AI homogenizes student writing, but whether the conditions under which students use it are designed to counteract a convergence that the technology produces by default.

### Q176 What does AI translation change about the case for learning a foreign language at school? {#q176}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI translation changes the case for school foreign-language learning by destroying its weakest justification — the purely instrumental one — while leaving its strongest justifications intact and, in some respects, strengthening them. The result is a recalibration rather than an abolition: the argument that students must learn a language to 'get by' in another country or to translate documents has largely collapsed, because real-time translation now handles transactional communication more fluently than most school leavers ever will. But the cognitive, cultural, and relational arguments for language learning survive, and the debate has shifted to whether schools can articulate them convincingly enough to resist the temptation to cut language programmes.

What AI translation actually removes. The instrumental case for language learning was always the most vulnerable. If the purpose of studying French or Japanese was to order food, ask directions, or read a menu, then a phone with live translation now outperforms a student with several years of classroom study. Generative translation tools handle transactional tasks — travel, basic correspondence, simple documents — with remarkable proficiency, and they are improving. This is why researchers describe the traditional goal of native-level fluency in school settings as increasingly unrealistic and, in a sense, beside the point: the technology has already achieved the communicative competence that the classroom was struggling to produce. The honest conclusion is that the 'usefulness' argument for language learning, in its narrow form, is no longer defensible, and curricula that rest on it are exposed.

What survives: the cognitive case. The cognitive benefits of language learning are independent of translation technology. Acquisition of a second language is associated with enhanced executive function, cognitive flexibility, and neuroplasticity: the brain's constant suppression of one language while selecting another trains the very control processes that underpin problem-solving and multitasking. Language learning also develops 'theory of mind' — the capacity to understand and adopt the perspectives of others — which is a critical skill in globalized professional and civic life. These benefits accrue from the process of learning, not from the resulting ability to communicate, and no translation tool confers them. A student who relies on AI translation gains none of the cognitive training that a student who actually learns the language receives.

What survives: the cultural and relational case. The cultural argument is where the debate has moved. Because AI translation struggles with the intangible elements of communication — sarcasm, humour, idiom, and deep cultural context — and because human bonds formed through direct interaction in another language are not replicable by a device, educators argue that language classrooms should pivot from linguistic proficiency toward cultural competence and global awareness. The foreign-language classroom is described as the optimal environment for fostering global competence: the ability to recognize diverse perspectives, understand human interdependence, and navigate intercultural situations. In this framing, AI is a 'flower in the bouquet' of communication rather than a replacement — it assists with practical tasks but cannot substitute for the personal transformation that occurs through genuine language learning. The pedagogical implication is that language courses should spend less time on grammar drills that AI can now perform and more time on cultural depth, critical evaluation of machine output, and human interaction.

What the evidence says about motivation. A common fear is that AI translation will demotivate students — why study for years what a device does instantly? The empirical picture is more complex. A recent study found that 61.6% of language learners reported that machine translation had not diminished their motivation to continue studying, while 38.4% reported a decline. Other research shows that machine translation can reduce foreign-language anxiety and enhance confidence, particularly among lower-level learners who otherwise feel overwhelmed — suggesting that for many students, the tool functions as a supportive scaffold rather than a reason to quit. The motivational effect appears to depend heavily on how the tool is integrated: students trained to use translation critically, for post-editing and error identification, develop metacognitive awareness and autonomy, while untrained use is associated with disengagement. The risk to motivation is therefore real but conditional on pedagogy.

The systemic risk: administrative capitulation. The most serious threat identified in the literature is not that students stop wanting to learn languages, but that administrators and policymakers use AI translation as a cost-saving substitute for language programmes. Researchers warn of 'administrative capitulation': underfunded or rural districts may view language learning as purely transactional and cut programmes, widening the gap between affluent students — who will continue to receive the cognitive and cultural benefits of language education — and disadvantaged students who will not. Defending language programmes in the age of AI therefore requires a shift in rhetoric: the case must be made in terms of global citizenship, cultural heritage, and cognitive development, not utility. The evidence supports this case, but it must be made explicitly, because the default administrative reading of AI translation is that it makes language teaching redundant.

The bottom line. AI translation changes the case for learning a foreign language at school by forcing it onto its strongest ground. The instrumental justification is gone; the cognitive, cultural, and relational justifications remain and are arguably more important than ever, precisely because they are what the technology cannot provide. Schools that continue to teach languages will need to teach them differently — with less emphasis on the transactional fluency AI has already achieved and more on the human capacities that AI cannot replicate — and they will need to defend the subject in those terms. The question is no longer whether AI makes language learning obsolete, but whether education systems can articulate, and fund, the reasons it is not.

### Q228 What does evidence show about AI-supported second-language acquisition, and what linguistic inequities does it create? {#q228}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI and Second-Language Acquisition: Evidence, Opportunities, and Linguistic Inequities

The application of artificial intelligence to second-language acquisition (SLA) has generated one of the most active research literatures in AI and education. AI tools for language learning — from intelligent tutoring systems and conversational agents to AI-powered writing feedback and pronunciation coaching — have proliferated rapidly, and the evidence on their effectiveness is more developed than in many other areas of AI in education. However, this evidence also reveals significant linguistic inequities: the benefits of AI language learning tools are not distributed equally across languages, learner populations, or educational contexts.

The Evidence Base

A scoping review of AI in SLA published in 2024 examined 49 empirical studies conducted from January 2023 through December 2024. The review found consistent evidence of positive effects on language learning outcomes, particularly in writing and speaking skills, with AI tools providing immediate, personalised feedback that would otherwise require teacher attention. A systematic review of AI-powered conversational agents in language learning found that they reduce communication anxiety, increase motivation, and provide more practice opportunities than traditional classroom instruction allows.

The strongest evidence for AI in SLA comes from applications in writing feedback and pronunciation coaching. AI writing feedback tools — including tools that provide grammar correction, style suggestions, and discourse-level feedback — have been shown to improve writing quality in controlled studies. AI pronunciation coaching tools, which use speech recognition to provide real-time feedback on pronunciation accuracy, have shown positive effects on pronunciation development, particularly for learners who lack access to native-speaker interaction.

The Linguistic Concentration Problem

The most significant finding in the AI and SLA literature is the extreme concentration of research and tool development on English. The 2024 scoping review found that 93.0% of studies focused on English as the target language, with the remaining 7% distributed across a small number of other languages. This concentration reflects the broader pattern of AI development: the largest and most capable language models are trained predominantly on English-language data, and the most sophisticated AI language learning tools are designed primarily for English learners.

This concentration has direct equity implications. Learners of English — the world's dominant language of international communication — have access to a rich ecosystem of AI language learning tools. Learners of other languages — including many of the world's most widely spoken languages, such as Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, and the indigenous languages of the Americas — have access to far fewer and less capable tools. This disparity risks reinforcing the linguistic hierarchies that already disadvantage speakers of minority and low-resource languages.

Skill Imbalances

The 2024 scoping review also found that AI language learning research emphasises writing and speaking more than listening and reading. This imbalance reflects the technical capabilities of current AI systems: writing feedback and speech recognition are more technically mature than listening comprehension assessment and reading support. However, it means that the evidence base for AI in SLA is incomplete, and that tools designed to support the full range of language skills are less developed than those focused on writing and speaking.

Conversational AI and Communication Anxiety

One of the most promising applications of AI in SLA is the use of conversational agents to provide low-stakes speaking practice. Research consistently finds that learners experience less communication anxiety when speaking with AI than with human interlocutors, and that this reduced anxiety leads to more practice and better outcomes. Conversational AI can provide unlimited speaking practice opportunities, immediate feedback, and patient, non-judgmental interaction — qualities that are particularly valuable for anxious learners.

However, conversational AI also has significant limitations as a language learning tool. Current AI conversational agents are not yet capable of the kind of nuanced, contextually sensitive interaction that characterises authentic human communication. They may reinforce non-native patterns rather than correcting them, and they cannot provide the cultural and pragmatic knowledge that is essential for genuine communicative competence.

Implications for Language Education Policy

The evidence on AI in SLA has clear implications for language education policy. Investment in AI language learning tools should be accompanied by explicit attention to linguistic equity — ensuring that tools are developed for a diverse range of languages, not just English. Research funding should prioritise under-resourced languages and learner populations. And language educators should be equipped to critically evaluate AI language learning tools, including their linguistic assumptions, their evidence base, and their equity implications.

### Q242 What does research say about AI translation's role in foreign-language learning — does it support or substitute genuine language acquisition? {#q242}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Machine translation has moved from a curiosity to a constant presence in the lives of language learners. Neural systems and, more recently, general-purpose language models produce fluent translations instantly and at no cost, and many students use them whether or not their teachers permit it. The question of whether this supports or substitutes for genuine language acquisition does not have a single answer. The research to date suggests that outcomes depend on how the tool is used, by whom, and for what purpose.

Second-language acquisition theory offers a useful starting point. Most accounts hold that acquisition requires meaningful input, opportunities to produce language, attention to the gap between one's own output and target forms, and feedback that prompts revision. Any tool that removes the learner's need to produce language, or that delivers finished output without engagement, risks bypassing these processes. Conversely, a tool that helps learners notice discrepancies between what they wrote and what a proficient speaker might write could, in principle, accelerate learning.

Empirical studies of guided use tend to support the second possibility. Sangmin-Michelle Lee, in a 2020 study in Computer Assisted Language Learning, asked Korean university students to write first in their native language, translate their own text into English without assistance, and then use machine translation as a reference to compare and revise their work. Text analysis indicated that this process reduced lexico-grammatical errors and improved revisions, and interviews suggested that students came to see writing as a multi-stage activity. A follow-up study by Lee and Briggs in ReCALL in 2021 found that students who used machine translation to mediate revision significantly reduced several categories of errors in academic writing, with more proficient students correcting a larger share. In both designs, the learner produced the text first and used translation as a mirror rather than a substitute.

Systematic reviews reinforce this pattern while noting important qualifications. Klimova and colleagues, in a 2023 PRISMA-based review in Education and Information Technologies drawing on Scopus and Web of Science, concluded that neural machine translation can support productive skills such as writing and speaking, receptive skills such as reading, and mediation skills relevant to translation. They also concluded that the tools appear best suited to advanced learners, who have enough proficiency to evaluate and reflect on machine output, whereas beginners may lack the knowledge needed to detect errors or understand why a translation differs from their own attempt. The reviewers emphasised that teachers need to guide students in understanding both the benefits and limitations of the technology.

Urlaub and Dessein, writing in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence in 2022, argued that educators' frequent hostility to machine translation, often framed as a problem of cheating, has obscured its pedagogical potential. They proposed that tools could be redesigned with educational modes that encourage learners to negotiate meaning, compare alternatives, and reflect on choices rather than simply accept output. Their argument is conceptual rather than experimental, but it highlights an important point: most commercial translation tools are designed for efficient communication, not for learning, and their default behaviour encourages substitution.

The risks of substitution are real, even if less studied with rigorous designs. When students paste assignments into a translator and submit the result, they may complete the task without engaging the cognitive processes that build vocabulary, grammar, and fluency. Teachers report difficulty assessing what students can actually do, and assessment validity suffers. Large language models intensify this problem because they can generate original text in the target language from a prompt in the learner's native language, removing even the act of composition. UNESCO's 2023 guidance on generative AI in education cautions more generally that these tools can undermine the development of human capabilities if used to replace rather than support learning activities.

Several design principles emerge from the evidence. Learners appear to benefit most when they produce language first and consult translation second, when tasks require them to explain or justify changes, when teachers explicitly teach the strengths and failure modes of translation tools, and when use is matched to proficiency, with more restricted use for beginners and more open, critical use for advanced learners. Assessment that includes spoken interaction, in-class writing, and reflective commentary on tool use can help distinguish learning from outsourcing.

The theoretical basis for the noticing function deserves elaboration because it explains why the same tool can help or hinder. Richard Schmidt's noticing hypothesis, set out in Applied Linguistics in 1990, proposed that input becomes intake for learning only when it is consciously registered, so that learners must notice features of the target language in order to acquire them. Merrill Swain's output hypothesis, developed in the 1980s and 1990s, added that producing language pushes learners to process grammar more deeply than comprehension alone and creates opportunities to notice gaps between what they want to say and what they can say. When a learner composes a sentence, compares it with a machine translation, and asks why the two differ, both mechanisms are engaged. When a learner simply reads a machine translation of a task they did not attempt, neither is engaged in any meaningful way. The theory therefore predicts the empirical pattern found by Lee and colleagues: benefits appear when learners produce first and compare second.

The broader literature confirms that this is a long-standing debate rather than a new one. Jolley and Maimone, in a 2022 review in the L2 Journal covering roughly three decades of research on machine translation in language teaching, traced the evolution of attitudes from early rejection of crude rule-based systems through ambivalence toward statistical systems to more nuanced engagement with neural translation. They found that instructors' attitudes had softened as quality improved but that many still regarded the tools primarily as a threat to academic integrity, while studies of student use consistently found widespread, often covert, reliance. The authors called for explicit pedagogical integration and for professional development that helps teachers move beyond prohibition.

Quantitative synthesis offers some support for guided use. Sangmin-Michelle Lee's systematic review and meta-analysis in Computer Assisted Language Learning, published online in 2021 and in print in 2023, synthesised experimental and quasi-experimental studies on machine translation in foreign-language education and reported a positive overall effect on language learning outcomes, with larger effects for writing and for more proficient learners. Lee cautioned that the included studies were relatively few, often small, and heterogeneous in design, and that most measured short-term writing quality rather than durable acquisition. The meta-analysis is therefore consistent with the view that guided use can improve the quality of written work and may support learning, without settling whether long-term acquisition benefits.

Practitioner research has proposed concrete classroom strategies. Ducar and Schocket, writing in Foreign Language Annals in 2018, argued for making peace with Google Translate by teaching students how machine translation works, where it fails, and how to use it as one resource among others. They suggested activities such as having students critique machine translations of idiomatic or culturally loaded texts, compare multiple tools, and back-translate to detect errors, while redesigning assessments so that unassisted performance is measured in contexts where tools are unavailable. Their work illustrates how instructors can turn an unavoidable technology into an object of linguistic analysis.

Large language models change the landscape in ways that research is only beginning to address. Unlike dedicated translation engines, general-purpose models can explain grammatical choices, offer alternative phrasings with differing registers, correct learner text with commentary, and conduct conversations in the target language. Robert Godwin-Jones, in a 2022 article in Language Learning and Technology, argued that intelligent writing assistance is becoming so embedded in everyday writing tools that the boundary between assisted and unassisted writing is dissolving, and that language teaching should therefore focus on developing learners' ability to partner critically with AI rather than attempting to exclude it. Kasneci and colleagues, in a widely cited 2023 review in Learning and Individual Differences, similarly identified language learning among the areas where large language models offer opportunities, such as personalised practice and feedback, while warning of risks including overreliance and reduced effort.

The conversational capacity of language models may offer something translation engines could not: abundant opportunities for interaction. Interactionist accounts of second-language acquisition, associated with researchers such as Michael Long, emphasise that negotiation of meaning in conversation, including clarification requests and recasts, promotes acquisition. A language model can engage a learner in sustained dialogue at their level, recast errors, and adapt topics to interests, offering practice that many learners lack, particularly in contexts where speakers of the target language are scarce. Early studies of chatbot-based speaking practice report that learners often feel less anxious speaking with a machine than with peers or teachers, which may encourage more production. However, rigorous evidence that such practice translates into measurable gains in spoken proficiency remains limited, and machine interlocutors may not provide the pragmatic and cultural richness of human interaction.

Language-specific factors also shape outcomes. Translation and language models perform best for language pairs with abundant parallel data, such as English with major European languages, and less well for languages with fewer resources or with structures very different from English. For learners of less commonly taught languages, outputs may contain more errors, which both reduces the tool's usefulness and increases the risk that learners absorb incorrect forms. Conversely, for learners of high-resource languages, the quality of output may be so high that the temptation to substitute it for effort is stronger.

Assessment is the arena where substitution becomes most visible. Written homework completed outside class can no longer be assumed to reflect unassisted ability, and detection tools have proven unreliable, with research by Liang and colleagues finding that AI-text detectors disproportionately flag writing by non-native English speakers as machine-generated. Language teachers have responded by increasing in-class writing, oral assessment, portfolios that document drafting processes, and tasks that require reflection on tool use. Some programmes have adopted explicit tiers of permitted use, distinguishing tasks in which translation is prohibited, tasks in which it is allowed for reference after a first attempt, and tasks in which it is fully integrated, so that students understand the purpose of each activity.

There are also motivational and affective questions. Some researchers and teachers worry that easy access to translation may reduce learners' motivation to invest in learning a language at all, particularly for instrumental purposes such as travel or basic communication. Others argue that the deeper reasons for language learning, including cultural understanding, cognitive benefits, personal relationships, and identity, are not satisfied by translation and may become more salient precisely because routine communication can be outsourced. Surveys of enrolment trends and learner motivation in the era of generative AI have not yet produced clear evidence on this question, and it remains an important area for future research.

Curriculum frameworks have also shifted in ways that complicate a simple ban. The Council of Europe's 2020 Companion Volume to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, the document that underpins language syllabuses and examinations across Europe and well beyond it, expanded the framework's treatment of mediation, describing the ability to relay, explain and adapt meaning across languages as a competence in its own right alongside reception, production and interaction. It also elaborated descriptors for plurilingual and pluricultural competence, treating a learner's existing languages as resources rather than interference. Read alongside the machine translation literature, this framing suggests that translation activity is not inherently a shortcut that bypasses learning; deciding whether a machine rendering preserves tone, register and intent is itself a mediation task that the framework recognises and that examiners can, in principle, assess. The Companion Volume predates the spread of generative AI and says nothing about specific tools, so it does not endorse any particular classroom practice. What it offers is a vocabulary that lets teachers distinguish between activities in which a machine does the mediating on the learner's behalf and activities in which the learner evaluates, corrects and justifies machine output. That distinction maps closely onto the support–substitution question and gives curriculum designers a principled basis for writing tool use into syllabuses rather than treating it only as an integrity problem.

The research base has limitations. Many studies are small, focus on university students in East Asian contexts, and measure short-term changes in written accuracy rather than long-term acquisition or speaking ability. Few use randomised designs. Nonetheless, the consistent message is that machine translation is not inherently supportive or destructive; it supports acquisition when it is positioned as feedback on the learner's own effort and substitutes for it when it replaces that effort.

### Q243 How do cultural assumptions embedded in dominant AI language models affect the teaching of history, social studies, and humanities in non-Western educational contexts? {#q243}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

History, social studies, and the humanities are the subjects in which cultural perspective matters most. They ask students to interpret the past, understand societies, and reason about values, and the answers they reach depend on whose narratives, categories, and moral frameworks are treated as normal. When students in non-Western contexts consult AI language models trained largely on English-language and Western sources, the cultural assumptions embedded in those models become a quiet participant in their education.

Evidence that such assumptions exist has grown steadily. Tao, Viberg, Baker, and Kizilcec, in a 2024 study in PNAS Nexus, compared the responses of several GPT models with nationally representative survey data on cultural values from more than one hundred countries. They found that the models' default responses most closely resembled the values of English-speaking and Protestant European countries, positioning them toward self-expression and secular-rational values. When the researchers used cultural prompting, asking the model to respond as a person from a particular country, alignment improved for a large majority of countries, between roughly 71 and 81 percent depending on the model, though not for all, and some distortions remained.

Atari and colleagues, in a 2023 working paper titled Which Humans?, compared language model responses on psychological measures with cross-cultural data and found that model outputs most resembled people from Western, educated, industrialised, rich, and democratic societies, with similarity declining as cultural distance from the United States increased. Research by Durmus and colleagues at Anthropic, measuring how model responses to global opinion surveys matched those of different national populations, similarly found default responses closer to those of the United States and some European countries, and noted that prompting in other languages did not always shift responses toward the populations speaking those languages.

The roots of this pattern lie partly in training data. Joshi and colleagues, in an influential 2020 ACL paper, classified the world's languages by the availability of digital resources and showed that a small number of languages, led by English, dominate the data on which natural language processing systems are built, while the vast majority have few or no resources. Content about non-Western histories and societies exists in English, but it is often written from external perspectives, and local scholarship in local languages is underrepresented.

For history teaching, the effects can be subtle. A model asked to explain colonial history may default to periodisations, terminology, and emphases common in Western historiography, such as framing events around European actors, describing resistance movements in terms used by colonial administrations, or treating national independence as the endpoint of a story told from the metropole. Questions about religious traditions, kinship, governance, or land may be answered using categories that fit poorly with local understandings. Because outputs are fluent and seemingly neutral, students may not recognise them as perspectival.

In social studies and civics, the risk is that particular political values are presented as universal defaults. The PNAS Nexus findings suggest that models lean toward individualistic and secular orientations, which may conflict with community-oriented or religious frameworks in which students are raised. This does not mean that one set of values should be privileged over another, but it does mean that an AI tool is not a neutral arbiter in discussions where values are contested.

In literature and the humanities, models may have deep familiarity with canonical Western texts and comparatively shallow or inaccurate knowledge of regional literatures, oral traditions, and works in less-resourced languages. Students relying on AI for interpretation may receive richer support for some traditions than others, reinforcing existing hierarchies of prestige.

Responses proposed in the literature and in policy guidance fall into several categories. UNESCO's 2023 guidance on generative AI in education urges attention to linguistic and cultural diversity and cautions that generative models can homogenise perspectives. At the classroom level, teachers can treat AI outputs as primary sources to be analysed, asking students to identify whose perspective an answer reflects, what it omits, and how a local historian might frame the same events. Cultural prompting can partially improve alignment, as Tao and colleagues found, but it depends on the model's limited knowledge and can produce stereotyped representations. At the system level, governments and institutions can invest in local-language datasets, regionally developed models, and curriculum-aligned retrieval systems grounded in local scholarship.

The concept underlying much of this research comes from psychology. Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan argued in Behavioral and Brain Sciences in 2010 that most behavioural science had been based on samples drawn from Western, educated, industrialised, rich, and democratic societies, and that such populations were often outliers rather than representative of humanity on measures ranging from visual perception to moral reasoning and conceptions of the self. Their critique has become a touchstone for AI researchers because language models trained mainly on English-language internet text inherit a similar sampling bias. The resemblance is not coincidental: the people who write most of the text on which models are trained, and the annotators and companies who shape model behaviour through fine-tuning, are drawn disproportionately from the same narrow slice of humanity.

Research on whose opinions models reflect adds a further layer. Santurkar and colleagues, presenting at the International Conference on Machine Learning in 2023, compared language model responses with those of demographic groups in the United States using Pew Research Center survey data. They found substantial misalignment between models and many groups, and that fine-tuning with human feedback shifted model opinions toward those of liberal, higher-income, and highly educated respondents, while some groups, such as older people and some religious populations, were poorly represented. If models are skewed even within the United States, their misalignment with societies elsewhere is unsurprising. The finding also shows that the stages of model development after pretraining, which are controlled by developers, actively shape the values a model expresses.

Cultural bias appears even when models operate in non-Western languages. Naous, Ryan, Ritter, and Xu, in a paper presented at the Association for Computational Linguistics conference in 2024 titled Having Beer after Prayer?, constructed a benchmark contrasting entities associated with Arab and Western cultures, such as names, foods, and places, and evaluated multilingual and Arabic-specific models on tasks in Arabic. They found that models frequently favoured Western entities even when prompted in Arabic and in culturally Arab contexts, for example by completing a sentence about a gathering after evening prayer with a reference to alcohol. They traced part of the bias to pretraining data, noting that even Arabic text on the web includes substantial content translated from or influenced by Western sources. For educators, this suggests that interacting with a model in a local language does not guarantee locally grounded content.

Earlier qualitative work documented similar value conflicts. Johnson and colleagues, in a 2022 paper titled The Ghost in the Machine has an American accent, analysed GPT-3 outputs on prompts touching on contested values across cultural contexts and found that the model tended to reproduce dominant American norms and to present them as natural, even when prompts described other cultural settings. The authors argued that such patterns raise concerns about value imposition when models are deployed globally. Although the model studied has been superseded, the subsequent quantitative studies discussed above suggest that the underlying tendency has persisted.

Scholars working in decolonial theory have placed these findings within a broader historical frame. Mohamed, Png, and Isaac argued in Philosophy & Technology in 2020 that patterns of power established during colonialism, including the extraction of resources and the imposition of knowledge systems, are reproduced in AI through data extraction from the Global South, the outsourcing of annotation labour, and the export of technologies designed according to Western priorities. They proposed decolonial foresight practices, including reverse tutelage, in which developers learn from affected communities, and the creation of affective and political communities that can contest technological impositions. For education, their analysis implies that the question is not only whether AI outputs are culturally biased but also who decides what counts as accurate history or appropriate values in the systems that schools adopt.

Historiographical debates within the humanities provide resources for responding. Postcolonial scholarship, from Edward Said's analysis of Orientalism to Dipesh Chakrabarty's call to provincialise Europe, has long challenged the treatment of European categories as universal frameworks for interpreting other societies. History teachers in many countries already teach students to recognise perspective in textbooks, colonial archives, and international media. AI outputs can be added to this repertoire as a new kind of source with identifiable biases. A classroom exercise might ask an AI system to describe a national independence struggle, then compare its account with local textbooks, oral histories, and scholarship from the region, analysing differences in terminology, causation, and agency.

Regional efforts to build culturally grounded models offer another response. In the Arabic-speaking world, the Jais models developed by Inception, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, and Cerebras, described by Sengupta and colleagues in 2023, were trained with substantial Arabic data and designed to reflect Arabic language and culture. Similar initiatives include SEA-LION, developed by AI Singapore for Southeast Asian languages, and various Indian and African language models. Evidence on whether such models produce more locally appropriate educational content is still emerging, and they face challenges of data scarcity, evaluation, and funding. They also raise their own questions about whose culture is represented within national or regional models, since states may encode official narratives that marginalise minority perspectives.

This last point highlights a complication in the debate. Replacing a Western default with a national default does not necessarily produce a more pluralistic education. History is contested within societies as well as between them, and governments sometimes use curricula to promote particular political narratives. An AI model aligned with a state's preferred account of history may be more culturally local but less open to critical inquiry. The goal suggested by much humanities scholarship is not cultural alignment as such but epistemic pluralism, in which students encounter multiple perspectives and learn to evaluate them.

Teacher capacity is central to any of these responses. Teachers who recognise AI outputs as perspectival can turn bias into a teaching opportunity, but this requires professional development that addresses both the technical basis of bias and the disciplinary skills of source analysis. In systems where teachers are under pressure, have limited training, or lack access to diverse resources, AI tools may be used as authoritative references rather than as sources to be interrogated, which would magnify their influence. Policy responses therefore need to address teacher preparation as well as tool design.

Finally, students themselves bring diverse perspectives that can serve as a check on AI defaults. Classrooms in which students are encouraged to draw on family histories, community knowledge, and local languages can expose gaps and distortions in AI outputs more readily than classrooms in which the AI is treated as the expert. Participatory approaches that position students as critics and contributors rather than consumers may be among the most practical ways to counter embedded cultural assumptions.

The geography of the open web helps explain why these defaults are so persistent, because the encyclopaedic sources that models learn from are themselves unevenly authored. Mark Graham, Ralph Straumann and Bernie Hogan, writing in the Annals of the Association of American Geographers in 2015, mapped where Wikipedia's geotagged articles and their editors were located and found that content about places in Europe and North America was far denser than content about most of Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia, and that articles about many places in the global South were disproportionately written by editors located elsewhere. They described this as informational magnetism, in which regions already rich in content attract further contributions. Wikipedia is a prominent component of the text collections used to train widely used language models, so a history student in Accra or Dhaka who asks a model about their own region may receive an account shaped by outsiders' coverage, written in outsiders' categories. The study predates current models and measured participation rather than model behaviour, so it does not show directly how training data shape any specific answer. It does, however, offer a plausible structural mechanism for the patterns that value-alignment studies detect, and it points to a remedy that sits outside the models themselves: investment in locally authored, openly licensed historical and cultural content that future systems can learn from.

The research base remains mostly focused on measuring value alignment through surveys rather than on observing classroom effects, and direct evidence about how students' historical understanding changes through AI use is scarce. The existing findings nonetheless suggest that educators in non-Western contexts should regard dominant AI models as carrying a particular cultural vantage point and should teach students to interrogate it.
