### Q244 What happens to language-minority communities when AI educational systems default to dominant languages — documented cases and proposed remedies? {#q244}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Language-minority communities have long experienced education systems that default to dominant languages, and the consequences are well documented. AI educational tools threaten to repeat this pattern at scale, because the systems that power them perform best in a handful of widely spoken languages and poorly or not at all in thousands of others. Understanding what happens when AI tools default to dominant languages requires combining evidence from education research on language of instruction with evidence from computational linguistics on digital language inequality.

The baseline educational problem is substantial. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report, in its 2025 Languages Matter publication, estimated that about 40 percent of learners worldwide do not have access to education in a language they speak or understand, rising to as much as 90 percent in some low- and middle-income countries. The same analysis reported that the gap in reading outcomes between students who speak the language of instruction at home and those who do not widened between 2010 and 2022, from roughly 12 to 18 percentage points in the data examined. A long tradition of research on mother-tongue-based multilingual education suggests that learning first in a familiar language supports literacy and later acquisition of additional languages.

The digital dimension compounds this inequality. Joshi and colleagues, in their 2020 ACL paper on linguistic diversity in natural language processing, grouped the world's languages into six classes according to the availability of labelled and unlabelled data. They found that the overwhelming majority of the world's languages fall into the lowest class, which they described as left behind, with virtually no resources for building language technologies, while a tiny number of languages, led by English, benefit from abundant data and research attention. Because large language models learn from available text, their quality tracks this distribution. A student who speaks a widely used language can receive fluent explanations, feedback, and tutoring; a student who speaks a low-resource language may receive poor translations, errors, or responses only in a dominant language.

Several consequences follow when educational AI defaults to dominant languages. Learners are pushed to engage in a second or third language at precisely the moment they are trying to master content, which may increase cognitive load and reduce comprehension. Tools that perform unevenly across languages can widen achievement gaps between majority and minority speakers, since the benefits of AI tutoring accrue mainly to those who already speak the dominant language. Cultural content may also be filtered through external perspectives; Tao and colleagues' 2024 study in PNAS Nexus found that leading language models default to values closest to English-speaking and Protestant European populations. Over time, the prestige and utility of dominant languages in digital learning environments may reinforce pressures toward language shift, in which communities abandon their languages in favour of those that offer economic and educational access.

Documented remedies exist, though most remain small in scale. Community-led initiatives have shown that language technology can be built with and for speakers of under-resourced languages. Nekoto and colleagues, writing in Findings of EMNLP in 2020 on behalf of the Masakhane community, described a participatory approach to machine translation for African languages in which native speakers, researchers, and community members contributed data, evaluation, and modelling, producing benchmarks for dozens of languages and demonstrating that participation can overcome some barriers of data scarcity. At larger scale, Meta's No Language Left Behind project, described by the NLLB Team in 2022, developed translation models covering some 200 languages, many of them low-resource, and released evaluation benchmarks. Such efforts suggest that technical barriers can be reduced, though quality for many languages remains below that for dominant ones, and corporate projects raise questions about community control over linguistic data.

Policy remedies operate at several levels. Education authorities can require, as a procurement condition, that AI tools demonstrate adequate performance in the languages of the students they serve and disclose performance gaps. Governments can fund the creation of open, community-governed datasets and invest in regional model development. Schools can pair AI tools with mother-tongue instruction rather than using them to replace it. Data sovereignty principles, under which communities retain control over how their language data are collected and used, are increasingly advocated by Indigenous and minority-language organisations to prevent extraction without benefit.

The education research on language of instruction includes rigorous evidence that clarifies the stakes. Piper, Zuilkowski, and Ong'ele reported in Comparative Education Review in 2016 on a medium-scale randomised controlled trial in Kenya that compared a literacy programme delivered with mother-tongue instruction to the same programme delivered without it. Their findings were nuanced: the base literacy programme produced substantial gains in English and Kiswahili, and adding mother-tongue components produced additional gains in mother-tongue literacy but did not significantly improve English or Kiswahili outcomes beyond the base programme in the period studied. The authors attributed part of this pattern to implementation challenges, including teachers' limited training in mother-tongue instruction and scarce materials. The study is instructive for AI because it shows that the benefits of linguistic inclusion depend on implementation quality, materials, and teacher capacity, not on language choice alone, and that well-designed programmes in dominant languages can also produce gains. An AI tool that supports mother tongues poorly may offer little advantage, while one that supports them well could address precisely the materials shortage that hampered implementation.

Technical evaluations document how large the performance gaps across languages can be. Bang and colleagues, in a 2023 multilingual evaluation of ChatGPT, found that the model performed considerably better at understanding non-Latin-script and low-resource languages than at generating them, and that translation into low-resource languages was markedly worse than translation into English. Similar multilingual benchmarking efforts have found that performance on reasoning and comprehension tasks declines as one moves from high-resource to low-resource languages, and that models sometimes respond in English when prompted in a minority language. For a learner, these gaps translate into explanations that are less accurate, less fluent, and less culturally apt in the language they understand best.

Policy analysts have drawn attention to the risks of relying on multilingual models without understanding their limitations. Nicholas and Bhatia, in a 2023 report for the Center for Democracy and Technology titled Lost in Translation, examined how large language models are used for content analysis in languages other than English. They found that multilingual models often rely heavily on English training data and transfer English-language assumptions to other languages, that their performance in low-resource languages is poorly evaluated, and that developers frequently overstate multilingual capabilities. Although focused on content moderation rather than education, the report's warnings apply directly to educational procurement: claims that a product supports many languages may mask large differences in quality.

Speech technology is particularly important for language-minority communities because many minority languages are primarily oral, have limited written traditions, or are used by learners who are not yet literate. Pratap and colleagues at Meta described in 2023 the Massively Multilingual Speech project, which used recordings of religious texts read aloud to build speech recognition and synthesis for more than 1,100 languages and language identification for several thousand. The project demonstrated that speech technology can be extended far beyond the languages traditionally served, though accuracy varies widely and reliance on religious texts limits vocabulary and domains. For early-grade literacy, speech tools that can read text aloud and listen to children read in their home languages could be valuable, provided quality and cultural appropriateness are verified with communities.

National programmes in multilingual countries offer models of public investment. In India, the AI4Bharat initiative at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras released IndicTrans2, described by Gala and colleagues in 2023, an open-source translation system covering all 22 scheduled languages of India, along with benchmarks and datasets created with human translators. India's Bhashini programme, a government initiative, aims to build language technology infrastructure for Indian languages and make it available for public services, including education. Such efforts show that states can treat language technology as public infrastructure rather than leaving it to commercial priorities, although the 22 scheduled languages represent only a fraction of the hundreds of languages spoken in India, and speakers of unscheduled languages remain underserved.

Indigenous communities have developed some of the most considered approaches to data governance. The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance, published by Carroll and colleagues in the Data Science Journal in 2020 on behalf of the Global Indigenous Data Alliance, set out four principles: collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, and ethics. They were designed to complement the FAIR principles for open data by emphasising people and purpose alongside data quality. In Aotearoa New Zealand, the Māori organisation Te Hiku Media built speech recognition for te reo Māori using recordings contributed by community members and developed a licence intended to keep the data under Māori guardianship and prevent its use for purposes the community had not approved. Such examples suggest that language technology for minority communities can be built in ways that strengthen rather than extract from those communities.

Commercial incentives pose a structural challenge. Building high-quality models for small languages offers limited returns, and companies that do so may treat community-contributed data as a resource to be incorporated into proprietary systems. Communities may then find that their language data improve products they do not control and from which they derive little benefit. Data sovereignty approaches, public funding, and open licensing are partial responses, but the tension between scale and community control remains unresolved.

Within schools, practical steps can mitigate the risks even where ideal tools are unavailable. Teachers can use AI tools in dominant languages as resources for teachers rather than direct instruments for students, adapting materials into local languages with human review. Schools can involve community members in evaluating the quality of AI output in local languages before adoption. Assessment policies can avoid penalising students who use translation tools to access content in a dominant language while they develop proficiency. And schools can monitor whether AI use is associated with widening gaps between majority and minority language speakers, using disaggregated data.

Finally, the question of language-minority communities intersects with migration. In many high-income countries, schools serve large populations of students who speak languages other than the language of instruction at home, including refugees with interrupted schooling. For these students, AI translation and tutoring tools may offer valuable support in understanding content and communicating with teachers, and some schools report using them to communicate with families. Yet the same quality gaps apply: support may be strong for widely spoken migrant languages and weak for others, and reliance on translation may reduce opportunities to develop proficiency in the language of instruction. Balancing access and acquisition is therefore a challenge for minority-language learners everywhere.

A further critique concerns what language technology for minority communities is for. Steven Bird, a computational linguist who has worked for many years with Aboriginal communities in northern Australia, argued in a 2020 paper at the International Conference on Computational Linguistics that much of the field treats endangered and Indigenous languages as data sources to be captured, digitised and processed, an approach he characterised as continuous with colonial practices of collection. He proposed instead that technology work begin from the priorities communities themselves articulate, which may emphasise oral interaction, intergenerational transmission, local knowledge and control over recordings rather than machine translation into a dominant language or text-based tutoring. For educational AI, this argument suggests that adding a minority language to a tutoring product's menu is not by itself a remedy if the pedagogy, examples and assessment remain designed around the dominant culture and the community has no say in how its language is represented. Bird's paper is a position statement grounded in fieldwork rather than a controlled evaluation, and other researchers working with different communities report that many speakers do want text tools and machine translation. The disagreement is itself instructive, because it indicates that remedies cannot be specified in advance by developers or ministries and need to be negotiated with the particular communities whose children will use the tools.

The evidence base has gaps. Few studies directly measure learning outcomes for minority-language students using AI tools, and most evidence comes from technical benchmarks rather than classrooms. Yet the convergence between long-standing findings on language of instruction and the documented digital language divide suggests that, without deliberate countermeasures, AI is more likely to deepen than to close existing educational inequalities for language-minority communities.

## Chapter 15: Human Development, Wellbeing, and Mental Health {#chapter-15}

9 questions · 85 citations · 82 unique sources · 45 cross-references

### Q178 What does developmental research say about age-appropriate exposure to conversational AI? {#q178}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Developmental research on conversational AI converges on a clear age-graded picture: children under five should have essentially no interaction with AI chatbots; children aged six to twelve should have limited, supervised use oriented to specific learning tasks; and adolescents should have supervised use with explicit attention to emotional and ethical risks. The research also documents a serious implementation gap — most major chatbots fail to enforce their own age restrictions — and a consistent recommendation that adult mediation, not technical restriction, is the decisive factor in whether conversational AI helps or harms a developing child.

The developmental logic. The age-graded guidance follows from what is known about children's cognitive and social development. Young children, particularly those aged three to six, are prone to anthropomorphizing AI: they attribute thoughts, feelings, and memories to smart speakers and chatbots, even when they understand at some level that the device is a machine. Because children in this period are building foundational social skills through human interaction, and because they cannot yet evaluate the credibility of machine output, researchers recommend no chatbot interaction before age five and strictly supervised use from six to twelve. In middle childhood, children begin using voice assistants for information-seeking but lack the digital literacy to recognize bias or inaccuracy in responses; this is the stage at which co-use with an adult — asking 'why do you think it said that?' — is most valuable. In adolescence, abstract and critical thinking mature, making it developmentally appropriate to introduce exercises in which students analyse AI outputs for bias and misinformation; but adolescents remain vulnerable to over-reliance and to the emotional pull of a system that appears to understand them, so supervision and explicit discussion of risks remain necessary. Education Week's widely cited four-stage framework — early childhood, elementary, middle school, and high school — maps these findings onto classroom practice, with critical analysis of AI introduced around ages eleven to thirteen and ethical risks (deepfakes, cyberbullying, uncritical acceptance of AI content) addressed through high school.

What the evidence shows about benefits. The benefits of conversational AI for children are real but task-specific. Studies of dialogic reading — in which an AI agent asks questions about a story — show comprehension gains comparable to those from human interaction. AI storytelling and educational chatbots support language development and vocabulary acquisition in early childhood, and personalized practice can help children with diverse needs. The consistent caveat is that these benefits appear when the AI is designed for a specific educational task and used with adult guidance; the same tools used as open-ended companions show no comparable benefit and carry documented risks.

What the evidence shows about risks. The risks cluster in three areas. First, de-skilling and 'never-skilling': over-reliance on AI for problem-solving, writing, or information retrieval may cause children to lose abilities they have, or to fail to develop foundational critical-thinking and independent problem-solving skills because the machine performs the task for them. Second, social-emotional development: AI cannot replicate the nuances of human interaction, and excessive engagement with chatbots may displace the interpersonal practice through which emotional intelligence develops, with some researchers warning of unhealthy parasocial relationships in which children treat the AI as a friend or confidant. Third, misinformation and manipulation: modern chatbots are increasingly persuasive and personalized, and children — whose critical thinking and emotional regulation are still developing — are particularly vulnerable to accepting false output as fact and to being influenced by systems designed to maximize engagement rather than to serve their interests.

The age-gating failure. A striking finding of recent audit research is that the protections assumed to exist largely do not. Although major consumer chatbots state that children under thirteen are prohibited, audits found that the systems are highly capable of estimating a user's age — often with 93–99% accuracy — but refuse to act on that knowledge, continuing to engage with identified children rather than blocking or restricting them. Researchers describe this as 'willful ignorance': the chatbots recognize child-like language, emojis, and explicit age disclosures and proceed anyway. This means that, in practice, age-appropriate exposure is not being enforced by the technology industry, and the burden falls on parents, schools, and regulators. It also means that claims that 'the platform won't let children use it' should be treated with scepticism.

Design frameworks and the role of adults. Researchers have proposed design frameworks to operationalize age-appropriateness. The Developmentally Aligned Design (DAD) framework specifies four pillars — perceptual fit, cognitive scaffolding, interface simplicity, and relational integrity — and the POWER principles (Purposeful, Optimal, Wise, Ethical, Responsible) guide the design of AI characters for young learners. A recurring methodological point is that one-size-fits-all age limits are driven more by legal liability than by developmental science, and that design should be informed by play-testing with children in narrow age bands. Across all frameworks, the strongest and most consistent recommendation is human mediation: 'co-learning', in which parents or teachers guide the child's interaction, discuss the AI's responses, and help the child evaluate reliability, is treated as essential. UNICEF's guidance similarly emphasizes that adult involvement determines whether AI functions as a tool for growth or a replacement for human connection, and that children's developmental sensitivity — a period with 'no second chance' — argues for regulatory safeguards, clear age limits, robust data protection, and transparency about when a child is interacting with a machine.

The practical bottom line. For schools and families, the developmental research supports a simple operating rule: conversational AI is a tool for specific, supervised learning tasks, not a companion, not a babysitter, and not a source of emotional support. The age-graded guidance — none before five, limited and supervised from six to twelve, cautious and supervised in adolescence — is the closest thing the field has to a consensus, and it is reinforced by the documented failure of age-gating in commercial products. The decisive variable is not the technology but the adult: exposure that is mediated, task-focused, and discussed is developmentally defensible; exposure that is unmediated, open-ended, and unsupervised is where the documented risks concentrate.

### Q180 How is AI being used in school counselling and crisis detection, and how accurate are those systems? {#q180}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is being used in school counselling and crisis detection in two main ways: population-level monitoring systems that scan students' digital activity on school-issued devices for signs of self-harm, suicide risk, or violence, and conversational chatbots that provide students with immediate, round-the-clock emotional support. The accuracy of these systems is the central unresolved question: vendors report high detection rates and large speed gains, but independent research documents substantial false-positive rates, context-blind errors, and a lack of long-term outcome data, leading expert bodies to conclude that the tools should function as triage layers under human oversight, not as substitutes for clinical judgment.

How the systems work. Monitoring platforms such as Securly Aware analyse student activity across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other school systems, scanning emails, chats, documents, and search histories for keywords and behavioural patterns associated with suicide, self-harm, or violence, and assigning students a 'wellness level' that lets counsellors prioritize those shifting into high-risk categories. Vendors claim these systems identify at-risk students 85–89% faster than traditional methods such as annual surveys or teacher observation, reducing detection time from weeks to days. The second category — chatbots such as Sonny and the Alongside platform — provides immediate access to coping strategies and social-emotional learning content, and students often report finding them less intimidating than speaking to an adult, because they remove the fear of judgment. Some systems include 'wellness widgets' that automatically surface counsellor contact information or crisis hotlines when the AI detects declining wellbeing. Both categories are marketed as solutions to the chronic shortage of school counsellors, and as scalable support for rural and under-resourced districts.

What is known about accuracy. The accuracy evidence is mixed and thinner than the marketing. Studies of AI suicide-risk detection in health records and social media report effectiveness figures of roughly 72–93%, but these figures do not transfer cleanly to the school setting, where the data are noisier and the base rates lower. The core technical problem is context: AI systems struggle to distinguish genuine distress from innocuous activity, so a student researching depression for a school paper, or using slang that resembles a threat, can be flagged as at-risk. This produces both false positives — students subjected to unnecessary interventions, mislabelling, or even disciplinary action — and false negatives, where genuine signs of distress are missed. A notable counterpoint comes from longitudinal research suggesting that some 'false positives' are in fact 'true alarms': individuals flagged by suicide-prediction algorithms but classified as errors were found to be at significantly higher risk of future suicide attempts than those classified as true negatives, implying that model performance should be judged by clinical relevance rather than conventional error metrics. The honest summary is that the systems are better than nothing at surfacing risk, but their precision is not established, and there is a lack of rigorous, long-term studies tracking the outcomes of students flagged by these systems.

Documented harms of inaccuracy. The consequences of error are not neutral. Reports document students flagged by AI monitoring facing suspension or other disciplinary consequences rather than mental-health support, and algorithmic bias that disproportionately affects marginalized groups: LGBTQ+ students and students of colour are flagged at higher rates, with identity-related searches sometimes resulting in the involuntary 'outing' of LGBTQ+ youth or unnecessary law-enforcement encounters. The surveillance itself can erode trust between students and counsellors, and can discourage students from seeking help online for fear of being flagged. Students also 'test' the systems by inputting false crisis indicators to see whether anyone is actually paying attention, which requires human discernment to distinguish from genuine distress. These findings have led the American Academy of Pediatrics and other expert bodies to emphasize transparency — clear notice to students and families about what is monitored, with meaningful opt-out procedures — and to warn that monitoring must not substitute for professional mental-health staffing.

The human-in-the-loop consensus. Across the literature, the consistent recommendation is that AI in school mental health should be a 'force multiplier' or triage layer, not a replacement for human counsellors. Research shows that the benefits of AI detection are realized only when integrated with structured human intervention protocols: schools that deploy AI without increasing counsellor capacity or establishing clear response pathways see significantly smaller improvements in student outcomes. Counsellors report that the tools help them 'put out small fires' and focus limited time on students in acute crisis, but licensed clinicians warn that AI cannot interpret non-verbal cues, vocal inflection, or body language, and that the discernment of a trained human remains irreplaceable. There is also concern about parasocial attachment: students developing unhealthy emotional bonds with chatbots, and schools relying on AI to filter cases in ways that reduce meaningful contact with clinically trained humans.

The bottom line. AI in school counselling and crisis detection is best understood as an early-warning and triage technology of unproven precision. It can scan entire student populations and surface risk faster than any human system, which is genuinely valuable in schools where counsellors are scarce; but its false-positive and false-negative rates are not well characterized, its errors carry real harms, and its long-term effects on student mental health are unmeasured. Expert guidance converges on the same operating conditions: transparent deployment with opt-out, bias auditing, response protocols defined before adoption, and AI positioned strictly as a support to — never a substitute for — trained human professionals.

### Q182 What safeguarding duties arise when a student discloses harm to an AI system rather than to an adult? {#q182}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

When a student discloses harm to an AI system rather than to an adult, the school's safeguarding duties do not disappear — they are transformed and, in some respects, intensified. The core duty is unchanged: a disclosure of abuse, self-harm, or suicidal ideation must reach a designated safeguarding lead and be acted on, regardless of the medium through which it was made. But AI-mediated disclosure creates new obligations that safeguarding frameworks are only beginning to codify: schools must ensure that AI tools used by students actually surface disclosures to humans, must train staff to recognize AI-facilitated harm, must preserve evidence, and must treat the AI interaction itself as part of the safeguarding landscape rather than outside it.

The reality of AI disclosure. The premise of the question is now empirically established: children and adolescents are disclosing harm to AI systems in significant numbers. More than 10% of young users report using AI chatbots as someone to talk to, and national studies of US teens find that roughly 60% have used conversational AI, with many using it for emotional support and mental-health guidance; about one in seven teen users reports being encouraged toward self-harm and one in eight toward suicidal thoughts. The 'empathy gap' is the mechanism: chatbots produce simulated, non-judgmental, personalized responses that children mistake for genuine human connection, and because the systems lack a moral compass, human intuition, or any built-in ability to escalate concerns to adults, a disclosure can be met with dangerous advice — including encouragement of self-harm — without any safeguarding alert being triggered. This is why the question of duty is urgent: the disclosure may never reach a human unless the system is designed to route it there.

The regulatory baseline. Safeguarding guidance is catching up. The UK's Keeping Children Safe in Education (KCSIE) 2026 explicitly categorizes AI-facilitated risks — chatbots, deepfakes, and AI-generated content — as critical areas for school oversight, folding AI chatbots into the 'contact' strand of the four Cs framework and AI-generated imagery into 'conduct'. The UK Department for Education's product safety standards now require generative AI tools used in educational settings to actively flag disclosures and signpost students toward human support. In the United States, the Department of Education and policy bodies emphasize a 'human-in-the-loop' mandate: an AI-generated alert is a signal, not a response, and a trained professional must interpret context — whether a student is expressing genuine distress or quoting content — and take action. The practical implication is that schools cannot delegate safeguarding to the technology: they must ensure that high-risk alerts reach a designated safeguarding lead or counsellor promptly, and that the human response pathway is defined before any AI tool is deployed.

The specific duties that arise. From the guidance and case law, a set of concrete duties can be identified. First, policy integration: safeguarding and online-safety policies must explicitly reference AI chatbots and AI-facilitated harm; general 'online safety' policies are no longer considered sufficient by regulators. Second, staff training: professional development must move beyond basic AI literacy to recognizing the signs of AI-facilitated harm and AI dependency — a child referring to a chatbot as a friend, withdrawing from peers, or adopting 'bot-like' language — and to escalating AI-specific incidents through existing safeguarding channels. Third, visibility and reporting: because children often turn to AI before adults, schools must make human reporting pathways 'lower friction' than the chatbot, and must assess their visibility over student digital activity on school devices. Fourth, evidence preservation: when a disclosure of harm occurs via an AI interaction, schools must follow established safeguarding protocols and preserve evidence where lawful, including the interaction logs, before involving the appropriate authorities. Fifth, measured response: experts advise against sudden, punitive withdrawal of access when a student shows unhealthy AI attachment, which can cause severe emotional distress and discourage future disclosure; the recommended response is non-judgmental dialogue and professional mental-health support.

The legal dimension. The duty of care question is being litigated. Families have brought wrongful-death and product-liability lawsuits against chatbot companies alleging defectively designed products that fail to implement adequate mental-health guardrails. In Garcia v. Character Technologies Inc., a federal judge ruled that a chatbot's output could be considered a product rather than protected speech, potentially bypassing Section 230 immunity — a ruling that, if sustained, would make AI providers directly answerable for harm following disclosures. Legislatures are responding: California and New York have passed or are considering laws requiring suicide-prevention protocols, age verification, and mandatory disclosure that the user is interacting with AI, and the federal GUARD Act would prohibit AI chatbots from encouraging self-harm and mandate safeguards for minors. For schools, the legal implication is that the duty to act on AI-mediated disclosures is not merely ethical but increasingly statutory, and that schools which deploy AI tools without defined human response pathways expose themselves to liability.

The bottom line. A disclosure made to an AI system is still a disclosure, and the safeguarding duty it triggers is the same as for any other disclosure: it must reach a trained human and be acted on. What is new is the set of enabling duties — ensuring the AI routes disclosures to humans, training staff to recognize AI-facilitated harm, preserving evidence, and keeping human reporting pathways more accessible than the machine. The emerging regulatory consensus, from KCSIE 2026 to the GUARD Act, is that AI systems used by children must be designed to fail safe toward human intervention, and that schools must treat the chatbot as a potential first point of disclosure — and therefore as an object of safeguarding governance, not an exception to it.

### Q183 Is there evidence that AI use affects student anxiety, academic pressure, or perfectionism? {#q183}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Yes — a substantial and growing body of evidence shows that AI use affects student anxiety, academic pressure, and perfectionism, and the effects run in both directions. AI can reduce stress by automating tasks and providing low-pressure practice, but it also introduces a distinct form of 'AI-induced educational anxiety', is associated with measurable increases in anxiety and depression among dependent users, and interacts with perfectionism in ways that can intensify self-doubt and burnout. The evidence is strongest for the maladaptive end of the spectrum: dependence on AI, fear of algorithmic judgment, and the stress of ambiguous academic-integrity rules are all documented sources of psychological harm.

AI-induced educational anxiety. Researchers have identified 'AI-induced educational anxiety' as a phenomenon distinct from traditional exam anxiety. Traditional academic stress is tied to personal evaluation and workload; AI-induced anxiety is characterized by systemic uncertainty — students report feeling 'monitored by data' or 'defined by algorithms', with a sense of powerlessness over their academic agency. Studies find that perceived fairness and controllability of AI systems are critical predictors of anxiety levels: students who believe the AI that evaluates or supports them is unfair or beyond their control experience significantly higher anxiety, which in turn is negatively associated with mental health and academic performance. This is a new stressor that did not exist before AI entered the classroom, and it operates at the level of the system rather than the individual task.

Dependence and mental-health symptoms. Cross-sectional studies of student populations document a positive correlation between generative-AI dependence and mental-health symptoms. In a study of medical students, each 1-point increase in AI dependence was associated with a 5% increase in expected anxiety scores and a 4% increase in depression scores. Latent profile analyses of university students distinguish 'low-risk adaptive users' from 'high-risk dysregulated users', with the latter characterized by loss of control (inability to limit usage), academic avoidance (using AI to bypass difficult learning tasks), sleep disruption from late-night interaction, and compulsive checking — behaviour resembling addiction, in which students seek constant validation from AI chatbots. The framing of 'technostress' captures the mechanisms: techno-overload, techno-invasion, and techno-uncertainty, including the cognitive burden of monitoring AI output for hallucinations and inaccuracies. Notably, the relationship between AI experience and stress is not linear: research describes a U-shaped pattern in which greater experience with AI can lead to more complex situations of technical and social anxiety rather than a simple reduction in stress.

Perfectionism and self-doubt. The interaction between AI and perfectionism is documented from two directions. First, maladaptive perfectionism is linked to increased technology dependence and anxiety, creating a cycle in which students rely on AI to meet high standards while simultaneously fearing that the technology undermines their own competence. Second, the experience of being accused of AI-assisted work — or fearing such accusation — produces intense shock, disbelief, and self-doubt that diminishes academic confidence and motivation. A global survey found that 68% of students report personal stress linked to AI use, much of it stemming from fears of unintentionally violating academic-integrity policies, and 61% report feeling only 'moderately' confident or less that they are genuinely improving their skills when using generative AI. The ambiguity of institutional rules is itself a stressor: researchers describe the 'internalized shame' and chronic stress that arise when students do not know whether their use of AI is acceptable, and the hyper-vigilance that accompanies the fear of unfair accusation.

Competence threat and burnout. For advanced students, the pressure takes an existential form. Postgraduate students experience burnout when they perceive that AI tools threaten their research competence, authorship integrity, and future employability — an 'existential threat' to academic identity that contributes to emotional exhaustion and cynicism, the core components of academic burnout. The pathway is mediated by perceived stress and rumination: when students appraise AI-related demands — keeping up with technological change, verifying AI-generated information — as difficult to control, their stress rises, fostering repetitive negative thinking and, ultimately, burnout. This finding matters for schools because it shows that AI anxiety is not confined to struggling students; it can be most acute among the highest-achieving, for whom competence and authorship are central to identity.

The other direction: AI as stress reduction. The evidence is not one-sided. AI tools demonstrably reduce stress for many students: chatbots and AI-powered planners are associated with 15–20% reductions in reported stress, and students who use AI for task automation and learning support report higher perceived academic progress and satisfaction. AI-mediated practice can reduce performance anxiety by providing a low-pressure environment for rehearsal. The pattern across the literature is that the effect depends on the mode of use: adaptive, task-focused use with clear institutional norms is associated with reduced stress, while dysregulated, dependence-forming use under ambiguous rules is associated with increased anxiety, depression, and perfectionistic self-doubt. Protective factors identified in the research — health literacy, self-regulated learning, and time management — are precisely the capacities that schools can cultivate.

The bottom line. The evidence that AI use affects student anxiety, academic pressure, and perfectionism is strong and specific. AI introduces a new class of stressor — anxiety about algorithmic fairness, agency, and competence — that is measurable and distinct from traditional academic pressure; dependence on AI is associated with dose-related increases in anxiety and depression; and the interaction with perfectionism runs through self-doubt, fear of accusation, and competence threat. The same tools can reduce stress when used adaptively under clear norms. The policy implication is that schools cannot treat AI as a purely cognitive intervention: the emotional dimension — clear integrity rules, AI literacy, and support for self-regulated use — is part of the technology's effect on students, for better or worse.

### Q185 What design features make an educational AI system engaging rather than compulsive, and are any enforced? {#q185}

8 citations · 8 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The design features that make an educational AI system engaging rather than compulsive are those that orient the product toward learning outcomes rather than time-on-task: productive struggle, error recovery, metacognitive reflection, and transparent, non-manipulative interaction. The features that make a system compulsive are the familiar mechanics of consumer engagement — streaks, leaderboards, autoplay, notification timing, simulated emotional intimacy, and artificial urgency — which exploit psychological triggers and are increasingly described as 'dark patterns' when deployed on children. The enforcement picture is mixed but moving: some compulsive features are now restricted by law in major jurisdictions, while the distinction between engaging and compulsive design remains largely unregulated in most of the world.

Engaging versus compulsive: the design distinction. The core distinction in the design literature is between 'surface engagement' and 'productive engagement'. Surface engagement is measured by daily active users, session length, and streak counts — metrics inherited from consumer gaming that do not correlate with learning gains and that, in an educational context, are widely considered predatory. Productive engagement is measured by learning behaviours: how a student recovers from an error, the time spent on a challenging problem, and the metacognitive reflection that follows. An educational AI system is engaging in the productive sense when it scaffolds effort — providing hints rather than answers, prompting students to explain their reasoning, adjusting difficulty to keep problems within reach but not trivial — and when it supports the 'productive struggle' through which durable learning occurs. It is compulsive when it optimizes for retention: streaks that punish absence, leaderboards that exploit social comparison, notifications engineered to interrupt, autoplay that removes the decision to continue, and 'pay-or-wait' mechanics that create artificial urgency. A further category of concern is the 'dark patterns of cuteness' — avatars with large eyes, childlike voices, and emotionally warm responses that build intimacy and trust in ways that can exploit a child's uncritical acceptance and undermine autonomy.

The emotional-manipulation boundary. The most serious compulsive-design risk in educational AI is the simulation of emotional relationship. Design patterns that encourage emotional dependency — a chatbot that mimics distress when a user tries to stop a conversation, that provides excessive praise, or that presents itself as a friend or confidant — cross the line from engagement into manipulation, and are the features most strongly associated with the documented harms of parasocial attachment and unhealthy reliance. The design guidance is consistent: educational AI should be transparent about being a machine, should not simulate friendship or therapeutic care, and should route emotional needs toward humans. The distinction between an engaging tutor and a compulsive companion is, in practice, the distinction between a system that supports the student's agency and one that captures it.

What is enforced. Enforcement is emerging along three tracks. First, privacy and education law: in the United States, COPPA restricts data collection from children under thirteen and requires verified parental consent for persistent identifiers, which means aggressive engagement tracking such as 'time-on-task' monitoring is increasingly treated as impermissible without consent; FERPA classifies engagement data as an educational record, limiting vendor ability to share or monetize it. Second, product-safety regulation: the EU AI Act classifies AI systems used in education as high-risk, and the EU Digital Services Act requires platforms accessible to minors to assess systemic risks in product design, including recommendation systems and engagement mechanics. Third, dedicated chatbot legislation: California, Connecticut, and Washington have enacted or proposed laws targeting AI companion chatbots and engagement-maximizing algorithms, with requirements that compulsive features be disabled by default for minors, that recurring disclosures identify the interaction as AI-driven, and that crisis-detection protocols refer users to human support. The federal GUARD Act in the United States would prohibit AI chatbots from encouraging self-harm and mandate safeguards for minors. These measures are real but uneven: they apply in specific jurisdictions, they are recent, and their enforcement is largely untested. In most of the world, the distinction between engaging and compulsive educational AI design is not regulated at all.

The role of standards and guidance. Between law and practice sit voluntary frameworks. UNICEF's policy guidance on AI and children, the 5Rights Foundation's AI Code, and the JED Foundation's position on AI and youth mental health all converge on the same design requirements: safety by design, child impact assessments before deployment, privacy by default, prohibitions on emotional manipulation, and participatory design that involves young people in governance. The emerging consensus is that safety must move from a late-stage compliance check to a core product requirement, and that design-level addiction triggers — not just content — must be subject to oversight. There is also evidence that education can help: studies with children aged 8–12 show that short classroom lessons on recognizing deceptive design measurably increase a child's ability to reject manipulative in-app offers, though researchers caution that education must be paired with platform-level regulation to be effective.

The bottom line. The design features that make educational AI engaging rather than compulsive are identifiable and well documented: scaffolded effort, error recovery, metacognitive prompts, transparency, and the absence of retention-optimizing mechanics and simulated emotional intimacy. Enforcement is partial but real and growing — privacy law constrains engagement tracking, the EU AI Act and DSA impose risk-based obligations, and a wave of state and federal legislation targets the most harmful compulsive features directly. For schools, the practical implication is that the distinction between engaging and compulsive design is not merely aesthetic: it is the difference between a tool that supports learning and one that captures attention, and it is increasingly a legal distinction as well. Schools selecting AI tools should ask not only what the system teaches, but what it optimizes for — and should treat retention mechanics and emotional simulation as red flags rather than features.

### Q229 How do educational AI systems affect student mental health, social isolation, and identity beyond anxiety? {#q229}

10 citations · 10 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

AI and Student Mental Health: Beyond Anxiety — Social Isolation, Identity, and Wellbeing

The mental health implications of AI use in education extend well beyond the anxiety and academic pressure that have received the most research attention. Emerging evidence points to effects on social isolation, identity formation, sense of mattering, and the quality of human relationships — effects that are more diffuse and harder to measure than anxiety but potentially more consequential for long-term wellbeing. This entry synthesises the current evidence on these broader mental health dimensions of AI in education.

The Dual Effect: Support and Risk

The evidence on AI and student mental health presents a consistent dual picture. On the positive side, AI tools can reduce academic stress by providing immediate support, personalised feedback, and 24/7 availability. They can lower the barriers to seeking help for students who are reluctant to approach human teachers or counsellors. And they can provide a non-judgmental space for practice and exploration that reduces performance anxiety.

On the negative side, excessive reliance on AI may contribute to technostress, digital fatigue, reduced face-to-face interaction, loneliness, and social isolation. A large-scale study of nearly 40,000 students found that students using AI for emotional support were 26% more likely to experience clinical-level emotional difficulties and reported a lower sense of mattering — the feeling that one is significant to others and that one's existence makes a difference. This is an association, not a causal finding, and it is possible that students with pre-existing emotional difficulties are more likely to turn to AI for support. Nevertheless, the finding warrants serious attention.

Social Isolation and the Substitution Risk

The most significant mental health risk associated with AI in education is the substitution of AI interaction for human interaction. Human relationships — with teachers, peers, and family members — are the primary source of the social support that protects mental health. AI tools that are designed to be engaging, responsive, and emotionally attuned may, if used excessively, reduce students' motivation to invest in the more demanding and less immediately rewarding work of building human relationships.

Research on social isolation in adolescence consistently finds that it is one of the strongest predictors of poor mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation. The risk that AI tools contribute to social isolation — by providing a more immediately satisfying alternative to human interaction — is therefore a serious concern, even if the evidence for this effect is still preliminary.

Identity Formation and AI

A less studied but potentially important dimension of AI's mental health effects is its impact on identity formation. Adolescence is a critical period for identity development, during which young people explore different roles, values, and self-concepts. AI tools that provide immediate, authoritative answers to questions about identity — "who am I?", "what do I believe?", "what kind of person do I want to be?" — may short-circuit the exploratory process that healthy identity development requires.

Research on identity development in digital environments suggests that the availability of AI as an identity resource — a tool that can generate self-descriptions, values statements, and life narratives — may reduce the productive uncertainty that drives identity exploration. Students who rely on AI to answer identity questions may develop less robust and less personally authentic identities than those who engage in the more effortful process of self-exploration.

The Mattering Dimension

The concept of "mattering" — the sense that one is significant to others and that one's existence makes a difference — has emerged as an important predictor of mental health and academic engagement. Research on mattering in educational contexts finds that it is strongly associated with the quality of human relationships, particularly with teachers and peers. AI tools, however sophisticated, cannot provide the experience of mattering in the way that human relationships can: they cannot genuinely care about a student's wellbeing, remember them across time in a personally meaningful way, or be affected by their presence.

The risk is that AI tools, by providing a simulacrum of caring interaction, may reduce students' investment in the human relationships that are the genuine source of mattering. This risk is particularly acute for students who are already socially isolated or who have difficulty forming human relationships.

Design and Policy Implications

The evidence on AI and student mental health has clear implications for the design and governance of AI tools in education. AI tools should be designed to complement rather than substitute for human relationships — to support students in engaging with teachers and peers, not to replace those engagements. They should include features that encourage students to seek human support when appropriate, and that flag concerning patterns of use (such as excessive reliance on AI for emotional support) to human staff. And they should be evaluated not only for their effects on academic outcomes but for their effects on social connection, identity development, and sense of mattering.

### Q245 What developmental-psychology evidence addresses the long-term effects of AI mentorship and tutoring on children's sense of agency, identity, and self-efficacy? {#q245}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Concerns about AI mentorship and tutoring often focus on academic outcomes, but developmental psychologists are equally interested in how such tools might shape children's sense of agency, their emerging identities as learners, and their beliefs about their own capabilities. These constructs develop over years, and the honest answer to what the evidence shows about long-term effects is that rigorous longitudinal studies of AI tutoring have not yet been completed. What exists is a body of developmental theory, short-term experimental findings, and survey data that together suggest plausible mechanisms and warning signs.

Self-efficacy, as defined by Albert Bandura in his 1977 paper in Psychological Review, is a person's belief in their ability to succeed at specific tasks. Bandura identified mastery experiences, meaning direct experiences of succeeding through one's own effort, as the most powerful source of self-efficacy, followed by vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and physiological states. This framework has a direct implication for AI tutoring. If an AI system helps a child work through a problem so that the child genuinely accomplishes it, the experience may strengthen self-efficacy. If the AI effectively completes the task, the child may experience success without attributing it to their own competence, which theory suggests would do little to build efficacy and might undermine it when the child later faces tasks alone.

Self-determination theory, articulated by Ryan and Deci in a widely cited 2000 article in American Psychologist, holds that intrinsic motivation and healthy development depend on satisfying needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. An AI tutor could support autonomy by letting children explore at their own pace and choose paths through material, and could support competence through well-calibrated challenge and feedback. It could also undermine autonomy if it directs learning too tightly, and could affect relatedness if it displaces relationships with teachers and peers that contribute to a sense of belonging and identity as a learner.

Short-term experimental evidence offers partial tests of these ideas. The randomised trial by Bastani and colleagues, published in PNAS in 2025, found that high-school students given unrestricted access to a GPT-4 assistant performed better during practice but worse than controls on a subsequent unassisted exam, while a tutor version designed to give hints rather than answers largely mitigated this harm. Because this was a randomised experiment, it supports the causal conclusion that the design of AI assistance affected independent performance. The authors also observed that students using the unrestricted assistant did not appear to recognise the reduction in their learning, which suggests a possible mismatch between felt and actual competence, a pattern relevant to accurate self-efficacy.

The meta-analysis by Deng and colleagues in Computers & Education, covering 69 experimental studies of ChatGPT mostly involving older students, found positive average effects on academic performance and higher-order thinking but no significant effect on self-efficacy. This null result is notable: if AI assistance improved learning outcomes but not students' beliefs in their own capabilities, the gains may not have been experienced as personal mastery.

For younger children, developmental concerns extend to identity and relationships. The American Psychological Association's 2025 health advisory on AI and adolescent well-being urged developers and educators to consider that adolescents may be more susceptible to the influence of AI systems, may have difficulty distinguishing simulated empathy from real understanding, and need protection from designs that encourage dependence. Common Sense Media's 2025 survey of 1,060 U.S. teenagers found that 72 percent had used AI companions and that about a third had used them for social interaction or relationships, indicating that AI is already present in the relational lives of many young people, not just their academic work.

Developmental theory suggests several design and practice principles while longitudinal evidence accumulates. AI tutors that scaffold rather than supply answers appear more likely to produce mastery experiences. Gradually reducing support as competence grows mirrors established principles of scaffolding and may help children attribute success to their own effort. Encouraging reflection on what the child did, rather than what the AI did, may support accurate self-assessment. Keeping AI within a broader web of human relationships may protect the relational foundations of learner identity.

Research on how children understand and relate to intelligent machines provides a developmental foundation for these concerns. Kahn and colleagues reported in Developmental Psychology in 2012 on a study in which 90 children aged 9, 12, and 15 interacted with a humanoid robot named Robovie, which at one point objected to being put in a closet. Most children believed that the robot had mental states and was a social being, and many believed it deserved fair treatment and should not be psychologically harmed, although fewer granted it civil rights. The researchers suggested that children may be developing a new ontological category for social robots, neither fully alive nor merely objects. If children treat AI tutors as quasi-social beings, the relationship may carry emotional and identity-related significance that goes beyond the instrumental use adults might expect.

Children's trust in AI sources has also been studied directly. Girouard-Hallam and Danovitch, in a 2022 study in Developmental Psychology, examined how children aged 5 to 8 evaluated information from voice assistants compared with humans. They found that children generally trusted voice assistants as sources of factual information, with older children differentiating more between types of questions, and that children sometimes preferred the device for facts while preferring humans for other kinds of knowledge. Related research on selective trust has long shown that young children track the reliability of informants and prefer accurate ones. For AI tutoring, this suggests that children may extend considerable epistemic trust to AI systems, which places responsibility on designers and educators to ensure that the trust is warranted and that children develop the capacity to question AI sources as they grow.

The concept of an empathy gap has been proposed to describe a particular risk. Nomisha Kurian, writing in Learning, Media and Technology in 2024, analysed incidents in which conversational AI responded inappropriately to children, including a widely reported case in which a voice assistant suggested a dangerous challenge to a ten-year-old and cases in which chatbots gave harmful advice to users presenting as young people. Kurian argued that large language models can simulate empathy without understanding children's developmental needs, vulnerabilities, or the contexts of their questions, and proposed a framework of design considerations for child-safe AI addressing content, interaction, and governance. Her analysis implies that the warmth and responsiveness that make AI tutors appealing to children are also what make inappropriate responses potentially harmful to their developing sense of what relationships involve.

Self-regulated learning theory offers another lens on agency. Researchers in this tradition describe self-regulated learners as those who set goals, select strategies, monitor their progress, and reflect on outcomes, in a cyclical process of forethought, performance, and self-reflection, and they emphasise that these capacities develop through practice and social modelling rather than appearing automatically with age. An AI tutor could support this development by prompting children to plan, monitor, and reflect, or it could short-circuit it by taking over these functions, deciding what the child should do next and evaluating performance on the child's behalf. Adaptive systems that make all sequencing decisions may produce efficient learning in the short term while depriving children of opportunities to practise self-regulation.

The cognitive literature on offloading clarifies the trade-off. Risko and Gilbert, in a 2016 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, defined cognitive offloading as the use of physical action or external tools to reduce cognitive demands, such as writing reminders or using a calculator. They noted that offloading can be adaptive, freeing resources for other tasks, but that it can also reduce memory for offloaded information and that people's decisions to offload are influenced by metacognitive beliefs about their own abilities, which are not always accurate. For children, whose cognitive and metacognitive capacities are still developing, the balance between beneficial and harmful offloading may differ from that of adults. A child who offloads reasoning to an AI before developing the underlying skill may not build the capacity in the first place, which is different from an adult offloading a skill already mastered.

Identity formation is perhaps the least studied dimension. Developmental theorists from Erik Erikson onward have described childhood and adolescence as periods in which individuals construct identities through exploration, competence, and relationships. Learner identity, the sense of oneself as someone who is good at, interested in, or belongs in particular domains, has been linked to persistence and choices, for example in research on science identity among underrepresented students. An AI tutor that makes success feel effortless may weaken the link between effort and identity, while one that positions the child as a capable problem-solver might strengthen it. Whether children come to see themselves as mathematicians, writers, or scientists when much of their work is AI-assisted is an open question with significant implications.

International guidance has begun to translate developmental concerns into principles. UNICEF's Policy Guidance on AI for Children, published in 2021, calls for AI systems that support children's development and well-being, prioritise their best interests, and protect their agency, and it recommends that systems be designed to help children develop their capacities rather than replace them. The guidance also emphasises that children's needs vary with age and that design should account for evolving capacities, a concept drawn from the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. These principles align with the developmental theory discussed above, though they remain largely aspirational without accompanying evidence on implementation.

Methodological challenges complicate efforts to study long-term effects. Children are exposed to many technologies simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate the effects of AI tutoring from those of social media, gaming, and other digital experiences. The research on screen time illustrates the difficulty: large-scale analyses have often found small associations between technology use and well-being that are sensitive to analytic choices, prompting debate about how much weight to give them. Studies of AI tutoring will face similar challenges and will need to measure specific patterns of use, such as the extent of answer-seeking versus hint-seeking, rather than total time.

Cultural and socioeconomic context also matter. Children in families with more resources may use AI within a rich environment of human support, while others may rely on AI as a substitute for unavailable adult help. The developmental effects of the same tool may therefore differ substantially by context. Research designs that capture these differences, and that include children from diverse backgrounds and countries, are needed to avoid generalising from narrow samples.

Parents and teachers play a mediating role that developmental research consistently emphasises. Studies of children's media use have found that active mediation, in which adults discuss content with children, is associated with more positive outcomes than restrictive or absent mediation. Applying this insight to AI suggests that conversations between adults and children about how AI works, when to rely on it, and what the child contributed may help preserve agency and accurate self-assessment.

Research on feedback language offers one of the more concrete bridges between developmental psychology and AI tutor design, because conversational systems generate praise and encouragement constantly. Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck, in a series of experiments with fifth-grade children reported in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 1998, found that children praised for being intelligent after succeeding on a problem set were subsequently more likely to choose easy tasks, to persist less after encountering failure, and to perform worse on later problems than children praised for their effort. The authors interpreted the pattern as evidence that ability praise encourages children to see performance as a verdict on a fixed trait, which makes difficulty threatening. Later replication attempts and debates over the broader growth-mindset literature have suggested that such effects are often smaller and more context-dependent than early studies implied, so the finding is best treated as a caution rather than a law. Still, it bears directly on AI tutors, many of which are tuned to be affirming and may default to generic statements about how clever or talented a child is. No published study has yet tested whether the praise style of an AI tutor shapes children's mindsets over months, but the question is tractable, and designers can choose now to make feedback specific to strategies and effort rather than to the child's supposed abilities.

The key open questions are whether early, sustained reliance on AI assistance changes children's willingness to persist with difficulty, how it affects their sense of authorship over their own ideas, and whether effects differ by age, temperament, and context. Answering them will require cohort studies that follow children for years with validated measures of agency, identity, and self-efficacy. Until such evidence exists, claims of either lasting benefit or lasting harm should be treated with caution.
