### Q248 How are students with disabilities being helped or harmed by mainstream AI educational tools not specifically designed for their needs? {#q248}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Most AI tools used in classrooms were not designed with students with disabilities in mind. General-purpose chatbots, writing assistants, adaptive learning platforms, and proctoring systems are built for a presumed typical user, and students with disabilities encounter them as they would any mainstream technology, sometimes finding unexpected benefits and sometimes facing new barriers. The available evidence, though limited, suggests that both outcomes are common and that the balance depends on design, institutional policy, and the specific disability involved.

The benefits are real and often reported by students themselves. A study by Zhao, Cox, and colleagues at the University of Sheffield on disabled students' use of generative AI in higher education found that students with conditions including dyslexia, attention difficulties, chronic illness, and mental-health conditions used general AI tools to summarise long readings, restructure notes, check spelling and grammar, generate starting points for writing, and reduce the fatigue associated with study. Several participants described AI as filling gaps left by slow or inadequate formal accommodations. Mainstream features such as speech-to-text, text-to-speech, automatic captioning, and the ability to request simpler explanations can function as assistive technology without the stigma or administrative burden of specialised tools.

Harms arise in several ways. The first concerns accessibility of the tools themselves. Interfaces that rely on complex visual layouts, time-limited interactions, or inaccessible components can exclude students who use screen readers or alternative input devices. In the United States, the Department of Justice's 2024 rule under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act requires state and local government entities, including public schools and universities, to make web content and mobile applications conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 at level AA, with compliance deadlines beginning in 2026 for larger entities. The rule extends to content provided through contracted third parties, which brings many AI tools within scope. WCAG 2.2, published by the World Wide Web Consortium, offers further criteria relevant to cognitive accessibility.

The second harm concerns academic integrity enforcement. The Center for Democracy and Technology's 2024 report Up in the Air found that students with disabilities were more likely than their peers to report using generative AI and also more likely to report being disciplined in connection with it. AI detection tools, which some teachers rely on, have documented reliability problems. Liang and colleagues, in a 2023 study in Patterns, found that several widely used GPT detectors misclassified a majority of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated, and observed that detectors penalise text with lower linguistic variety. Students whose disabilities affect writing style, or who use assistive tools that alter text, may face similar risks of false accusation.

The third harm concerns surveillance and assessment. AI-based proctoring systems that flag unusual eye movements, body movements, or background noise may disproportionately flag students with conditions such as Tourette syndrome, autism, or visual impairments. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, in its 2024 report on AI in K-12 education, identified risks that AI systems used for monitoring, discipline, and placement could produce discriminatory outcomes for students with disabilities, and urged federal agencies to clarify how civil-rights protections apply.

The fourth harm concerns normative bias in outputs. General-purpose models tend to reflect typical communication patterns and may give advice or feedback that treats atypical expression as error. Students who rely on AI for writing feedback may be steered toward conventional styles in ways that erase legitimate differences.

The fifth harm concerns privacy. Students with disabilities may disclose sensitive information to AI tools in the course of seeking help, and mainstream tools often lack the data protections that would apply to formal special-education records.

These findings point toward several institutional responses. Procurement can require evidence of accessibility conformance and testing with disabled users. Integrity policies can recognise AI use as a legitimate accommodation where appropriate and prohibit reliance on detection tools as the sole basis for misconduct findings. Proctoring and monitoring systems can be evaluated for disparate impact before adoption. Accommodation processes can be updated to address AI explicitly, so that students are not forced to choose between using helpful tools and risking discipline.

The relationship between disability and educational technology has a long history that helps explain both the promise and the pattern of harm. Many technologies now taken for granted were developed first for disabled people or adopted by them early: optical character recognition and synthetic speech were combined in reading machines for blind users in the 1970s, speech recognition found an early market among people who could not type, and word prediction was refined for people with motor impairments. Each of these tools later moved into the mainstream. The reverse movement, in which mainstream tools are retrofitted for disabled users after the fact, has a less happy record, because accessibility added late is typically partial, fragile and expensive. The Universal Design for Learning framework developed by the nonprofit CAST, most recently revised as version 3.0 in 2024, was a response to that pattern. It asks educators and designers to anticipate learner variability from the outset by offering multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression, rather than designing for an imagined average learner and then accommodating exceptions. Generative AI could advance this aim, since it can present the same content as text, audio, simplified language or images on request. Whether it does so depends on whether the products schools adopt are built with that variability in mind or treat it as an edge case.

The rights framework is also relevant. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, adopted in 2006, commits states in Article 24 to an inclusive education system at all levels and to reasonable accommodation of individual requirements, and in Article 9 to measures ensuring access to information and communications technologies on an equal basis with others. The Convention reflects the social model of disability, associated with disabled scholars and activists in the United Kingdom from the 1970s onward, which locates disability not only in individual impairment but in environments and practices that exclude people with impairments. Seen through this lens, an AI tutor that cannot be operated with a screen reader, a proctoring system that flags involuntary movements, or a writing assistant that treats atypical expression as error is not a neutral tool that some students happen to find difficult. It is an environment that disables. The social model also underpins the disability movement's demand of nothing about us without us, which in the context of AI procurement means involving disabled students and staff in testing tools before adoption rather than consulting them only after problems appear.

There is solid evidence that some AI-adjacent tools help particular groups when used well. Sarah Wood, Jerad Moxley, Elizabeth Tighe and Richard Wagner, in a 2018 meta-analysis in the Journal of Learning Disabilities, synthesised studies of text-to-speech and related read-aloud tools for students with reading disabilities and found a small-to-moderate positive average effect on reading comprehension, with an overall effect size of about 0.35 standard deviations. They noted considerable variation across studies and cautioned that the tools support access to content rather than remediating underlying decoding difficulties. Modern AI systems extend these capabilities considerably, generating natural-sounding speech, summarising long texts, and answering questions about content in conversation. For blind and low-vision users, multimodal models have opened new possibilities. Be My Eyes, a service that previously connected blind users with sighted volunteers through video calls, introduced a feature in 2023 that uses OpenAI's GPT-4 to describe images and answer follow-up questions, which OpenAI and Be My Eyes presented as a way to give users greater independence. Accounts from users describe practical benefits such as reading labels, navigating documents and interpreting diagrams, though independent evaluations of accuracy in educational contexts remain limited and errors in describing technical images can mislead students who have no way of checking them.

Research on bias within language technologies shows why such tools can also embed exclusion. Ben Hutchinson and colleagues at Google, presenting at the Association for Computational Linguistics conference in 2020, examined widely used natural language processing models and found that sentences mentioning disability were scored as more toxic and more negative in sentiment than otherwise similar sentences, and that phrases referring to disability were associated in model representations with topics such as homelessness, drug use and violence. In educational settings, such associations could affect content moderation, automated feedback, or essay scoring, for instance by flagging a student's personal narrative about living with a disability as inappropriate or by producing examples that reproduce stereotypes. Speech technology presents parallel problems. Robert MacDonald and colleagues described in a 2021 Interspeech paper how Google's Project Euphonia collected more than one million recorded utterances from people with disordered speech, because standard automatic speech recognition systems performed poorly for speakers with conditions such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, cerebral palsy and Down syndrome. The project's premise was that mainstream systems trained on typical speech exclude these users by default, and that inclusion requires deliberate data collection with consent from the affected community. Students who rely on dictation or voice interfaces may therefore find mainstream AI tools least reliable precisely when they need them most.

Implementation in schools raises a further set of challenges that sit at the boundary between general and special education. In many systems, students with disabilities have formal plans, such as individualised education programmes in the United States, that specify accommodations and services. Mainstream AI tools are rarely referenced in these plans, so a student who depends on an AI reading assistant at home may find it prohibited in class or in examinations, while a tool introduced for all students may be inaccessible to the student it was supposed to help. Special educators report that they are seldom involved in district decisions about AI adoption and that guidance on whether AI assistance counts as an accommodation or as a breach of integrity is often absent. This creates inconsistency across classrooms and can force students and families to negotiate access repeatedly. Integrating AI into accommodation planning would mean documenting which tools a student uses, clarifying where they are permitted, ensuring examination rules recognise assistive uses, and training teachers to distinguish accommodation from substitution.

Equity considerations intersect with disability in ways that can compound disadvantage. Diagnosis and formal identification of disabilities vary by family income, language and race, so students whose disabilities are unidentified may use AI informally to manage difficulties without any protection when that use is questioned. Families with more resources can purchase premium tools, specialist software and private assessments, while others rely on whatever the school provides. Disabled students from low-income backgrounds may therefore experience the risks of mainstream AI, such as false accusations or inaccessible interfaces, without equal access to its benefits. Addressing this requires attention not only to the design of tools but to the systems of identification, procurement and assessment in which they are embedded, and to monitoring outcomes by disability status so that patterns of harm are detected rather than assumed away.

Assessment is where the tension between accommodation and integrity becomes sharpest for disabled students. Traditional accommodations such as extended time, a separate room, a reader or a scribe were designed to remove barriers to demonstrating knowledge without changing what was being measured. AI tools blur that line because the same system that reads a question aloud can also answer it, and the same assistant that helps a student with dysgraphia organise ideas can also write the essay. Institutions that respond by banning AI in assessment risk removing tools that function as genuine accommodations, while institutions that permit it without clear boundaries risk undermining the validity of the assessment for everyone. A more defensible approach starts from the construct being assessed. If an examination measures understanding of historical causation rather than spelling or handwriting, then a tool that converts speech to text or corrects surface errors may be a legitimate accommodation, whereas a tool that generates arguments is not. Making these distinctions requires collaboration among disability services, assessment designers and subject teachers, and it requires listening to disabled students themselves, who are often the most precise analysts of which forms of support help them demonstrate what they know and which would replace their own thinking.

The evidence base is thin, consisting mostly of surveys, qualitative studies, and policy analysis, and few studies disaggregate outcomes by disability type. Yet the pattern is consistent: mainstream AI tools can expand access when they are accessible and when institutions treat them as part of an inclusive learning environment, and can deepen exclusion when accessibility is neglected and enforcement practices fall hardest on those who depend on the tools most.

### Q249 What does the evidence show about AI's effect on first-generation and low-income college students — does it level or steepen the playing field? {#q249}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

First-generation and low-income college students face well-documented disadvantages in higher education, including less familiarity with institutional norms, fewer family resources to draw on for academic guidance, greater likelihood of working while studying, and lower completion rates. AI has been promoted as a democratising force that could provide every student with the kind of on-demand guidance that wealthier students obtain through tutors and networks. Whether it actually levels the playing field or steepens it depends on evidence that remains incomplete but is beginning to show a recognisable pattern.

The most rigorous evidence of a levelling effect comes from Georgia State University, an institution known for its large population of first-generation and low-income students. In a randomised study by Meyer, Page, and colleagues, students in an introductory government course received course-specific messages from an AI chatbot reminding them of deadlines, offering study support, and answering questions. Students in the treatment group earned higher final grades, and the effect was concentrated among first-generation students, who scored roughly eleven points higher on average and were about sixteen percent more likely to earn a B or above than comparable control students. Because assignment was random, the study supports causal conclusions about this specific intervention, and its distributional pattern suggests that structured AI support may help most those with the least access to informal guidance.

The nature of that intervention matters. The Georgia State chatbot was proactive, institutionally provided, and designed around known barriers such as missed deadlines and uncertainty about course expectations. It was not an open-ended generative tool that students had to discover, pay for, and learn to use well on their own.

Evidence on open-ended generative AI points in a more worrying direction. The Higher Education Policy Institute and Kortext Student Generative AI Survey 2025, covering 1,041 UK undergraduates, found that while AI use was nearly universal at 92 percent, there were differences by socio-economic background in patterns of use and in confidence with AI tools, with students from more advantaged backgrounds tending to report more frequent and more varied use. The survey's authors warned of a digital divide in AI skills that could compound existing inequalities. The Digital Education Council's 2024 global survey similarly found that many students felt they lacked adequate AI skills and that institutional training was insufficient, a gap likely to fall hardest on students without other sources of guidance.

Access to premium tools is another factor. The most capable AI models are often available through paid subscriptions, and students who can afford them may gain advantages in speed, quality, and features. Institutions that provide licensed tools to all students can reduce this gap, but provision varies widely. Evidence from the K-12 pipeline suggests that disparities begin before college: RAND's American School District Panel found that training on AI for teachers was considerably more common in low-poverty districts than in high-poverty districts, so students arrive at college with different levels of guided exposure.

The way students use AI also affects whether it helps. The randomised trial by Bastani and colleagues in PNAS found that unrestricted AI assistance improved practice performance but was associated with worse performance on later unassisted exams, while a guardrailed tutor design largely avoided the harm. Students with less academic preparation and less guidance on effective study strategies may be more likely to use AI in ways that substitute for learning, and less likely to recognise when this is happening. If so, unguided access could widen gaps in actual learning even as it narrows gaps in completed assignments.

The overall evidence suggests that AI does not have a fixed distributional effect. It appears to level the playing field when institutions deliberately design and provide support targeted at known barriers, make tools freely available to all students, and teach effective use. It risks steepening the field when access, skills, and guidance are left to individual resources, which track existing advantage.

Understanding why first-generation students face disadvantages helps clarify which kinds of AI support might address them. Anthony Abraham Jack, in his 2019 book The Privileged Poor, drew on interviews with undergraduates at an elite American university to distinguish between low-income students who had attended well-resourced private high schools, whom he called the privileged poor, and those who came from under-resourced public schools, whom he called the doubly disadvantaged. Both groups faced financial strain, but the doubly disadvantaged were far less likely to know the unwritten rules of college life, such as that attending office hours and building relationships with professors were expected and rewarded rather than signs of weakness. Nicole Stephens and colleagues, writing in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2012, offered a complementary account based on survey and experimental data. They argued that American universities emphasise independent norms, such as expressing one's own views and pursuing personal passions, while many first-generation students arrive with more interdependent norms centred on family and community, and that this cultural mismatch was associated with lower academic performance. In an experiment, framing the university's welcome in interdependent terms reduced the performance gap on a subsequent task. These accounts suggest that the barriers facing first-generation students are partly informational and partly cultural, which matters because AI tools are much better at supplying information than at changing institutional culture.

The history of earlier technologies promoted as equalisers offers a cautionary precedent. Massive open online courses were widely heralded in 2012 as a way to bring elite education to anyone with an internet connection. John Hansen and Justin Reich, writing in Science in 2015, analysed registration and completion data from Harvard and MIT courses on the edX platform and found that participants in the United States came disproportionately from more affluent and better-educated neighbourhoods, and that among those who enrolled, students from more advantaged backgrounds were more likely to earn certificates. Free availability, in other words, did not translate into equal use or equal benefit, because the capacity to take advantage of open resources itself depended on prior advantages. The parallel with generative AI is direct. Tools that are freely available but require self-direction, prior knowledge to evaluate outputs, and confidence to integrate them into study may disproportionately benefit students who already possess these resources. That pattern is consistent with the gaps reported in the HEPI survey, though the survey's cross-sectional design cannot establish whether AI is widening gaps or simply reflecting them.

Targeted design has been shown to change this dynamic in some cases. René Kizilcec, Andrew Saltarelli, Justin Reich and Geoffrey Cohen, reporting in Science in 2017, tested brief social-psychological interventions in online courses and found that a short values-affirmation writing exercise substantially improved course completion among learners in less developed countries, closing much of the gap with learners in more developed countries in the courses where it was tested, although the effects did not replicate uniformly in later, larger trials. Lindsay Page and Hunter Gehlbach, writing in AERA Open in 2017, evaluated Pounce, an AI-enabled text-messaging assistant that Georgia State University deployed to help admitted students complete the steps required before enrolment, such as financial aid forms, immunisation records and orientation registration. In their randomised trial, students who received the assistant were more likely to enrol on time, with an increase of about 3.3 percentage points, and the benefits appeared concentrated among students who might otherwise have been lost to summer melt. This earlier evidence, together with the later classroom chatbot study by Meyer and Page, indicates that AI support aimed at specific, well-understood barriers can narrow gaps, while open-ended tools left to individual initiative may do the opposite.

Help-seeking is one area where AI's potential to level the field is plausible but unproven. The research on first-generation students consistently finds that many are reluctant to ask professors or tutors for help, out of uncertainty about norms, fear of appearing unprepared, or the demands of work and family schedules that conflict with office hours. A chatbot available at any hour, which does not judge and cannot be embarrassed by basic questions, might lower these barriers. Several students quoted in qualitative studies describe AI in precisely these terms. Yet there is a risk that AI becomes a substitute for the human relationships that Jack identified as so consequential, such as mentoring that leads to research opportunities, recommendation letters and professional networks. If advantaged students use AI for routine questions while continuing to cultivate faculty relationships, and disadvantaged students use AI instead of those relationships, the result could be a widening of the social-capital gap even as informational gaps narrow. Institutions can mitigate this by designing AI tools that actively refer students to human advisers, office hours and mentoring programmes rather than serving as an endpoint.

Institutional provision of AI tools is spreading and may address one dimension of inequality. In 2025 the California State University system, which serves a large population of first-generation and low-income students across its campuses, announced a partnership to provide ChatGPT Edu to all students and faculty, framing the initiative partly as a matter of equitable access to tools that wealthier students might otherwise purchase for themselves. Such system-wide provision removes the cost barrier associated with premium subscriptions. It does not, by itself, address differences in the knowledge and confidence needed to use the tools well, and its effects on learning and completion have not yet been evaluated independently. Whether provision of this kind levels the playing field will depend on whether it is accompanied by instruction in effective use, by course designs that reward understanding rather than output, and by evaluation that disaggregates outcomes by first-generation status and income so that institutions can see whether gaps are narrowing.

There are also concerns about how AI may affect the labour market value of the credentials that first-generation students pursue. Students who enter college to secure economic mobility often concentrate in fields with clear occupational pathways, some of which involve routine cognitive tasks that AI may automate or reshape. If AI changes which skills employers reward, students with fewer networks and less access to career guidance may be slower to adjust their choices. Career services that integrate information about AI's effects on occupations, and curricula that develop judgement, communication and domain expertise alongside AI literacy, may help ensure that first-generation students are not disadvantaged twice, first in learning with AI and then in competing in labour markets shaped by it. Evidence on these longer-term effects does not yet exist, and claims in either direction should be treated as speculative.

Methodological choices will determine whether future research can answer the levelling question at all. Many existing studies report average effects of AI tools across all students, which can conceal opposite effects in different groups: a tool that helps confident, well-prepared students and slightly harms struggling ones may show a positive average while widening gaps. Studies that report effects separately for first-generation, low-income, part-time and working students, and that are designed with enough statistical power to detect differences between these groups, are needed to show whether particular tools narrow or widen disparities. Measures also matter. Course grades and completion rates capture outcomes institutions care about, but they can be inflated by AI-assisted work that does not reflect learning, so evaluations benefit from including unassisted assessments, persistence into subsequent courses, and longer-term outcomes such as graduation and employment. Qualitative work that asks students how they use AI, what they avoid and why, can explain the mechanisms behind quantitative patterns. The Georgia State studies are valuable partly because they were randomised and reported effects for students most at risk; replicating that rigour across institutions with different student populations and different kinds of AI support would give policymakers a far firmer basis than current surveys provide.

Important caveats remain. The Georgia State findings come from one institution and one type of intervention, and replication across contexts is needed. Survey data on socio-economic differences are correlational and may reflect other differences between groups. Few studies follow first-generation students over time to examine effects on persistence and graduation. Institutions seeking to use AI for equity would benefit from disaggregating outcomes by first-generation and income status, evaluating interventions with comparison groups, and treating equitable access and training as integral to any AI strategy rather than as afterthoughts.

## Chapter 17: Environmental and Material Costs {#chapter-17}

10 questions · 75 citations · 65 unique sources · 50 cross-references

### Q194 What is the estimated energy and water footprint of typical AI use in a school, per student per year? {#q194}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

No published study yet reports a direct per-student-per-year energy and water figure for AI use in schools, but the underlying per-query data are well established, and a transparent estimate can be constructed from them. The most commonly cited figure is that a standard conversational AI query consumes approximately 0.3–0.4 watt-hours (Wh) of electricity. This is consistent with the aggregate statistics for ChatGPT, which processes roughly 2.5 billion prompts per day and consumes on the order of 383 gigawatt-hours (GWh) per year — about 0.42 Wh per query. The per-query figure, however, is highly task-dependent: advanced 'reasoning' models can consume 10 to 70 times more energy per prompt than standard models, generating a single AI image can be roughly 1,450 times more energy-intensive than basic text classification, and a short AI-generated video can consume as much electricity as 200,000 spam classifications. Any per-student estimate must therefore be stated as a range that depends on how the tool is used.

A worked estimate for a typical student. Consider a student who uses a standard conversational AI model for homework and study support for roughly 30 minutes per day during a 180-day school year, making about 30 queries per session. At 0.4 Wh per query, this yields approximately 5,400 queries per year and about 2.2 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of direct query energy. If the same student regularly uses reasoning-class models, the figure rises to roughly 22–150 kWh per year. For comparison, a typical laptop consumes on the order of 30–60 kWh per year in normal use, so AI query energy for a moderate user is small relative to the device itself, but for a heavy user of advanced models it can exceed the device's own consumption. The water footprint follows from the energy: data centres require roughly 1–2 litres of water per kilowatt-hour of energy consumed, combining on-site evaporative cooling with the indirect water used in electricity generation. On this basis, a moderate student user's AI use corresponds to roughly 2–4 litres of water per year, while a heavy user of reasoning models corresponds to roughly 20–300 litres per year. These are illustrative calculations based on published per-query and per-kWh figures, not measured school-level data; the true figure for any school depends on model choice, task mix, and the carbon and water intensity of the local grid.

Sensitivity to usage patterns. The range of plausible per-student footprints is wide because school AI use varies enormously. A primary school that uses AI for occasional read-aloud support will consume a fraction of the energy of a secondary school whose students run reasoning models for mathematics and generate images for project work. The Earth Day Network's analysis of the cost of individual prompts emphasises that the same tool can be used in ways that differ in energy intensity by orders of magnitude, and that users rarely see or are told about these differences. Schools that adopt explicit usage policies — limiting multimodal generation, choosing standard models for routine tasks — can hold their per-student footprint near the bottom of the range, while schools that encourage unrestricted use of frontier models will sit near the top. This variability is itself a finding: the per-student environmental cost of AI in schools is not fixed by the technology but is substantially determined by institutional choices.

The aggregate context. The per-student figures sit within a rapidly growing aggregate footprint. Global data centre electricity consumption reached approximately 448 TWh in 2025, with AI systems' power demand estimated at 23 GW, and projections place global data centre electricity demand at roughly 945 TWh by 2030, with an associated water footprint of about 9.3 trillion litres — a volume comparable to the annual domestic water needs of 1.3 billion people in Sub-Saharan Africa. Inference — the continuous running of models to answer prompts — accounts for 80–90% of total AI energy consumption, which is why per-query figures matter more than training costs for ongoing use. The UN University's Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH) analysis emphasises that the environmental cost of a single query varies by orders of magnitude depending on the task, and that a single complex AI-generated video can consume over 4 litres of water — equivalent to two days of drinking water for a human.

Caveats and measurement problems. Several caveats apply to any per-student estimate. First, the figures above exclude the embodied energy and water of the devices students use, the network infrastructure, and the data centre share attributable to the school's other digital services. Second, published per-query figures vary by source and model generation, and vendors do not disclose facility-level data that would allow precise attribution. Third, the water intensity of electricity varies dramatically by region: grids dominated by fossil-fuel or nuclear generation have large indirect water footprints, while wind and solar have near-zero water requirements for generation. Fourth, the 'rebound effect' documented in the literature — efficiency gains that lower cost per query and thereby increase total usage — means that per-query improvements do not automatically reduce aggregate consumption. The practical conclusion for schools is that the per-student footprint of typical AI use is real but modest in absolute terms — on the order of a few kWh and a few litres to a few hundred litres per year depending on usage — while the system-level footprint is large and growing, and both are sensitive to choices about model selection and task mix that schools can influence.

### Q195 How do AI's environmental costs in education compare with those of the technologies it displaces? {#q195}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Comparing AI's environmental costs with those of the technologies it displaces in education requires distinguishing three different baselines: print materials, conventional digital tools, and the human activities AI substitutes for. The honest answer is that the comparison is favourable in some cases, unfavourable in others, and complicated everywhere by the fact that AI is largely additive — it is layered on top of existing technologies rather than cleanly replacing them.

AI versus print. The print-versus-digital literature provides the most developed comparison. Print textbooks carry significant lifecycle costs: deforestation, energy-intensive manufacturing, chemical processing, binding, global transport, and eventual landfilling, where discarded books contribute methane emissions. Digital alternatives carry the embodied costs of device manufacturing — rare-earth mineral extraction, water- and energy-intensive production — plus ongoing electricity for charging and data centre operations)Skip. The break-even analysis is well established: an e-reader becomes more sustainable than print only if the user reads roughly 13–20 books per year over the device's three-year lifespan. For a student who reads fewer titles, print is greener; for a heavy reader, digital wins. AI adds a new layer of per-use energy and water on top of the digital baseline, so an AI-enabled digital textbook system is environmentally more expensive than either plain print or plain digital — the question is whether it displaces enough print to compensate, which depends on usage intensity. The most environmentally favourable option in this comparison is neither print nor digital but the circular economy: libraries and second-hand markets that spread the production cost of a single book across many readers.

AI versus conventional digital tools. The comparison between AI and the digital tools it displaces is more direct. A generative AI query is substantially more energy-intensive than a conventional web search: estimates place a standard conversational query at roughly 0.3–0.4 Wh, several times the energy of a typical search request, and reasoning models and image generation are orders of magnitude more expensive still. When AI replaces a search engine for the same task — finding information, checking a fact — the environmental cost rises. When AI replaces a more expensive activity, the comparison flips. The UNU-INWEH analysis notes that a single AI-generated video can consume as much electricity as 200,000 spam classifications, but also that the task mix determines the total: using the lightest model for a simple task is dramatically cheaper than using a heavy model. The key structural difference is that AI systems run inference continuously on cloud infrastructure, whereas conventional digital tools rely more on local processing and lighter server loads — which is why inference accounts for 80–90% of AI's energy consumption.

AI versus the human activities it substitutes. A third comparison is against the activities AI replaces in education: human tutoring, teacher preparation time, and physical travel. The online-learning literature finds that digital delivery can be significantly less carbon-intensive per credit hour than in-person models, because it eliminates campus building energy and commuting. An AI tutor that substitutes for a parent driving a child to a tutoring centre, or for a teacher commuting to produce materials, may have a lower net footprint. The Netnada analysis of the education sector notes that online learning shifts the carbon burden from physical campuses to data centres and student devices, and that the comparison depends on which emissions are counted. However, the evidence does not support the strong claim that AI tutoring is environmentally superior to human tutoring: the per-hour footprint of a human tutor is mostly the tutor's own commuting and materials, which is small, while the per-hour footprint of AI tutoring scales with usage and is not negligible.

The rebound problem. The most important complication is that AI does not simply displace other technologies; it generates new demand. The literature documents a rebound effect — the Jevons paradox — in which efficiency gains lower the cost per query and thereby increase total usage, so that aggregate energy consumption rises even as per-query efficiency improves. In education, AI is typically adopted alongside existing devices, platforms, and print materials rather than instead of them, so the realistic comparison is not AI versus displaced technology but AI plus everything else. Schools that adopt AI while retaining print textbooks, 1:1 devices, and cloud platforms are adding a new energy and water load to an existing one.

Assessment. The defensible conclusion is that AI's environmental cost per unit of educational activity is higher than that of the conventional digital tools it most directly displaces (search, basic software), comparable to or lower than print for heavy-use scenarios, and highly sensitive to task mix and model selection. Because AI is largely additive in practice, the system-level effect is an increase in education's environmental footprint, and the most effective mitigation is not to compare AI with alternatives but to reduce the footprint of the AI use itself — choosing the lightest model for each task, limiting multimodal generation, and ensuring that AI displaces genuinely higher-footprint activities rather than being layered on top of them.

### Q196 Do education AI vendors disclose environmental data, and is any of it independently verified? {#q196}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The short answer is that education AI vendors — like the broader AI industry — disclose very little environmental data, and almost none of it is independently verified. The core problem is structural: corporate environmental reports rarely distinguish AI-specific workloads from general computing, so even the data that is published cannot be used to attribute environmental impact to AI products, let alone to the education segment of a vendor's business. Research on data centre sustainability finds that fewer than one in five companies disclose project-level emissions, and only about 7% report water consumption, despite the significant water stress caused by data centre cooling. These figures apply to companies covered by stringent regulations such as the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, which means the disclosure gap is not simply a matter of weak regulation — even regulated companies are not providing the granular data that would allow schools, investors, or the public to assess the environmental cost of AI services.

What vendors do disclose. The largest AI and cloud vendors publish corporate sustainability reports with aggregate figures: total data centre electricity consumption, renewable-energy procurement percentages, and in some cases water-use efficiency metrics. These reports are useful for understanding a company's overall trajectory but are inadequate for education-specific questions. A school cannot determine from a vendor's annual report how much energy its students' queries consumed, what the carbon intensity of that energy was, or what water was withdrawn to cool the servers that processed them. The Cell Press analysis of AI's environmental footprint documents that companies frequently exclude indirect water consumption — the water used by power plants to generate the electricity data centres draw — and do not separate AI-related usage from other workloads, producing footprints that are systematically mismeasured and understated.

Verification gaps. Independent verification is the exception rather than the rule. Corporate sustainability data is typically self-reported, and while some figures are audited as part of financial reporting, the environmental metrics most relevant to AI — per-workload energy, water withdrawal by facility, carbon intensity of purchased power — are not subject to standardised third-party verification. The research literature identifies this as a 'governance gap': the rapid expansion of hyperscale data centres has outpaced the accounting and assurance frameworks that would make their impacts verifiable. Emerging verification mechanisms include blockchain-backed carbon records, which create immutable logs of emissions data, and investor-led due diligence frameworks such as those developed by the Environmental Defense Fund and Nuveen, which provide structured questions for assessing data centre sustainability across the value chain — from chip manufacturers to utilities. These tools exist but are not yet widely applied to education procurement.

The education-specific problem. Education vendors add a further layer of opacity. Many AI tools used in schools are built on top of third-party foundation models, so the education vendor itself may not control — or even know — the environmental footprint of the underlying infrastructure. A school purchasing an AI tutoring platform is typically several layers removed from the data centre that processes its students' queries, and each layer has weaker incentives to disclose than the last. The OECD's work on AI in education has noted that procurement decisions are made with almost no environmental information, and the sustainability literature on the education sector finds that ICT and data centre emissions are rarely itemised in institutional carbon accounting. The practical consequence is that schools cannot currently make informed environmental choices between AI vendors, because the data needed to do so does not exist in comparable, verified form.

The gap between marketing and measurement. The disclosure problem is compounded by the way environmental claims are made. Vendors advertise renewable-energy commitments and carbon-neutrality targets prominently, and these claims are not false — but they describe corporate averages, not the services a school buys. A company can be 100% renewable on an annual accounting basis while the specific data centre serving a school's region runs on fossil-heavy grid power at the moment of use, because renewable procurement is often matched on an annual, not hourly, basis. The research literature on data centre sustainability notes that this temporal mismatch means corporate green claims can coexist with significant real-world emissions, and that no standard exists for reporting the carbon intensity of a specific workload at a specific time. For schools, the practical implication is that a vendor's headline sustainability figures are a weak basis for procurement decisions, and that requests for facility-level, time-matched data are the only way to obtain information that reflects the actual service.

What would change the picture. The research points to three developments that would improve disclosure and verification: standardised reporting requirements that force facility-level, workload-specific disclosure of energy, water, and carbon; independent assurance of those figures; and procurement standards that make environmental data a condition of contract. The EU's evolving sustainability reporting regime and the growth of investor due-diligence frameworks are moving the industry in this direction, but neither yet reaches the granularity that education buyers need. Until it does, the defensible position for schools is to treat vendor environmental claims as unverified marketing, to request facility-level data in procurement processes, and to assume that the true footprint of AI services is larger than published figures suggest.

### Q197 Should schools account for AI emissions in their sustainability reporting, and do any currently do so? {#q197}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Schools should account for AI emissions in their sustainability reporting, and the case for doing so is strong on both accounting and pedagogical grounds — but very few currently do. The accounting case rests on the structure of Scope 3 emissions. Under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, Scope 3 covers all indirect emissions in an institution's value chain that it does not own or control, and the World Resources Institute divides these into fifteen categories, including purchased goods and services, capital goods, and upstream and downstream activities. For educational institutions, Scope 3 is typically the largest share of the footprint: at Yale University, Scope 3 was estimated to represent 57% of the total footprint in 2022. AI services fall squarely within Scope 3 — the energy consumed by the data centres that process students' queries is an indirect emission of the school that purchases the service — and the same logic applies to the cloud platforms, learning management systems, and streaming services that schools already use. If a school reports its Scope 3 emissions at all, AI emissions are already, in principle, part of what it should be reporting.

The current state of practice. In practice, almost no schools account for AI emissions specifically. The sustainability literature on the education sector documents a persistent lack of standardisation in how institutions measure ICT-related emissions, with inconsistent time metrics, functional units (per student versus per square metre), and emission factors for digital services. Most institutions that report Scope 3 use spend-based modelling — estimating emissions from the monetary value of purchased goods and services using environmentally extended input-output models — which cannot distinguish AI services from other cloud purchases. Process-based accounting, which would require suppliers to provide actual energy and emission data, is more accurate but far more time-consuming. The result is that AI emissions, if captured at all, are buried inside broad procurement categories. Universities are further along than schools: higher education institutions with net-zero commitments, particularly those aligned with the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), are under increasing pressure to include Scope 3 in their targets, and some are beginning to engage suppliers on data centre emissions. K-12 school systems, which rarely have dedicated sustainability teams, are almost entirely absent from this picture.

Why schools should report. Beyond the accounting logic, there are three reasons schools should account for AI emissions. First, materiality: as AI use grows, the associated emissions grow with it, and the OECD and UN analyses project data centre electricity demand to roughly double by 2030. An institution that reports sustainability data while omitting its fastest-growing emission source is producing misleading information. Second, procurement leverage: the Scope 3 literature shows that institutions can influence supplier behaviour through their purchasing power — inserting climate-related requirements into contracts and engaging top-tier suppliers on sustainability reporting. If schools asked for environmental data in AI procurement, vendors would have an incentive to provide it, which is currently the single most effective lever available. Third, pedagogy: schools that teach sustainability while operating unmeasured, unexamined AI infrastructure are vulnerable to the charge of hypocrisy, and accounting for AI emissions turns the school's own operations into a teachable case study in environmental responsibility.

The pedagogical case. There is also a teaching argument for accounting that goes beyond compliance. Schools that report their AI emissions can use the numbers in the classroom: students can examine the school's own footprint, compare it with published benchmarks, and evaluate mitigation options — turning sustainability reporting into a live case study in environmental accounting. The sustainability-in-education literature argues that institutions teach as much by their operations as by their curriculum, and that a school which measures and discloses its digital footprint models the transparency and accountability that sustainability education aims to cultivate. Conversely, a school that teaches climate science while refusing to examine its own fastest-growing emission source invites the charge of greenwashing, and students are increasingly equipped to notice the inconsistency.

Methodological challenges. The obstacles to reporting are real. AI emissions are difficult to attribute: a school's queries are processed on shared infrastructure with other customers, vendors do not disclose workload-level data, and the carbon intensity of the electricity varies by hour and region. Spend-based methods cannot capture this granularity, and process-based methods depend on vendor cooperation that is rarely forthcoming. The literature also notes that online learning shifts emissions from campus buildings to data centres and student devices, so a school that reports only its own facilities is systematically understating its footprint. These challenges are not reasons to avoid reporting; they are reasons to report transparently with stated assumptions, as the emerging university practice does.

Assessment. The defensible conclusion is that AI emissions belong in school sustainability reporting as a matter of accounting integrity, that the methodological tools exist (spend-based as a floor, process-based as the target), and that the current practice is close to zero — with universities beginning to move and K-12 systems not yet engaged. The most practical first step for a school is to include AI and cloud services in its Scope 3 procurement estimates, request environmental data from vendors as a condition of contract, and report the resulting figures with their assumptions stated. This is not yet standard practice anywhere, but it is the direction in which the accounting standards, the net-zero movement, and the growth of AI use are all pushing.

### Q198 What device-lifecycle and e-waste consequences follow from AI-driven hardware requirements in schools? {#q198}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The device-lifecycle and e-waste consequences of AI-driven hardware requirements in schools are substantial and are already visible in the largest 1:1 device programmes. The core problem is that AI raises the hardware bar — modern AI features require more memory, more processing power, and newer operating systems — at the same time that the dominant school device, the Chromebook, is subject to a lifecycle constraint that retires functional hardware on a fixed schedule. The result is a convergence of two forces that shortens device lifespans and increases e-waste: AI-driven hardware requirements pushing devices out of service, and manufacturer-controlled update policies pulling them out.

The Chromebook churn. Chromebooks have become the standard for 1:1 learning environments because of their low initial cost and ease of management, but their lifecycle is dictated by Google's Automatic Update Expiration (AUE) policy. Google sets an expiration date for each model based on its certification date rather than its purchase date, and once that date passes, the device stops receiving security updates and may lose compatibility with essential educational websites and testing platforms. Because schools typically buy, configure, and deploy devices over a period of months, the remaining update window for a new fleet can be as short as four to five years. The PIRG Education Fund's investigation of 'Chromebook churn' documented that this policy forces schools to retire devices that are still physically functional, generating e-waste that is entirely avoidable in hardware terms. The scale is significant: research suggests that doubling the lifespan of the millions of Chromebooks sold in 2020 could save taxpayers \$1.8 billion and prevent millions of tons of CO2-equivalent emissions — comparable to removing nearly a million cars from the road for a year.

The repairability gap. A second factor compounding the e-waste problem is the difficulty and cost of repairing school devices. Manufacturers often fail to provide affordable, accessible spare parts, leading school IT departments to scavenge components from other broken machines. Design changes between models — minor variations in bezels, clips, and connectors — prevent parts from being interchangeable, and the cost of individual replacement parts such as keyboards can approach half the price of a new low-cost Chromebook, making repair financially irrational for districts. The combination of AUE-driven retirement and poor repairability means that the school device fleet is on a treadmill: devices are discarded while functional, and the ones that break cannot be economically fixed.

AI's additional pressure. AI adds a new dimension to this problem. AI-enabled features — on-device assistants, real-time translation, image and speech processing — require more RAM, faster processors, and newer operating systems than the devices many schools currently deploy. The AI access gap literature reports that only 27% of rural students possess devices compatible with advanced AI tools, compared with 70% of urban students, and the gap is partly a hardware gap. As schools adopt AI, they face pressure to refresh fleets faster than the already-short AUE cycle, either because existing devices cannot run the tools or because the tools run poorly. This accelerates the retirement of devices that would otherwise have years of service left, converting a software-driven adoption decision into a hardware replacement decision. The environmental cost is double: the embodied carbon and materials of the discarded devices are wasted, and new devices carry their own manufacturing footprint.

E-waste management and the circular economy. The responses available to schools are well documented. Internal repair programmes — such as the student-led 'Chrome Squad' at Royse City ISD in Texas — keep devices in service longer while teaching students repair skills. Trade-in and buyback programmes with original equipment manufacturers or third-party vendors convert aging fleets into service credits or refurbished units. Repurposing legacy hardware for administrative tasks, library loaner programmes, or low-intensity classroom activities extends useful life before recycling. Software alternatives such as ChromeOS Flex can modernise older PCs and Macs, though the process is technically labour-intensive. Each of these measures reduces both cost and e-waste, and the PIRG analysis is explicit that the single most effective intervention is extending device lifespans through policy change — longer update windows and better repairability — rather than managing the waste after the fact.

Assessment. The device-lifecycle consequences of AI in schools are therefore a compound problem: AI raises hardware requirements, the dominant device platform retires hardware on a fixed schedule, and the repair market cannot economically extend lives. The e-waste outcome is predictable — larger, faster device turnover and more discarded hardware — unless schools and manufacturers act. The levers are policy (longer update windows, right-to-repair provisions), procurement (repairability and longevity as contract criteria), and practice (repair programmes, repurposing, and buybacks). The environmental stakes are not trivial: the embodied carbon in a school device fleet is a significant share of the sector's footprint, and every year shaved off a device's life multiplies the manufacturing burden that AI adoption is already increasing.

### Q199 How should the contradiction between teaching sustainability and operating energy-intensive AI be handled? {#q199}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The contradiction between teaching sustainability and operating energy-intensive AI is real, and the emerging consensus among educators is that it should be handled not by hiding it, banning AI, or pretending it away, but by making the contradiction itself part of the curriculum. The 'sustainability paradox' is well documented: schools use carbon-intensive technologies to teach about climate mitigation, and a single generative AI query can consume significantly more electricity than a standard search request, while the data centres behind the tools draw water for cooling and rely on grids that frequently include fossil fuels. When schools introduce AI modules while ignoring the environmental footprint of the underlying infrastructure, they risk teaching a 'wrong lesson' — that digital convenience is free, that the cloud is clean, and that environmental values apply to everything except the technology in front of the student. The AAUP's analysis of teaching climate change in the age of ChatGPT describes this as an ethical dilemma that educators must confront explicitly rather than avoid.

The spectrum of ethical stances. The literature identifies a spectrum of defensible positions for educators, from 'conscientious objection' — declining to use AI where its environmental cost is not justified — to 'compensation' — acknowledging the footprint and advocating for, or using, models powered by renewable energy. Between these poles lies the mainstream position: critical digital literacy, in which the environmental impact of technology is integrated directly into course material. The National Science Teaching Association, for example, recommends assignments in which students calculate the energy and carbon costs of their own digital habits — comparing the footprint of streaming video, web search, and AI chatbots — so that the abstract concept of a data centre becomes concrete and personal. The National Education Association similarly frames AI's environmental impact as a teachable topic in its own right, connecting the technology students use daily to the sustainability principles they are taught in science and social studies.

Systemic thinking rather than binary judgment. A recurring recommendation is to move beyond the 'AI is good or bad' binary and help students understand AI as a systems-level issue involving energy production, resource management, and social justice. This framing connects the environmental question to the equity questions that students already study: data centres are disproportionately sited in rural and low-income communities, their water use competes with municipal and agricultural needs, and their electricity demand can raise residential rates. Teaching AI's environmental cost as a systems problem turns the contradiction into an analytical opportunity — students can examine trade-offs, evaluate mitigation options, and consider what responsible use looks like, rather than simply being told that AI is either a tool or a threat. The Modern Diplomacy analysis of school curricula argues that the current separation of 'digital skills' and 'sustainability' as distinct subjects is outdated, and that the future of both fields lies in teaching them together.

The scale of the contradiction. The size of the environmental cost matters for how the contradiction should be framed. The UNU-INWEH analysis projects global data centre electricity demand to reach roughly 945 TWh by 2030, with an associated water footprint of about 9.3 trillion litres, and inference — the continuous running of models to answer prompts — accounts for 80–90% of AI's energy consumption. These are system-level figures, but they translate into per-use costs that students can grasp: a single AI-generated image can be roughly 1,450 times more energy-intensive than basic text classification, and a short AI-generated video can consume as much electricity as 200,000 spam classifications. Presenting these figures to students converts the abstract paradox into a concrete, quantifiable trade-off, and it gives students the tools to make their own informed judgments about when AI use is justified.

Institutional practice. Beyond the classroom, the contradiction should be handled through institutional practice that models the values being taught. This includes measuring and disclosing the school's own AI-related emissions (as discussed in the analysis of sustainability reporting), choosing vendors and models with lower footprints, using AI where it provides unique value — such as climate modelling — while avoiding unnecessary high-energy tasks, and being transparent with students about the school's own trade-offs. The 'hybrid pedagogy' approach — using AI as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, traditional teaching methods — reduces unnecessary energy use while preserving the pedagogical benefits. The key principle is alignment: the tools of instruction should not contradict the values of the subject matter, and where they do, the contradiction should be acknowledged and examined rather than concealed.

The risk of greenwashing. The literature is explicit about the risk of greenwashing: institutions that teach sustainability while operating unexamined, energy-intensive AI infrastructure without disclosure are vulnerable to the charge that their environmental commitments are performative. The response is not to abandon AI — which is increasingly essential to the modern workforce and to climate science itself — but to integrate the environmental dimension into AI governance, procurement, and curriculum simultaneously. The defensible position is that the contradiction between teaching sustainability and operating energy-intensive AI is not a problem to be solved by choosing one side, but a tension to be managed through transparency, measurement, and pedagogy. Schools that handle it well treat the contradiction as a teaching opportunity: the same students who learn that AI has an environmental cost can learn that responsible use, informed choice, and institutional accountability are the tools for managing it.

### Q200 What practical measures reduce the environmental cost of AI use in education without abandoning it? {#q200}

6 citations · 6 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

A substantial body of 'Green AI' research identifies practical measures that reduce the environmental cost of AI use in education without abandoning the technology. The measures fall into four levels: task selection, model selection, infrastructure choices, and institutional policy. The unifying principle is that most AI energy consumption is discretionary — it depends on how the tool is used, not on the fact that it is used at all — and schools therefore have significant control over their footprint.

Task selection: use the lightest tool for the job. The single most effective measure is matching the tool to the task. The energy cost of AI varies by orders of magnitude across tasks: a standard conversational query consumes roughly 0.3–0.4 Wh, reasoning-class models consume 10 to 70 times more per prompt, generating an image can be roughly 1,450 times more energy-intensive than basic text classification, and video generation is more expensive still. The UNU-INWEH analysis recommends 'efficiency by design' — choosing the lightest model that can perform a given task, and avoiding multimodal generation where text suffices. For schools, this translates into concrete rules: use standard models for summarisation and drafting, reserve reasoning models for genuinely difficult problems, and treat image and video generation as an occasional, justified activity rather than a default. A school that adopts this practice can reduce its AI energy footprint by an order of magnitude without reducing educational benefit.

Model selection and efficiency techniques. The technical literature documents a range of efficiency techniques that reduce the energy cost of AI itself. Pruning removes redundant weights and neurons from a neural network, reducing computation with minimal accuracy loss; quantization converts high-precision parameters into lower-bit formats, cutting memory and energy use; and knowledge distillation trains smaller 'student' models to replicate larger 'teacher' models. These techniques are implemented by vendors, but schools can influence them through procurement: choosing tools built on efficient, smaller models rather than frontier models for routine use. The MIT Sloan analysis of data centre energy costs notes that model choice is a decision that users and buyers can influence, and that the gap between the most and least efficient models for a given task is large.

Infrastructure choices: edge computing and carbon-aware scheduling. At the infrastructure level, two measures stand out. Edge computing — processing data locally on devices rather than in cloud data centres — can reduce energy consumption by 100 to 1,000 times per task, according to World Economic Forum analysis, because it avoids the network and data centre overhead. For schools, this means favouring on-device AI features (which increasingly run on modern laptops and phones) for tasks that do not require cloud-scale models. Carbon-aware scheduling — shifting non-time-sensitive workloads to times and regions where renewable energy is abundant — is a vendor-side measure, but schools can support it by choosing vendors that practice it and by avoiding peak-hour, latency-sensitive AI use where possible. Power capping, which limits the wattage supplied to processors, is another vendor-side technique that reduces both energy and heat.

Institutional policy and procurement. The institutional level is where schools have the most direct control. Procurement criteria can require environmental data from vendors — energy and water disclosure, renewable-energy procurement, and efficiency practices — which both reduces the school's footprint and creates market pressure for greener products. Usage policies can encode the task-selection principle: guidelines for when to use AI, which models to use for which tasks, and when not to use AI at all. The Environmental and Energy Study Institute's analysis of data centres notes that cooling choices matter too: schools that host any infrastructure can favour facilities using efficient cooling, and schools that buy cloud services can ask about the water intensity of the facilities that serve them. Device longevity is a further institutional lever: extending device lifespans through repair and repurposing reduces the embodied carbon of the fleet, which for many schools exceeds the operational energy of AI use.

Behavioural measures. Institutional culture matters as well as technology. Schools that normalise asking 'is AI necessary for this task?' before using it, that designate AI-free zones and activities, and that teach students the environmental rationale for restraint, reduce usage without reducing capability. The rebound effect documented in the Green AI literature — efficiency gains that lower cost per query and increase total usage — means that behavioural norms are a necessary complement to technical efficiency: without them, savings are consumed by additional use.

Measurement and accountability. Finally, the Green AI literature is unanimous that measurement is a precondition for reduction. Schools that track their AI-related energy and water use — even with rough estimates — can set targets, evaluate interventions, and report progress. The rebound effect documented in the literature — efficiency gains that lower cost per query and increase total usage — means that efficiency measures must be paired with usage awareness, or the savings will be consumed by additional use. The practical package for a school is therefore: lightest-model rules, on-device processing where possible, procurement criteria that demand environmental data, usage policies that discourage gratuitous multimodal generation, device longevity programmes, and periodic measurement of the resulting footprint. None of these measures requires abandoning AI; together they can reduce its environmental cost by a large factor while preserving its educational value.

### Q201 Are data-centre siting decisions affecting the communities whose schools use these systems? {#q201}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Data-centre siting decisions are affecting the communities whose schools use these systems, and the effects are increasingly documented as an environmental justice problem. The AI boom has driven a rapid expansion of hyperscale data centres, and the evidence shows that they are disproportionately sited in regions facing water scarcity and in communities already carrying environmental burdens. A 2026 analysis of California data centres found that newer facilities are frequently proposed in areas that score highly on both social vulnerability and water scarcity indices. Nationally, approximately two-thirds of data centres built since 2022 are located in water-stressed regions, and of 809 planned data centres examined in a 2026 analysis, 517 are in areas that experienced drought conditions over the past year. The World Resources Institute's analysis of U.S. data centre growth documents that these facilities are increasingly concentrated in census tracts that already face poor air quality and water pollution — the classic pattern of environmental injustice, in which industrial burdens fall on communities with the least capacity to resist or absorb them.

Water competition. The most direct community impact is water competition. Large hyperscale facilities can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day — equivalent to the daily use of a city of 10,000 to 50,000 residents — primarily for evaporative cooling. In water-stressed regions such as the Colorado River Basin and groundwater-dependent areas like Gilroy, California, this demand competes directly with municipal, agricultural, and ecological needs. The Next 10 analysis emphasises that the risks extend beyond a facility's immediate footprint: reliance on imported water or shared groundwater basins means a single data centre's consumption can contribute to basin-wide depletion and reduced drought resilience for distant, often more vulnerable, populations. During droughts, local water authorities may be forced to choose between residential access and industrial operations — a choice that communities with less political power tend to lose.

Electricity, rates, and air quality. Data centres also strain local electricity grids. Utilities are investing billions in new transmission lines and power plants to meet data centre demand, and the costs are frequently passed on to residential ratepayers; in Northern Virginia's 'Data Center Alley', residents have reported significant spikes in electricity bills. Projections indicate U.S. data centre energy demand could nearly double between 2025 and 2028, reaching roughly 150 gigawatts, and the 'Field of Dreams' pattern — building facilities in anticipation of power that may not be available — can destabilise local energy markets. Air quality is a further concern: thousands of on-site diesel backup generators produce nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, and cooling systems using chemical additives — biocides and corrosion inhibitors — can, if mismanaged, introduce heavy metals, salts, and PFAS into local soil and groundwater. These impacts fall disproportionately on communities that already suffer from high asthma rates and other health disparities.

Transparency and governance. A recurring finding is the lack of transparency in siting decisions. Many developers use non-disclosure agreements with local officials, limiting public access to information about a project's scale and resource requirements, and fewer than one-third of operators are estimated to track their water consumption. This 'data desert' prevents water providers and local governments from accurately assessing long-term impacts on local supplies. In response, some communities are implementing moratoria, forming task forces, and negotiating community benefits agreements that mandate the use of reclaimed water, secure local economic benefits, and require transparent reporting. The Lincoln Institute's analysis of the land and water impacts of data centres notes that the facilities are 'extractive' in character: they provide relatively few long-term jobs relative to their massive land and resource footprint, so the economic benefits to host communities are often smaller than promised.

Cumulative and regional effects. The impacts are not confined to the immediate vicinity of a facility. Because data centres draw on shared grids and water basins, their effects propagate regionally: a facility in one county can contribute to rate increases or water restrictions in neighbouring communities, and the cumulative demand of many facilities can reshape regional energy planning. The Next 10 analysis of California found that the water risks of data centre development extend beyond the host site to the basins and utilities that serve it, and that cumulative impacts are poorly captured by project-by-project review. This regional dimension matters for schools because the communities affected by data centre siting are often the same communities whose schools depend on the digital infrastructure — the burden and the benefit are connected, but the burden is concentrated while the benefit is diffuse.

The connection to schools. The connection to schools is twofold. First, schools are among the institutions that use these systems — their AI tools, learning platforms, and cloud services run on the same infrastructure — so the environmental cost of educational AI is borne, in part, by the communities where data centres are sited, which are often not the communities whose schools benefit most. Second, schools in host communities experience the impacts directly: water competition, rate increases, and air quality effects can affect the same families whose children use AI in the classroom. The environmental justice literature concludes that siting decisions should be subject to standardised disclosure of water and energy use, inclusive siting criteria that avoid disproportionately burdened areas, and community participation in decision-making. For schools, the practical implication is that the footprint of educational AI is not abstract — it is tied to concrete communities, and procurement and advocacy decisions by school systems can influence where and how that burden falls.
