### Q250 How should schools account for the full lifecycle carbon and water footprint of AI infrastructure, from hardware manufacture through data-centre operation to device disposal? {#q250}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

When schools consider the environmental cost of AI, attention usually falls on the electricity consumed when a student types a question and receives an answer. Lifecycle thinking, a standard approach in environmental assessment, suggests this is only one part of the picture. The footprint of AI also includes the energy and materials used to manufacture servers and chips, the water consumed to cool data centres and generate their electricity, the energy used to train models before any student uses them, and the waste generated when hardware, including the devices students use, reaches the end of its life.

Embodied emissions from hardware manufacture are often overlooked. Luccioni, Viguier, and Ligozat, in a 2023 lifecycle assessment of the BLOOM language model published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research, estimated that the final training run emitted about 24.7 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent from dynamic power consumption, but that the total rose to roughly 50.5 tonnes when idle power, infrastructure, and the embodied emissions of the servers and graphics processors were included. Embodied hardware emissions alone accounted for an estimated 11.2 tonnes, and the authors noted that this was a lower bound because manufacturers do not disclose full data. Their analysis suggests that accounting only for operational electricity can substantially understate the footprint.

Operational energy demand is growing quickly. The International Energy Agency's 2025 Energy and AI report estimated that data centres consumed about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5 percent of global electricity use, and projected that consumption could more than double to roughly 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI the primary driver. The carbon intensity of that electricity depends heavily on location and time, so the same AI query can have very different emissions depending on where and when it is processed.

Water is a second dimension. Li, Yang, Islam, and Ren, in their study Making AI Less Thirsty, estimated that training GPT-3 in Microsoft's U.S. data centres could have directly evaporated around 700,000 litres of clean freshwater, with total water use including electricity generation considerably higher, and projected that global AI demand could account for 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027. Water use varies with climate, cooling technology, and the water intensity of the local grid, and data centres in water-stressed regions raise particular concerns.

The type of model also matters. Luccioni, Jernite, and Strubell, in their 2024 FAccT paper Power Hungry Processing, measured the energy used by 88 models across ten tasks and found that general-purpose generative models consumed far more energy per inference than smaller task-specific models, sometimes by orders of magnitude, with image generation especially energy-intensive. This finding implies that using a large generative model for a task that a smaller tool could handle carries an avoidable environmental cost.

End-of-life is the final stage. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024, produced by the United Nations Institute for Training and Research and the International Telecommunication Union, reported that 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were generated worldwide in 2022 and that only 22.3 percent was documented as formally collected and recycled. AI contributes through accelerated replacement cycles for data-centre hardware and through pressure on schools to upgrade student devices to run newer AI features.

Schools face real constraints in measuring these impacts, since vendors rarely disclose lifecycle data and individual institutions lack the expertise to conduct full assessments. Several practical approaches are nonetheless available. Procurement can require vendors to disclose the energy and water intensity of their services, the location and energy mix of data centres, and any emissions reporting under recognised frameworks, and can give weight to vendors who provide such information. Schools can estimate their footprint using published per-query or per-user estimates while acknowledging uncertainty, and can include AI services within broader sustainability reporting.

Use policies can also reduce impact. UNESCO and University College London's 2025 report Smarter, Smaller, Stronger found that using smaller task-specific models could cut energy use by up to 90 percent in some tasks and that shortening prompts and responses could reduce energy use by more than half, suggesting that proportionate use, matching the tool to the task, has measurable benefits. Device policies that extend the life of student hardware, prioritise repair, and ensure certified recycling address the end-of-life stage.

The question of AI's footprint sits within a longer debate about the environmental cost of information and communication technology as a whole. Charlotte Freitag, Mike Berners-Lee and colleagues at Lancaster University and Small World Consulting, writing in the journal Patterns in 2021, reviewed the main published estimates and concluded that the sector accounted for between about 2.1 and 3.9 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions once the full supply chain and lifecycle were included, a range comparable to or larger than aviation. They emphasised that earlier, lower estimates often omitted embodied emissions from manufacturing and parts of the supply chain, and they cautioned against assuming that efficiency improvements would automatically reduce total emissions, because historically efficiency gains in computing have been accompanied by even faster growth in demand. Their analysis was completed before the surge in generative AI and therefore does not capture its recent effects, but it established a framework that schools can apply: count the whole lifecycle, be sceptical of figures that cover only operational electricity, and recognise that adoption decisions contribute to aggregate demand even when each individual use seems negligible. The same authors noted that much of the data needed for complete accounting is held by companies that are not obliged to disclose it, a constraint that remains acute for AI.

Accounting conventions matter more than many schools realise. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the most widely used corporate emissions standard, developed by the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development, distinguishes direct emissions, emissions from purchased electricity, and indirect emissions across the value chain, known respectively as Scopes 1, 2 and 3. For a school, almost all of the footprint of a cloud-based AI service falls into Scope 3, which is the category organisations report least consistently. The Protocol's 2015 Scope 2 guidance also requires companies to report electricity emissions in two ways: a location-based figure reflecting the average emissions of the grid where electricity is consumed, and a market-based figure that can reflect purchases of renewable energy certificates and power purchase agreements. Technology companies often highlight market-based figures that can appear close to zero, while location-based figures, which better reflect the physical emissions from grids where data centres operate, can be considerably higher. Schools evaluating vendor sustainability claims therefore benefit from asking which method was used, whether embodied emissions from hardware are included, and whether water consumption is reported at the level of the specific data centres serving the school's region rather than as a global average.

The manufacturing stage deserves particular attention for the devices that schools buy, not just for the data centres they rent. Udit Gupta and colleagues at Harvard and Meta, presenting at the IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture in 2021, analysed corporate sustainability reports and lifecycle assessments and found that, for many consumer devices such as phones and laptops, emissions from manufacturing the hardware, including chip fabrication, accounted for the majority of lifetime carbon emissions, exceeding those from operating the devices. They also showed that, as data-centre operators shifted toward renewable electricity, the relative share of embodied emissions in data-centre hardware rose. For schools, the implication is that device lifespan may be the most powerful lever they control directly. A laptop kept in service for six years rather than three spreads its manufacturing footprint over twice the period of use, and the environmental benefit of choosing a slightly more efficient AI service may be small compared with the benefit of avoiding a premature device replacement cycle. This consideration is particularly relevant where AI features are used to justify upgrading hardware that otherwise remains functional.

Device policy in school systems illustrates how software decisions shape hardware lifecycles. The U.S. PIRG Education Fund's 2023 report Chromebook Churn examined the low-cost laptops widely used in American schools and argued that automatic expiration of software updates was forcing schools to retire devices that still worked, generating electronic waste and costs. The report estimated that doubling the lifespan of Chromebooks purchased in a single pandemic-era year could save taxpayers about 1.8 billion dollars, and it urged manufacturers to extend support. Google later announced that it would extend automatic updates for Chromebooks to ten years. The episode shows that procurement and advocacy can lengthen device life, and it offers a template for AI. As vendors introduce AI features that require newer processors or on-device accelerators, schools face pressure to replace hardware. Lifecycle-aware procurement would weigh the educational value of such features against the embodied emissions of new devices, favour vendors who commit to long support periods, and ensure that retired equipment enters certified refurbishment or recycling streams rather than informal export.

Regulation is beginning to make data-centre impacts more visible. The European Union's revised Energy Efficiency Directive, adopted in 2023, requires operators of data centres above a power threshold of 500 kilowatts to report key performance information, including energy consumption, water use and the share of renewable energy, to a European database, with the stated aim of enabling a common rating scheme. Although the reporting is designed for regulators and aggregated publication rather than for individual customers, it creates a basis that schools and education authorities could draw on when asking vendors where their workloads run and how efficiently. Company reports provide another, less standardised source. Microsoft's annual environmental sustainability reports, for instance, have disclosed substantial increases in total water consumption in years of rapid AI expansion, and independent journalists have connected such increases to data centres in water-stressed regions. These disclosures are partial and use company-chosen metrics, but they show that the information exists and that public pressure can increase its availability.

Equity considerations extend beyond the school gate. The communities that host data centres, mines that supply minerals for chips, and facilities that process electronic waste are often distant from the schools that use AI services, and they may bear water stress, pollution or noise without sharing in the benefits. Lifecycle accounting that stops at a carbon number can obscure these distributional effects. Schools that teach about AI's environmental footprint can include them, asking students to trace where minerals are mined, where models are trained and served, and where devices end up, and to consider who decides whether these costs are worth bearing. Such an approach connects environmental accounting to questions of justice that are central to sustainability education, and it acknowledges that the choice to use AI in education carries consequences for people who are not consulted.

Rebound effects complicate any accounting. If AI tools become more efficient per query, schools may use them more often, for more tasks and with more students, so that total consumption rises even as unit costs fall. This pattern, known since the nineteenth century as the Jevons paradox, implies that efficiency targets alone are insufficient. Schools may need to complement efficiency measures with sufficiency principles, asking not only how to perform a task with less energy but whether the task requires AI at all, and setting expectations that generative tools are used where they add clear educational value rather than by default.

For a school or district that wants to act on these considerations, a staged approach is realistic. A first step is an inventory of AI services in use, the devices they run on, and the regions where vendors process data. A second is a standard set of procurement questions covering location-based and market-based emissions, embodied hardware emissions, water consumption at the serving data centres, device support periods and take-back arrangements. A third is a set of internal guidelines that favour smaller or task-specific tools where they suffice and reserve the most resource-intensive models for uses with clear educational value. None of these steps requires a full lifecycle assessment, which few institutions could conduct, but together they move decisions from an exclusive focus on cost and features toward a fuller picture of consequences, and they signal to vendors that environmental transparency affects purchasing.

Finally, environmental accounting can become part of the curriculum. Students who learn to ask what resources lie behind a digital service develop a form of AI literacy that connects technology to sustainability. The evidence base has gaps, especially regarding inference at scale and embodied emissions of specialised chips, but the lifecycle research available suggests that schools that consider only electricity at the point of use will consistently underestimate the environmental cost of AI.

### Q251 What evidence exists that smaller, locally deployed AI models can achieve comparable educational outcomes at significantly lower energy cost? {#q251}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

As concern about the energy and water footprint of large AI models has grown, attention has turned to smaller models that can run on school servers, laptops, or even phones. Such models promise lower energy use, reduced data-transfer and privacy risks, independence from internet connectivity, and lower costs. The central question for education is whether they can deliver learning outcomes comparable to those achieved with large cloud-hosted models. The evidence that bears on this question is substantial for energy efficiency, moderate for general task performance, and thin for educational outcomes specifically.

The energy evidence is strong. Luccioni, Jernite, and Strubell, in their 2024 FAccT paper Power Hungry Processing, measured energy use across 88 models and ten tasks and found that multi-purpose generative models consumed substantially more energy per inference than task-specific models, often by large factors, even for tasks such as classification or question answering where smaller models performed adequately. UNESCO and University College London's 2025 report Smarter, Smaller, Stronger reported experiments in which smaller task-specific models reduced energy use by up to 90 percent while maintaining performance on targeted tasks, and in which model compression through quantisation saved up to 44 percent of energy. The report also found that reducing prompt and response length cut energy by more than half.

General capability evidence comes from technical benchmarks. Microsoft's Phi-3 technical report, by Abdin and colleagues, described a 3.8-billion-parameter model small enough to run on a smartphone that scored around 69 percent on the MMLU knowledge benchmark, a level the authors compared to considerably larger models from a year or two earlier. Similar results have been reported for other compact open models. These benchmarks suggest that small models can handle many tasks relevant to education, such as explaining concepts, generating practice questions, or providing feedback on short texts, though they typically lag frontier models on complex reasoning, specialised knowledge, and multilingual performance. Benchmark performance is also an imperfect proxy for pedagogical quality, since it measures answer accuracy rather than the ability to scaffold, question, and adapt to a learner.

Direct evidence on educational outcomes is the critical gap. The most cited positive experimental results for AI tutoring have used large frontier models. Kestin and colleagues, in a 2025 randomised crossover study in Scientific Reports involving 194 Harvard physics students, found that students using a carefully designed AI tutor built on a large model learned more in less time than in an in-class active learning session. Bastani and colleagues' PNAS trial, which showed that guardrails determined whether AI helped or harmed independent learning, also used GPT-4. To date, there appear to be few if any published randomised studies comparing learning outcomes from small locally deployed models with those from large models under otherwise identical pedagogical designs.

Indirect evidence suggests why comparable outcomes are plausible for some uses. Both the Kestin and Bastani studies indicate that pedagogical design, including structured prompts, step-by-step solutions supplied by teachers, and limits on answer-giving, strongly shapes outcomes. If much of the educational value comes from design rather than raw model capability, smaller models grounded in curated content through retrieval may achieve similar results for well-defined tasks. Kestin and colleagues reported that supplying step-by-step solutions in system prompts reduced errors, a technique that could also compensate for weaker knowledge in smaller models.

Indirect evidence also suggests limits. Smaller models are more prone to factual errors on topics outside their training, perform worse in low-resource languages, and may struggle with long, multi-turn tutoring dialogues. For subjects requiring complex reasoning or broad knowledge, the performance gap could translate into poorer explanations or more misconceptions. Local deployment also shifts responsibility for updates, safety filtering, and maintenance onto schools that may lack technical capacity.

The interest in small, local models continues a longer tradition of designing educational technology for settings where connectivity, power and budgets are limited. Long before generative AI, organisations such as Learning Equality built offline-first platforms, most notably Kolibri, which allows schools to distribute curated educational content and exercises over a local network from a single low-cost device, synchronising with the internet only when a connection is available. Such platforms were developed for refugee camps, rural schools and other contexts in which reliance on cloud services was impractical, and they established design principles that remain relevant: content must be curated and aligned with local curricula, devices must tolerate intermittent power, and teachers need tools to monitor progress without constant connectivity. The International Telecommunication Union's Facts and Figures 2024 report estimated that about 2.6 billion people, roughly a third of the world's population, remained offline, with the gap concentrated in low-income countries and rural areas. For these learners, the relevant comparison is not between a small local model and a frontier cloud model but between a small local model and no AI at all. That framing changes how the evidence should be weighed, since a tool that is somewhat less capable but actually available may deliver more educational value than a superior tool that cannot be reached.

Technical advances explain why smaller models have become more capable. Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals and Jeff Dean described in 2015 a technique they called knowledge distillation, in which a smaller student model is trained to reproduce the output probabilities of a larger teacher model, transferring much of the teacher's capability into a more compact form. Distillation has since become a standard method for producing small models from large ones. Quantisation, which stores model weights with fewer bits, offers further savings. Tim Dettmers and colleagues, presenting QLoRA at the NeurIPS conference in 2023, showed that a model with 65 billion parameters could be fine-tuned on a single graphics processor with 48 gigabytes of memory by combining four-bit quantisation with low-rank adaptation, while preserving performance close to full-precision fine-tuning on the benchmarks they tested. These techniques mean that education ministries, universities or regional consortia could adapt open models to local curricula and languages without access to massive computing clusters. They also mean that the capability gap between small and large models is not fixed; it depends on how much effort goes into distilling, compressing and specialising smaller models for particular purposes.

Retrieval augmentation is another reason that small models may perform adequately in bounded educational tasks. Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, presenting at NeurIPS in 2020, introduced retrieval-augmented generation, in which a model retrieves relevant passages from a document collection and conditions its answer on them, and found that this approach improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and produced more specific and factual responses than a comparable model relying on its internal parameters alone. In an educational setting, a small model connected to a curated library of textbooks, worked examples and teacher materials does not need to store vast general knowledge, because it can draw on vetted sources for the content it explains. This design also supports transparency, since answers can be linked to the passages they rely on, and it allows schools to control the content students encounter. Retrieval does not eliminate errors, as models can still misread or misapply retrieved passages, and the quality of the library becomes critical. But it shifts part of the burden of accuracy from model size to curriculum curation, a task in which educators have expertise.

The closest experimental evidence on low-cost AI tutoring comes from a study in Ghana. Owen Henkel and colleagues at Rising Academies reported in a 2024 working paper on a randomised controlled trial of Rori, a mathematics tutor delivered through WhatsApp on low-cost phones, in which students in participating schools used the tutor during short weekly sessions over about eight months. The authors reported that students with access to Rori scored significantly higher on a mathematics assessment than the control group, with an effect size of about 0.37 standard deviations, at a low reported cost per student. Rori relied on a cloud-hosted language model for parts of its interaction rather than running entirely on local hardware, so the study does not directly test a small locally deployed model. It does, however, show that a lightweight, low-bandwidth tutor with tightly structured content and limited open-ended generation can produce meaningful learning gains in a low-resource context, which is the type of design small local models are best suited to. The paper had not been peer reviewed at the time of release and the trial was conducted in a limited number of schools, so the result warrants replication before broad conclusions are drawn.

The energy comparison is less straightforward than it may first appear. In 2025 Google published a methodology paper by Cooper Elsworth and colleagues estimating that the median text prompt to its Gemini assistant consumed about 0.24 watt-hours of energy when accounting for accelerators, host systems, idle capacity and data-centre overhead, along with small amounts of water and emissions, and reported large efficiency gains over the preceding year. The figures were produced by the company itself and cover only the median prompt, not long or multimodal interactions, but they suggest that per-query energy for highly optimised cloud services can be lower than earlier estimates implied. Running a model locally on an inefficient laptop or server may therefore not always use less energy per interaction than a well-utilised data centre, especially if schools buy new hardware to host models, adding embodied emissions. The environmental case for local deployment is strongest when existing devices are used, when models are small enough to run efficiently, and when the alternative cloud service relies on very large models for tasks that do not need them. A full comparison requires lifecycle accounting rather than per-query electricity alone.

Implementation challenges also deserve attention. Running local models requires technical capacity to install, update and secure them, and many schools lack dedicated IT staff. Models need periodic updating to correct errors and incorporate curriculum changes, and without central support local deployments can become outdated. Safety filtering, which cloud providers maintain centrally, must be configured and maintained locally. These costs can be shared by regional or national programmes that prepare, test and distribute curriculum-aligned small models and the content libraries they draw on, much as earlier offline content platforms were maintained by organisations rather than individual schools. Such programmes also offer an opportunity to evaluate educational outcomes systematically, comparing local and cloud deployments on the same tasks with the same students, which would address the central gap in the current evidence.

Small local models offer an advantage that is not environmental but often decisive for schools: control over student data. When a model runs on a school server or a student's device, prompts and responses need not leave the institution, which simplifies compliance with data-protection regimes such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation and with national rules on children's data. It also reduces the risk that student interactions will be retained or used for model training by a commercial provider, a concern that education authorities in several countries have raised about cloud AI services. This benefit has to be weighed against security responsibilities, since a poorly maintained local system can expose data in other ways, and against capability limits, particularly in languages with little training data, where small models tend to perform markedly worse than large ones. For many schools the choice will not be binary. A hybrid architecture, in which routine and privacy-sensitive tasks run locally while a limited set of demanding tasks are routed to a cloud model under strict data agreements, may capture most of the energy and privacy benefits of small models while preserving access to greater capability when it is genuinely needed.

The practical implication is that small, locally deployed models are a credible option for specific, bounded educational tasks, particularly when paired with curated content and strong pedagogical design, and that their energy advantages are well established. Claims that they achieve comparable educational outcomes in general, however, outrun the evidence. Schools and researchers could close this gap by running head-to-head evaluations that hold pedagogical design constant and vary model size, measuring both learning outcomes and energy use. Such studies would allow education systems to make informed trade-offs rather than defaulting to the largest available model.

## Chapter 18: Higher Education and Research {#chapter-18}

10 questions · 80 citations · 72 unique sources · 50 cross-references

### Q202 What is happening to the undergraduate essay as an assessment instrument? {#q202}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The undergraduate essay is undergoing its most significant destabilisation since the rise of mass higher education, and the cause is not a change in pedagogy but a change in the technology available to students. Generative AI can now produce, in seconds, prose that is structurally competent, grammatically fluent, and topically plausible — precisely the qualities that the traditional take-home essay was designed to elicit and reward. The result is a definitional crisis: institutions are being forced to decide what an essay is for, what it certifies, and whether the instrument can survive in its current form.

The definitional problem. Historically, plagiarism was defined as the unacknowledged copying of another person's identifiable work. AI-generated text has no human author, so the old conceptual architecture does not map cleanly onto it. Institutions have responded by extending their academic integrity codes to treat the unacknowledged submission of AI-generated content as a form of misrepresentation — a distinct category from plagiarism but one that carries similar penalties. This shift is documented across policy reviews in multiple jurisdictions, and it represents a genuine conceptual change: the offence is no longer theft of another's words but the false claim that machine output is one's own intellectual labour.

Three policy stances. Institutional responses fall broadly into three categories. Prohibitive policies ban any AI assistance for graded work, on the grounds that the intellectual struggle of writing is itself the learning outcome. Permissive-with-disclosure policies permit specific uses — brainstorming, outlining, language polishing — provided students cite the tool, reproduce their prompts, and take responsibility for verifying accuracy. Assignment-specific governance delegates rule-setting to individual instructors, who must communicate expectations for each task in the syllabus. Survey evidence indicates that approximately 68 percent of universities still have no explicit AI assessment policy, though this does not immunise them from applying existing academic integrity standards to AI-assisted submissions.

The failure of detection. A central empirical finding is that neither human markers nor automated detection software can reliably distinguish human-authored from AI-assisted work. Detection tools operate on statistical proxies such as perplexity and burstiness, and they produce both false positives and false negatives at rates that make them unsuitable as sole instruments of discipline. The bias is not random: a 2023 study found that AI detectors misclassified over 61 percent of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated, and a 2026 follow-up reported a 61.3 percent false-positive rate for essays by Chinese students compared with 5.1 percent for U.S. students. The consequences are real and documented: in Newby v. Adelphi University, a court annulled an academic-integrity finding based on a 100 percent AI-generated score from Turnitin, and Australian Catholic University ceased using AI detection software in 2025 after a high volume of referrals based on tool scores were dismissed on investigation. The consensus across the literature is that detection scores should never be the sole basis for disciplinary action.

Assessment redesign as the emerging consensus. Because detection cannot police the essay, institutions have moved toward a 'pedagogical-first' orientation. The recommended alternatives cluster into three families. Authentic and performative assessments — tasks requiring personal reflection, local context, or primary data that AI cannot plausibly generate — reduce the incentive for substitution. Synchronous and interpersonal assessments, including oral examinations, vivas, and in-class presentations, allow examiners to probe depth of understanding in real time. Process-oriented submissions — incremental drafts, annotated bibliographies, reflective journals tracing the development of an argument — make the intellectual journey visible and harder to outsource. Frameworks such as the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) formalise this by categorising assignments along a spectrum from 'no AI' to 'full AI', giving educators a structured vocabulary for deciding what each task is meant to certify.

What the evidence does and does not show. Systematic reviews find that AI-assisted feedback can improve the structural, grammatical, and cohesive quality of student writing)Skip, and is associated with higher self-efficacy and motivation in some cohorts. The same literature flags risks of over-reliance, erosion of critical thinking, and the well-documented problem of AI 'hallucinations' — plausible-sounding but false information that students may accept uncritically and incorporate into assessed work. A persistent debate concerns whether blanket prohibition is feasible or desirable given that AI is already standard in many professional contexts graduates will enter. Critics of prohibition argue that it delays necessary skill development and places institutions in the position of policing undetectable behaviour; proponents argue that the formative value of struggling to produce original thought justifies restriction during degree programmes. Current evidence does not resolve this debate: there are no longitudinal studies demonstrating that either prohibitive or permissive policies produce better learning outcomes over time.

The trajectory. The institutional consensus as of the mid-2020s is that protecting credential value requires students to engage honestly with course material, and that the vehicle for this is assessment redesign rather than technological policing. The undergraduate essay is not disappearing, but it is being repositioned: increasingly it is either performed under controlled conditions, embedded in a visible process, or explicitly framed as a human-AI collaboration in which the student's contribution is the judgment, verification, and argumentation that the machine cannot supply. Whether this repositioning delivers the intended outcomes — particularly in under-resourced departments without capacity for oral examination at scale — remains an open empirical question. What is no longer in doubt is that the essay's authority as a standalone, unsupervised instrument of certification has been permanently weakened.

### Q203 How is AI changing doctoral supervision and research training? {#q203}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Generative AI has entered the doctoral supervisory relationship as what one body of scholarship describes as a 'socio-technical force' — not merely a tool that candidates use, but an active participant that reconfigures the ecology of supervision itself. The traditional dyad of supervisor and candidate is increasingly supplemented, or covertly complicated, by AI acting as an unacknowledged third party: generating draft literature syntheses, cleaning data, suggesting analytical framings, and providing rapid text feedback between scheduled meetings. When this use remains hidden, it can confer undue agency to the technology and erode the trust on which effective mentorship depends.

The unchanged standard, the new verification problem. The core institutional principle, affirmed by bodies including King's College London, the University of Toronto, and the Open University, is that the doctoral thesis must represent the candidate's own account of their investigations. Candidates are expected to remain the intellectual authors of their work, capable of defending every element of it in an oral examination. This standard has not changed, but AI complicates its verification: examiners cannot rely on detection software to flag AI contributions with acceptable accuracy, and viva voce examination has consequently been reaffirmed as the primary mechanism of authenticity verification. Several universities now explicitly warn that a candidate who cannot justify or explain the content of their thesis during the oral examination may fail, regardless of the thesis's written quality.

The green-amber-red framework. Institutional policy frameworks have broadly converged on a tiered categorisation of permissible AI use. Green activities — brainstorming, style suggestions, grammar improvement, formatting — are generally permitted without special approval. Amber activities — paragraph-level drafting, data cleaning, literature organisation — typically require documented supervisory approval, recorded in writing through email or meeting minutes. Red activities — drafting core analysis, discussion, or conclusions that substitute for the candidate's reasoning, and any AI use during viva examinations — are prohibited as academic misconduct. Transparency is a near-universal requirement: candidates are expected to disclose GenAI use in supervision meeting minutes, thesis front matter, methods sections, or dedicated appendices, and to document the prompts and outputs involved.

Data privacy as a contractual and legal obligation. A distinct and serious concern is data privacy. Public-facing AI tools typically retain user inputs for training purposes. Doctoral research often involves unpublished empirical data, proprietary datasets, commercially sensitive partner information, or pre-publication findings from collaborative grants. Institutions consistently advise against uploading such material to commercially operated AI platforms, recommending instead institutionally sandboxed or approved environments. This is not merely a policy recommendation but a potential contractual and legal obligation under research agreements with industry or government funders, and a breach can constitute a confidentiality violation with real consequences for the candidate and the institution.

The recalibration of supervision itself. The supervisory relationship requires recalibration because AI-generated feedback differs in kind from supervisory feedback. AI feedback tends to be task-oriented and immediate but lacks the relational, contextual, and developmental character of supervisory feedback that fosters evaluative independence over time. Research distinguishes clearly between these two feedback types, noting that reliance on AI for formative feedback may impair the candidate's development of the independent judgment that the doctorate is meant to certify. Supervisors now face a more complex set of responsibilities: they must help candidates navigate the pedagogical and ethical implications of AI-mediated work, distinguishing AI as a support mechanism from AI as a substitute for the intellectual struggle central to developing an independent scholarly identity. Activity-theory analyses of doctoral training document the resulting friction between groups of students and supervisors with divergent attitudes toward technology adoption, and the tension between productivity-oriented practices and traditional norms of scholarly formation.

Training and evidence gaps. Professional development needs for supervisors are substantial: they require ongoing training on evolving AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, and institutional policy — a need that many universities have not yet met systematically. There is currently no longitudinal evidence that institutions with more permissive or more restrictive AI policies produce better doctoral outcomes, better-prepared researchers, or different rates of research misconduct. The evidence base consists largely of policy documents, case studies, and small-scale qualitative studies rather than controlled comparisons. What is documented is the direction of travel: disclosure, tiered permission, data protection, and the reaffirmation of oral examination as the ultimate test of authorship. The doctorate is being preserved as a certification of individual intellectual contribution, but the machinery for verifying that contribution is being rebuilt around a technology that makes the boundary between the candidate's mind and the machine's output increasingly difficult to draw.

Comparative policy and the open questions. The policy landscape is genuinely international but uneven. Universities in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and continental Europe have published comparable guidance documents, yet the specificity and enforcement of those documents vary widely: some institutions require written supervisory approval for any AI use, while others rely on general academic-integrity codes that mention AI only in passing. Research training itself is being reshaped in ways that extend beyond the thesis: doctoral programmes are adding AI literacy modules, research-methods courses now routinely address the use of AI in data analysis and literature review, and candidates are being trained to use AI critically rather than merely to avoid it. The open questions are empirical. There is no longitudinal evidence on whether candidates who use AI extensively during their doctorate are better or worse prepared for independent research careers, whether the green-amber-red framework changes actual behaviour or merely formalises existing practice, or whether the reaffirmation of the viva as the authenticity mechanism will hold as AI systems become capable of generating and defending plausible accounts of research that the candidate did not conduct. What is clear is that doctoral supervision has become a site of active institutional experimentation, and that the norms being established now — around disclosure, tiered permission, and the primacy of oral defence — will shape the next generation of researchers' understanding of what it means to be the author of one's own work.

### Q204 What is AI doing to peer review and scholarly publishing, and how are journals responding? {#q204}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

AI is simultaneously transforming the production, evaluation, and integrity of the scholarly record, and the publishing community's response has been to build a normative framework around a single non-negotiable principle: accountability must remain human. The three principal organisations governing research publication ethics — the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), and the World Association of Medical Editors (WAME) — have converged on a policy framework whose core elements are now relatively stable, though implementation and enforcement remain inconsistent across journals and publishers.

Authorship. The position on authorship is unambiguous: AI tools cannot be listed as authors or co-authors. The reasoning is grounded in authorship criteria that require legal accountability, the capacity to take public responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the work, management of conflicts of interest, and the ability to sign legal publishing agreements. Because AI systems are not legal entities, they cannot meet any of these criteria. Human authors who use AI retain full responsibility for all content, including any errors, biases, fabrications, or plagiarism that AI may introduce; authors cannot exculpate themselves from misconduct by attributing problematic content to a tool. This principle is affirmed by ICMJE guidance updated in 2024 and 2025 and by COPE's standing position documents.

Disclosure. All major frameworks require transparency about AI use, but the required level of specificity varies. The ICMJE specifies that AI used for writing assistance should be disclosed in the acknowledgements section, while AI used for data collection, analysis, or figure generation should be described in the methods section with sufficient detail to allow scientific scrutiny. Some journals additionally require disclosure of specific tools, version numbers, query dates, and the purpose of each application. ICMJE's 2024–2025 updates also clarify the handling of AI in images and figures: generative AI must not be used to create or manipulate primary research images in ways that would misrepresent the underlying data, and where AI is used for legitimate illustrative purposes, full disclosure and verification against source data are required.

Peer review. The consensus on peer review is more cautious. Uploading a manuscript to a public AI platform constitutes a confidentiality breach, because these tools typically retain input data for training purposes, potentially exposing pre-publication research. ICMJE, COPE, WAME, and the STM association all characterise this as a violation of the privileged relationship between authors and journals. Peer reviewers who wish to use AI assistance are generally required to seek explicit permission from the handling editor before doing so, and must disclose both the tool used and the purpose. The reliability concern is equally important: AI-generated review comments can contain hallucinated citations, inaccurate claims, and assessments that are systematically biased in ways that human reviewers, relying on professional expertise, are better positioned to avoid. Empirical evidence confirms the scale of the problem: analysis of the ICLR 2024 conference found that 15.8 percent of peer reviews were LLM-assisted, and Stanford research suggests that up to 17 percent of computer science peer-review sentences are generated by LLMs.

The integrity crisis and publisher responses. The normative framework has been built under pressure from an unprecedented integrity crisis. The Wiley-Hindawi case is the most documented single episode: over 11,300 papers were retracted from that portfolio between 2022 and 2024, at an estimated cost to the publisher of \$35–40 million, driven by paper mills that use large language models to mass-produce plausible manuscripts with fabricated data and hallucinated citations. Globally, over 10,000 fraudulent articles were estimated to have been withdrawn in 2023 alone. Publisher responses have become increasingly multilayered: forensic screening for 'tortured phrases' (machine-paraphrased synonyms such as 'nucleic corrosive' for 'nucleic acid'), network analysis through initiatives such as the STM Integrity Hub, which screens over 125,000 manuscripts monthly, and convergence on policies prohibiting AI authorship and requiring disclosure. A 2024 review of top medical journals found that 78 percent now provide specific guidance on AI, with 59 percent prohibiting its use and 39 percent allowing it under specific conditions.

The enforcement gap and the direction of travel. The central unresolved problem is enforcement. While most major publishers now mandate disclosure of AI use, there is no reliable mechanism to verify compliance: survey data from 2025 suggests that 57 percent of scientists used AI for writing assistance, yet formal disclosure rates in submitted manuscripts are substantially lower. COPE's guidance is explicit that AI detection software should not be used as a primary basis for rejection decisions, because its inconsistency produces both false positives and false negatives at rates that make threshold-based rejection arbitrary and potentially unjust — and false positives disproportionately affect early-career and non-native-English-speaking researchers. Editors are instead advised to focus on scholarly merit, adherence to journal policy, and the author's willingness to assume full accountability, with an educational response preferred over immediate rejection where authors demonstrate genuine accountability. More systemic reform proposals — reducing reliance on high-volume journal publication in promotion criteria, expanding preprint culture with post-publication review — have been advanced but not yet widely institutionalised. The trajectory is clear: the era in which peer review and publishing could assume that submissions were human-authored is over, and the system is adapting through disclosure norms, human-accountability rules, and upstream detection — while acknowledging that none of these mechanisms is yet reliable enough to fully police the boundary between human and machine authorship.

### Q205 What research-integrity failures attributable to AI have been documented, and at what rate? {#q205}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Bibliometric and systematic-review evidence confirms a marked increase in retractions attributable to AI-related misconduct between 2022 and 2025, with 2023 emerging as the peak year in the period studied. One 2026 systematic review identified 335 retracted AI-related publications, with 2023 accounting for approximately 46.3 percent of the total retraction volume. A separate analysis of 764 retracted papers in PubMed found a similar surge, with 667 retractions recorded in 2023 alone. The trend continued into 2024 and 2025, reflecting an ongoing struggle by institutional safeguards to keep pace with AI-assisted paper mills operating at industrial scale.

The dominant driver: compromised peer review. The most commonly cited driver of AI-related retractions is compromised peer review integrity, not manuscript-level misconduct alone. Research indicates that peer review pipelines are being systematically targeted: analysis of the ICLR 2024 conference found that 15.8 percent of peer reviews were LLM-assisted, and that nearly half of all submissions received at least one AI-assisted review. Stanford research suggests that up to 17 percent of computer science peer-review sentences are generated by LLMs. AI-assisted reviews have been shown to systematically inflate scores, which creates selection pressure that distorts the scientific literature independently of whether the papers themselves are fraudulently generated. Approximately 82.2 percent of retracted AI-related articles were published in special issues, which were found to have significantly faster submission-to-acceptance timelines than regular issues — a structural vulnerability that paper mills exploit.

Manuscript-level misconduct. At the manuscript level, approximately one-third of AI-related retractions are directly linked to the use of large language models to generate manuscripts without disclosure. Common signatures include 'tortured phrases' — machine-paraphrased synonyms that replace standard terminology with nonsensical alternatives (the documented example 'nucleic corrosive' for 'nucleic acid') — hallucinated citations, and fabricated data. The 'Problematic Paper Screener' has flagged over 15,000 papers using tortured-phrase heuristics. The Wiley-Hindawi portfolio retraction of over 11,300 papers between 2022 and 2024, at a cost to the publisher of an estimated \$35–40 million, represents the most documented single instance of paper-mill-driven industrial-scale fraud. Paper mills sell authorship slots on fabricated manuscripts at prices documented as low as \$500, creating a market where the financial return on fraudulent publication — through academic promotion, grant eligibility, and institutional rankings — far exceeds the cost of production.

Geographic and disciplinary concentration. Geographic and disciplinary concentration is well-documented. Up to 72.2 percent of retracted AI-related articles in one systematic review originated from China. Engineering accounts for approximately 30.4 percent of AI-related retractions, followed by education and medical therapeutics. Whether geographic concentration reflects differential enforcement, differential publishing pressure, or actual differential rates of misconduct cannot be determined from retraction data alone, and caution is warranted in attribution.

The persistence of retracted work. Retracted articles continue to influence the scholarly record after formal withdrawal. More than 50 percent of retracted AI-related articles maintained a field citation ratio greater than one, indicating continued citation after retraction. The median time from publication to retraction is approximately 510 to 550 days, creating a substantial window during which compromised findings may be cited and built upon. Journal editors remain the primary initiators of retractions (98.5 percent of cases), and LLMs themselves are not effective at flagging retracted or unreliable sources, creating a compounding problem when AI tools are used to conduct literature reviews.

The enforcement gap. The 'enforcement gap' is a central concern: while most major publishers now mandate disclosure of AI use, there is no reliable mechanism to verify compliance. Survey data from 2025 suggests that 57 percent of scientists used AI for writing assistance, yet formal disclosure rates in submitted manuscripts are substantially lower, indicating widespread undisclosed use. False-positive rates from detection tools disproportionately affect early-career and non-native-English-speaking researchers, creating equity and reliability problems with enforcement approaches. The documented rate of AI-attributable failure is therefore best understood as a floor rather than a ceiling: the 335 retracted articles identified in the systematic review are those that were caught, and the gap between measured use and disclosed use suggests that the true prevalence of undisclosed AI involvement in the scholarly record is substantially higher than retraction data alone can reveal.

Rates in context. To interpret these rates, comparison with the pre-AI baseline is instructive. Retractions were already rising before generative AI became widely available in late 2022, driven by image manipulation, data fabrication, and paper mills using older methods, but the scale and speed of the post-2022 increase are without precedent: the Wiley-Hindawi episode alone exceeded the total annual retraction volume of any prior year in the modern era. The rate question also has a qualitative dimension. AI does not merely increase the volume of misconduct; it changes its character. Traditional fabrication required deliberate human effort and left detectable traces; AI-generated manuscripts can be produced at scale with minimal human involvement, and the 'tortured phrase' signatures that detection tools rely on are already being refined away as models improve. The documented rate of AI-attributable failure is thus a moving target: the 46.3 percent concentration in 2023 reflects both the peak of the paper-mill wave and the beginning of detection improvements, and the persistence of elevated retraction volumes into 2024 and 2025 suggests that the enforcement gap is structural rather than transitional. For institutions and researchers, the practical implication is that AI-related integrity failure is now a normal risk of the publication system — to be managed through disclosure norms, upstream screening, and post-publication vigilance — rather than an exceptional event that detection tools can be expected to eliminate.

### Q206 How are admissions systems responding to AI-written applications and personal statements? {#q206}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The use of generative AI by applicants to draft or refine personal statements and supplemental essays has forced higher education institutions to develop admissions-specific policies, though the landscape remains heterogeneous and rapidly evolving. Survey research documents four policy categories: outright prohibition, line-level editing only, brainstorming-only permission, and no explicit policy at all. The last category covered approximately 68 percent of surveyed institutions, though the absence of an explicit AI policy does not preclude enforcement of existing academic honesty standards — and in practice, most institutions treat AI-generated application content as a violation of the integrity statement that applicants sign.

Institutional stances. Among institutions with explicit stances, Brown University and the University of Melbourne prohibit AI-assisted drafting outright, and Yale has stated that an AI-generated essay violates its admissions policy. Institutions such as Cornell University permit AI for brainstorming but not drafting; Caltech requires disclosure of AI tool use; Cambridge and Michigan's Rackham Graduate School offer guidance discouraging AI drafting while warning against inauthentic submissions. The consequences for violation are severe in prohibitive institutions: rescinding of offers, suspension, or expulsion have all been cited as potential penalties. The Common App, which processes applications for over a thousand member institutions, has formalised the issue by defining fraud to include submitting 'the substantive content or output of an artificial intelligence platform, technology, or algorithm' as one's own original work.

The authenticity problem. The primary concern driving these policies is the loss of authentic voice. Admissions committees are looking for evidence of individual motivation, character, and readiness for advanced study. AI-generated prose tends toward formulaic structures, generic phrasing, and what admissions officers describe as 'hollow' writing that lacks the specific detail and idiosyncrasy of lived experience. Human reviewers are trained to identify stylistic inconsistencies between application materials and other evidence such as interview performance. However, the reliability of this human review is itself contested: one study found that human reviewers correctly identified AI authorship only approximately 56 percent of the time, and some reviewers assigned higher quality scores to AI-generated essays, suggesting that quality and authenticity are being partially conflated.

Detection technology. Detection technology presents similar difficulties. Turnitin and other platforms have added AI-detection modules, but these generate false positives and false negatives at rates that make them unsuitable as sole arbiters of authenticity — a problem compounded in admissions by the fact that applicants, unlike enrolled students, are not available for follow-up interviews or process-based verification. Some institutions are exploring baseline in-person writing samples or proctored essays to provide a comparison text against which submitted materials can be evaluated stylistically. UCAS in the United Kingdom uses centralised anti-plagiarism software to flag similarities across submissions.

The equity debate. A normative debate concerns equity and access. Advocates for permissive approaches argue that AI tools democratise a process previously skewed toward applicants with access to expensive private college counsellors: AI provides brainstorming and editing support to first-generation applicants who lack that coaching advantage. Critics respond that applicants without AI literacy training are more likely to misuse tools in ways that constitute unintentional plagiarism, and that the gap in AI capability between premium and free-tier tools replicates rather than reduces advantage. The equity question is unresolved, and the empirical evidence is thin on both sides.

AI evaluating applicants. A separate and emerging strand involves institutions using AI to evaluate applicants rather than merely to police their submissions. Approximately half of U.S. admissions offices have used AI at some stage of the process, primarily for administrative tasks such as transcript processing and keyword screening, but increasingly for summarising essays and recommendation letters. Fine-tuned language models trained on admissions data have been used experimentally to assess personal qualities — leadership, prosocial motivation, resilience — by analysing essay text. These systems aim to make holistic review more systematic and less resource-intensive. However, they face substantial criticism regarding 'black box' algorithmic opacity, the risk of perpetuating historical bias encoded in training data, and the absence of robust external auditing. The National Association for College Admission Counseling has established working groups to monitor the ethical use of AI in admissions, and jurisdictions such as New York City have begun requiring bias audits for AI hiring tools — a regulatory trajectory that may extend to admissions. This represents a different and potentially more consequential use of AI in admissions than applicant-side drafting assistance, but the evidence base remains thin, and the interaction between AI-written applications and AI-read applications — machines evaluating machines — is only beginning to be studied.

The international dimension and the trajectory. The response is not confined to the United States. In the United Kingdom, UCAS has issued guidance on academic honesty and AI in applications and uses centralised anti-plagiarism software to flag similarities across submissions, while individual universities have adopted a range of stances from prohibition to disclosure-based permission. Australian institutions, including the University of Melbourne, have been among the most explicit in prohibiting AI drafting, and European universities are navigating the same policy space under the additional constraint of the EU AI Act's transparency requirements. The trajectory is toward convergence on a disclosure-based norm: rather than attempting to detect AI use, a growing number of institutions are requiring applicants to declare any AI assistance and to certify that the substantive content and personal narrative are their own. This approach acknowledges the detection problem while preserving the integrity function of the personal statement — the applicant's account of their own motivation and experience. The unresolved questions are whether disclosure requirements are honoured in practice, whether the equity benefits claimed for permissive approaches materialise, and whether the shift toward AI-assisted evaluation of applications will make the process more systematic or simply more opaque. What is already clear is that the personal statement, like the undergraduate essay, has lost its status as an unproblematic sample of unaided applicant writing, and that admissions systems are adapting through a combination of policy, disclosure, and — increasingly — the use of AI on both sides of the application.

### Q207 What are the economic consequences of AI for universities' teaching-revenue models? {#q207}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

The economic consequences of AI for universities' teaching-revenue models are best understood against the pre-existing structure of higher education finance, which is already characterised by a persistent misalignment between what students pay and what institutions spend on instruction. Total expenditures for U.S. higher education reached \$712 billion in 2021–22, yet the share of spending directed to instruction has remained relatively flat or declined as a proportion of total budgets, even as tuition prices have risen substantially. The student share of total education revenue rose from 20.9 percent in 1980 to 38.4 percent by 2025, reflecting the long-term withdrawal of state appropriations rather than proportional increases in instructional quality or delivery costs. AI enters this landscape as a technology that could, in principle, lower the marginal cost of instruction — and as a technology that threatens the value proposition on which tuition revenue depends.

Two competing theories of cost. The economics literature offers two competing explanations for why higher education costs rise, and they frame the AI question differently. Howard Bowen's 'revenue theory of costs' (1980) holds that institutions raise as much revenue as possible and spend all they raise, so unit costs are primarily a function of revenue rather than efficient delivery. On this view, AI-driven savings would be absorbed into expanded administrative and facilities expenditure rather than returned to students through lower tuition — a pattern consistent with the observed growth of administrative positions far faster than instructional ones. The competing framework, Baumol's 'cost disease', holds that higher education is a labour-intensive service industry that cannot easily substitute capital for labour without quality loss, so it must raise wages to remain competitive with more productive sectors. Cross-sectional analysis by Archibald and Feldman finds stronger empirical support for cost disease. The policy implications diverge sharply: if the revenue theory is correct, restricting revenue streams would control costs; if cost disease dominates, capping revenue without enabling productivity-enhancing delivery changes would degrade quality without reducing costs. AI is precisely the kind of capital-for-labour substitution that the cost-disease model assumes is impossible without quality loss — which is why its arrival is economically significant.

The adjunct labour model as the current mechanism. The adjunct labour model represents the primary institutional mechanism for managing instructional costs against rising non-instructional expenditure. By replacing tenure-track positions with contingent, per-course contracts, institutions dramatically reduce instructional salary expenditure. The national median pay per credit hour for adjunct faculty is \$1,166, or approximately \$3,498 for a standard three-credit course; annualised for a full-year teaching load, this produces an estimated income of approximately \$41,976 — below the median income for full-time U.S. workers. In documented cases, a single course generating tens of thousands of dollars in tuition revenue may be staffed by an adjunct earning \$3,500–\$4,100 for that course. AI enters this picture as a technology that could automate precisely the instructional labour that adjuncts perform — grading, discussion facilitation, routine feedback — raising the question of whether institutions will use AI to reduce costs further, to reallocate savings toward higher-value instruction, or to absorb savings into non-instructional expenditure.

The threat to the revenue model itself. Beyond cost structure, AI threatens the revenue model from the demand side. The traditional business model relies on the standardised, high-cost delivery of information, and generative AI now provides personalised tutoring and content generation at a fraction of the cost. As AI automates routine intellectual tasks, the value of a degree solely as a labour-market signalling mechanism is being questioned, and students and employers increasingly demand evidence of tangible skills rather than credentials alone. Some analysts describe this as a 'seismic shift' comparable to the arrival of the internet, with institutions responding along a spectrum from incremental adoption (integrating AI tools into existing workflows) to disruptive innovation (AI-tutor-centric models enabling compressed degree programmes). The economic logic of disruption is straightforward: if a student can obtain comparable learning outcomes through AI-mediated instruction at lower cost, the tuition premium for traditional delivery becomes harder to defend — particularly in large, standardised programmes where AI's cost savings are greatest, as opposed to high-contact or specialised programmes where human instruction retains its value.

The empirical bottom line. The measured economic consequences so far are modest but directional. AI is shifting cost structures in teaching delivery and student services, and institutions that leverage it can reduce the cost-to-serve per student — but achieving these gains requires granular, programme-level cost models and intentional instructional design rather than ad-hoc adoption. The savings are uneven: significant in large, standardised programmes, limited in high-contact ones. The Federal Reserve has documented that educational exposure to generative AI is concentrated in ways that may reshape both labour demand and the value of specific credentials. What is not yet established is whether AI will produce the cost-disease-breaking productivity gains that economic theory predicts, or whether the revenue theory will prove more accurate and the savings will be absorbed into the institution rather than returned to students. The answer will depend on competitive pressure, regulatory intervention, and the willingness of institutions to treat AI as an opportunity to restructure delivery rather than simply to defend existing revenue streams.

### Q208 How is AI changing the value and delivery of graduate professional programmes? {#q208}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

Generative AI has demonstrated a capacity to pass the high-stakes professional examinations that graduate programmes in medicine, law, and business use as gatekeeping mechanisms — and this documented capability has destabilised the validity of conventional assessment formats and, with them, the value proposition of the programmes themselves. In law, large language models can apply IRAC (Issue, Rule, Analysis, Conclusion) methodology at a level sufficient to pass bar-style problem questions, and GPT-4 and subsequent models have achieved passing scores on the Uniform Bar Examination. In medicine, AI systems have outperformed student cohorts on standardised exams and clinical reasoning assessments. In business, AI tools perform routine market analysis, case structuring, and report drafting at a quality that renders traditional take-home assignments vulnerable to full substitution.

The failure of the initial response. The initial institutional response — deploying detection tools and issuing prohibitive policies — has broadly been characterised as ineffective. Detection software is unreliable in professional programme contexts, where prose sophistication is expected and AI can be deployed with sufficient human editing to pass existing detectors. Research across law, medicine, and business schools now identifies a shift toward what is variously termed 'authentic', 'AI-inclusive', or 'AI-proof' assessment. The common thread is a preference for assessment forms that either require human-specific capabilities or explicitly integrate AI as an object of evaluation. Authentic assessments in legal education include live advocacy, client simulations, and negotiation exercises that reward empathy, judgment, and real-time adaptability. Medical education is shifting toward clinical simulation, communication skills assessment, and tasks requiring the interpretation of AI-generated diagnostic outputs rather than mere information recall. Business schools are emphasising process documentation, team-based projects with individual accountability mechanisms, and reflective journals alongside case competitions.

AI literacy as a professional competency. A significant curricular response is the formal integration of 'AI literacy' or 'digital professionalism' as a graduate-level competency. This framing positions the ability to use AI tools ethically, critically, and effectively — including identifying hallucinations, understanding algorithmic bias, and maintaining human oversight of AI outputs — as a substantive professional skill rather than a threat to academic integrity. Legal programmes, such as those at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School and Georgetown Law, are developing curricula around regulatory compliance with frameworks such as the EU AI Act, professional duty-of-competence obligations in an AI-integrated practice environment, and the ethics of AI-assisted legal advice. In medicine, the emphasis is on 'human-in-the-loop' workflows: final medical decisions and academic evaluations remain the responsibility of human professionals, and students must learn to validate AI-generated content rigorously. In business education, the shift is from AI literacy to AI fluency: Harvard Business School has mandated a 'Data Science & AI for Leaders' course for all first-year students, Stanford GSB integrates AI across roughly three dozen courses, and Wharton has launched a full MBA major in Artificial Intelligence for Business. The pedagogical logic is that students now arrive with a higher baseline of knowledge, which sharpens classroom discussion and allows case-method teaching to focus on judgment, ethics, and strategy rather than information transmission.

The value question. The value of professional degrees is being renegotiated in two directions simultaneously. On one side, the credential's signalling value is threatened: if AI can perform the analytical tasks that professional programmes certify, employers may discount the degree's ability to predict job performance. On the other side, the degree's value is being redefined around precisely the capabilities AI cannot supply — professional judgment, ethical discernment, client-facing communication, and the ability to manage AI systems themselves. Surveys indicate that while students are often self-taught in AI tools, there is a significant gap between the skills students acquire in professional programmes and the proficiency expected by employers, suggesting that programmes that close this gap can increase their value. The delivery model is also changing: AI enables compressed degree formats, personalised pacing, and simulation-based practice at scale, which some institutions are using to offer accelerated or competency-based pathways.

Equity and regulatory tension. Equity concerns persist. Students with access to premium AI model subscriptions may have a systematic advantage over those using free-tier versions, replicating and potentially amplifying pre-existing digital divides — particularly acute in professional programmes where international students and those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds are already navigating additional barriers. Policy responses to this equity dimension remain underdeveloped. A further tension exists between the slower pace of professional regulatory reform and the faster pace of curriculum change: some professional regulatory bodies still mandate traditional supervised, in-person examination as the primary competency verification mechanism, even as the underlying competencies they certify are being redefined. The prevailing academic consensus is that AI is a 'catalyst for enhancement' rather than simply a threat, but causal evidence that redesigned assessments actually produce better-prepared graduates — rather than graduates who have simply been assessed differently — does not yet exist. The direction of travel is clear: professional programmes are moving from certifying the ability to perform analytical tasks to certifying the ability to exercise judgment over tasks that machines can perform, and the value of the credential will increasingly depend on how convincingly that new certification is delivered.
