### Q209 What is AI doing to the academic labour market, including adjunct and teaching-assistant work? {#q209}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

AI is entering an academic labour market that has already undergone a structural transformation since the 1970s, shifting from a system primarily composed of tenured and tenure-track faculty to one in which contingent appointments constitute the majority of instructional labour. AAUP data indicate that in fall 1987, approximately 53 percent of faculty held tenured or tenure-track positions; by fall 2023, that proportion had fallen to approximately 32 percent, with contingent appointments representing approximately 68 percent of all faculty roles. At two-year institutions, contingent appointments can reach 83 percent of total faculty. The question posed by AI is whether it will accelerate this trajectory, reverse it, or simply redistribute the remaining human labour.

The adjunct workforce AI encounters. CUPA-HR's 2024–25 survey, covering 43,279 reported adjuncts across 263 institutions, provides the most granular available compensation data. The median adjunct pay is \$1,166 per credit hour and \$3,498 per three-credit course; annualised estimates for full-time course loads produce approximately \$41,976 per year. Job security is structurally precarious: at 70 percent of institutions, courses are cancelled when enrolment falls below threshold, leaving the adjunct unpaid for scheduled work, and 67 percent of institutions do not expect or compensate adjuncts for activities beyond direct instruction. The graduate teaching assistant (GTA) segment is a distinct and substantial category: the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported approximately 145,960 individuals in the 'Teaching Assistants, Postsecondary' category as of May 2023, with median annual wages of approximately \$43,750, though stipends frequently range from \$20,000 to \$35,000 for nine-month contracts supplemented by tuition waivers. The number of graduate student employees with teaching and research responsibilities grew by over 40 percent between 2002 and 2023.

The displacement risk. The displacement risk from AI is concentrated precisely where contingent labour is concentrated: high-enrolment survey courses, discussion sections, routine grading, and introductory instruction. These are the instructional tasks that AI can most plausibly automate or augment — automated grading, AI-mediated discussion facilitation, and AI-generated feedback are already deployed in these settings. Research on the impact of AI on academic work identifies adjunct faculty in high-enrolment courses as at the highest risk of displacement, with institutions increasingly relying on automated systems to manage instructional tasks with minimal faculty oversight. The Federal Reserve has documented that educational exposure to generative AI is unevenly distributed across fields and institutions, and the AAUP has warned that AI initiatives are frequently spearheaded by university administrations with little input from faculty, staff, or students — raising governance questions about who decides which academic work is automated.

Work intensification versus substitution. The evidence suggests that AI's effect on academic labour is not simply substitution but also work intensification. Rather than uniformly reducing the burden on educators, AI integration often adds to existing workloads by requiring faculty to manage new, data-intensive systems — learning management systems with predictive analytics, AI-detection tools, and the administrative apparatus of AI governance — often without the faculty's explicit awareness or consent. The 'hidden labour' problem documented in the teacher-workload literature applies equally in higher education: time saved on generation is partially offset by time spent reviewing, correcting, and reworking AI output. At the same time, AI-assisted productivity gains for individual contingent instructors raise an open empirical question: whether they will translate into improved compensation or simply increased institutional extraction of labour value. The historical pattern of adjunctification — in which productivity gains in instructional delivery were captured by institutions rather than instructors — suggests the latter is the more likely default.

Governance and collective response. The academic labour response has been to organise around transparency and shared governance. The AAUP has emphasised that faculty must maintain primary responsibility for instructional and curricular policies involving AI, and academic workers are increasingly demanding disclosure of AI usage, 'AI-free' course designations, protection of faculty and student data from third-party AI training, and the incorporation of AI guardrails into faculty handbooks and collective bargaining agreements. Where faculty unions exist, they demonstrably improve conditions — documented salary improvements of 25–40 percent in unionised settings — and collective bargaining by GTAs at major research universities has produced secured stipend increases. The interaction between AI and this organised response is only beginning: the first collective bargaining agreements to address AI use in teaching are being negotiated, and their terms will shape whether AI-driven efficiency gains are shared with the academic workforce or captured entirely by institutions. The direction of travel is that AI is accelerating the long-term recomposition of academic labour — fewer human hours on routine instructional tasks, more on oversight, mentorship, and the relational work that machines cannot perform — but whether this recomposition improves the conditions of adjuncts and GTAs or further degrades them depends on governance decisions that are currently being made with limited faculty participation.

The 'freeway flyer' and the union counterweight. The precariousness of the contingent workforce is embodied in the 'freeway flyer' phenomenon — adjuncts driving between multiple campuses to cobble together survivable income — which reflects an institutional strategy of capping course loads to avoid triggering benefits obligations. Where faculty unions exist, they demonstrably improve conditions: documented salary improvements of 25–40 percent in unionised settings, along with improved job security, are observed in systems such as CUNY, and collective bargaining efforts by GTAs at major research universities, affiliated with unions including the United Auto Workers and the American Federation of Teachers, have produced secured stipend increases and improved working conditions. The interaction between AI and this organised response is only beginning: the first collective bargaining agreements to address AI use in teaching are being negotiated, and their terms will shape whether AI-driven efficiency gains are shared with the academic workforce or captured entirely by institutions. The supply-side driver — an oversupply of individuals with advanced degrees who accept contingent employment in the absence of tenure-track alternatives — has historically depressed wages and limited collective leverage, and AI's capacity to automate routine instructional tasks may either intensify that oversupply by reducing demand for instructional labour or redirect it toward the higher-level oversight roles that AI creates. The empirical literature has not yet resolved which path dominates, but the structural position of adjuncts and GTAs — excluded from institutional governance, compensated per course, and first in line for automation — makes them the most exposed segment of the academic labour market to AI-driven change.

### Q252 What is AI doing to the academic conference system, preprint culture, and peer review — and are hallucinated citations appearing in published literature? {#q252}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

The academic publishing system rests on a chain of trust: authors report work honestly, reviewers evaluate it carefully, and citations connect claims to verifiable evidence. Generative AI is placing pressure on each link of that chain. The evidence now available suggests that AI is reshaping peer review, accelerating submission volumes, altering the language of published research, and, in a measurable number of cases, introducing fabricated citations into the published record.

Peer review was among the first areas where AI use was measured at scale. Liang and colleagues, in a study presented at ICML 2024, developed a method for estimating the proportion of text substantially modified by large language models across a corpus. Applying it to peer reviews at ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023, and EMNLP 2023, they estimated that between 6.5 and 16.9 percent of review text could have been substantially modified by LLMs. They found that such reviews were more likely to be submitted close to deadlines and were associated with lower reviewer confidence and fewer scholarly citations, suggesting that AI use may correlate with rushed or less engaged reviewing.

AI-assisted writing has also spread through published papers. Kobak and colleagues, in a 2025 Science Advances study, analysed vocabulary changes in more than fifteen million biomedical abstracts indexed in PubMed and identified a sharp rise in words characteristic of LLM output after 2022. They estimated that at least 13.5 percent of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs, with rates as high as 40 percent in some subgroups defined by country, field, or journal. Using AI to polish language is not inherently problematic, but the scale of change indicates how rapidly authoring practices have shifted.

Conference systems are straining under growing volumes. Reporting on NeurIPS indicated that the conference received 21,575 submissions in 2025, an increase of more than 200 percent since 2020. While not all of this growth can be attributed to AI, the ability to draft papers more quickly adds to the load on volunteer reviewers, whose numbers have not kept pace. Preprint servers face similar pressure, and several have introduced policies to limit low-quality or automatically generated submissions.

Hallucinated citations have now been documented in published literature. Walters and Wilder's 2023 Scientific Reports study established that ChatGPT frequently fabricated references, with 55 percent of citations from GPT-3.5 and 18 percent from GPT-4 in their sample being non-existent. In January 2026, an audit by the AI-detection company GPTZero, reported by TechCrunch and other outlets, identified at least 100 hallucinated citations across 51 papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025 after scanning 4,841 of the 5,290 accepted papers, with each flagged citation verified manually. The fabrications included non-existent authors, invented titles, and real papers with added fictitious co-authors. The NeurIPS board responded that incorrect references did not necessarily invalidate the research itself. Because the audit was conducted by a company that sells detection tools, its findings warrant independent replication, but the manual verification of each case lends them credibility.

Institutions have responded with policies. The U.S. National Institutes of Health, in notice NOT-OD-23-149 issued in 2023, prohibited reviewers from using generative AI tools to analyse or formulate peer-review critiques, citing confidentiality obligations. The European Commission's Living Guidelines on generative AI in research, updated in May 2026, advise researchers against using generative AI substantially in sensitive activities such as peer review and evaluation and maintain that AI cannot be an author. Many conferences and journals now require disclosure of AI use in writing and prohibit uploading manuscripts under review to external AI tools.

These developments raise deeper questions about the future of scholarly communication. If AI drafts papers and AI assists reviews, the human judgement that peer review is meant to provide may be diluted. If fabricated references enter the record, they may be cited by later work, creating chains of error. Some researchers propose technical remedies, such as automated reference verification at submission, while others argue for structural changes, including smaller conferences, reviewer compensation, and greater emphasis on replication.

It helps to remember that peer review, in the form most researchers now take for granted, is a relatively recent institution. The historian Melinda Baldwin, writing in Isis in 2018, traced how the term and the practice became central to scientific legitimacy in the United States only in the second half of the twentieth century, in part as a response to congressional scrutiny of federally funded research during the 1970s. Many prominent journals had long relied on editors' judgement rather than systematic external review; Nature, for example, did not require external refereeing for all papers until 1973. Baldwin's account shows that peer review was adopted not because it had been proven to detect error reliably but because it offered a way for the scientific community to demonstrate accountability while retaining autonomy over its own standards. This history is relevant because it suggests that the system now under pressure from AI is itself a historically contingent arrangement, adapted repeatedly in response to changes in the scale of science, funding structures and public expectations. It also tempers nostalgia. Peer review was never a guarantee of quality, and research before generative AI documented inconsistency between reviewers, bias against unconventional work and difficulty in detecting fraud. AI adds new pressures to a system that was already stretched rather than corrupting one that was functioning flawlessly.

Automated generation of fake papers also predates large language models. In 2005 graduate students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology released SCIgen, a program that generated nonsensical computer science papers complete with graphs and citations, originally to expose conferences with weak review. Cyril Labbé, a computer scientist at Joseph Fourier University in Grenoble, later developed methods to detect SCIgen output and found that such papers had been published in conference proceedings from established publishers. Richard Van Noorden reported in Nature in 2014 that Springer and the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers were removing more than 120 such papers from their subscription services after Labbé's analysis. A subsequent line of detection work by Guillaume Cabanac, Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov, released in 2021, identified what they called tortured phrases, such as counterfeit consciousness in place of artificial intelligence, produced when paraphrasing software was used to disguise plagiarised text. They found clusters of such phrases in papers published in established journals, including in one journal where problematic articles were concentrated in a short time window. These episodes indicate that the publishing system's vulnerability to machine-generated text was visible years before ChatGPT, and that detection has relied on painstaking work by a small number of volunteers and specialists. Generative AI makes fabricated text more fluent and harder to spot by surface features, which raises the stakes for such detection work.

AI's role in peer review is not exclusively a threat. Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford, reporting in NEJM AI in 2024, built a pipeline that used GPT-4 to generate structured feedback on scientific manuscripts and compared that feedback with human reviews for thousands of papers from Nature family journals and from the International Conference on Learning Representations. They found that the overlap between points raised by GPT-4 and by human reviewers was comparable to the overlap between two human reviewers, and in a prospective user study with researchers, more than half found the AI feedback helpful, with many saying it was more useful than at least some human reviews they had received. The authors stressed that AI feedback tended to be more generic, rarely engaged deeply with methodological novelty, and should complement rather than replace expert review. The study suggests a plausible role for AI in helping authors, particularly early-career researchers and those without access to well-connected mentors, improve manuscripts before submission. It also suggests that reviewers tempted to outsource their reports would produce reviews that look adequate but lack the specific expert judgement that justifies the system's existence, a concern consistent with Liang's ICML findings that AI-modified review text was more common in reviews submitted close to deadlines.

Preprint servers have been forced to adapt their policies. In October 2025 arXiv announced that its computer science category would no longer accept review articles and position papers unless they had already been accepted through peer review at a journal or conference, explaining that moderators had been overwhelmed by a surge of submissions, many of which it described as little more than annotated bibliographies, and that generative AI had made such papers easy to produce. The decision was notable because arXiv's model has long relied on light-touch moderation rather than review, on the premise that rapid open dissemination benefits science more than gatekeeping. The policy change illustrates how increased volume, partly attributable to AI, can push open infrastructures toward more restrictive rules, with potential costs for researchers who use preprints to share legitimate syntheses quickly. It also indicates that the burden of AI-generated content falls disproportionately on volunteer moderators and non-profit infrastructures that lack the resources of commercial publishers.

Manipulation of AI-assisted review has also appeared. Nikkei Asia reported in July 2025 that it had found research papers posted on arXiv, from authors at institutions in several countries, that contained hidden instructions, written in white text or very small fonts, directing AI tools to give only positive reviews or to praise the paper's rigour and novelty. Some authors defended the practice as a countermeasure against reviewers who improperly relied on AI, while institutions involved announced reviews or withdrew papers. The episode illustrates a vulnerability known in computer security as prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in content alter the behaviour of a language model processing it. If reviewers paste manuscripts into AI tools, hidden instructions can bias the resulting reviews without the reviewer noticing. The incident led some conferences to clarify that hidden prompts constitute misconduct, and it strengthened the argument for prohibiting the upload of confidential manuscripts to general-purpose AI tools, a rule the National Institutes of Health had already adopted for grant review in 2023.

The citation problem is in part an infrastructure problem with available remedies. Scholarly metadata systems such as Crossref, which registers digital object identifiers for most journal articles, already allow automated checking of whether a cited work exists and whether its title, authors and year match the reference. Some publishers and conference organisers have begun running reference lists through such checks at submission, and tools that flag non-existent or mismatched references are becoming available to editors and reviewers. Crossref's acquisition of the Retraction Watch database in 2023 and its decision to make the data openly available also allow automated flagging of citations to retracted work. These checks cannot verify that a real paper actually supports the claim attributed to it, which is a subtler form of citation error that AI tools also produce, but they can catch outright fabrication at low cost. Making such verification routine at the point of submission, rather than relying on readers to discover problems after publication, is one of the more tractable responses available to the publishing system.

The pressures on peer review also have an equity dimension. Researchers who write in English as an additional language have long faced reviewer criticism of their prose and the cost of professional editing. AI writing assistance can reduce these barriers, and some researchers in non-Anglophone countries describe it as levelling a playing field long tilted toward native speakers. At the same time, AI-text detectors have been shown to flag non-native English writing disproportionately, so policies that rely on detection risk penalising the same researchers who benefit most from legitimate language assistance. Publishing policies that focus on disclosure and on accountability for content, rather than on detecting stylistic markers of AI use, are more consistent with fairness to the global research community.

Underlying many of these problems is an incentive structure that rewards volume. Researchers are evaluated heavily on publication counts and citations, conferences compete on submission numbers, and reviewing remains largely unpaid and unrecognised. Generative AI lowers the cost of producing papers and reviews without changing these incentives, so it is unsurprising that submissions rise faster than the pool of qualified reviewers. Responses that address only the technology, such as detection or disclosure rules, leave the incentives intact. Some communities are experimenting with structural changes, including limits on the number of submissions per author, requirements that submitting authors also review, formal recognition or payment for reviewing, and evaluation practices that emphasise the quality of a small number of contributions rather than the quantity of outputs. Whether these measures can keep pace with AI-driven growth is not yet known, but they acknowledge that the strain on scholarly communication is as much institutional as technical.

The evidence base has limitations. Detection methods estimate rather than identify AI use, and their accuracy varies by domain and language. Counts of hallucinated citations depend on the scope of audits. Nonetheless, multiple independent lines of evidence converge on the conclusion that AI is materially changing how research is written, reviewed, and cited, and that verification practices have not yet caught up.

### Q253 How are universities restructuring research data management and open-science policies in response to AI tools that can process, summarise, and generate research outputs? {#q253}

12 citations · 12 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Research data management and open science developed over the past two decades around a set of assumptions: that data and publications would be read and reused primarily by humans, that sharing would accelerate discovery, and that confidentiality could be protected through access controls and ethics review. AI tools that can ingest, summarise, analyse, and generate research outputs at scale unsettle several of these assumptions. Universities and the funders that shape their policies are responding, though unevenly and often provisionally.

The most visible change concerns disclosure and responsibility. The European Commission's Living Guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research, first issued in 2024 and updated in a third edition in May 2026, set out principles for researchers, research organisations, and funders. They hold that researchers remain responsible for scientific output, that AI cannot be listed as an author, and that substantial use of generative AI should be disclosed. They also advise research organisations to provide training, monitor the use of AI tools, and integrate the guidelines into their own research-integrity frameworks. Many European universities have since revised integrity codes to reference these principles.

Funders have set rules for confidential processes. The U.S. National Institutes of Health, in notice NOT-OD-23-149, prohibited reviewers from using generative AI to analyse or critique grant applications, reasoning that uploading applications to AI tools would breach confidentiality. UK Research and Innovation adopted a policy in September 2024 requiring applicants to disclose substantive generative AI use and prohibiting assessors from using AI in assessment except for limited language refinement, with the possibility of sanctions for misuse. These funder policies have pushed universities to issue matching guidance to staff who serve as reviewers and applicants.

Data protection is a second area of restructuring. Research data frequently include personal, sensitive, or commercially confidential information subject to ethics approvals and data-sharing agreements. Uploading such data to an external AI service may violate consent terms, data-protection law, or contractual obligations, particularly if the provider retains inputs or uses them for training. Universities have responded by publishing lists of approved tools, negotiating enterprise licences with contractual protections against training on inputs, offering institutionally hosted models for sensitive data, and adding AI-specific questions to ethics applications and data management plans. The NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy, effective since January 2023, requires researchers to plan for data sharing and protection, and institutions increasingly ask how AI tools will be used in processing within those plans.

Open science presents a more complicated tension. Open-access publications and openly licensed datasets are now routinely used to train AI models, sometimes in ways authors did not anticipate. Some researchers welcome this as an extension of openness, while others worry about attribution, misrepresentation, and commercial capture of publicly funded work. Universities and repositories are debating whether existing licences adequately express authors' wishes about machine use, whether to adopt signals that opt out of AI training, and how to balance openness with protection of research participants whose data could be re-identified through AI-assisted linkage.

Research integrity offices also face new categories of misconduct. Kobak and colleagues' 2025 analysis in Science Advances, estimating that at least 13.5 percent of 2024 biomedical abstracts were processed with large language models, illustrates how quickly AI has entered scholarly writing. Integrity frameworks are being revised to address fabricated citations, AI-generated images or data, and undisclosed AI use, alongside traditional concerns about plagiarism and falsification.

In education, sector bodies have set expectations that shape research cultures as well. The Russell Group's 2023 principles on generative AI in education committed its universities to supporting AI literacy among students and staff and to adapting teaching and assessment, and many of these institutions extended similar commitments into research training for doctoral students.

The frameworks now being revised were themselves products of an earlier attempt to make research outputs usable by machines. Mark Wilkinson and an international group of co-authors published the FAIR Guiding Principles in Scientific Data in 2016, proposing that research data should be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. A distinctive feature of the principles was their emphasis on machine actionability: the authors argued that, given the volume and complexity of modern data, computational agents rather than humans would increasingly discover and integrate datasets, so metadata, identifiers and licences needed to be structured for automated processing. FAIR quickly became embedded in funder requirements, including those of the European Commission's research programmes, and in university data management policies. In a sense, AI systems that ingest and summarise research outputs are a realisation of the machine-actionable future the FAIR authors anticipated. The difficulty is that the principles were written with a model of reuse in which machines served scientific discovery under the norms of research communities, not one in which commercial models absorbed large corpora to produce general-purpose products. Universities restructuring their policies are therefore not abandoning FAIR so much as confronting questions it left open, such as whether reusability should include training commercial models and who should benefit when it does.

International policy reflects the same tension. UNESCO's Recommendation on Open Science, adopted by its member states in 2021, set out a broad vision of open scientific knowledge, open infrastructures and the participation of societal actors, and it emphasised equity, inclusiveness and benefit-sharing, particularly for researchers in low- and middle-income countries. The Recommendation also acknowledged that openness should be balanced against legitimate concerns, including privacy, security, intellectual property and the rights of Indigenous peoples over their knowledge, summarised in the phrase as open as possible, as closed as necessary. Generative AI sharpens these balancing questions. A dataset of oral histories made openly available for scholarly reuse may become training data for models whose outputs reproduce or distort community knowledge, and openly published research from under-resourced institutions may enrich commercial systems that those institutions then pay to use. Universities aligning their policies with the Recommendation are beginning to ask whether open science should be reconceived to include conditions on downstream AI use, or whether such conditions would undermine the openness that makes science cumulative.

Licensing is where these questions become operational. Most open-access articles and many open datasets are released under Creative Commons licences. Creative Commons, in guidance published in 2023, stated its view that training AI on openly licensed works may often be permissible under copyright exceptions such as fair use or text and data mining provisions regardless of the licence chosen, and that licence conditions such as attribution or non-commercial use may not straightforwardly govern training where such exceptions apply. In the European Union, the 2019 Directive on copyright in the Digital Single Market created two text and data mining exceptions: one in Article 3 for research organisations and cultural heritage institutions conducting scientific research, and a broader one in Article 4 that applies to anyone but allows rights holders to reserve their rights in a machine-readable way. This framework gives universities, as research organisations, relatively secure grounds to mine literature and data for research, while allowing them, as rights holders, to opt out of commercial mining of their own outputs. Few universities have yet adopted coherent positions on whether to exercise that opt-out, and doing so for open-access repositories would sit uneasily with commitments to openness.

The commercial dimension has become impossible to ignore. Diana Kwon, writing in Nature in 2024, described deals in which academic publishers had sold access to research content to technology companies for AI training, including a reported agreement between Taylor and Francis and Microsoft and disclosures by Wiley of substantial revenue from AI-related content licensing. Kwon reported that many authors had not been consulted and would not share in the proceeds, and that it was difficult for researchers to determine whether their own work had been used. These arrangements have prompted some universities and researchers to reconsider copyright transfer agreements and rights-retention policies, under which authors keep the right to deposit accepted manuscripts in institutional repositories. Rights retention was originally adopted to support open access, but it is now also seen as a way for institutions to retain some influence over how their research outputs are licensed, including for AI training. Whether universities will use that influence to restrict, permit or monetise such uses remains unsettled.

Researchers' own attitudes shape how policies land in practice. Richard Van Noorden and Jeffrey Perkel reported in Nature in 2023 on a survey of more than 1,600 researchers about artificial intelligence in science. Respondents expected AI tools to become increasingly important to research, with many anticipating benefits such as faster data processing and computation, while expressing concerns about the spread of misinformation, the ease of plagiarism and fraud, and the risk that reliance on pattern recognition without understanding would entrench bias and reduce reproducibility. The survey was not a random sample of researchers and respondents were self-selected, so the balance of opinion may not represent the research workforce as a whole. It nonetheless indicates that researchers are not uniformly enthusiastic or resistant and that policies imposed without engagement may struggle to gain compliance. Universities that involve researchers in drafting AI guidance, and that distinguish clearly between uses that raise integrity or confidentiality concerns and routine uses such as coding assistance or language editing, may find policies easier to implement.

Reproducibility is a particular concern for data management offices. When AI tools are used to clean, code, analyse or summarise data, the steps they perform may not be fully documented, and proprietary models can change behaviour between versions without notice. A result produced with a commercial model in one month may not be reproducible with the same prompt a few months later. Data management plans have traditionally asked researchers to describe how data will be collected, stored and shared, but they rarely asked researchers to record the software versions, prompts and parameters used in analysis. Some institutions and journals are beginning to request this information, along with archiving of inputs and outputs where licences permit, and to favour open models with fixed versions for analyses that need to be reproducible. These requirements add documentation burdens, but they extend long-standing principles of methodological transparency to a new class of tools.

Capacity and equity shape what restructuring is possible. Well-resourced universities can provide institutional licences for AI tools with contractual data protections, secure computing environments for sensitive data, and specialist staff to advise researchers. Smaller institutions and those in lower-income countries may lack these resources, leaving researchers to use consumer tools with weaker protections or to forgo AI assistance altogether. National and regional consortia, shared infrastructure and open models can help reduce this gap. Without such efforts, AI could reinforce existing inequalities in research capacity even as open-science policies aim to reduce them.

Practical restructuring often begins with data classification. Many universities already sort research data into tiers, from public through internal and confidential to highly restricted, with corresponding rules on storage and sharing. Institutions are now mapping AI tools onto these tiers, specifying which tools may be used with which categories of data. Public or published material may be processed with consumer tools, while confidential or personal data may be processed only with enterprise services under contracts that prohibit retention and training, or with models running in the university's own secure computing environment. Highly restricted data, such as identifiable health records, may be excluded from AI processing unless an ethics committee has approved a specific protocol. Ethics review forms are being revised to ask whether AI tools will be used to transcribe interviews, code qualitative data or analyse participant information, and consent documents increasingly mention such uses so that participants can make informed choices. These changes are incremental and administrative rather than dramatic, but they translate abstract principles into decisions that researchers face every day, and they show how existing governance structures can absorb new tools without being rebuilt from scratch.

The overall pattern is one of incremental adaptation rather than wholesale restructuring. Policies are frequently labelled interim or living, reflecting uncertainty about how tools will evolve. Implementation varies widely, with well-resourced institutions able to provide secure internal tools and dedicated support, while others rely on guidance alone. There is little evaluation of whether these policies change behaviour or protect data effectively. The direction of travel nonetheless appears clear: universities are moving toward treating AI use as a dimension of research data management and integrity that requires disclosure, secure infrastructure, and explicit attention to how openly shared outputs are reused by machines as well as people.

## Chapter 19: Teacher Formation and the Profession {#chapter-19}

9 questions · 70 citations · 60 unique sources · 45 cross-references

### Q210 What must initial teacher education now include about AI, and what do programmes actually teach? {#q210}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Initial teacher education (ITE) programmes globally are in an early and largely uncoordinated phase of AI competency integration. Research identifies a significant gap between the rapid deployment of AI tools in schools and the systematic inclusion of AI-related knowledge, skills, and ethical dispositions in the formal preparation of teachers. Systematic reviews of ITE programmes find that most current interventions are short-term, embedded opportunistically within existing courses, and focused on tool familiarity rather than the deeper conceptual and ethical competencies that effective AI integration requires.

What must be included: the conceptual core. The conceptual landscape distinguishes between AI literacy — a foundational knowledge base regarding how AI systems work, their limitations, and their societal impacts — and AI competency, defined as the professional capacity to apply this knowledge in context-specific teaching, learning, and assessment situations. Frameworks such as 'Intelligent-TPACK' (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge adapted for AI) attempt to integrate these dimensions with established models of professional knowledge, emphasising that AI competency is not additive to existing professional knowledge but transformative of it. Teachers need not merely know how to use AI tools; they need pedagogical judgment about when, whether, and how AI use changes the nature of learning tasks and student development. The UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), released during Digital Learning Week 2024, provides the most comprehensive global reference point. It defines 15 competencies across five dimensions — human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI for professional learning — at three progression levels: Acquire (basic literacy), Deepen (pedagogical integration), and Create (innovation and leadership). By 2022, only seven countries had established national AI frameworks for teachers, indicating the novelty of the policy landscape into which the UNESCO framework enters.

What programmes actually teach. Curriculum provision in ITE programmes shows several documented patterns. Project-Based Learning (PBL) is identified as an effective strategy for bridging AI theory and classroom practice, fostering teacher autonomy through authentic problem-solving. A five-dimension progression — from guided tool exploration to autonomous critical application — appears in effective programme designs. Most existing interventions follow a common structure: a preparatory phase involving concept introduction, a practical phase involving guided to autonomous exploration of AI tools, and a final phase of critical reflection. Content typically addresses foundational concepts (machine learning, prompt engineering), ethical implications, and data privacy. Evaluations using instruments such as the PAICE questionnaire show that even concise, concept-driven instruction can significantly improve pre-service teachers' self-assessed knowledge and perceived self-efficacy, though trust in AI systems does not always show statistically significant growth after short-term training.

The teacher-educator confidence gap. Teacher educators, who are responsible for modelling AI-integrated practice to pre-service teachers, frequently report feeling underprepared themselves, creating a confidence gap that cascades into inconsistent instruction. Studies from Norway and Hong Kong document that while teacher educators recognise generative AI's transformative potential, many hesitate to model its use in their own teaching. This is a structural problem: ITE cannot teach what its own instructors do not yet confidently practise, and the professional development of teacher educators has not kept pace with the technology.

Documented gaps. Several persistent gaps are documented in the literature. There is an absence of longitudinal studies tracking AI competency development over time; most studies assess attitudes or confidence at a single point. Standardised assessment instruments for measuring AI literacy and competency are scarce, though the Teacher AI Competence Self-Efficacy (TAICS) scale represents an emerging effort. There is a noted underrepresentation of educational-sciences perspectives in AI literacy framework development, with computer-science viewpoints dominating at the expense of classroom-grounded pedagogical knowledge. Training equity is a documented concern: low-poverty districts are significantly more likely to provide AI professional development than high-poverty districts, with U.S. data showing approximately half of districts providing some form of AI training as of fall 2024 — up from lower rates the previous year — but often as voluntary opt-in sessions rather than systematic provision. There is also a mismatch between the technical training offered by some higher education institutions and the specific pedagogical needs of teachers in the classroom, and a lack of formal policies or guidance regarding generative AI in many ITE institutions.

The direction of travel. The trajectory is toward treating AI competency as a core professional competence rather than an optional technical skill. International policy frameworks — UNESCO's AI CFT, the European Union's Digital Education Action Plan, and emerging national frameworks — have formally recognised AI literacy as part of teacher preparation, and 'train-the-trainer' models are being developed to build faculty capacity. The EQUIP framework (Ethical Governance, Qualified Professional Learning, Unified Collaborative Partnerships, Implementation Readiness, Progressive Adaptation) exemplifies the move beyond ad-hoc training toward systemic integration. But the gap between policy aspiration and classroom reality remains wide: most programmes still treat AI as an add-on module rather than a transformative dimension of professional knowledge, and the evidence base for what works in ITE is dominated by short-term attitude studies rather than longitudinal measures of classroom competence. The honest summary is that initial teacher education knows what it should include — the UNESCO dimensions, the ethical and pedagogical judgment to use AI well — but is not yet systematically teaching it, and the programmes that do integrate AI are the exception rather than the rule.

### Q211 How is AI being used in teacher recruitment, evaluation, and classroom surveillance? {#q211}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

Artificial intelligence is being applied to teacher-facing processes — hiring, performance evaluation, and classroom monitoring — at a pace that substantially outstrips the development of governance frameworks, professional standards, or evidence-based protocols. The resulting policy landscape is characterised by uncoordinated adoption, significant equity concerns, and an unresolved tension between efficiency gains and the professional autonomy central to effective teaching.

Recruitment. In recruitment, approximately 53 percent of school district recruiters in the United States now employ AI tools to screen résumés, rank candidates, and generate interview questions. Some districts deploy hiring agents based on models such as Google's Gemini to analyse redacted résumés and quantify candidate strengths. Despite this prevalence, only 2 percent of teacher applicants report being aware that AI is involved in evaluating their applications, representing a transparency deficit. Research into the use of natural language processing to analyse applicants' short-answer responses aims to identify quantitative predictors — language clarity, affect, concreteness — that correlate with teacher effectiveness and retention; a project funded by the Institute of Education Sciences is currently testing whether such applicant characteristics predict in-service teacher quality and retention. Proponents argue that AI reduces human bias by standardising the initial screening process; critics counter that AI trained on historical data reproduces historical biases, including demographic patterns encoded in which characteristics are associated with 'successful' past hires. The 'automation bias' finding is particularly concerning: human recruiters follow AI recommendations approximately 90 percent of the time, even when they perceive the output as low quality, creating a practical situation where algorithmic decisions are effectively final despite nominal human oversight. Regulatory responses are emerging — New York City has begun requiring independent bias audits for AI hiring tools and mandatory notifications for job-seekers — but most districts operate without such oversight, and few collective bargaining agreements address AI in hiring.

Evaluation. In performance evaluation, AI is being explored as a supplement to traditional, resource-intensive classroom observation. Computer vision systems using object detection algorithms can track teacher positioning, student participation, and use of instructional materials, generating quantitative key performance indicators. Machine learning analysis of video-recorded lessons has been shown to reliably measure certain indicators of teaching effectiveness — particularly those involving linguistic cues such as instructional clarity and eliciting student thinking — where AI can outperform human raters in consistency. However, AI currently struggles with context-dependent classroom management situations where nuance and real-time judgment are essential. The consensus in this literature is that AI-assisted observation should function as a reflection tool supporting professional development rather than as a mechanism for high-stakes personnel decisions such as contract renewal or dismissal. Commercial tools such as TeachFX (which analyses the proportion of teacher talk versus student talk) and Edthena's AI Coach are explicitly positioned as private, non-supervisory professional development aids, and providers emphasise that observation data is encrypted)Skip, not used to train third-party models, and kept within district control — a design choice intended to preserve teacher trust. There is significant resistance to using AI-driven insights for formal evaluation, on the grounds that introducing a supervisory relationship would discourage teachers from using the tools at all.

Classroom surveillance. Classroom surveillance applications extend to student-facing monitoring: computer vision, audio analysis, and engagement tracking systems are deployed at some institutions, with proponents claiming attendance and discipline improvements. In some regions, such as Mashan County, China, dynamic evaluation models utilising computer vision and machine learning have been implemented to automate monitoring and reduce the subjectivity of traditional evaluation methods. These systems raise serious concerns about the normalisation of constant surveillance, the chilling effects on natural classroom interaction, and the data privacy rights of students who are minors subject to FERPA and COPPA protections. The surveillance trajectory is the least governed of the three applications, with the weakest evidence base for claimed benefits and the most direct conflict with established norms of professional and student privacy.

The autonomy dimension. The professional autonomy dimension is contested. UNESCO, the OECD, and major teacher unions — including the National Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers — consistently emphasise that AI should support rather than displace teacher professional judgment, and that mandated AI use or algorithmic performance metrics reduce teacher agency in ways that are associated with lower job satisfaction and higher turnover. The OECD's 'driver's seat' principle holds that educators must actively select, evaluate, and shape AI tools used in their practice rather than being passive recipients of algorithmic outputs. State-level frameworks in the United States generally affirm teacher authority over instructional decisions and establish that AI should not determine final grades or disciplinary outcomes without human review. The gap between these normative commitments and the actual pace of adoption — particularly in recruitment, where transparency is minimal and automation bias is strong — is the defining feature of the current landscape. The evidence base for AI's effects on teacher evaluation quality, hiring outcomes, and surveillance-related outcomes remains thin, and the most rigorous finding in the adjacent literature — the Education Endowment Foundation's randomised controlled trial showing that ChatGPT-assisted lesson planning reduced planning time by 31 percent without measurable quality degradation — addresses workload, not the personnel processes examined here.

### Q212 What measured effect does AI have on teacher workload and burnout? {#q212}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 established

Teacher burnout is well-documented as a systemic crisis. Survey estimates indicate that 44 to 60 percent of K-12 teachers report high or very frequent burnout. The 2024 TALIS results indicate that 17 percent of teachers intend to leave the profession within five years, rising to 20 percent among educators under 30. Turnover costs are estimated at \$8,000–\$21,000 per departing teacher. A 2022 meta-analysis of over 50,000 teachers identifies administrative burden as the strongest predictor of burnout — outweighing student behaviour — followed by role ambiguity and lack of autonomy. Teachers work an average of 53 hours per week, with only approximately 23–25 hours on direct instruction; the remainder is consumed by grading, lesson planning, documentation, and compliance. The question is whether AI measurably reduces this burden, and the answer, on the current evidence, is: modestly, conditionally, and not yet at the level of burnout itself.

The strongest experimental evidence. The most rigorous evidence on AI's workload effects comes from the Education Endowment Foundation's cluster-randomised controlled trial involving 259 secondary science teachers across 68 English schools. Teachers using ChatGPT with a structured implementation guide reduced lesson and resource preparation time by an average of 25.3 minutes per week — a 31 percent reduction in planning time relative to controls (56.2 minutes per week versus 81.5 minutes). Independent expert panels found no measurable difference in lesson quality between AI-assisted and standard materials. This is the strongest experimental evidence currently available, and it is important to note what it does and does not show: it demonstrates a real, statistically significant reduction in one specific component of workload (planning time) without quality loss, but it does not establish effects on total working hours, burnout, retention, or learning outcomes. Vendor surveys and opt-in studies reporting larger savings (5.9 to 6.5 hours per week in some estimates) do not meet experimental standards and reflect self-selected adopters, likely overestimating benefits.

Documented application areas and the hidden-labour problem. AI's documented application areas include lesson plan generation (reported time savings of 60–80 percent for initial scaffolding, though substantial revision is typically required), rubric-aligned feedback on structured assessments (grading time reductions of up to 80 percent for specific task types), and routine parent communication drafting (30–60 minutes per week). The 'hidden labour' problem is important: empirical studies find that teachers spend significant time reviewing, correcting factual errors, adjusting for local curriculum standards, and reworking AI-generated content to meet pedagogical specificity. AI output is frequently described as too generic, bland, or contextually misaligned, requiring substantive editing. Time savings from generation are thus partially offset by time spent on revision — a finding absent from survey-based estimates. Critically, reported time savings do not establish that total working hours decrease: approximately half of teachers report AI eases workload, but only one-third report a reduction in actual hours, as reclaimed time is absorbed by other professional demands.

The psychological pathway. The psychological pathway from AI use to burnout reduction is better described as mediated than direct. Structural equation modelling demonstrates that AI-assisted teaching does not directly reduce burnout; rather, it improves teachers' sense of efficacy — their belief in their capacity to manage professional responsibilities — which then reduces emotional exhaustion. This mediating role of efficacy means that AI tools are more effective for teachers who already feel relatively competent and supported. For teachers experiencing anxiety about technological replacement, skill obsolescence, or professional surveillance through AI monitoring, the relationship can reverse: AI anxiety depletes emotional resources and increases burnout, particularly when institutions impose rigid algorithmic control rather than teacher-directed adoption. The 'digital burden' pathway — where constant connectivity, learning curves, and the monitoring of student AI misuse add new forms of invisible labour — is documented particularly among early adopters in high-adoption environments.

Structural limitations. Several structural limitations on AI's burnout-mitigating potential are documented. AI cannot address role ambiguity — conflicting demands from administrators, parents, and regulators — which is a primary burnout driver. AI does not resolve inadequate compensation, excessive class sizes, or dysfunctional school leadership. Research indicates that AI only significantly reduces the burnout effects of workload among teachers with high self-efficacy; those with low self-efficacy are not protected by AI access alone. Implementation evidence consistently emphasises professional development as a precondition for benefit realisation: teachers who feel well-prepared for AI integration report burnout rates of approximately 43 percent, while those who feel unprepared report approximately 72 percent. Only around one in five teachers work in schools with formal AI policies as of the mid-2020s, and rural schools show lower AI adoption rates (approximately 57 percent) than suburban schools (approximately 65 percent). The EEF is currently conducting a follow-on trial of 'Aila', Oak National Academy's purpose-built AI lesson assistant, with 450 Key Stage 2 teachers across 86 primary schools, with results expected in autumn 2026. The measured bottom line is that AI produces real but bounded workload reductions in specific tasks, mediated by teacher efficacy and preparation, and that no peer-reviewed experimental evidence yet establishes that AI adoption causes sustained reductions in burnout or measurable improvements in retention.

### Q214 How does mandated AI use affect teachers' professional autonomy and judgment? {#q214}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

The integration of AI into schools is occurring against a backdrop of long-term deprofessionalisation, in which teachers increasingly face scripted curricula, rigid pacing mandates, and standardised accountability measures. The question of how mandated AI use affects professional autonomy and judgment must therefore be read in this context: AI enters a profession whose autonomy is already under pressure, and the technology can either reinforce that pressure or, under different implementation conditions, help reverse it. The evidence and policy analysis converge on a central finding — the effect of AI on teacher autonomy depends less on the technology itself than on how it is implemented.

The threat model: top-down mandates. Systems that mandate specific lessons without teacher input, platforms that track 'fidelity' to AI-generated pacing, and AI detection tools that override a teacher's professional judgment regarding student work are cited as the major threats to autonomy. When AI policies and platforms are imposed without educator input, they implicitly devalue teacher expertise and reduce educators to implementers of algorithmic outputs. This 'top-down' approach creates a disconnect between the intended use of AI tools and the actual, diverse needs of students, and it risks shifting the focus from teaching to what one strand of scholarship calls 'learnification' — the automation of instructional tasks sidelining the teacher's role in meaning-making. The replacement mode of AI integration, in which AI independently executes tasks such as grading or lesson planning, carries the highest risk of 'competence atrophy', where teachers may lose essential diagnostic and evaluative skills through disuse. Research on teacher agency identifies this as the most damaging configuration: when AI replaces rather than augments professional tasks, the teacher's capacity to exercise judgment atrophies precisely because it is no longer exercised.

The support model: complementarity and augmentation. AI can support autonomy when it serves as a tool for teacher-led decision-making. This includes automating routine tasks — grading objective items, generating resource options, drafting routine communications — which frees time for higher-level professional activities like providing personalised student feedback and designing instruction. The research literature distinguishes three modes of AI integration with different implications for agency: replacement (automation), which risks competence atrophy; complementarity, in which AI extends the teacher's capabilities while the teacher remains in full control; and augmentation, in which human-AI teams perform tasks more effectively than either could alone. Complementarity is generally viewed as the most supportive model for maintaining professional agency, and augmentation can enhance teacher competence when teachers remain the orchestrators of the human-AI relationship. Professional judgment is increasingly viewed not just as a preference but as a core competency required for effective teaching in a post-digital landscape: a teacher's decision to use AI is itself a professional judgment shaped by the interplay of efficiency demands, pedagogical goals, risk management, and the desire to maintain professional autonomy.

Policy responses: human-in-the-loop as the emerging norm. State-level education departments have responded with guidance that consistently mandates human oversight. Alabama and Arizona explicitly require human verification of AI-generated content and grading to ensure AI supplements rather than replaces human instruction. Georgia's guidance distinguishes high-stakes from non-high-stakes uses, explicitly prohibiting AI for educator evaluations, individualised education programme goals, and subjective grading to protect the integrity of professional judgment. Alaska's guidance promotes a flexible, recommendation-based approach rather than strict mandates, encouraging districts to move away from blanket bans to foster local autonomy and culturally responsive teaching. Some institutions have implemented 'traffic light' or 'red-yellow-green' systems that empower teachers to determine the appropriate level of AI use for individual assignments, effectively granting them the autonomy to decide how technology fits their specific curriculum and student needs. The Teacher Task Force and researchers argue that without deliberate efforts to centre teachers in AI integration, the education sector risks systemic de-professionalisation, and policy dialogues increasingly call for evidence-informed strategies that prioritise teacher-AI interactions that bolster, rather than diminish, the teacher's role as the primary orchestrator of the classroom.

The empirical bottom line. The empirical evidence on mandated AI use is thinner than the policy discourse suggests. What is documented is correlational: teachers who report that AI is imposed on them without consultation also report lower job satisfaction and higher turnover intentions, while teachers who report agency over AI adoption report more positive outcomes. The 'structured flexibility' model — where teachers adhere to common standards but retain autonomy over instructional methods — has shown success in improving both teacher satisfaction and student outcomes in the broader autonomy literature, and it is the model most frequently recommended for AI governance. What is not yet established is a causal chain from specific mandate designs to specific autonomy or judgment outcomes. The direction of travel, however, is clear: the emerging consensus across international bodies, state frameworks, and teacher unions is that AI should function as an advisory tool under human oversight, that teachers must retain final authority over instructional decisions, and that the professional judgment of the teacher — not the output of the algorithm — is the ultimate arbiter of what happens in the classroom. Whether that consensus is honoured in practice, particularly in districts where AI is adopted as a cost-saving measure, remains the open question.

### Q215 Is AI affecting teacher recruitment and retention, and in which direction? {#q215}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

AI is affecting teacher recruitment and retention in two distinct directions simultaneously: it is reshaping the hiring process through automation, and it is being deployed as a tool to reduce the workload drivers of attrition. The net direction of the effect is not yet measurable in rigorous longitudinal terms, but the component effects are documented with increasing clarity.

Recruitment: automation with an 'automation paradox'. On the recruitment side, over 50 percent of district recruiters now employ AI tools to assist in the hiring process, including AI-powered recruitment marketplaces, autonomous hiring agents that crawl the web for qualified candidates, resume screening, and candidate-strength analysis against job postings. These tools are adopted primarily to manage the volume of applications in a context of chronic teacher shortage and to reduce time-to-hire, which is significantly higher in education than in other sectors. The documented 'automation paradox' is that while districts use AI to handle high volumes of applications, approximately 30 percent of candidates have withdrawn from job applications because the process felt too robotic or impersonal. The direction of this effect is negative for recruitment: automation that depersonalises the hiring experience can deter precisely the candidates districts most want to attract, and experts emphasise that human interaction remains essential for conveying school culture. There is also a transparency deficit — only 2 percent of teacher applicants report being aware that AI is involved in evaluating their applications — and a bias risk, since AI models trained on historical hiring data may reproduce past exclusions, such as de-prioritising candidates based on alma mater, caregiving gaps, or demographic markers. Only about one in ten school districts has a formal AI policy, and fewer still address AI in hiring. On the positive side, some districts use AI to redact identifiable information and standardise screening, which can reduce human bias in initial filtering, and research funded by the Institute of Education Sciences is testing whether natural language processing of applicant responses can predict in-service teacher quality and retention, potentially improving the match between candidates and districts.

Retention: workload reduction as the mechanism. On the retention side, the mechanism is workload reduction. Teacher retention is strongly correlated with burnout, and 44 percent of teachers report high levels of burnout, driven primarily by administrative burden. AI tools are being deployed to automate the most time-intensive tasks: AI-assisted grading can reduce grading time by up to 78 percent for structured assessments, AI content generators can produce standards-aligned materials in minutes, and AI chatbots can manage routine parent and student inquiries. Districts implementing comprehensive AI tools report improvements in year-over-year retention rates of 28 to 41 percent in some cases, with one middle school reporting approximately \$180,000 in avoided turnover costs in a single year after improving retention by 41 percent through AI-assisted support. AI is also being used to enhance organisational responsiveness: tools that rapidly process thousands of open-ended staff survey responses allow administrators to identify professional development needs and workplace concerns and act on them faster, and teachers' sense of being heard by administration is a documented correlate of retention.

The limits of the evidence. The direction of the retention effect is positive but bounded. The strongest experimental evidence — the Education Endowment Foundation's randomised controlled trial — shows that ChatGPT-assisted planning reduced planning time by 31 percent without quality loss, but it does not measure retention. The larger retention figures come from vendor-affiliated and opt-in studies that do not meet experimental standards and reflect self-selected adopters. Critically, AI cannot address the systemic drivers of attrition: role ambiguity, lack of autonomy, inadequate compensation, and working conditions. Research is explicit that AI is a partial, limited response to the retention crisis, and that effective implementation requires a phased approach starting with high-volume routine tasks, with organisational support that removes barriers to AI usage rather than mandating it. There is also a supply-side hypothesis worth noting: if AI-driven disruption of the broader graduate labour market pushes more talented graduates toward teaching as a stable career path, the recruitment pool could improve in quality — historical evidence shows that teachers who enter the profession during economic instability are often more effective — but this is speculative and not yet supported by data.

The net direction. The net direction of AI's effect on recruitment and retention is therefore mixed and conditional. On recruitment, AI improves efficiency and reach but risks depersonalisation and bias, with a documented deterrent effect on a substantial minority of candidates. On retention, AI reduces the administrative burden that drives burnout, with correlational and quasi-experimental evidence of improved retention in adopting districts, but with no rigorous evidence that it changes the systemic conditions — compensation, autonomy, role clarity — that ultimately determine whether teachers stay. The most defensible summary is that AI is a positive but partial contributor to retention and a double-edged contributor to recruitment, and that its net effect will be determined by implementation choices: transparency, human-in-the-loop design, and the protection of the relational aspects of hiring and teaching.

### Q216 What new professional roles are emerging in schools because of AI? {#q216}

7 citations · 7 sources · 5 cross-references

#### Claim 1 emerging

The integration of AI into schools is generating two distinct families of new professional roles: formal, titled positions created to govern and coordinate AI adoption, and informal, classroom-embedded leadership roles that emerge as teachers experiment with AI in practice. Both families are documented in the emerging literature, and both reflect a broader shift in how schools organise expertise in a period of rapid technological change.

The formal role: AI Coordinator. The most visible new formal role is the AI Coordinator, a position emerging across K-12 districts, county offices, and higher education institutions. The AI Coordinator serves as a central resource for navigating the rapid evolution of AI, bridging the gap between emerging technology and institutional mission, and ensuring that AI adoption is equitable, transparent, and aligned with strategic goals. Core responsibilities include leading the development of AI policies and guardrails for data privacy (FERPA and COPPA compliance), academic integrity, and risk management regarding bias or data misuse; acting as a liaison between staff, students, families, and external partners, including facilitating task forces, advisory councils, and community forums; designing and delivering professional development on prompt engineering and AI literacy; and managing pilot programmes with performance metrics to inform scaling decisions. The role typically requires a bachelor's degree in computer science, information systems, educational technology, or public policy, with strong communication skills for translating complex technical concepts to non-technical audiences. The emergence of this role reflects a broader trend of institutions moving from ad-hoc AI use toward structured integration.

Formal leadership variants. Beyond the coordinator role, institutions are beginning to prepare professionals for related formal career paths. The AI Instructional and Curriculum Leader is responsible for integrating AI into the pedagogical framework and ensuring curriculum remains aligned with AI-supported learning objectives. The AI Transformation Officer navigates the organisational, ethical, and policy-related shifts required for responsible AI adoption at district or school level. The Education Technology and AI Systems Integrator focuses on the technical and data-driven aspects, ensuring tools are interoperable, secure, and aligned with privacy regulations. These roles are emerging in job markets and university programmes alike, with educational leadership degrees beginning to incorporate AI-specific competencies.

Informal, classroom-embedded leadership. The second family of roles is informal and distributed. As AI technology evolves rapidly, traditional centralised decision-making often struggles to keep pace, and a model of 'leading from the classroom' has emerged. Teachers who experiment with AI tools — creating custom chatbots for student feedback, redesigning assessment practices, differentiating instruction — become in-house experts who influence their peers by modelling practice, sharing effective prompts and artifacts, shaping norms around ethical AI use and academic integrity, and facilitating professional learning communities where both successful experiments and failed attempts are shared. This distributed leadership model is defined by influence and practice rather than hierarchy, and principals increasingly view these 'irreplaceable' teachers as essential leaders who bridge the gap between technological potential and pedagogical reality. The shift is characterised by four movements: from control to trust (districts trusting teachers to experiment and refine practices in real time), from roles to practices (recognising leadership based on tangible contributions rather than formal titles), from compliance to inquiry (moving from one-off professional development toward ongoing, inquiry-based learning), and from individual experts to distributed leadership (avoiding a single 'AI expert' in favour of building capacity across the entire faculty).

The governance and leadership dimension. The rise of AI is also reshaping school leadership itself. Digital-savvy principals are increasingly delegating lower-level administrative tasks to AI, allowing them to focus more on instructional leadership and the human-centred aspects of schooling. The new roles are emerging against a governance gap: only about one in five teachers works in a school with a formal AI policy, and the coordination function that the AI Coordinator role provides is precisely the function that is missing in most schools. The evidence base on these roles is largely descriptive — job postings, case studies, and practitioner accounts — rather than evaluative, and there is no rigorous research yet on whether schools with dedicated AI coordination roles achieve better outcomes than those without. What is documented is the direction of travel: schools are creating formal positions to govern AI, cultivating informal teacher leadership to model it, and restructuring leadership practice around it, in a pattern that mirrors earlier waves of educational technology adoption but with a faster pace and a higher stakes governance component.

The governance gap and the evidence base. The new roles are emerging against a documented governance gap: only about one in five teachers works in a school with a formal AI policy, and the coordination function that the AI Coordinator role provides is precisely the function that is missing in most schools. This gap explains both the demand for the role and its ambiguity — in the absence of established professional standards, the AI Coordinator's authority, reporting lines, and scope vary widely between institutions, and the role risks becoming either a purely technical position (tool procurement and troubleshooting) or a purely compliance position (policy writing and risk management) rather than the pedagogical leadership function its proponents describe. The evidence base on these roles is largely descriptive — job postings, case studies, and practitioner accounts — rather than evaluative, and there is no rigorous research yet on whether schools with dedicated AI coordination roles achieve better outcomes than those without, whether the distributed-leadership model produces more durable capacity than the single-expert model, or how the new roles interact with existing structures such as instructional coaching, educational technology departments, and data-protection officers. What is documented is the direction of travel: schools are creating formal positions to govern AI, cultivating informal teacher leadership to model it, and restructuring leadership practice around it, in a pattern that mirrors earlier waves of educational technology adoption but with a faster pace and a higher-stakes governance component. The professionalisation of these roles — through credentialing, salary scales, and career pathways — is only beginning, and the outcome will determine whether AI coordination becomes a recognised teaching-career destination or remains an additional duty assigned to already-overloaded staff.
